Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager is explaining to a sponsor what an organisation can and cannot expect from operating in a matrix structure. Which of the following is NOT a benefit of a matrix organisational structure?
o: Access to specialist expertise from functional departments
Clear, single-point leadership from project manager
Governance Arrangements.w: In matrix structures, leadership is shared, not fully held by the project manager.

n.0: Matrix structures allow dynamic resource sharing.
n.1: Matrix enables use of cross-functional specialists.
n.2: Collaboration improves due to cross-functional involvement.
n.3: Shared resources can be allocated efficiently.

Governance Arrangements.q: Team members on a project are receiving instructions from both their department head and the project manager, leading to disputes over priorities. Which structure may result in this confusion over authority and dual reporting lines?
Governance Arrangements.w: Matrix structures often result in employees reporting to both functional and project managers.

n.0: Project structures have centralised authority with the project manager.
n.1: Agile teams are self-organising with clear role boundaries.
n.2: Functional structures have clear single reporting lines.
n.3: Product-based organisations typically follow a clear reporting structure.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager is establishing how a new project will be controlled and reported within its host organisation. An organisation's governance approach will typically influence which of the following?
o: The project life cycle, controls, and reporting structures
The technical design of the product
The funding source used for a project
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance impacts how the project is structured, controlled, reviewed, and reported.

n.1: Technical design is determined by solution teams.
n.2: Funding is decided more by business case or sponsor.
n.3: External consultants may or may not be influenced by governance.
n.4: Innovation level depends more on project goals and context.

Governance Arrangements.q: A sponsor is concerned that projects in one part of the organisation receive little oversight because departmental managers make most decisions. In which structure is project governance likely to be weakest?
Governance Arrangements.w: In functional structures, project governance is minimal and decisions are led by functional management.

n.0: Strong matrix supports governance through project leadership.
n.1: Hybrid structures include formalised project governance.
n.2: Project-based structures typically feature defined governance models.
n.3: Balanced matrix structures maintain some level of project governance.

Governance Arrangements.q: A senior manager values keeping staff within their departments to support long-term development, but a project manager worries this limits how much attention projects receive. Which structure often improves staff continuity and career development but may reduce project focus?
Governance Arrangements.w: Functional structures keep staff within departments, supporting career development but reducing project focus.

n.0: Project-based structures remove staff from departmental paths.
n.1: Agile squads focus fully on delivery.
n.2: Strong matrix prioritises projects more heavily.
n.3: Hybrid can balance both staff development and project focus.

Governance Arrangements.q: A sponsor wants to appoint a project manager who will hold complete accountability for the budget, schedule and the people delivering the work. Which organisational structure enables the project manager to have full control over budget, schedule, and resources?
Governance Arrangements.w: Project-based structures provide the project manager with maximum authority over all aspects of delivery.

n.0: Strong matrix provides significant but not total control.
n.2: Balanced matrix shares control with functional managers.
n.3: Weak matrix structures limit project manager authority.
n.4: Functional structures centralise control with departmental heads.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project operating in a balanced matrix structure is facing delays. Team members are unsure which tasks to prioritise. What is the likely cause?
o: Insufficient stakeholder buy-in and engagement in the project
Conflicting direction from functional and project managers
Excessive reliance on rigid formal governance review processes
Inadequate project funding to complete the scheduled work
Absence of an approved and documented business case
Governance Arrangements.w: In balanced matrix structures, dual authority can cause confusion over task prioritisation.

n.0: Stakeholder buy-in affects support, not task direction.
n.2: Governance processes help control, not cause confusion.
n.3: Funding issues are financial, not decision-based.
n.4: The business case justifies the project, not task assignment.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation that runs dedicated project teams finds it hard to bring in niche technical expertise that normally sits within its functional departments. Which of the following is a key challenge of project-based structures that this illustrates?
o: Delayed decision-making due to governance layers
Governance Arrangements.w: Project-based teams may struggle to access specialist knowledge that remains in functional departments.

n.1: Projects typically align to strategic objectives.
n.2: Project-based models usually streamline decision-making.
n.3: Roles are usually clearly defined in project structures.
n.4: Project managers have high authority in this structure.

Governance Arrangements.q: A manufacturing company has recently strengthened how it runs its change programmes. Every project must now pass formal stage gate reviews before continuing, and each is given tightly defined tolerances for scope and cost. What does this way of working best reflect?
Governance Arrangements.w: Stage gates and tolerances are hallmarks of strong, proactive governance to manage risk and control delivery.

n.0: Stage gates are more typical of linear models than iterative.
n.1: Formal processes suggest structured, not informal, governance.
n.3: The organisation clearly has controls in place.
n.4: This describes strong, not weak, governance.

Governance Arrangements.q: A newly appointed project manager is briefed on how governance is expected to operate across the organisation's portfolio, and is given a list of characteristics associated with well-controlled projects. Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of strong project governance?
Governance Arrangements.w: Strong governance avoids ad hoc decisions by enforcing structure and consistency.

n.0: Stage boundaries mark progress points.
n.1: Strong governance clarifies all roles.
n.2: Reporting lines are essential for oversight.
n.4: Escalation paths are clearly defined.

Governance Arrangements.q: A sponsor is concerned that a large transformation project may drift away from the organisation's wider strategic priorities as delivery progresses. Which governance feature is most important for ensuring alignment between the project outcomes and the business strategy?
Governance Arrangements.w: Steering groups provide strategic oversight and help align project outcomes with business goals.

n.0: Risk registers manage uncertainty, not alignment.
n.2: Lessons learned support future improvement.
n.3: Stand-ups are for operational updates, not strategic alignment.
n.4: Change control manages scope but not strategy alignment.

Governance Arrangements.q: A consultancy runs many concurrent client engagements and frequently needs to move specialists between them as demands shift week to week. Which organisational structure provides the most flexibility in allocating staff based on project need?
Governance Arrangements.w: Matrix structures enable cross-functional resource sharing based on changing project demands.

n.0: Functional structures allocate staff based on department, not project flexibility.
n.1: Agile teams are cross-functional but often stable.
n.3: Project-based teams are dedicated and not easily reallocated.
n.4: Hierarchical structures are slow to adapt resource needs.

Governance Arrangements.q: A weak matrix structure will most likely result in:
o: Functional managers having full control over resources
Project managers having direct authority over budgets
Project team members being fully dedicated to the project
Governance Arrangements.w: In weak matrix structures, functional managers retain primary control over resources and decision-making.

n.0: Accountability is fragmented between managers.
n.2: Budget authority rests with functional managers.
n.3: Governance remains under functional control.
n.4: Team members are shared, not dedicated.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager working within an organisation where staff report both to functional heads and to project leads is finding that decisions are approached differently depending on who is consulted. In this setting, what is a primary governance challenge?
Governance Arrangements.w: Dual authority in matrix structures can lead to inconsistent decisions across functional and project lines.

n.0: Formal initiation can still occur in matrix models.
n.1: Strategic goals are typically clear, but execution may vary.
n.3: Stakeholders are often well engaged across departments.
n.4: Performance is still tracked in well-governed matrices.

Governance Arrangements.q: A time-critical initiative needs to make and act on delivery decisions quickly, without repeatedly seeking approval from separate departmental managers. In which type of organisational structure would you typically expect to see the most rapid project-level decisions?
Governance Arrangements.w: Project-based structures concentrate authority within the project team, enabling fast decisions.

n.0: Balanced matrix shares decision-making, slowing speed.
n.1: Hierarchical models tend to delay approval and decisions.
n.2: Decisions in functional structures require departmental approval.
n.4: Weak matrix prioritises functional leadership.

Governance Arrangements.q: A team member complains that their line manager and their project manager keep giving them competing instructions about which work to do first. Which organisational structure is most likely to result in conflicting priorities of this kind due to dual reporting lines?
Governance Arrangements.w: Matrix structures often lead to conflicting priorities due to shared authority between project and functional managers.

n.0: Product-centric teams have defined ownership, reducing conflict.
n.1: Functional structures involve clear departmental authority.
n.2: Agile teams are usually self-organising and not subject to multiple reporting lines.
n.4: Project-based structures have a single reporting line to the project manager.

Governance Arrangements.q: A public sector body has introduced a policy requiring that every project include formal stage reviews and independent assurance before proceeding to the next phase. This governance approach is most likely to:
o: Reduce the need for stakeholder engagement
Avoid the use of tolerances and escalation paths
Enable structured oversight and risk management
Encourage autonomous team delivery with minimal oversight
Governance Arrangements.w: Formal stage reviews and assurance are key elements of structured governance to manage risk and maintain control.

n.0: Stakeholder engagement is typically stronger, not reduced.
n.1: Tolerances and escalation paths are central to formal governance.
n.3: Governance adds oversight, not removes it.
n.4: Formal governance prefers structured reporting.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager has been asked to deliver a change initiative using staff who continue to report to their departmental heads, and finds they must request people rather than direct them. In which organisational structure does the project manager typically have no direct authority over team members?
Governance Arrangements.w: In functional structures, project managers must request resources from functional heads and have little authority.

n.1: Hybrid varies but usually includes some project manager control.
n.2: Strong matrix provides significant project manager authority.
n.3: Balanced matrix shares authority between PM and functional leads.
n.4: Project managers have full authority in this structure.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation is weighing whether to move its delivery model so that dedicated teams are permanently assigned to individual projects. As it reviews the trade-offs, which of the following is a disadvantage of project-based structures?
o: Lack of role clarity for team members
Inefficient use of specialist resources across projects
Governance Arrangements.w: Specialists may be isolated in project teams, making cross-project resource use less efficient.

n.0: Governance can be streamlined in project-based environments.
n.1: Decisions are typically fast due to direct control.
n.2: Roles are clearly defined in most project teams.
n.3: Reporting lines are usually clear under the project manager.

Governance Arrangements.q: A PMO is trying to roll out a single, consistent governance model across an organisation that delivers work using a mix of predictive and iterative approaches side by side. Which structure creates the greatest challenge for applying a consistent governance model across projects?
Governance Arrangements.w: Hybrid structures combine different delivery methods, making consistent governance harder to apply.

n.0: Project-based structures apply uniform governance.
n.1: The V-model applies structured delivery with clear governance.
n.2: Functional structures are consistent but not project-focused.
n.3: Agile frameworks have consistent but adaptive governance.

Governance Arrangements.q: Across an organisation, a well-established PMO enforces the use of consistent templates, mandatory reviews and standard reporting for every project. This arrangement is best described as an example of:
Governance Arrangements.w: Enforcing templates and reporting is part of establishing a robust governance framework.

n.0: Portfolio management is broader and strategic.
n.2: Siloed delivery reflects separation, not structured oversight.
n.3: Risk management is a component, not the structure itself.
n.4: Alignment focuses on direction, not control.

Governance Arrangements.q: An engineering firm is concerned that placing staff into permanent, dedicated delivery teams could reduce how easily people draw on specialists based in other departments. Which of the following structures most likely limits access to shared functional expertise?
Governance Arrangements.w: Project-based teams may not have regular access to specialists from other departments.

n.0: Hybrid models often maintain access to functional support.
n.1: Balanced matrix promotes collaboration between functions.
n.3: Functional structures centralise expertise.
n.4: Matrix structures allow sharing of specialists.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation's governance model requires that, at the end of each stage, progress is formally reviewed against the agreed success criteria before the project is allowed to continue. This requirement most directly supports:
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance ensures assurance activities like reviewing progress against criteria for control and alignment.

n.0: Governance may reduce flexibility to maintain control.
n.1: Engagement may be part of governance, but this is about control.
n.3: Testing relates more to product quality than governance stages.
n.4: Formal communication is typically preferred in governance models.

Governance Arrangements.q: A junior team member is confused about who they report to, as they have worked across several different delivery models. A colleague explains that one structure gives each person a single manager to whom they answer. Which structure provides the clearest reporting line for team members?
Governance Arrangements.w: Project-based structures provide a single, clear reporting line to the project manager.

n.0: Functional reporting is clear but not aligned to project delivery.
n.1: Hybrid may create blurred reporting depending on delivery mode.
n.2: Matrix structures involve dual reporting lines.
n.3: Agile reporting is shared across roles, not always formalised.

Governance Arrangements.q: A strong governance model typically improves project performance by:
o: Eliminating the need for communication plans
Governance Arrangements.w: Good governance defines direction, roles, escalation, and performance measures to improve delivery confidence.

n.0: Governance reinforces the need for communication planning.
n.1: Stakeholder engagement is a core part of governance.
n.2: Collaboration is often enhanced by clarity and governance.
n.4: Escalation paths are clearly defined in strong governance.

Governance Arrangements.q: Midway through delivery, the market conditions underpinning a project have shifted and questions are raised about whether the investment is still worthwhile. Within the project's governance, who is primarily accountable for ensuring the business case remains valid throughout the project?
Governance Arrangements.w: The project sponsor is accountable for ensuring continued business justification.

n.0: Project team members contribute specialist work but do not ensure business case validity.
n.2: The project manager delivers the project but isn't accountable for business justification.
n.3: The board secretary may support administration but has no role in the business case.
n.4: The product owner defines and prioritises product requirements, not the business case.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager notices a delay in a supplier delivery and wants to adjust the plan. Who should they consult first to assess impact on strategic objectives?
Governance Arrangements.w: The sponsor provides strategic oversight and can judge impact against the business case.

n.0: User representatives input requirements but don’t own strategy.
n.1: Procurement handles contracts, not strategic decisions.
n.2: The product owner focuses on product needs, not strategic alignment.
n.3: The team leader helps manage tasks, not strategic decisions.

Governance Arrangements.q: A software project is being delivered using an agile approach, and the team needs someone to decide what functionality matters most and in what order it should be built. Which of the following is a primary responsibility of the product owner?
Governance Arrangements.w: The product owner ensures the product meets the user's needs by defining and prioritising features.

n.0: Procurement is managed by specialised roles or the PM.
n.2: Team management is the role of the project manager.
n.3: Regulatory compliance is typically a shared or delegated responsibility.
n.4: The sponsor owns the business case, not the product owner.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager is clarifying which governance roles are involved in the running of the project from one day to the next, so that responsibilities are understood by all. Which role is NOT typically responsible for day-to-day project delivery?
Governance Arrangements.w: The project sponsor provides strategic oversight but is not involved in daily project delivery.

n.0: The Scrum Master facilitates daily agile delivery.
n.1: The project manager leads the daily execution of the project.
n.2: Team leaders help coordinate daily tasks and resources.
n.4: Work package owners are accountable for specific deliverables.

Governance Arrangements.q: A senior executive has agreed to take on a governance role for a major project and wants to understand what will be expected of them at that level. The responsibilities of a project sponsor typically include:
o: Facilitating daily stand-ups, tracking sprints, and grooming the product backlog
Providing resources, championing the project, and ensuring alignment with strategy
Maintaining the issue log, risk register, and daily timesheets
Writing detailed test cases, quality checklists, and acceptance criteria
Operating the financial software and reconciling costs each day
Governance Arrangements.w: Sponsors provide strategic leadership, resource access, and alignment with organisational goals.

n.0: These are tasks typically done by agile team roles like the Scrum Master.
n.2: The issue log is maintained by the project manager or support roles.
n.3: These are quality assurance tasks, not sponsor duties.
n.4: This is a task for project support or administrators.

Governance Arrangements.q: A software development project uses agile delivery. Who typically acts as the voice of the customer to ensure value delivery?
Governance Arrangements.w: The product owner represents stakeholders and ensures the team delivers value.

n.0: The Scrum Master facilitates process, not value direction.
n.1: The sponsor provides oversight but not day-to-day product direction.
n.2: The project manager handles coordination, not stakeholder representation.
n.4: The technical lead ensures technical quality, not value.

Governance Arrangements.q: As a project passes key milestones, both the sponsor and the project manager are expected to play a part in checking that the investment still stacks up. Which activity is typically shared between the project sponsor and project manager?
o: Defining the detailed user acceptance criteria for each deliverable
Creating and prioritising the team's sprint backlog items
Leading the technical design workshops with the delivery team
Drafting and completing the individual change request forms
Reviewing the project business case at key milestones
Governance Arrangements.w: Both the sponsor and manager have roles in reviewing business justification at milestones.

n.0: User criteria are usually set by users and product owners.
n.1: Sprint backlogs are agile team responsibilities.
n.2: Technical workshops are usually led by specialists or architects.
n.3: The PM may draft change requests, not typically sponsors.

Governance Arrangements.q: Having secured approval and appointed a project manager, the sponsor steps back to allow day-to-day execution to proceed under the manager's control. During which stage does the project sponsor most often delegate authority to the project manager?
Governance Arrangements.w: During delivery, the project manager is empowered to lead day-to-day execution.

n.1: Handover is a joint responsibility but led by the PM.
n.2: Post-project reviews are sponsor-influenced activities.
n.3: Initiation involves sponsor-driven decisions.
n.4: Benefits realisation is typically sponsor-led.

Governance Arrangements.q: A senior user complains that the deliverables don’t meet expectations. Who should the project manager collaborate with to reassess requirements?
Governance Arrangements.w: The product owner ensures user requirements are correctly prioritised and met.

n.0: The architect focuses on design, not user needs.
n.1: The sponsor focuses on strategic fit, not user detail.
n.2: The board secretary is not involved in requirements.
n.4: The PMO may offer support, not requirement management.

Governance Arrangements.q: A newly formed delivery team needs someone to translate project objectives into clear task allocations and make sure everyone knows what they are expected to produce. Which of the following roles is primarily responsible for ensuring the project team understands their assigned work?
Governance Arrangements.w: The project manager communicates objectives and manages task allocation.

n.1: The product owner manages product priorities, not task allocation.
n.2: The sponsor offers high-level guidance, not task instructions.
n.3: The change manager handles change impacts, not daily task clarity.
n.4: Senior users give input but don't lead the team.

Governance Arrangements.q: Some months after a new system has been handed over to operations, the organisation wants to confirm that the anticipated efficiency savings are actually being achieved. Who is ultimately responsible for the realisation of benefits after the project has been completed?
Governance Arrangements.w: The project sponsor is accountable for ensuring the planned benefits are realised post-project.

n.0: Users benefit from outcomes but are not accountable for realisation.
n.1: Work package owners are responsible for deliverables, not benefits.
n.2: The project manager's role typically ends at project handover.
n.4: The product owner focuses on product delivery, not benefit tracking.

Governance Arrangements.q: A conflict arises between two departments over resource allocation. Who should resolve this issue in a way that aligns with project priorities?
Governance Arrangements.w: The project manager is responsible for resolving resource conflicts and keeping the project on track.

n.0: Team leaders handle team performance, not inter-department issues.
n.2: Schedulers assist with planning, not conflict resolution.
n.3: Stakeholder officers support engagement but not resource resolution.
n.4: The sponsor intervenes in high-level escalations, but resource conflicts are usually handled by the PM.

Governance Arrangements.q: A stakeholder new to project working asks how the two most senior project roles differ, given that both are heavily involved in the initiative's success. What distinguishes the responsibilities of a project sponsor compared to a project manager?
o: The sponsor delivers products; the manager signs off outputs
The sponsor manages day-to-day tasks; the manager manages benefits
The sponsor maintains the risk register; the manager handles benefit realisation
The sponsor defines team tasks; the manager approves the business case
The sponsor focuses on strategic alignment; the manager focuses on delivery
Governance Arrangements.w: Sponsors ensure strategic oversight; project managers handle execution and delivery.

n.0: Product delivery is coordinated by the PM; sign-offs are joint.
n.1: Sponsors are not involved in day-to-day operations.
n.2: Risk management is usually managed by the PM with sponsor oversight.
n.3: Task definition is the manager's responsibility, not the sponsor’s.

Governance Arrangements.q: On an agile initiative, the governance board wants assurance that the most valuable work is being done first and that scarce development effort is focused correctly. In this context, what is the product owner's main governance responsibility?
o: Prioritising backlog items to maximise value
Governance Arrangements.w: The product owner ensures value delivery by prioritising items in the backlog.

n.0: Budget responsibility lies with the sponsor or project manager.
n.2: Sprint retrospectives are managed by the Scrum Master.
n.3: The benefits approach is owned by the sponsor or senior leadership.
n.4: Issue tracking is a project support or PM task.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project is being set up with a steering group that will provide oversight and make key decisions, and a chair must be identified to lead it. Which of the following would be most likely to chair a project steering group?
Governance Arrangements.w: The sponsor often chairs the project board or steering group to ensure strategic control.

n.0: Analysts provide input but don’t lead governance structures.
n.1: The product owner manages product features, not project governance.
n.3: Team leaders operate at the delivery level.
n.4: The project manager reports to the steering group, not chair it.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager finds that delivery is stalling because a decision that only the steering group can make has not been reached, and the schedule is beginning to slip. What should the project manager do?
o: Change the project plan without approval
Request a team member to make the decision
Stop the project until approval is given
Governance Arrangements.w: Escalating delays to the sponsor is appropriate as they can unblock governance decisions.

n.0: Changing plans without approval risks misalignment with governance.
n.1: Finance may not have authority or context for project decisions.
n.3: Team members do not have decision-making authority at this level.
n.4: Halting a project should follow formal processes, not reactive action.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation is initiating a new project and needs to formally establish who holds the various governance roles before delivery begins. Who is responsible for appointing the project manager in most governance frameworks?
Governance Arrangements.w: The sponsor typically appoints the project manager and remains their key point of escalation.

n.0: The team is managed by the PM; they don’t appoint leadership.
n.1: Business analysts support requirements, not leadership roles.
n.3: Suppliers influence delivery but not PM appointments.
n.4: The PMO may advise but doesn’t usually appoint roles.

Governance Arrangements.q: On a product development initiative, the governance structure needs someone to represent the interests of those who will use the deliverables and confirm the outputs are fit for their needs. Which project role is typically responsible for ensuring that the project outputs meet user needs?
Governance Arrangements.w: The product owner ensures outputs align with stakeholder needs and priorities.

n.0: Secretaries support administration, not governance validation.
n.1: The Scrum Master ensures agile practices, not product validation.
n.2: The sponsor ensures strategic fit but not detailed product requirements.
n.3: Finance officers handle cost tracking, not product quality.

Governance Arrangements.q: A governance review is clarifying which activities sit with the project manager as opposed to the sponsor or board. Which of the following tasks would the project manager most likely be accountable for?
o: Managing delivery plans and reporting progress
Governance Arrangements.w: The project manager delivers the plan and provides regular status updates to governance bodies.

n.0: Sponsors and governance boards authorise the business case.
n.2: Governance strategy is a board-level responsibility.
n.3: Funding is allocated at a senior governance level, not by the PM.
n.4: Benefit realisation is typically sponsor-led.

Governance Arrangements.q: During a governance workshop, participants are asked to describe how the two most senior project roles interact and where the boundary between them lies. Which statement best describes the relationship between the project sponsor and the project manager?
o: The sponsor and manager perform identical, fully interchangeable governance roles
The sponsor reports to the manager and takes on operational delivery tasks
The manager owns the business case; the sponsor merely advises on it
The sponsor provides strategic direction; the manager delivers within those parameters
The manager sets strategic direction; the sponsor delivers within those limits
Governance Arrangements.w: The sponsor sets the strategic direction while the manager executes and controls delivery.

n.0: They have distinct, non-interchangeable responsibilities.
n.1: Sponsors do not report to the manager.
n.2: The benefits plan is typically sponsor-owned.
n.4: Stakeholder alignment is sponsor-led, not instructed by the manager.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project board has been convened to oversee a significant organisational change, and its members want to be clear about the purpose their group serves. What is the primary governance responsibility of the project steering group (or board)?
o: To write the quality management approach
To conduct sprint reviews and retrospectives
To manage the daily progress of the project team
To provide strategic direction and decision-making
Governance Arrangements.w: The steering group ensures alignment with organisational objectives and makes key decisions.

n.0: Quality plans are typically produced by the project manager or quality role.
n.1: Sprint reviews are agile ceremonies managed by delivery teams.
n.2: Daily progress is the responsibility of the project manager.
n.3: Work packages are implemented by delivery teams.

Governance Arrangements.q: A dispute has arisen between two departments over competing priorities that is affecting a shared project and needs resolution at a senior level. Which project role is best positioned to resolve strategic conflicts between departments?
Governance Arrangements.w: Strategic alignment and conflict resolution at a senior level fall under the sponsor’s role.

n.0: Configuration managers oversee technical integrity, not strategy.
n.1: Product owners focus on prioritising product value, not organisation-level strategy.
n.3: The project manager manages operational issues, not strategic departmental conflicts.
n.4: The Scrum Master facilitates agile processes, not inter-department resolution.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project sponsor observes that, over several reporting periods, the project manager has consistently failed to meet the agreed progress milestones. What action should the sponsor most appropriately take?
o: Hold a formal review and consider corrective action
Override the manager’s authority and take control of delivery
Reassign the project team without consulting the manager
Report the project manager to human resources immediately
Governance Arrangements.w: The sponsor is responsible for project oversight and should address issues through review and intervention.

n.1: The sponsor does not typically take over project delivery directly.
n.2: Team changes require collaboration with the project manager.
n.3: Cancellation must follow proper governance review processes.
n.4: Escalating to HR without review is inappropriate in governance terms.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager is reviewing their remit to confirm which responsibilities genuinely sit with them and which belong to more senior governance roles. Which of these is NOT typically a responsibility of the project manager?
Governance Arrangements.w: Executive funding is a governance board or sponsor responsibility, not the PM’s.

n.0: Progress monitoring is a core PM duty.
n.2: The PM ensures outputs are delivered on time and to spec.
n.3: The PM manages risks within governance thresholds.
n.4: The PM communicates with both internal and external stakeholders.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project is facing repeated delays due to lack of user input. Who should the project manager escalate this issue to?
Governance Arrangements.w: The sponsor can engage senior stakeholders and ensure user support is provided.

n.1: Team leads cannot compel user input from outside their delivery group.
n.2: Product owners manage product decisions, not stakeholder engagement.
n.3: Scrum Masters facilitate teams, not resolve external user delays.
n.4: The secretary documents meetings but does not have decision authority.

Governance Arrangements.q: A busy executive questions why they should stay engaged as sponsor once a project is underway, rather than leaving it entirely to the project manager. What is one reason the project sponsor should remain involved throughout the project?
o: To draft the detailed delivery plans and work schedules
To manage the delivery team's day-to-day operational workload
To ensure strategic oversight and alignment with business case
To sign off each work package description and estimate
To configure and prioritise the team's sprint backlogs
Governance Arrangements.w: The sponsor owns the business case and ensures it remains valid throughout the project.

n.0: Delivery planning is part of the PM’s remit.
n.1: Daily workload is managed by the project manager.
n.3: Work packages are created and approved at a delivery level.
n.4: Sprint planning is typically agile-team specific, led by product owners or scrum masters.

Governance Arrangements.q: As a project moves into its handover phase and the deliverables are transferred into operational use, the sponsor turns their attention to what matters most at their level. Which of the following would most likely be a project sponsor's concern during the handover phase?
o: Whether daily tasks are completed on time
Whether the team’s morale is high
Whether the project will deliver long-term benefits
Whether the risk log is up to date
Governance Arrangements.w: Sponsors are accountable for ensuring benefits realisation beyond the immediate project delivery.

n.0: Daily task tracking is managed by the PM.
n.1: Team morale is important but not a sponsor’s core concern.
n.3: Configuration management is a technical role.
n.4: Risk log updates are the project manager's responsibility.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation is defining its governance framework and debating whether the sponsor and project manager roles could be combined for smaller projects. In governance terms, why is it important that roles such as sponsor and project manager remain distinct?
o: To maintain accountability and prevent conflict of interest
So the sponsor can lead the team's day-to-day work
To remove the need for formal reporting to the board
So that the project manager can replace the sponsor if needed
So that the project manager can own the business case
Governance Arrangements.w: Separating direction (sponsor) from management (project manager) keeps accountability clear and gives independent oversight: the person challenging performance and owning the business case is not the person delivering it.

n.1: The sponsor directs and supports; day-to-day management is the project manager's role.
n.2: Distinct roles strengthen, rather than remove, formal reporting to the board.
n.3: The roles are not interchangeable; the project manager does not stand in for the sponsor.
n.4: The sponsor owns the business case; the project manager provides input to it.

Governance Arrangements.q: A significant change request has been raised that would affect the project's scope, timescale and budget, and it is unclear who should decide on it. Which responsibility is typically shared between the project manager and the sponsor?
o: Completing all individual team member performance reviews
Installing and configuring the technical tools and software
Maintaining the issue log and daily progress records
Approving changes that impact scope, time, or cost
Drafting the detailed content of each work package
Governance Arrangements.w: Major changes must be escalated and agreed upon by both the PM and sponsor.

n.0: Performance reviews are a line management responsibility.
n.1: Technical setup is not a governance responsibility.
n.2: The issue log is maintained by the PM or project support.
n.4: Work packages are typically created by workstream leads.

Governance Arrangements.q: On an agile project, the steering group needs to stay informed about delivery direction and the relative importance of the work being undertaken. In agile governance, what is one way the product owner supports the steering group?
o: By tracking hours worked by developers
By communicating product progress and user priorities
By signing off the business case
Governance Arrangements.w: The product owner ensures the steering group is updated on value delivery and user needs.

n.0: Tracking hours is a delivery management task.
n.1: Risk procedures are usually handled by the PM or governance officer.
n.2: Financial control is sponsor or finance-owned.
n.4: Business cases are approved by governance bodies, not the PO.

Governance Arrangements.q: When setting up the governance structure for a new operational system, the sponsor insists that those who will actually use the solution are clearly represented. Why is it important for users to be clearly identified within project governance structures?
o: They ensure the solution meets operational needs
They design the high-level business case
They are responsible for supplier contracts
They approve funding for each project stage
Governance Arrangements.w: Users validate that the solution aligns with how it will be used in practice.

n.1: The business case is created by the project manager or sponsor.
n.2: Tolerances are governed by the sponsor and project board.
n.3: Supplier management is handled by procurement roles.
n.4: Funding is typically authorised by sponsors or boards.

Governance Arrangements.q: A trainee project professional is trying to understand how accountability is divided between the two most senior project roles on their assignment. What distinguishes the project sponsor from the project manager in terms of responsibility?
o: The sponsor manages sprint backlog items; the manager funds the project
The sponsor owns the business case; the manager delivers it
The sponsor writes technical specifications; the manager reviews the strategy
The sponsor monitors timesheets; the manager approves the business case
The sponsor plans daily work schedules; the manager sets objectives
Governance Arrangements.w: The sponsor ensures continued business justification, while the PM leads delivery.

n.0: Sprint backlog items are managed by product teams.
n.2: Technical documents are produced by technical teams or the PM.
n.3: Timesheet tracking is an operational task for the PM or support staff.
n.4: Work scheduling is managed by the PM.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation runs its new mobile-banking initiative using an agile approach, with a cross-functional team delivering in short iterations. The steering group wants to clarify how governance is exercised over what gets built. What is a key governance role performed by the product owner in this environment?
o: Prioritising product features to maximise value
Governance Arrangements.w: The product owner ensures features are developed in a value-driven order.

n.0: Organisational policy is outside the remit of the product owner.
n.1: Stakeholder management is led by the PM.
n.2: Comms planning is part of the PM's responsibility.
n.3: Budget approvals are typically sponsor or board-level.

Governance Arrangements.q: On a manufacturing project, individuals have been assigned specific tasks from the breakdown structure and report progress to their team leader. A new joiner asks how their own accountability fits into the governance structure. Which of the following best describes the responsibility of project team members?
o: To deliver work packages as assigned
Governance Arrangements.w: Team members are responsible for completing assigned work within agreed parameters.

n.1: Benefit realisation is a sponsor-led activity.
n.2: Milestone sign-off is done at a governance level.
n.3: Exceptions are approved by project boards or sponsors.
n.4: Only sponsors or boards authorise budget changes.

Governance Arrangements.q: A newly appointed project manager and an experienced project sponsor are agreeing how they will work together on a business-change project. The sponsor wants their respective governance accountabilities set out clearly from the outset. What differentiates the responsibilities of the project manager from those of the project sponsor?
o: The project manager signs off programme-level funding
The project manager approves the business case
The project manager manages delivery; the sponsor ensures justification
The project manager oversees the benefits review
The project manager defines organisational policy
Governance Arrangements.w: The PM ensures delivery of outputs; the sponsor ensures the project remains viable and justified.

n.0: Programme-level funding is outside the PM’s remit.
n.1: The sponsor owns the business case.
n.3: Benefits are reviewed by the sponsor or benefits owner.
n.4: Policy is defined at the organisational level, not by the PM.

Governance Arrangements.q: During delivery of a system-integration project, a serious disagreement develops between the project team and a group of external users over acceptance criteria, and it cannot be settled at working level. Considering the governance structure, who should step in to mediate the issue?
Governance Arrangements.w: The sponsor can engage senior stakeholders to resolve cross-functional conflicts.

n.0: Team leaders may manage internal conflict, but sponsors handle external escalations.
n.1: Support officers facilitate admin, not conflict resolution.
n.2: Product owners represent users but don’t mediate cross-team issues alone.
n.4: Finance managers handle cost reporting, not team dynamics.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project board relies on a monthly information pack to authorise continuation of a large infrastructure programme. The board chair asks how the project manager contributes to sound governance during the delivery phase. How does a project manager support good governance during delivery?
o: By ensuring progress, risk and issue reports are accurate and timely
By defining the organisation's strategic business objectives and priorities
By approving the membership and terms of the governance board
By personally signing off and awarding all procurement contracts
By setting the organisation's company-wide governance policies and standards
Governance Arrangements.w: Accurate reporting enables the board to make timely and informed decisions.

n.1: Strategic objectives are defined by senior leadership.
n.2: Board composition is typically organisationally controlled.
n.3: Contracts are signed at sponsor or procurement level.
n.4: Policies are set by leadership, not project managers.

Governance Arrangements.q: A product owner on an agile software project is reviewing the boundaries of their remit with the project sponsor, who wants to avoid any overlap of accountabilities. Which of these activities would fall outside the governance responsibility of a product owner?
o: Representing user needs to the team
Governance Arrangements.w: Product owners do not sign off the business case — this is a sponsor/board responsibility.

n.0: Backlog prioritisation is a core product owner responsibility.
n.2: They act as a voice of the user throughout delivery.
n.3: Product owners clarify acceptance with the team.
n.4: They liaise with users to gather feedback.

Governance Arrangements.q: Midway through a transformation project, market conditions shift and questions are raised about whether the investment is still worthwhile. The governance board looks to the sponsor for assurance. Which statement best reflects the sponsor's role in maintaining governance over project success?
o: Running the daily agile stand-ups and sprint ceremonies
Managing the delivery team's individual performance reviews and appraisals
Writing the user documentation and operating instructions manuals
Assigning and scheduling individual development tasks to team members
Ensuring the project continues to support the business case
Governance Arrangements.w: The sponsor ensures the project remains aligned with its justification throughout.

n.0: Stand-ups are delivery-focused and facilitated by the scrum master or team.
n.1: Performance reviews are handled at team lead or HR level.
n.2: User documentation is typically written by the delivery team.
n.3: Task assignment is a project manager or team lead responsibility.

Governance Arrangements.q: On a high-profile organisational-change project, the sponsor is described in the governance documentation as the project's 'champion'. A new board member is unsure what this actually involves in practice. What does it mean if a project sponsor acts as the 'champion' of the project?
o: They step in to replace the project manager when absent
They track and appraise each individual team member's performance
They take direct responsibility for all technical development work
They promote the project to stakeholders and defend its value
They personally perform the code reviews and product testing
Governance Arrangements.w: The sponsor champions the project’s value and ensures continued support from senior stakeholders.

n.0: The sponsor does not substitute for the PM operationally.
n.1: Performance management is the PM or team lead's role.
n.2: Technical development is handled by delivery roles.
n.4: Code review is not a sponsor responsibility.

Governance Arrangements.q: A new project involves multiple subcontractors and strict regulatory requirements. Why is it critical to implement robust governance arrangements in this context?
o: To accelerate the supplier procurement process
To monitor the marketing team's campaign performance
To reduce the number of governance meetings
To ensure policies and procedures are consistently followed
To remove the need for separate quality assurance
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance ensures that project activities align with regulations and internal procedures, especially when subcontractors and compliance are involved.

n.0: While governance may influence procurement, its main role is broader.
n.1: Marketing performance is not the focus of governance structures.
n.2: Governance often increases structured communication, not reduces it.
n.4: Quality assurance is part of governance, not a result of avoiding it.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation is setting up governance arrangements for its portfolio of change projects and wants to define what these arrangements should contain. A consultant is asked to identify the core components. Which of the following identifies two functions typically included in project governance arrangements?
Governance Arrangements.w: Approval processes and delegation of authority are core components of project governance.

n.0: While important, these are team management tools, not governance elements.
n.2: These are more aligned with corporate image than project governance.
n.3: These are financial tactics, not governance functions.
n.4: These relate to operations or communications, not governance.

Governance Arrangements.q: A regulated financial-services firm is establishing governance for a compliance-driven project and must ensure its work meets both corporate strategy and external rules. Complete the statement: effective governance ensures that project ______ are aligned with organisational objectives and regulatory requirements.
Governance Arrangements.w: Processes are the mechanisms through which governance ensures compliance and alignment.

n.0: Graphics are irrelevant to governance.
n.1: Celebrations are cultural, not governance-related.
n.2: Colours have no bearing on governance.
n.4: Deliveries are outputs, not governance mechanisms.

Governance Arrangements.q: A PMO is explaining to senior managers why decision-making authority is distributed to defined levels within the governance structure rather than held centrally. One manager challenges the rationale. Which of the following is NOT a reason to establish delegated authority within project governance?
o: To reduce bottlenecks in decision making
To ensure decisions can be made at the right level
Governance Arrangements.w: Delegation reduces the need for excessive oversight by distributing authority effectively.

n.0: One goal of delegation is decision-making at appropriate levels.
n.1: Delegation helps define who is responsible for what.
n.2: Delegation distributes authority, not increases oversight.
n.3: Delegated authority assigns decision-making responsibility.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project sponsor wants to change a major deliverable. Which governance element should define who has the authority to approve this change?
Governance Arrangements.w: Delegated responsibilities clearly define who is authorised to make project decisions.

n.0: WBS defines tasks, not authority levels.
n.1: The comms plan outlines information flow, not governance authority.
n.2: Resource calendars relate to availability, not approval rights.
n.4: Team charters guide team dynamics, not formal approval authority.

Governance Arrangements.q: A newly formed project team is documenting the mechanisms that will guide behaviour and decisions throughout their governance framework. They need to select an appropriate example. Which of the following pairs best represents governance mechanisms in project management?
Governance Arrangements.w: Policies (the organisation's rules) and procedures (consistent, repeatable ways of working) are governance mechanisms: they guide behaviour and decisions and provide accountability and control.

n.0: Estimates and resource histograms are planning outputs, not mechanisms that set rules for behaviour and decisions.
n.1: Stakeholder maps and personas support stakeholder analysis and design, not the rules that guide project decisions.
n.2: Gantt and burndown charts show schedule and progress; they are planning and reporting tools, not governance mechanisms.
n.3: The WBS and CBS are planning tools that break down the work and costs; they do not govern how decisions are made.

Governance Arrangements.q: When designing governance for a phased construction project, the sponsor insists the framework be tied to the stages of the life cycle. A team member asks what this alignment is intended to achieve. The governance framework should be aligned with the project's life cycle to ensure what key benefit?
o: Decisions are made at appropriate stages
Governance Arrangements.w: Aligning governance with the life cycle supports effective decision making at relevant phases.

n.0: Bonuses are unrelated to governance design.
n.2: Speed isn't the core goal—appropriate timing is.
n.3: Meeting reduction is not a direct governance goal.
n.4: Supplier payment terms are contractual, not governance-driven.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project delivering a product across three countries faces different legal obligations in each jurisdiction, and the sponsor is concerned about staying compliant everywhere. Which governance tool helps ensure compliance in this situation?
Governance Arrangements.w: Compliance across several jurisdictions is achieved by identifying the regulations that apply in each country and setting policies that require the project to meet them. Policies and regulations are core elements of governance.

n.0: Burn charts track progress in iterative delivery and give no control over legal compliance.
n.1: Engagement and communication plans manage relationships and information flow; they do not define the legal obligations the project must meet.
n.2: Product-based planning defines deliverables and their sequence, not compliance with local law.
n.4: Earned value measures cost and schedule performance, not compliance with regulations.

Governance Arrangements.q: In project governance, delegated authority helps to:
o: Replace the need for governance policies
Governance Arrangements.w: Delegated authority ensures the right people can make timely decisions within governance limits.

n.0: Documentation is still essential, even with delegation.
n.1: Escalation routes remain necessary for unresolved issues.
n.2: Policies are part of, not replaced by, delegation.
n.4: Stakeholder engagement remains important.

Governance Arrangements.q: A key risk in poorly governed projects is:
Governance Arrangements.w: Without governance, authority and responsibility may be unclear, leading to delays and confusion.

n.0: Skilled resources are beneficial, not a risk.
n.2: Celebrations are not a risk issue.
n.3: RAID logs support governance rather than hinder it.
n.4: Stakeholder support is generally positive.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project in its initiation phase requires formal reviews before moving to the next stage. Which governance component ensures these reviews occur?
Governance Arrangements.w: Decision gates are formal go/no-go control points at the end of each phase where the business case, readiness and funding are re-confirmed before the next phase is authorised.

n.0: Updating the risk register is continuous monitoring, not a formal review before the next stage.
n.1: Retrospectives are team learning sessions at the end of an iteration, not governance approval points.
n.2: Change control assesses individual change requests; it does not mandate phase-end reviews.
n.4: Stand-ups coordinate the team's daily work; they are not formal governance reviews.

Governance Arrangements.q: A programme office is strengthening its governance framework so that breaches of standards do not go unaddressed and corrective action is triggered promptly. Complete the statement: governance frameworks often include _______ to address non-compliance and enforce corrective actions.
Governance Arrangements.w: Escalation procedures route breaches of standards or tolerances to the level of authority able to act, so non-compliance is addressed and corrective action is triggered promptly.

n.0: Benefits profiles describe each benefit, its measure and its owner; they do not deal with non-compliance.
n.2: Resource histograms show resource demand over time and have no role in enforcing standards.
n.3: Lessons learned logs capture experience for the future; they do not enforce corrective action on a current breach.
n.4: Stakeholder registers record who the stakeholders are and their interests, not how breaches are handled.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation is defining what decisions individuals may take without referring upward on its projects. The governance lead wants to specify the typical delegated authorities. Which of the following identifies two delegated authorities that are typically defined in project governance?
o: Critical path analysis and resource smoothing
Defect logging and test script writing
Governance Arrangements.w: Delegated authority defines what each role may decide without referring upward, most commonly the authority to approve changes and the limits of financial authority (the spend each role may commit before escalating).

n.0: Sequencing and duration estimating are planning activities, not limits on what a role may approve.
n.2: Stakeholder mapping and communication planning are management activities, not decision rights delegated by the governance framework.
n.3: Critical path analysis and resource smoothing are scheduling techniques, not authorities delegated through governance.
n.4: Defect logging and test script writing are quality control tasks done by the team, not delegated authorities.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project support officer is compiling a checklist of the activities that make up their organisation's project governance, and one proposed item does not seem to belong. Which of the following is NOT a typical governance activity?
Governance Arrangements.w: Informal social activities are not a formal part of governance procedures.

n.0: Risk assessments are a key governance control.
n.2: Charter approval is a core governance milestone.
n.3: Defining roles is fundamental to governance.
n.4: Reporting processes enforce accountability.

Governance Arrangements.q: During execution of a resource-constrained project, two work streams begin competing for the same scarce specialists and their leads cannot agree a way forward. A governance mechanism that helps resolve such conflicts is:
Governance Arrangements.w: When leads cannot agree within their own authority, escalation procedures pass the decision to the level that can resolve it, such as the project manager, sponsor or board, which can set priorities across work streams.

n.1: Benefits reviews check whether benefits are being realised, not who gets scarce resources.
n.2: Post-project reviews happen after closure, too late to resolve a conflict during execution.
n.3: Configuration audits check that items match their records and requirements; they do not resolve priority disputes.
n.4: A lessons learned log captures experience for the future; it does not settle a live conflict.

Governance Arrangements.q: Your project is halfway through its lifecycle and requires additional funding. According to governance limits, you must seek _______ from the project board.
Governance Arrangements.w: Additional funding beyond delegated limits must be approved by the level that holds that financial authority, here the project board.

n.1: Configuration sign-off confirms the status of items and versions, not spending.
n.2: Quality acceptance confirms outputs meet acceptance criteria; it does not release extra funds.
n.3: Technical assurance gives confidence in the solution; it is not a funding approval.
n.4: Benefits sign-off concerns realised benefits, not authority to spend more.

Governance Arrangements.q: A sponsor is explaining to a sceptical department head why the effort of maintaining clear governance procedures is worthwhile for their project. One claimed advantage, however, is not something governance actually provides. Which is NOT a benefit of having clear governance procedures?
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance sets limits; it does not grant unlimited spending power.

n.0: Transparency is a key governance outcome.
n.1: Procedures help avoid repeated work.
n.2: Stakeholders trust clear governance.
n.3: Consistency in decisions comes from defined procedures.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project coordinator is assembling the documentation that describes how their governance process operates day to day. They must choose genuine governance content for it. Which two items would you find in a governance process?
o: Test scripts and defect resolution logs
Detailed design specifications and technical drawings
Supplier price lists and delivery notes
Governance Arrangements.w: A governance process documents who is accountable for what and how and when performance is reported upwards, so decisions and oversight happen consistently.

n.0: Test scripts and defect logs are quality control records.
n.1: Durations and float are schedule content, not governance.
n.2: Design specifications and drawings describe the solution, not how it is governed.
n.3: Price lists and delivery notes are commercial and logistics records.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project is approaching closure and an assurance reviewer asks the project manager to evidence that all key decisions and approvals were properly recorded during delivery. Which governance document provides a record of all decisions made?
Governance Arrangements.w: A decision log records each significant decision, who made it, when and why, giving the audit trail an assurance reviewer needs.

n.1: The risk register records risks, their assessment, owners and responses, not every decision taken.
n.2: A benefits profile defines a benefit, its measure, owner and timing, not project decisions.
n.3: The lessons learned log captures experience to pass on, not a formal record of approvals.
n.4: The stakeholder register records who the stakeholders are and their interests and influence.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation is formalising how the order and authority of project decisions are set out within its governance arrangements. Complete the statement: governance ________ define the sequence and authority for project decisions.
Governance Arrangements.w: Procedures outline the steps and authority levels for decisions in governance.

n.0: Recipes have no role in governance.
n.1: Festivities are unrelated to decision-making.
n.2: Celebrations don’t guide governance steps.
n.3: Themes are design-related, not governance frameworks.

Governance Arrangements.q: An external regulatory audit of a completed project finds that several key documents were released without the required sign-off. The sponsor asks which governance element broke down. Which governance element failed?
Governance Arrangements.w: Documents released without the required sign-off show that the approval process, which defines who must authorise what before it is issued, was not followed or enforced.

n.1: Resource planning decides who is needed and when; it does not control document sign-off.
n.2: Benefits management tracks and realises benefits; it does not govern the approval of documents.
n.3: Scheduling sets the timing of work; the breach here was a missing authorisation, not a timing problem.
n.4: Lessons learned capture experience for future projects; a missing sign-off is a failure of a control, not of learning.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project board is concerned that spending on a capital project stays within authorised limits and wants to embed suitable controls in its governance arrangements. Which two practices help maintain financial control within governance limits?
o: Budget review meetings and delegated authority
Stakeholder mapping and engagement plan reviews
Governance Arrangements.w: Regular budget reviews compare spend and forecast against the authorised budget, and delegated authority sets how much each role may approve before escalating.

n.0: Levelling and float management are scheduling techniques, not financial controls.
n.2: These gather and test requirements; they do not keep spend within authority.
n.3: These develop the team; they are not financial governance controls.
n.4: These support stakeholder engagement, not spending limits.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project has suffered repeated unauthorised additions to its scope because it was never clear who could approve changes. The sponsor argues that better governance would have prevented this. Complete the statement: effective governance reduces the risk of _______ by ensuring clear decision paths and accountability.
Governance Arrangements.w: Clear governance prevents uncontrolled scope changes by defining who can approve changes.

n.0: Allocation is a planning activity, not a risk.
n.1: Engagement is a positive outcome, not a risk.
n.2: Quality control is managed by governance but not described as a risk.
n.3: Collaboration is aided by governance but not a risk it reduces.

Governance Arrangements.q: A PMO is drafting the standard contents of its project governance framework and reviewing a list of candidate items, one of which belongs in each individual project's own plan instead. Which of the following is NOT typically included in a governance framework?
Governance Arrangements.w: A governance framework sets the rules for direction and control: decision rights, escalation, reporting and delegated authority. Detailed activity schedules are produced for each project in its own plan.

n.0: Authority levels define what each role may approve.
n.1: Decision rights procedures are core to governance.
n.3: Reporting requirements provide transparency to the board.
n.4: Escalation paths make sure issues reach the right level.

Governance Arrangements.q: During delivery of a project, the project manager realises that committing to a supplier invoice would take spending beyond their agreed authority limit. In line with the governance arrangements, the next step is to:
Governance Arrangements.w: Overspend breaches governance limits and must be escalated for board approval.

n.0: Scope changes require proper approval, not blind changes.
n.1: Parties don’t resolve authority breaches.
n.2: Ignoring financial breach violates governance.
n.3: Rescheduling tasks doesn’t address financial breaches.

Governance Arrangements.q: Which two documents illustrate delegated responsibilities and approval thresholds?
o: Work breakdown structure and Gantt chart
Quality plan and acceptance test strategy
Risk register and issue resolution log
Governance Arrangements.w: A governance charter sets out roles and decision rights, and an authority matrix shows which role can approve what, up to which threshold.

n.0: These show scope and timing, not who may approve what.
n.1: These cover who stakeholders are and how to communicate with them.
n.2: These define quality standards and testing, not approval limits.
n.3: These record risks and issues, not delegated thresholds.

Governance Arrangements.q: An assurance reviewer is confirming that a project's governance ensures compliance with the rules and obligations that genuinely apply to it. One listed item, however, is not something governance enforces. Governance is required to ensure compliance with all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Draft industry guidance not yet adopted
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance ensures compliance with the rules that actually apply to the project: external regulations and the organisation's own policies, procedures and delegated authorities. Draft guidance that has not been adopted or made mandatory is not something governance enforces.

n.0: Standard operating procedures set consistent ways of working that governance requires the project to follow.
n.1: Corporate policies are the organisation's own rules, and governance makes sure projects follow them.
n.2: Delegated authorities define who may decide or spend what, and governance enforces those limits.
n.4: Statutes are external legal requirements, and governance must ensure the project complies with them.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation is documenting how problems that cannot be resolved at working level are formally raised and dealt with under its governance arrangements. Complete the statement: a governance framework defines the _______ for raising and resolving project issues.
Governance Arrangements.w: The escalation process defines how issues beyond a role's tolerance are formally raised to the right level and resolved.

n.0: The work breakdown structure breaks the scope into work packages.
n.1: A configuration audit checks items against their records and requirements.
n.2: A resource histogram shows resource demand over time.
n.3: A benefits profile describes a benefit and how it will be measured.

Governance Arrangements.q: A governance lead is explaining why a project manager's spending authority is greater in some phases than others. A colleague asks what actually determines these limits. Which two factors influence the limits of financial authority in a project?
o: Team size and the project manager's preference
Amount of float and the length of the critical path
Number of defects found and test pass rate
Project life cycle stage and delegated authority
Number of stakeholders and meeting frequency
Governance Arrangements.w: Limits of financial authority are set through delegation from the sponsor or board and are often released phase by phase, so the life cycle stage affects what can be committed.

n.0: Limits are set by governance, not by team size or personal preference.
n.1: Float and the critical path are schedule measures, not authority settings.
n.2: Defect and test measures relate to quality, not delegated spend.
n.4: Stakeholder numbers and meeting frequency affect communication, not spending limits.

Governance Arrangements.q: A quality reviewer is assessing whether a project's governance arrangements are sound and is testing them against the hallmarks of good practice. One proposed trait clearly does not belong. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of effective governance?
Governance Arrangements.w: Effective governance requires accountability, not its absence.

n.0: Procedures must be documented for consistency.
n.1: Decision paths ensure clarity in authority.
n.2: Escalation routes are critical for issue resolution.
n.3: Reviews monitor adherence to governance.

Governance Arrangements.q: During the initiation phase of a large infrastructure project, stakeholders question who can authorise budget changes. Which governance tool clarifies spending limits at each level?
Governance Arrangements.w: An authority matrix maps out who can approve different levels of expenditure.

n.1: The project schedule sets timelines, not approval limits.
n.2: A resource histogram shows staffing levels, not spending approval.
n.3: A risk register logs risks, not financial authorities.
n.4: A communication plan defines information flow, not budget limits.

Governance Arrangements.q: Which two items are central to a governance charter?
o: Defect logs and test completion reports
Roles and responsibilities and escalation paths
Activity network diagram and critical path analysis
Skills matrix and training needs analysis
Governance Arrangements.w: A governance charter defines who is accountable for what and how decisions and issues are escalated.

n.0: These are quality control records.
n.2: These are scheduling tools, not governance content.
n.3: These support team development, not governance structure.
n.4: These are planning products produced during delivery.

Governance Arrangements.q: A sponsor is explaining why the spending limits delegated to project roles change as the project moves through its stages, and what exposure this variation is intended to manage. Complete the statement: delegated spending limits vary across the project life cycle to control _____ risk.
Governance Arrangements.w: Delegated spending limits (limits of financial authority) set the maximum each role may commit before escalating. Varying them as commitments and spend change through the life cycle controls financial risk.

n.0: Technical risk is managed through design reviews, testing and specialist input, not through spending limits.
n.1: Safety risk is controlled through health and safety management and legislation, not financial delegation.
n.3: Cultural factors are addressed through leadership and engagement; spending limits do not control them.
n.4: Quality risk is managed through quality planning, assurance and control, not delegated spending limits.

Governance Arrangements.q: A department head questions whether the effort of maintaining a clear governance framework really pays off for a project. One of the advantages being claimed for it, however, is not something governance delivers. Which of the following is NOT a benefit of clear governance frameworks?
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance defines limits rather than granting unlimited power.

n.1: Consistency comes from defined decision paths.
n.2: Governance ensures financial authority remains controlled.
n.3: Accountability is a core outcome of good governance.
n.4: Stakeholders gain confidence when governance is clear.

Governance Arrangements.q: A healthcare IT project must comply with patient privacy laws. Governance _____ outline how policies are enforced and breaches handled.
Governance Arrangements.w: Procedures specify the steps for enforcing policies and managing violations.

n.0: Timelines set deadlines, not policy enforcement processes.
n.2: Resources are assets, not governance instructions.
n.3: Templates provide formats, not procedural guidance.
n.4: Budgets allocate funds, not enforcement steps.

Governance Arrangements.q: A global finance project missed deadlines due to decision bottlenecks. Which of the following is NOT a governance failure that would cause this issue?
Governance Arrangements.w: Having controlled budget thresholds is a positive governance practice, not a failure.

n.0: Undefined decision rights cause confusion and delays.
n.1: Inconsistent procedures lead to unpredictable processes.
n.2: Without escalation paths, critical issues remain unresolved.
n.3: Lack of delegation forces bottlenecks at higher levels.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project office is selecting the governance documents that will set out both who may approve what, and how unresolved problems are escalated and settled. Which two governance documents specify approval levels and issue resolution pathways?
Governance Arrangements.w: An authority matrix defines approval limits and an escalation procedure defines how to resolve issues.

n.0: Resource and budget plans forecast needs but don’t define escalation.
n.2: Schedules and comms plans manage timing and info flow, not approvals.
n.3: Checklists and tests support quality but don’t set authority.
n.4: These capture risks and lessons but not authority or escalation.

Governance Arrangements.q: A software rollout involves several external vendors, each with different working practices, and the sponsor insists governance policies be in place before work starts. A vendor asks why these policies matter so much here. In this project, governance policies are critical because they:
o: Transfer all delivery risk onto the vendors
Provide formal rules for project conduct
Remove the need for a contract with each vendor
Guarantee code quality without further testing
Replace the need for a detailed project schedule
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance policies set the formal rules for how the project is conducted, so several vendors with different practices work to the same standards, approvals and accountabilities from the start.

n.0: Risk is allocated through contracts and risk management; policies do not shift all delivery risk to suppliers.
n.2: Policies complement contracts; each vendor still needs a contract setting out its obligations and terms.
n.3: Policies can require quality standards, but they cannot guarantee quality; testing and quality control are still needed.
n.4: Policies do not replace planning; a schedule is still needed to coordinate the vendors' work.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation is deciding what will set the benchmarks and the authority required to accept its project deliverables under the governance arrangements. Complete the statement: governance ________ define the criteria and authority for accepting project deliverables.
Governance Arrangements.w: Standards set the benchmarks and approval authority for deliverable acceptance.

n.0: Budgets allocate funds but don’t set acceptance criteria.
n.1: Templates provide formats, not approval authority.
n.2: Reports capture information but don’t set criteria.
n.3: Schedules define timelines, not acceptance benchmarks.

Governance Arrangements.q: An international aid project spanning many partners needs consistent oversight, and the sponsor is reviewing proposed measures to strengthen its governance. One suggestion would actually weaken it. Which of the following would NOT improve governance in this scenario?
Governance Arrangements.w: Randomly assigning decisions undermines clarity and accountability.

n.0: Escalation paths ensure issues can be raised effectively.
n.1: Frequent updates keep stakeholders informed.
n.2: Common templates standardise information for oversight.
n.3: Delegation clarifies who makes which decisions.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project operating in a heavily regulated sector must keep track of every policy, standard and statute it has to comply with. The project manager needs the governance tool that captures these obligations. Which governance tool lists applicable policies and regulations for a project?
Governance Arrangements.w: A policies and regulations register captures all relevant rules that must be complied with during the project.

n.0: A risk register logs project risks, not policy requirements.
n.1: An issue log records problems, not governance policies.
n.2: A stakeholder map identifies stakeholders, not policy details.
n.3: A communication plan defines information flow, not regulations.

Governance Arrangements.q: Which pair of elements does an organisation's governance framework set out so that projects follow consistent, repeatable and accountable ways of working?
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance sets the policies (the organisation's rules) and procedures (consistent, repeatable ways of working) that every project follows, giving accountability, consistency and control.

n.0: Training and development plans build capability; they are an HR and line management matter, not governance rules.
n.2: Schedules and resource histograms are project planning outputs, not governance elements.
n.3: Stakeholder maps and communication plans are project-level engagement tools rather than governance rules.
n.4: Quality metrics and test scripts are used in quality management and control, not set by the governance framework.

Governance Arrangements.q: Governance ___ specify how decisions escalate to higher authority.
Governance Arrangements.w: Procedures define the formal steps for escalating decisions within governance structures.
