n.0: Templates provide formats, not decision pathways.
n.1: Schedules set timelines, not authority routes.
n.3: Budgets allocate funds but don’t outline escalation steps.
n.4: Checklists help with tasks, not formal escalation.

Governance Arrangements.q: A new project administrator is sorting proposed items into those that form part of project governance and those that are delivery techniques used by the team. Which of the following does NOT form part of project governance?
Governance Arrangements.w: Resource smoothing is a scheduling technique used by the project manager and team. Governance covers roles, escalation, reporting and delegated authority.

n.1: Escalation paths make sure issues are handled at the right level.
n.2: Delegated authority specifies who can make which decisions.
n.3: Defined roles clarify decision rights, a governance function.
n.4: Reporting processes give the board visibility and accountability.

Governance Arrangements.q: On a fast-track construction project where waiting for sign-off would jeopardise the schedule, the sponsor wants a governance approach that keeps routine decisions moving. Which governance approach helps reduce decision delays?
Governance Arrangements.w: Delegated authority allows decisions to be made quickly at appropriate levels, reducing delays.

n.0: Social events don’t impact formal decision processes.
n.1: Weekly meetings can still cause delays between sessions.
n.2: More approval layers typically increase delays, not reduce them.
n.3: Extended reporting adds work and can slow decisions.

Governance Arrangements.q: When setting up governance for a multi-party project, the sponsor wants to make explicit who is permitted to take which decisions and at what level. What is the primary purpose of delegated responsibilities in governance?
o: To clarify who can make decisions
Governance Arrangements.w: Delegated responsibilities specify who has authority to make which project decisions.

n.0: Budgets are financial controls, not directly defined by delegation.
n.1: Resource allocation is managed separately from delegation authority.
n.3: Communication planning is distinct from delegation of decision rights.
n.4: Task scheduling is part of planning, not the purpose of delegation.

Governance Arrangements.q: Which two items are defined in governance procedures?
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance procedures define who does what and how issues are escalated within the framework.

n.0: These are stakeholder management tools, not procedural definitions of authority.
n.2: These support quality control, not governance.
n.3: These are commercial records, not governance procedures.
n.4: These are planning products, not governance procedures.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project's governance arrangements set out how much each role is allowed to commit financially without seeking approval. Complete the statement: limits of financial authority are set by delegated ___ within the governance framework.
Governance Arrangements.w: Delegated responsibilities include defined spending limits for different roles.

n.0: Standards set quality benchmarks, not financial limits.
n.1: Policies guide behaviour but don’t specify individual authority limits.
n.2: Procedures outline steps but don’t themselves set limits.
n.3: Templates provide formats, not authority definitions.

Governance Arrangements.q: A newly appointed project board is defining which responsibilities fall within its remit as opposed to those handled by the project manager and delivery team during day-to-day execution. Reviewing a proposed list of activities, which of the following is NOT a role typically covered by project governance?
Governance Arrangements.w: Producing and maintaining the schedule is a day-to-day planning activity for the project manager and team. Governance approves the baseline and takes decisions on exceptions, but it does not build the schedule itself.

n.0: Assurance gives the board confidence that the project is on track and is part of governance, ideally independent of the delivery team.
n.1: Governance sets the delegated authority and tolerances within which the project manager may act.
n.3: Approving the budget and releasing funding is a core governance responsibility.
n.4: Go/no-go decisions at decision gates are taken by the sponsor and board as part of governance.

Governance Arrangements.q: Midway through a warehouse automation project, the sponsor notices a major discrepancy between planned and actual expenditure and asks for evidence so corrective action can be authorised at the next board meeting. Which governance report is designed to highlight this variance?
Governance Arrangements.w: Financial status reports compare planned vs. actual costs to identify variances.

n.0: Risk reports identify potential issues, not cost variances.
n.1: Change logs track scope changes, not expenditure variances.
n.2: Quality audits assess product standards, not finances.
n.3: Registers list stakeholders, not financial data.

Governance Arrangements.q: A national retailer is launching a new inventory tracking system, and the sponsor insists the initiative be traced back to the corporate business plan before funding is released. Why must this project be linked to the organisation's overall strategy?
o: To ensure the system supports strategic goals
Governance Arrangements.w: Linking ensures the project delivers value that aligns with and advances the organisation’s strategic goals.

n.0: Bonuses are HR matters, not a purpose of strategic linkage.
n.2: Code review frequency isn’t determined by strategic objectives.
n.3: UI complexity is a design concern, not a strategic alignment issue.
n.4: Office space isn’t influenced by project–strategy alignment.

Governance Arrangements.q: A portfolio director is deciding how to distribute limited funding and specialist staff across competing initiatives, and reviews how each connects to the organisation's stated objectives. What primary benefit does linking a project to organisational objectives provide in this situation?
o: Removal of the need for a business case
Scope fixed for the whole life cycle
Governance Arrangements.w: Linking projects to objectives lets leaders direct scarce funding and people to the initiatives that contribute most to strategy, and stop those that no longer fit.

n.0: Strategic fit is shown through the business case; alignment does not replace it.
n.1: Alignment does not reduce the number of stakeholders who need engagement.
n.3: Scope can still change through change control; alignment does not freeze it.
n.4: Alignment justifies the investment but does not remove delivery risk.

Governance Arrangements.q: A software rollout overran its approved budget, and a post-project review concluded that the work had drifted away from the business goals it was meant to serve. Which practice could have prevented this outcome?
o: Focusing solely on delivering the technology features
Extending the project scope without formal approval
Eliminating the regular governance and gate reviews
Ensuring project objectives align with organisational strategy
Reducing the amount of project documentation produced
Governance Arrangements.w: Alignment with strategy keeps projects focused on delivering business value within approved budgets.

n.0: Technology focus alone may ignore business priorities.
n.1: Scope extensions increase budget risk.
n.2: Governance reviews are essential for alignment checks.
n.4: Documentation reduction doesn’t guarantee alignment.

Governance Arrangements.q: Project alignment with organisational ____ ensures strategic relevance.
Governance Arrangements.w: Projects exist to deliver organisational strategy, so alignment with organisational objectives is what makes a project strategically relevant.

n.0: Alignment with procedures gives consistency and compliance, not strategic relevance.
n.2: Hierarchies define reporting lines, not strategic aims.
n.3: Budgets constrain spend but do not define strategic purpose.
n.4: Timescales are planning constraints, not the strategic intent.

Governance Arrangements.q: After a programme office links each project's objectives to the corporate goals and communicates the connection to delivery teams, the sponsor lists the improvements she expects to see across the portfolio. Which of the following is NOT an expected outcome of this linkage?
Governance Arrangements.w: Linkage yields coordination, not uncoordinated efforts.

n.0: Resources get focused on strategic work.
n.2: Alignment enhances decision clarity.
n.3: Stakeholders back well-aligned projects.
n.4: Success is measured against strategic criteria.

Governance Arrangements.q: Linking project objectives to business aims helps in:
Governance Arrangements.w: Strategic alignment clarifies which initiatives should be prioritised.

n.0: Stakeholder buy-in typically increases.
n.1: Random tasks conflict with strategic focus.
n.3: Alignment doesn’t inherently extend duration.
n.4: Social events aren’t a strategic outcome.

Governance Arrangements.q: A hospital implements an electronic records system aligned with its objective to improve patient care and reduce errors. Which two practices highlight this alignment?
o: Setting patient outcome targets and mapping features to them
Tracking spend against budget and reporting milestone progress
Choosing the lowest-cost supplier and fixing the go-live date
Delivering every requested feature and maximising module count
Writing user manuals and scheduling classroom training
Governance Arrangements.w: Alignment is shown by measurable targets tied to the objective (better care, fewer errors) and by tracing each system feature to those targets, in the same way as a benefits map.

n.1: These are cost and schedule controls, not evidence of strategic alignment.
n.2: Cost and date decisions concern delivery constraints, not alignment with patient-care objectives.
n.3: Delivering more features is not the same as delivering the objective; scope should be justified by benefits.
n.4: These prepare users for transition but do not show the link to objectives.

Governance Arrangements.q: During a governance workshop, a project manager is asked to justify why every proposed initiative must be mapped against the organisation's strategy before approval. Which of the following is NOT a valid reason to align project objectives with organisational strategy?
Governance Arrangements.w: Alignment ensures projects remain relevant, not irrelevant.

n.1: Resources are better allocated to strategic initiatives.
n.2: Clarity in decisions is improved by alignment.
n.3: Stakeholders back strategically linked projects.
n.4: Supporting goals is the core purpose of alignment.

Governance Arrangements.q: A local council deploys a citizen portal to improve transparency. Ensuring project objectives align with the council’s mission helped gain ______ approvals.
Governance Arrangements.w: Showing strategic fit with the council's mission strengthens the business case, which is what funding (budgetary) approvals are based on.

n.0: Technical approvals depend on the design and architecture.
n.2: Planning approvals relate to physical development and land use.
n.3: Security approvals depend on meeting security standards.
n.4: Regulatory approvals depend on legal compliance, not mission alignment.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project sponsor wants a single term to describe the discipline of ensuring that a new digital-services project's goals actively support and advance the organisation's strategic aims. Which term best describes this process?
Governance Arrangements.w: Strategic alignment is making sure a project's objectives and benefits support the organisation's strategy, through the business case, portfolio prioritisation, the sponsor and decision gates.

n.0: Configuration management controls the versions of project items and products, not strategic fit.
n.1: Scope creep is uncontrolled growth in scope, the opposite of disciplined alignment with strategy.
n.3: Risk management deals with uncertain events that could affect objectives, not with linking objectives to strategy.
n.4: Quality assurance gives confidence that processes will deliver fit-for-purpose outputs; it does not link goals to strategy.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project sponsor asks the project manager to explain why an assurance function is being applied throughout the project. What is the primary purpose of assurance within a project?
o: To provide confidence that processes and deliverables meet required standards
To schedule and run project team meetings
To manage and control the project budget
To negotiate contracts with external suppliers
To design and develop the project products
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance provides stakeholders with confidence that project processes and deliverables comply with required standards.

n.1: Scheduling meetings is part of project administration, not assurance.
n.2: Managing budgets is a financial control activity, not assurance’s main purpose.
n.3: Contract negotiation falls under procurement, not assurance.
n.4: Designing products is a development activity, not assurance.

Governance Arrangements.q: A newly appointed project manager wants to understand exactly what the assurance activities on their project will examine. Which of the following best describes the scope of assurance activities in project management?
o: Reviewing processes, deliverables, and governance to ensure compliance
Tracking the performance of marketing campaigns
Negotiating contracts with the project's suppliers
Managing the schedules of team members
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance covers process, deliverable, and governance reviews to confirm compliance with standards.

n.1: Marketing tracking is outside assurance’s remit.
n.2: Contract negotiation is a procurement function.
n.3: Schedule management is part of planning and control, not assurance.
n.4: UI design is a development activity, not assurance.

Governance Arrangements.q: Why is objectivity important in assurance activities?
o: To provide unbiased assessments of project processes
Governance Arrangements.w: Objectivity ensures assurance findings are impartial, credible, and trusted by stakeholders.

n.0: Approval speed depends on many factors beyond objectivity.
n.1: Cost reduction is an outcome of control, not objectivity itself.
n.2: Morale may be affected indirectly, but it’s not the primary reason for objectivity.
n.3: No assurance activity can guarantee success.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager assigns an independent team to perform a process audit after identifying quality concerns with deliverables. Which strategic aim does this assurance activity support?
Governance Arrangements.w: Independent audits reassure stakeholders that quality issues are being addressed objectively.

n.0: Assurance audits don’t inherently reduce project scope.
n.2: Audits don’t aim to delay project timelines.
n.3: Workload may change, but the primary aim is confidence, not increased effort.
n.4: User involvement is managed separately, not minimised by assurance.

Governance Arrangements.q: During a mid-project audit, the assurance team discovers that documentation lacks traceability. What should be the next priority for assurance activities?
Governance Arrangements.w: Strengthening documentation control restores traceability and ensures future compliance can be verified.

n.0: Outsourcing may help, but first internal controls should be enhanced.
n.1: More meetings do not directly fix traceability issues.
n.3: Freezing change requests doesn’t address documentation gaps.
n.4: Reducing audits would risk further non-compliance going undetected.

Governance Arrangements.q: A quality assurance team carries out compliance checks on deliverables supplied by an external vendor. Which aspect of assurance does this activity best illustrate?
Governance Arrangements.w: Checking vendor deliverables for compliance exemplifies external verification of standards adherence.

n.0: Team morale is a human resources concern.
n.1: Budget forecasting is a financial activity, not assurance.
n.2: Negotiation is handled by procurement, not assurance.
n.3: Compression refers to schedule adjustments, not verification.

Governance Arrangements.q: In an assurance review, auditors find that risk documentation is outdated. Updating the risk register primarily supports which strategic aim?
Governance Arrangements.w: Current risk information is essential for leaders to make informed decisions about mitigation and planning.

n.0: Assurance values appropriate documentation, not its minimisation.
n.2: Timeline extension is not an assurance objective.
n.3: Product release timing is not the main aim of assurance updates.
n.4: Social events are unrelated to risk documentation.

Governance Arrangements.q: Which two perspectives are balanced by assurance activities?
o: Stakeholder engagement and maximisation of benefits
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance gives stakeholders confidence that the project is being managed properly: it verifies compliance with governance, standards and plans, and feeds its findings back to improve delivery.

n.0: Allocating resources and developing the team are management activities, not assurance perspectives.
n.1: Engagement and benefits are managed by the project and sponsor; assurance may review them, but balancing them is not its purpose.
n.3: Assurance should be independent of the delivery team, so it does not carry out day-to-day delivery or task management.
n.4: Cost reduction and speed are delivery aims; assurance checks that the project is on track, not that it is cheap or fast.

Governance Arrangements.q: Which two strategic aims are typical for assurance activities?
o: Providing independent evaluation and supporting continuous improvement
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance offers impartial assessment and drives ongoing enhancements in processes and quality.

n.0: Bureaucracy and slowdowns are undesirable, not strategic assurance aims.
n.2: Stakeholder elimination contradicts governance principles.
n.3: Profit maximisation is a business aim, not assurance.
n.4: Communication restrictions undermine transparency.

Governance Arrangements.q: Which two methods are commonly employed in assurance activities?
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance gives stakeholders confidence that the project is being managed properly and will meet its objectives. Audits and compliance reviews (with health checks and gateway reviews) are typical, ideally independent, assurance methods.

n.0: Stakeholder mapping and communication planning are delivery activities in stakeholder management, not assurance.
n.1: Gathering requirements and designing the solution are delivery work that assurance may review, not assurance methods themselves.
n.2: Levelling and schedule optimisation are planning techniques used by the delivery team.
n.3: Progress reporting and variance analysis are the project manager's monitoring and control activities; assurance independently checks them rather than producing them.

Governance Arrangements.q: Your project is preparing for a governance review, and the assurance team is asked to cover both product quality and process compliance. Which two focus areas should the assurance checklist include?
o: Product deliverable inspections and process conformity checks
Earned value cost variances and updated schedule forecasts
Team performance appraisals and individual training records
Supplier selection criteria and contract award decisions
Benefits tracking reports and stakeholder satisfaction surveys
Governance Arrangements.w: The brief covers product quality (are the deliverables right?) and process compliance (are the agreed processes being followed?), so the checklist needs deliverable inspections and process conformity checks.

n.1: Cost and schedule performance data shows progress against the baseline, not whether products and processes conform.
n.2: Appraisals and training records are HR and line-management matters; they do not test product quality or process compliance.
n.3: Supplier selection and award decisions belong to procurement; they are not the focus areas the review was asked to cover.
n.4: Benefits tracking and satisfaction surveys concern outcomes and stakeholders, not the quality of deliverables or process conformity.

Governance Arrangements.q: During a review of a safety-critical system, stakeholders request updates on both compliance and risk reduction. Which two reporting elements should assurance provide?
o: Stakeholder engagement levels and the communication log
Resource utilisation figures and team velocity metrics
Software version history and the latest release notes
Budget burn rate and the current cost performance index
Compliance status summary and risk mitigation progress
Governance Arrangements.w: Stakeholders asked about compliance and risk reduction, so assurance should report compliance status and how far risk responses have reduced exposure.

n.0: Engagement levels and a communication log track stakeholder management, not compliance or risk.
n.1: Utilisation and velocity describe team productivity, not compliance or risk reduction.
n.2: Version history and release notes are configuration information, not evidence of compliance or reduced risk.
n.3: Burn rate and CPI report cost performance, which is not what the stakeholders requested.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project board requests assurance outputs that address both financial control and regulatory adherence. Which two assurance activities would meet these requirements?
o: Financial audit and regulatory compliance review
Schedule health check and critical path review
Stakeholder survey and communication plan review
Skills audit and team performance review
Governance Arrangements.w: Financial control is assured by a financial audit and regulatory adherence by a regulatory compliance review, so this pair addresses both requirements.

n.0: Benefits reviews and lessons-learned workshops look at benefits and learning, not financial or regulatory compliance.
n.2: Schedule reviews give confidence about time, not money or regulatory adherence.
n.3: Surveys and communication reviews concern stakeholder engagement, not financial control or compliance.
n.4: A skills audit and performance review assess people capability, not financial control or regulation.

Governance Arrangements.q: Assurance provides ____ by evaluating adherence to defined processes.
Governance Arrangements.w: By verifying process compliance, assurance instills confidence in project integrity.

n.1: Assurance reduces risk exposure but does not provide ‘risk’.
n.2: Delays are a risk, not a benefit of assurance.
n.3: Ambiguity is reduced by assurance, not provided.
n.4: Complexity is a challenge, not an output of assurance.

Governance Arrangements.q: Assurance activities often involve independent ____ to maintain objectivity.
Governance Arrangements.w: Independent reviews ensure impartial evaluation of project adherence to standards.

n.0: Designs are deliverables, not assurance activities.
n.2: Regular meetings occur, but ‘independent reviews’ is the key term.
n.3: Budgets are financial documents, not assurance methods.
n.4: Contracts are agreements, not assurance techniques.

Governance Arrangements.q: When drafting an assurance plan at the start of a project, the project manager sets out what will be examined and how often. An assurance plan should define the ______ and frequency of reviews.
Governance Arrangements.w: Defining the scope clarifies exactly what will be reviewed and how often.

n.0: Location is logistical detail, not the review’s scope.
n.1: Budget details belong in cost management plans.
n.2: Resources are allocated but scope defines review content.
n.4: Duration is part of scheduling, not scope definition.

Governance Arrangements.q: During a review meeting, the team notes that several deliverables do not align with the agreed standards. Assurance activities on the project aim to ensure ______.
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance checks that deliverables meet defined quality standards.

n.0: Cost is monitored under financial control, not primary assurance focus here.
n.2: Risk management addresses potential issues, not deliverable quality.
n.3: Time relates to schedule control, not directly to this alignment.
n.4: Scope control manages requirements, not quality alignment specifically.

Governance Arrangements.q: After an audit identifies deviations from the project's defined ways of working, the assurance reviews focus on uncovering ______ in the project's processes.
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance seeks to identify gaps where practices diverge from standards.

n.0: Synergy relates to team collaboration, not deviations.
n.2: Events are occurrences, not the core finding in audits.
n.3: Feedback is collected but not the primary focus of deviation analysis.
n.4: Profits are financial outcomes, not process deviations.

Governance Arrangements.q: When auditors discover that the project's risk logs are incomplete, the assurance mandate includes validating the ______ of such records throughout the project.
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance verifies that all required risk information is complete and up to date.

n.0: Efficiency is a performance metric, not directly completeness.
n.1: Popularity is irrelevant to risk documentation.
n.2: Creativity is not an assurance criterion.
n.4: Redundancy refers to duplication, not thoroughness.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager is clarifying the boundaries of the assurance function with the delivery team. Which of the following is NOT typically within the scope of assurance activities?
Governance Arrangements.w: Approving designs is a governance or technical activity, not assurance’s verification role.

n.0: Quality assessment is part of assurance checks.
n.1: Assurance directly verifies standards compliance.
n.2: Auditing processes is a core assurance task.
n.3: Governance reviews fall under assurance scope.

Governance Arrangements.q: Which is NOT a benefit of assurance activities?
o: Guaranteeing project success regardless of risks
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance cannot guarantee success, but it helps manage risks and quality.

n.0: Process quality is improved through assurance feedback.
n.1: Corrective actions are initiated based on assurance findings.
n.3: Early issue identification is a key assurance benefit.
n.4: Stakeholders gain confidence from objective reviews.

Governance Arrangements.q: Which activity is outside the remit of assurance?
o: Performing root cause analysis for test failures
Governance Arrangements.w: Budget development is a planning activity, not part of assurance verification.

n.0: Checking process compliance is at the heart of assurance.
n.2: Governance reviews are a core assurance function.
n.3: Recording audit findings is central to assurance reporting.
n.4: Root cause analysis informs assurance on non-conformities.

Governance Arrangements.q: During a stage boundary review, a project board member argues that because an independent assurance function is in place, the project's success is effectively guaranteed. As the project manager, you want to correct this misunderstanding of what assurance can and cannot do. Which statement is NOT correct about assurance activities?
o: They identify areas for potential improvement
They support the project's compliance objectives
They evaluate adherence to defined processes
They provide evidence to support decision making
They replace the need for project management oversight
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance complements but does not replace overall project management oversight.

n.0: Finding improvement areas is a key assurance benefit.
n.1: Ensuring compliance is a primary objective of assurance.
n.2: Evaluating adherence is a fundamental assurance task.
n.3: Evidence provision aids informed decisions.

Governance Arrangements.q: During a compliance review, a team suggests assurance can eliminate all risks. Which of the following is NOT a realistic objective of assurance?
Governance Arrangements.w: No assurance process can remove every risk; it helps identify and mitigate them.

n.1: Confidence building is a core benefit.
n.2: Strengthening governance is a strategic assurance aim.
n.3: Corrective recommendations arise from assurance reviews.
n.4: Finding deviations from standards is a realistic goal.

Governance Arrangements.q: In a scenario where a sponsor expects assurance to replace all governance processes, which expectation is NOT aligned with the purpose of assurance activities?
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance supplements governance; it does not replace governance frameworks themselves.

n.0: Transparency is enhanced by assurance activities.
n.1: Independent evaluation is a core assurance role.
n.3: Driving improvement aligns with assurance aims.
n.4: Compliance verification is fundamental.

Governance Arrangements.q: A delivery team proposes three options to recover schedule slippage. The project board chooses the cheapest option without considering risk or benefit impact. What has most clearly failed?
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance decisions should consider balanced criteria, not cost alone.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager escalates a supplier dispute to the sponsor because it threatens delivery tolerances. The sponsor criticises the escalation as unnecessary detail. What is the best assessment?
o: The sponsor is correct because supplier issues are never governance matters
The team should resolve all supplier issues without escalation
The project manager acted appropriately because tolerances were threatened
The dispute should only be reported after project closure
Escalation should be avoided unless costs have already been incurred
Governance Arrangements.w: Issues threatening tolerances should be escalated so governance roles can make or support required decisions.

Governance Arrangements.q: A governance group approves a project but does not define decision rights, tolerance limits or escalation thresholds. What is the most likely consequence?
o: The project will need less reporting
The project manager will have clearer autonomy
Decisions will become inconsistent and accountability unclear
The project board will be unnecessary
Governance Arrangements.w: Without decision rights and escalation thresholds, governance becomes inconsistent and accountability weakens.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project governance board requests assurance reports from an independent reviewer. What is the main purpose of this oversight activity?
o: To take over the project manager's delivery responsibilities
To approve each operational decision made during delivery
To provide confidence that the project is controlled and aligned
To transfer accountability from the sponsor to the reviewer
To remove the need for any further stakeholder consultation
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance gives governance bodies confidence that delivery, risks and controls remain appropriate.

Governance Arrangements.q: On a business-change project, the individual who represents the end users has been left out of governance decisions that set the priorities for accepting deliverables. The project manager is concerned about the consequences of this omission. What is the most likely risk that results?
o: The project manager will lose all delivery authority
The governance board will become too large
Decisions may not reflect user needs or acceptance criteria
The escalation process will become unnecessary
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance decisions need appropriate representation so user needs and acceptance priorities are considered.

Governance Arrangements.q: A sponsor wants to assure herself that the governance board is genuinely providing oversight rather than merely receiving reports. She is looking for the signs that oversight is working effectively across the project. Which TWO features indicate effective project governance oversight?
o: Avoiding escalation to preserve delivery speed
Delegating sponsor accountability to the project team
Regular review of alignment with business objectives
Approval of every minor team-level decision
Monitoring whether tolerances remain under control
Governance Arrangements.w: Effective oversight checks strategic alignment and whether the project remains within agreed controls.

Governance Arrangements.q: A newly appointed project manager is clarifying with the sponsor when matters should be raised to the governance board rather than handled within the team. He wants to recognise the circumstances that ought to prompt escalation. Which TWO situations should normally trigger escalation within project governance?
o: A routine task completed by the team
A planned meeting taking place as scheduled
A forecast breach of agreed tolerance
A decision needed beyond the project manager's delegated authority
A minor update to a team checklist
Governance Arrangements.w: Escalation is appropriate when tolerances are threatened or decisions exceed delegated authority.

Governance Arrangements.q: A newly formed governance board wants its decision-making to be consistent and defensible, so that similar requests are handled the same way each time rather than case by case. The sponsor asks what the framework must set out. Which TWO elements should a governance decision framework normally clarify?
o: Authority required for different decision types
Technical method to be used for each work package
Named owners for each risk in the risk register
Governance Arrangements.w: A decision framework makes decisions consistent and defensible by setting out the criteria used to compare options and the level of authority needed for each type of decision, so similar requests are judged the same way and taken at the right level.

n.1: Team membership is set out in the organisation structure and resource plans; it does not tell the board how to make or authorise decisions.
n.2: Technical methods are a delivery matter for the team and specialists, not something a governance decision framework prescribes.
n.3: Risk owners are recorded in the risk register as part of risk management; they do not define how the board compares options or who may decide.

Governance Arrangements.q: An assurance reviewer has found that a portfolio's governance oversight is applied only intermittently and superficially. She is preparing to explain to the sponsor the dangers this creates for projects running beneath it. Which TWO risks are created by weak governance oversight?
Governance Arrangements.w: Weak oversight can allow projects to drift and issues to surface too late.

Governance Arrangements.q: Following an incident where a serious problem was raised too late and to the wrong manager, a sponsor wants to make escalation more disciplined on future projects. She asks which measures would achieve this. Which TWO actions would strengthen escalation discipline in a project?
o: Encourage informal escalation to any senior manager
Clarify who has authority to approve exceptions
Define tolerance thresholds at the start
Remove the project manager from decision-making
Delay reporting until a problem is irreversible
Governance Arrangements.w: Clear tolerances and approval authority make escalation controlled and timely.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project is delivered on time and within budget, but the intended operational improvements are not realised and stakeholders are dissatisfied. Which judgement best reflects project success?
o: The project is partially successful because outputs were delivered
The project cannot be assessed without reviewing technical quality
The project is successful because it met time and cost constraints
The project is successful because governance objectives were met
The project is unsuccessful because benefits and stakeholder satisfaction were not achieved
Project Success & Benefits.w: Success is defined by benefits and stakeholder satisfaction, not just time, cost, and quality.

n.0: Outputs alone are insufficient to determine success.
n.1: The failure in benefits and satisfaction is already clear.
n.2: Time and cost alone do not define success.
n.3: Governance success does not equal project success.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project sponsor tells the team that the project will be judged a success purely on whether it is delivered within the approved budget, and sets no other measures of any kind. What is the most significant risk of defining success in this way?
o: The project life cycle may need to be redefined midway
The project may deliver outputs that fail to realise intended benefits
The governance structure may grow unnecessarily complex over time
The project manager may lose authority over key delivery decisions
The project team may neglect stakeholder engagement to protect the budget
Project Success & Benefits.w: Focusing only on cost risks ignoring whether the project delivers value or benefits.

n.0: Lifecycle choice is not the main issue.
n.2: Governance complexity is unrelated.
n.3: Authority is not directly affected.
n.4: Engagement may suffer, but the core issue is benefits.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project delivers a high-quality product, but stakeholders reject it because it does not meet their evolving needs. What does this demonstrate?
o: Success criteria must include stakeholder satisfaction and not just technical quality
Stakeholders should not be allowed to influence success measures
Technical quality is the single most important success criterion here
Projects should prevent any requirement changes once delivery begins
High technical quality inevitably guarantees full stakeholder acceptance
Project Success & Benefits.w: Stakeholder satisfaction is a key success criterion beyond technical quality.

n.1: Stakeholders are central to success.
n.2: Quality alone does not ensure success.
n.3: Change is often necessary.
n.4: Quality does not guarantee acceptance.

Project Success & Benefits.q: At the initiation stage of a new project, the project manager is establishing how success will ultimately be judged once the work is complete, and wants to set criteria that reflect a mature view of success. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Focus on outputs rather than outcomes to simplify measurement
Define success only in terms of time, cost, and quality
Include benefits, stakeholder satisfaction, and alignment with objectives
Avoid defining success criteria until delivery is complete
Use only financial measures to ensure objectivity
Project Success & Benefits.w: Comprehensive success criteria include benefits, satisfaction, and alignment.

n.0: Outcomes are critical to success.
n.1: Triple constraint is insufficient alone.
n.3: Success must be defined early.
n.4: Financial measures alone are insufficient.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A completed project is being evaluated against the success criteria agreed at the outset, and the review panel is specifically looking for evidence of a genuine gap between what was intended and what was achieved. Which scenario best illustrates a mismatch between defined success criteria and actual project outcomes?
o: A project consumes more resources than were initially planned
A project requires several additional governance reviews before approval
A project meets its schedule but slightly overspends its budget
A project experiences repeated stakeholder conflict throughout its delivery
A project delivers outputs that do not achieve intended organisational benefits
Project Success & Benefits.w: Success requires benefits, not just outputs.

n.0: Resource use is not the main issue.
n.1: Governance reviews do not define success.
n.2: This relates to constraints, not success mismatch.
n.3: Conflict does not necessarily mean failure.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A long-running project is still consuming resources even though the business need it was set up to address has since changed, and it no longer supports the organisation's objectives. What does this situation indicate about its success criteria?
o: They were not communicated to the project team
They were not aligned with organisational strategy
They are overly focused on stakeholder satisfaction
They were based only on quality measures
They were too detailed to be useful
Project Success & Benefits.w: Success criteria must align with evolving organisational strategy.

n.0: Communication is not the primary issue.
n.2: Stakeholder focus is not the issue.
n.3: Quality focus is not the issue.
n.4: Detail is not the main problem.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project management trainer asks a group of delegates to move beyond a narrow, constraint-focused view and describe what genuinely characterises project success in practice. Which statement best reflects a mature understanding of project success?
o: Success is achieved when outputs are delivered as planned
Success is determined by the project manager’s performance
Success depends on delivering benefits and satisfying stakeholders
Success is achieved when risks are minimised
Success is defined by meeting time, cost, and quality targets
Project Success & Benefits.w: Success is broader than constraints and focuses on value and satisfaction.

n.0: Outputs alone are insufficient.
n.1: Success is not based solely on the project manager.
n.3: Risk management alone does not define success.
n.4: Triple constraint is incomplete.

Project Success & Benefits.q: After delivery, senior management regard a project as a clear success, while the end users who now have to work with its outputs consider it a failure. What does this difference in judgement most strongly suggest?
o: Success criteria were not consistently defined across stakeholders
The chosen project life cycle was fundamentally inappropriate
The project delivered outputs of poor technical quality
The governance structures overseeing the project were ineffective
The project significantly exceeded its approved budget
Project Success & Benefits.w: Different stakeholder perspectives indicate unclear or inconsistent success criteria.

n.1: Lifecycle is not the issue.
n.2: Quality is not necessarily the issue.
n.3: Governance is not the main issue.
n.4: Budget is not mentioned.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project meets all agreed constraints but is terminated early due to lack of expected benefits. What is the most accurate conclusion?
o: The project should have continued to recover costs
The project should not have defined benefits initially
The project was successful because constraints were met
The project failed because benefits were not realised
The project manager did not control scope effectively
Project Success & Benefits.w: Benefits realisation is central to success.

n.0: Continuing may worsen losses.
n.1: Benefits must always be defined.
n.2: Constraints alone do not define success.
n.4: Scope is not the issue.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is drafting the success criteria for a new initiative and wants to ensure the measures capture more than simply delivering the work on time. Which TWO factors should be included when defining project success criteria?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Benefits and stakeholder satisfaction are key success measures.

n.0: Governance avoidance is not relevant.
n.3: Time alone is insufficient.
n.4: Workload is not a success criterion.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which TWO scenarios indicate poor definition of success criteria?
o: Success includes measurable benefits and outcomes
Success criteria are agreed at project initiation
Different stakeholders have conflicting views of success
Success is defined only as delivering on time
Project Success & Benefits.w: Narrow definitions and conflicting views indicate poor criteria.

n.0: This is good practice.
n.1: Defining early is correct.
n.2: Stakeholder satisfaction is appropriate.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project's success is defined exclusively in terms of meeting its time, cost and quality targets, with no wider measures agreed by the sponsor or stakeholders. Which TWO consequences are most likely to result from framing success in this way?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Focusing only on constraints risks missing benefits and value.

n.0: Alignment may be lost.
n.2: Satisfaction may decrease.
n.4: Engagement is still required.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is explaining to stakeholders the difference between judging success on the deliverables produced and judging it on the lasting value those deliverables create once in use. Which TWO elements distinguish outcomes-based success criteria from output-based criteria?
o: Focus on value realised after delivery
Project Success & Benefits.w: Outcomes-based criteria focus on value and benefits.

n.0: Resource tracking is not outcome-based.
n.1: This relates to outputs.
n.3: Schedule is not outcome-focused.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project continues despite clear evidence that costs now outweigh expected benefits. What is the most fundamental failure of the business case?
o: It has not been updated to reflect current viability
It was not approved by the project manager
It does not include stakeholder communication plans
It was not created at project initiation
Project Success & Benefits.w: The business case must be maintained to reflect ongoing viability; failure to update undermines justification.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A sponsor approves a project primarily because it aligns with strategic goals, despite uncertain financial returns. What aspect of the business case is being prioritised?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Business cases consider strategic alignment alongside financial metrics.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A proposed transformation project offers substantial benefits but carries extremely high delivery risk, and the board is deciding whether to authorise it. What should the business case primarily assess before proceeding?
o: Whether the risks can be transferred entirely to the suppliers
Whether the project remains viable when risk is considered
Whether the delivery schedule can be shortened to reduce exposure
Whether the delivery team has enough available specialist capacity
Whether all stakeholders are fully satisfied with the approach
Project Success & Benefits.w: Viability requires balancing benefits, costs and risks, not considering them in isolation.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Under intense pressure to hit deadlines, a project manager concentrates solely on producing the agreed outputs and rarely refers back to the business case. What is the primary risk of working this way?
o: Loss of alignment with business value
Project Success & Benefits.w: Ignoring the business case risks delivering outputs that do not provide value.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project is technically feasible and within budget but no longer supports organisational priorities. What should the business case drive?
o: Delegation of decision to the project team
Reassessment of justification and possible termination
Project Success & Benefits.w: Business cases ensure continued justification aligned with organisational priorities.

Project Success & Benefits.q: During an approval review, a board member notes that the submitted business case sets out the costs in considerable depth but says very little about the benefits the project would deliver. What is the main weakness?
o: It focuses too heavily on delivery planning
It fails to demonstrate value and justification
Project Success & Benefits.w: A business case must demonstrate value through benefits, not just costs.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project is authorised largely because several comparable initiatives delivered well in previous years, with little fresh analysis of the current situation. What is the governance concern regarding the business case?
o: It omits a detailed stakeholder communication and engagement plan
It relies on assumptions rather than current justification
It overstates the available technical capability of the team
It disregards the resource and capacity constraints on delivery
It prioritises operational delivery over strategic project outcomes
Project Success & Benefits.w: Business cases must be based on current context, not past assumptions alone.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A governance board meets at a defined review point to consider whether a piece of work is still worth pursuing before releasing further funding. Which scenario best demonstrates the purpose of a business case in decision making?
o: Determining whether the project should start or continue
Selecting the best technical solution for delivery
Project Success & Benefits.w: The business case supports key decisions on whether to initiate or continue a project.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project continues because significant investment has already been made, despite poor future outlook. What bias is affecting the business case?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Sunk cost bias leads to continuation despite lack of future justification.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A long-running programme prepared a thorough business case at the outset but has not looked at it again, even as market conditions and priorities have shifted considerably. What is the main governance risk?
o: It creates unnecessary duplication of the project documentation
It weakens ongoing stakeholder engagement across the project
It may fail to reflect changing viability and context
It increases the technical complexity of the delivery work
It slows down day-to-day project delivery decisions
Project Success & Benefits.w: Business cases must be reviewed to ensure ongoing justification.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A completed project handed over all of its agreed outputs on time, yet a year later the organisation finds the expected benefits never materialised. What does this indicate about the business case?
o: It focused on delivery rather than value realisation
It underestimated the technical complexity of the outputs
It depended too heavily on early stakeholder engagement
It lacked accuracy in the delivery schedule estimates
It contained an excessive level of financial detail
Project Success & Benefits.w: A strong business case must ensure outputs translate into benefits.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is drafting a business case and must include the core information the board will need to judge whether the work is genuinely worthwhile. Which TWO elements are essential to justify a project in a business case?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Justification requires understanding benefits and costs.

Project Success & Benefits.q: When appraising whether a proposed project should go ahead, the governance board wants to understand what genuinely determines whether it is worth pursuing. Which TWO factors determine project viability within a business case?
o: Balance of cost, benefit and risk
Project Success & Benefits.w: Viability considers cost-benefit balance and feasibility.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Midway through delivery, a project manager is deciding when the business case genuinely needs re-examining rather than being left unchanged. Which TWO situations should trigger a review of the business case?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Changes in benefits or risk affect justification and require review.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Throughout a project's life, responsibility for keeping the business case current and credible needs to sit clearly with the right people. Which TWO roles are most involved in maintaining the business case?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Sponsor owns justification, project manager supports with delivery data.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which TWO outcomes indicate a strong business case?
o: Demonstrated value exceeding cost and risk
Project Success & Benefits.w: Strong business cases show alignment and value.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A submitted business case sets out impressive expected benefits but leaves the delivery costs unquantified, and the board must now decide whether to proceed. What is the most significant weakness in this business case?
o: It removes the need for governance reviews
It limits the ability to assign project roles
It prevents accurate assessment of overall viability
Project Success & Benefits.w: Without cost information, the balance between cost and benefit cannot be assessed, undermining viability.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project delivers strong financial benefits but has an extended timescale that delays value realisation significantly. What is the key concern within the business case?
o: The governance structure is too complex
The delivery team is too small
The timing of benefits may reduce overall value
Project Success & Benefits.w: Timescale affects when benefits are realised, which impacts overall value and viability.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A quick and inexpensive project is proposed to the board, but the benefits it would actually deliver to the organisation are very small. What does this indicate about the business case?
o: The project is automatically viable due to low cost
The project lacks sufficient justification despite efficiency
The project should proceed due to reduced risk
The project requires no further analysis
The project is strategically aligned by default
Project Success & Benefits.w: Low cost alone does not justify a project if benefits are insufficient.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A business case sets out the expected benefits and costs in careful detail, but makes no mention of the risks involved in delivering the work. What is the most likely consequence?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Ignoring risk can lead to unrealistic expectations of viability.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project offers moderate benefits but requires a long timescale with increasing uncertainty. What should the business case primarily assess?
o: Whether the extended timescale increases risk beyond acceptable levels
Whether the suppliers can compress the overall delivery timescale
Whether the stakeholder communication plan covers the full timescale
Whether the project manager has enough delivery experience
Whether team members can be reassigned to other projects
Project Success & Benefits.w: Longer timescales often increase uncertainty and risk, affecting viability.

Project Success & Benefits.q: While reviewing the standard components of a business case, a board member wants to identify which one exists specifically to capture the things that might go wrong. Which component of a business case is most directly concerned with uncertainty and potential negative impacts?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Risk captures uncertainty and potential threats or opportunities.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project promising strong long-term benefits will require a large investment before any return is seen, and the board is weighing whether to commit the funds. What must the business case demonstrate?
o: That the project has minimal risk
That the team can deliver quickly
That the benefits outweigh the costs over time
Project Success & Benefits.w: Viability requires demonstrating that benefits justify the costs.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project is low risk and low cost but delivers limited benefit over a long timescale. What is the most likely conclusion?
o: The project may not be justified due to limited value
The project should proceed because its overall cost is low
The project should be prioritised ahead of higher-value work
The project can proceed with only minimal governance oversight
The project is clearly viable because its risk is low
Project Success & Benefits.w: Limited benefits may not justify even low-cost, low-risk projects.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A reviewer is assessing several submitted business cases in order to identify one that is poorly balanced across its key components. Which scenario best demonstrates an imbalance in business case components?
o: Costs, benefits and risks are all clearly defined and balanced
Benefits align with strategy, and costs and risks are proportionate
Costs are high, benefits are unclear, and risks are not assessed
Benefits exceed costs, and the identified risks are fully assessed
Timescales are realistic, costs justified, and benefits clearly stated
Project Success & Benefits.w: Unclear benefits and missing risk assessment create imbalance and weak justification.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A proposed solution would deliver benefits soon after go-live but would then carry noticeably higher operational costs for years afterwards. What should the business case take into account?
o: Only the immediate cost of initial project delivery
The overall complexity of the detailed project plan
The total number of stakeholders involved in delivery
The frequency of progress reporting to the sponsor
The balance between short-term benefits and long-term costs
Project Success & Benefits.w: Business cases must consider both short-term and long-term cost-benefit relationships.

Project Success & Benefits.q: The governance board is presented with a project offering high potential benefits but also carrying a high level of risk to delivery. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this proposal?
o: The project can proceed without any formal governance oversight
The project may be viable if risks are understood and managed
The project is certain to succeed given its high benefits
The project should be rejected automatically because the risk is high
The project manager alone should decide whether to proceed
Project Success & Benefits.w: High benefit projects can be viable if risks are acceptable and managed.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is deciding which information the board most needs in order to judge whether a proposed project is genuinely viable. Which TWO components are essential for assessing project viability in a business case?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Cost and benefit are fundamental to viability assessment.

Project Success & Benefits.q: During appraisal of a proposed project, stakeholders want to understand when the value it promises is likely to be realised. Which TWO factors influence the timing of value delivery in a business case?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Timescale and benefit timing determine when value is realised.

Project Success & Benefits.q: When building a robust business case, a project manager must ensure that the two most fundamental elements are properly weighed against each other. Which TWO elements must be balanced to ensure a strong business case?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Balancing cost and benefit is central to justification.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A quality reviewer is examining a submitted business case for signs that risk has been handled poorly during its preparation. Which TWO scenarios indicate poor consideration of risk in a business case?

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project delivers all outputs successfully, but no mechanism exists to track whether expected benefits are realised. What is the primary failure?

Project Success & Benefits.w: Benefits must be tracked and managed beyond delivery; otherwise value cannot be confirmed.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project's business case lists an important benefit, but no individual has been made responsible for delivering or tracking it once the work completes. What is the most likely outcome?

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project clearly sets out the benefits it intends to deliver, but it never defines how each of those benefits will actually be measured. What is the key issue this creates?
o: The project will exceed its budget
The benefits may not be aligned with strategy
The benefits cannot be verified or tracked effectively
The team will not understand their roles
Project Success & Benefits.w: Measurement criteria are essential to confirm whether benefits have been achieved.

Project Success & Benefits.q: After a project has formally closed and been handed over to the business, the project manager decides to take on ongoing responsibility for realising its benefits. What is the main concern with this?

The team will not deliver outputs
The project will require less governance

Assigning all benefits to the project manager
Defining measurable indicators and monitoring them over time
