Escalate all issues rather than resolving them locally
Reduce stakeholder interaction to maintain focus
Project Success & Benefits.w: Continuous improvement requires ongoing evaluation and adaptation rather than waiting until the end.

n.1: End-only reviews miss opportunities to improve during delivery.
n.2: Rigid adherence prevents improvement.
n.3: Escalation alone does not drive improvement.
n.4: Reduced interaction limits feedback.

Project Success & Benefits.q: During delivery of a software project, the team runs regular retrospectives and gathers stakeholder feedback, yet the same problems keep recurring because nothing changes as a result. From a continuous improvement perspective, what is the MOST significant issue here?
o: Feedback is not being converted into actionable improvements
The project schedule is too rigid
The team lacks sufficient governance controls
The project manager is over-communicating with stakeholders
Stakeholders are providing too much feedback
Project Success & Benefits.w: Continuous improvement requires both feedback and action; without action, feedback has no value.

n.1: Schedule rigidity is not the main problem.
n.2: Governance is not the primary issue.
n.3: Communication is not the root issue.
n.4: The issue is not quantity but lack of action.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A programme manager wants to see feedback loops working well across the projects she oversees. Considering how information should flow while work is still under way, which scenario BEST demonstrates the effective use of feedback loops in a project?
o: Feedback is collected at the end of the project for documentation purposes
Stakeholder input is gathered and used to refine outputs during delivery
Feedback is used only to update project reports
The project team reviews performance only at major stage gates
Stakeholder feedback is filtered through a single individual
Project Success & Benefits.w: Effective feedback loops involve continuous input and adaptation during delivery.

n.0: End-only feedback limits improvement opportunities.
n.2: Reporting does not ensure improvement.
n.3: Infrequent reviews reduce responsiveness.
n.4: Filtering reduces insight.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager encourages small, incremental changes based on feedback rather than waiting for major redesigns. What is the MOST appropriate interpretation?
o: This approach increases risk due to frequent changes
This approach replaces formal governance processes
This approach supports continuous improvement through iterative adjustments
This approach reduces the need for stakeholder engagement
This approach is only suitable for linear projects
Project Success & Benefits.w: Continuous improvement often involves incremental adjustments based on feedback.

n.0: Incremental change can reduce risk.
n.1: Governance still applies.
n.3: Stakeholder engagement remains important.
n.4: It is suitable across different life cycles.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A newly appointed project manager is explaining to junior team members why the project establishes regular feedback loops with its users and sponsor throughout delivery. What is the PRIMARY purpose of a feedback loop in a project environment?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Feedback loops allow continuous refinement and improvement during delivery.

n.0: Documentation alone is insufficient.
n.1: Reporting remains necessary.
n.2: Compliance is not the main purpose.
n.3: Scope control is separate.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Over the course of a lengthy delivery, a project team notices its performance steadily improving because it reviews results at the end of each cycle and adapts its processes accordingly. What does this behaviour BEST demonstrate?
o: Strict adherence to initial planning assumptions
Continuous improvement driven by feedback and learning
Project Success & Benefits.w: Continuous improvement involves learning from experience and adapting processes.

n.0: Risks are managed, not eliminated.
n.1: Adaptation contradicts strict adherence.
n.2: Stakeholder input supports improvement.
n.4: Governance alone does not drive improvement.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is defining the ways of working for a new team and wants to build continuous improvement into everyday delivery rather than leaving it to chance. Which TWO of the following practices would MOST effectively support continuous improvement in the project?
o: Regularly reviewing performance and adapting processes
Fixing the project plan and avoiding changes
Deferring all improvements until project closure
Using feedback to refine outputs during delivery
Limiting stakeholder input to reduce complexity
Project Success & Benefits.w: Continuous improvement requires regular review and active use of feedback.

n.1: Avoiding changes prevents improvement.
n.2: Deferring improvements misses opportunities.
n.4: Limiting input reduces learning.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A sponsor is concerned that a project rarely gathers or acts on information about how delivery is going until issues have already escalated. If the project's feedback loops remain weak, which TWO of the following risks are MOST likely to result?
o: Increased rework due to late corrections
Project Success & Benefits.w: Weak feedback loops delay issue detection and increase rework.

n.1: Alignment typically worsens.
n.2: Satisfaction is likely to decrease.
n.4: Reviews remain necessary.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which TWO actions BEST demonstrate effective continuous improvement?
o: Applying lessons learned during the project
Ignoring minor issues to maintain progress
Making incremental changes based on feedback
Waiting until closure to implement improvements
Project Success & Benefits.w: Continuous improvement involves applying lessons and making adjustments during delivery.

n.1: Ignoring issues prevents improvement.
n.3: Avoiding change limits improvement.
n.4: Delayed action reduces effectiveness.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which TWO characteristics define an effective feedback loop?
o: Using feedback only for reporting purposes
Clear mechanisms for acting on feedback
Timely collection and use of feedback
Project Success & Benefits.w: Effective loops require timely input and action.

n.0: Reporting alone is insufficient.
n.2: No action means no improvement.
n.4: Limiting input reduces insight.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager discovers an unplanned scope increase midway through execution. What should they do first regarding the business case?
o: Reassign project resources to cover the extra work
Inform the sponsor immediately without any impact analysis
Revise the requirements document to add the scope
Review the business case against the original baseline
Update the project schedule to absorb the change
Project Success & Benefits.w: The first step is to compare the change against the original business case baseline to assess impact.

n.0: Reassigning resources is premature before impact analysis.
n.1: Informing without analysis skips the necessary assessment.
n.2: Revising requirements should follow a business case review.
n.4: Updating the schedule comes after assessing impact on the business case.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Partway through delivery, the project's actual expenditure starts to climb noticeably above the figures set out in the approved budget. To respond appropriately within project governance, what should the project team do?
o: Adjust only the schedule to recover the cost
Delay the scheduled stakeholder progress reviews
Revisit the business case to assess impact
Archive the original business case without any change
Raise the project's quality thresholds and standards
Project Success & Benefits.w: Cost overruns require a business case review to understand viability and options.

n.0: Adjusting the schedule alone doesn’t address budget issues.
n.1: Delaying reviews ignores critical information.
n.3: Archiving skips necessary updates.
n.4: Quality thresholds are unrelated to cost overruns.

Project Success & Benefits.q: During execution, tracking shows that the benefits the project is expected to deliver are now forecast to come in well below the estimates used to justify it. Faced with this shortfall against the original projections, what should the project sponsor do?
o: Approve additional funding without any supporting analysis
Conduct a business case review and update forecasts
Ignore the deviations and continue as planned
Reduce the project scope without consulting stakeholders
Cancel the project immediately without further review
Project Success & Benefits.w: Low benefit projections must be validated and forecasts updated via a business case review.

n.0: Funding without analysis bypasses good governance.
n.2: Ignoring deviations risks project failure.
n.3: Scope reduction requires impact assessment first.
n.4: Immediate cancellation is premature without review.

Project Success & Benefits.q: While a project is underway, an unexpected change in legislation significantly increases the cost of remaining compliant. As part of sound project governance, what is the appropriate next step for the project team to take?
o: Hold a stakeholder communication workshop only
Modify the project's quality metrics and thresholds
Review and update the business case assumptions
Redefine the project team roles and responsibilities
Proceed with the original plan unchanged
Project Success & Benefits.w: Regulatory changes require revisiting business case assumptions to reassess viability.

n.0: Workshops alone don’t update core assumptions.
n.1: Quality metrics don’t address compliance cost impacts.
n.3: Role definitions aren’t the primary concern.
n.4: Proceeding unchanged ignores new constraints.

Project Success & Benefits.q: During a routine risk workshop, the project team uncovers a significant new threat that had not featured anywhere in the original risk analysis or the approved business case. Having identified this previously unrecognised risk, what should the team do next?
o: Assess its impact on the business case
Assign the risk to the sponsor
Project Success & Benefits.w: New risks must be evaluated to see how they affect the business case baseline.

n.1: Ignoring risks postpones essential analysis.
n.2: Ownership assignment follows impact assessment.
n.3: Communication updates are secondary to impact assessment.
n.4: Cancelling risk registers is inappropriate.

Project Success & Benefits.q: At a monthly project review, the board notes that the delivery timeline has slipped noticeably from what was originally agreed. Before deciding on any corrective action, what should the board do first?
o: Immediately lower the project's quality standards
Change the project delivery methodology entirely
Expand the team to recover the schedule
Compare actual performance to the business case baseline
Shift the remaining deliverables to later dates
Project Success & Benefits.w: Comparing performance against the baseline shows if the slip threatens business case viability.

n.0: Quality standards adjustment doesn’t address baseline alignment.
n.1: Methodology changes require a full review first.
n.2: Team expansion is a solution, not an analysis step.
n.4: Shifting deliverables may hide underlying issues.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Midway through execution, an influential stakeholder asks the project manager to add several new features that were not part of the agreed scope. Before committing to anything, what should the project manager's immediate action be?
o: Notify the team without assessing impact
Update only the project's risk register
Evaluate the impact on the business case
Reject and lock the current requirements
Implement the requested changes straight away
Project Success & Benefits.w: Any change request must be assessed against the business case baseline before action.

n.0: Notification without analysis is insufficient.
n.1: Risks are relevant but secondary to baseline impact.
n.3: Locking requirements prevents proper change control.
n.4: Direct implementation skips governance.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Updated cost forecasts now indicate that the project is heading for a 15% overrun against its approved budget. In line with good practice, what must the project team do in response to this projected overspend?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Projected overruns require a business case reassessment to guide decisions.

n.0: Reducing testing may introduce quality risks.
n.1: Contract terminations aren’t the first step.
n.2: Deadline extensions need baseline analysis first.
n.4: Budget increases demand justification.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Three months into delivery, monitoring reveals that the benefits actually being realised are trailing well behind the levels set out in the plan. Given this growing gap between planned and actual benefits, what should the project sponsor do?
o: Shift baselining to the quality plan
Review and update the business case
Project Success & Benefits.w: Lagging benefits require a formal business case review and update.

n.0: Scope expansion may worsen issues.
n.1: Baselining quality plan doesn’t address business case.
n.2: Archiving skips corrective action.
n.3: Proceeding ignores critical benefit shortfalls.

Project Success & Benefits.q: An organisation's executive board meets each quarter to confirm that its portfolio of projects still represents a worthwhile investment and remains justified. When judging whether a given project is still viable, against what should the board compare its progress?
Project Success & Benefits.w: The business case baseline is the primary reference for viability assessments.

n.1: Communication plan guides messaging, not viability.
n.2: Stakeholder map identifies roles, not performance metrics.
n.3: Risk tolerance register tracks risk levels, not overall viability.
n.4: Quality plan addresses standards, not viability directly.

Project Success & Benefits.q: In a quarterly review, the project board aims to ensure strategic alignment and accurate forecasts. Which two objectives should this review achieve?
o: Rebaseline the schedule and update the quality plan
Validate benefits forecasts and confirm strategic alignment
Archive previous reports and start a new budget
Conduct team morale survey and adjust budget
Assess vendor performance and lock scope
Project Success & Benefits.w: Reviewing benefits forecasts and strategic fit are core to business case reviews.

n.0: Schedule and quality are important, but strategic/fiscal alignment takes priority.
n.2: Budget archiving/start is administrative, not a review objective.
n.3: Morale surveys are outside business case scope.
n.4: Vendor performance is secondary to business case validity.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Following a major approved change to a live project, the project manager must bring the business case up to date so it still reflects reality. Which TWO of the following actions are essential when carrying out this update?
o: Revise test scripts and reassign work packages
Update the RACI chart and team structure
Archive the original and close the change log
Lower benefit targets to match the new costs
Project Success & Benefits.w: The business case justifies the project by comparing benefits with costs and risks. After a major change, costs must be reforecast and the assumptions behind them recorded, so the justification can be re-tested against the new position.

n.0: Test scripts and work package assignments are delivery details held in the quality and schedule plans, not the business case.
n.1: The RACI chart and team structure belong to the project management plan and resource planning, not the business case.
n.3: The business case remains a live document, and the change log stays open to control future changes.
n.4: Benefit targets are not adjusted to make the case look viable; the case must honestly show whether benefits still justify the revised cost.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A business case review should ideally:
o: Re-baseline costs without checking the benefits
Identify deviations and recommend corrective action
Assume the original justification still holds
Confirm the project manager's individual performance
Focus only on whether the schedule is on track
Project Success & Benefits.w: A business case review checks whether the project is still justified, identifying deviations in costs, benefits, risks or the environment and recommending action (continue, re-plan or close).

n.0: Changing costs without re-checking benefits ignores whether the project still makes sense.
n.2: The purpose of a review is to test whether the justification still holds, not to assume it.
n.3: The review assesses the project's justification, not an individual's performance.
n.4: Schedule is one input; the review weighs benefits against costs and risks.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is explaining to a new sponsor why the business case should be revisited at regular intervals throughout the life cycle. Of the outcomes listed below, which one is NOT a genuine benefit of reviewing the business case regularly?
Project Success & Benefits.w: No review can eliminate all risks; it can only identify and manage them.

n.0: Informed decision-making relies on up-to-date business case data.
n.1: Forecast adjustments are a key output of reviews.
n.3: Regular reviews help keep the project aligned with its goals.
n.4: Early issue identification is a core benefit.

Project Success & Benefits.q: During a formal business case review meeting, the project team works through the agreed governance activities for keeping the case current and controlled. Which of the following actions should NOT be taken during such a review?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Baselines must not be changed without the proper approval process.

n.0: Cost estimate revisions are a primary review activity.
n.2: Expectations should be updated to reflect changes.
n.3: Documenting impacts is essential.
n.4: Benefit realisation assessment is crucial.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is chairing a scheduled business case review and wants to ensure the team follows sound governance throughout. Of the practices listed, which one should NOT take place during a business case review?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Ignoring new risks would leave the business case outdated and incomplete.

n.0: Validating assumptions ensures accuracy.
n.1: Reforecasting aligns expectations with reality.
n.2: Recording decisions provides an audit trail.
n.4: Comparisons identify variances.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project management office is drafting guidance on the circumstances that should prompt a formal review of the business case during delivery. Which of the following would NOT be a valid trigger for such a review?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Re-sequencing work within float does not change the end date, cost or benefits, so the justification is unaffected and it is managed within the project manager's tolerances.

n.0: New regulation can change assumptions, costs and risks.
n.2: Benefit shortfalls go to the heart of the justification.
n.3: Variances beyond tolerance affect viability.
n.4: Significant scope changes alter costs and benefits.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is reinforcing with the team the disciplines required to keep the business case baseline under proper control. Of the behaviours below, which one is NOT aligned with maintaining that baseline?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Undocumented changes break control over the baseline.

n.1: Deviation tracking is essential governance.
n.2: Sponsor approval ensures formal baseline updates.
n.3: Impact communication keeps stakeholders informed.
n.4: Documentation provides traceability.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is explaining to the team how the business case is used throughout delivery to judge whether the project is performing as intended. Complete the statement: the business case provides a ______ against which project performance is measured.
Project Success & Benefits.w: The business case baseline is the reference for measuring performance.

n.0: Stakeholder registers track people, not performance metrics.
n.1: Scope is one aspect of the case, not the measuring baseline.
n.2: Schedules are separate planning tools.
n.3: Budgets derive from the baseline but are not the case itself.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A sponsor asks the project manager why the business case must be reviewed periodically rather than simply approved once and filed away. Complete the statement: regular reviews help to ______ the assumptions underpinning the business case.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Validating assumptions ensures they remain accurate over time.

n.0: Disregarding assumptions undermines the review.
n.1: Duplicating assumptions adds no value.
n.2: Ignoring assumptions risks outdated analysis.
n.4: Finalising prematurely removes needed flexibility.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Partway through delivery, a stakeholder secures approval for a significant change to the project's scope. Explaining the governance consequence to the team, the project manager notes that a scope change of this kind must trigger a business case ______.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Scope changes always require a formal review of the business case.

n.0: Handover occurs during project closeout.
n.1: Closure happens at project end.
n.3: Cancellation is a possible outcome, not the trigger.
n.4: Archival is for completed documents.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is warning the team about the consequences of neglecting to assess the impact of emerging changes on the business case. Complete the statement: failing to review impacts can lead to ______ deviations going unnoticed.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Significant deviations threaten project success if not detected early.

n.0: Planned deviations are accounted for.
n.2: Minor deviations may also matter, but the focus is on significant ones.
n.3: Predictable deviations are usually anticipated.
n.4: Irrelevant deviations by definition don’t matter.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A sponsor wants assurance that variances from plan will be picked up promptly rather than surfacing too late to act on. Complete the statement: effective ______ of the business case ensures early detection of variances.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Monitoring the business case keeps track of performance against the baseline.

n.1: Delegation isn’t relevant to variance detection.
n.2: Closure happens at project end.
n.3: Documentation supports monitoring but isn’t the activity itself.
n.4: Planning is done upfront, not for variance detection.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Regular reviews support informed ______.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Up-to-date business case data underpins informed decision-making.

n.0: Reports communicate decisions, not support them.
n.1: Budgets are outputs, not the primary support.
n.3: Schedules are planning tools, not the main support.
n.4: Meetings are forums, not the direct output of reviews.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is explaining to a new team member what governance relies on when a project is first put forward for authorisation. Complete the statement: the business case is the primary ______ for project approval.
Project Success & Benefits.w: The business case document captures justification needed for approval.

n.0: Tool is generic; the business case is specifically the document.
n.1: Measurement is an activity, not the approval basis.
n.3: Issue is a problem, not the approval basis.
n.4: A form is a format, but the content is the document itself.

Project Success & Benefits.q: When a project team revisits the business case during a scheduled review, certain core components almost always need refreshing to reflect the latest position. Which TWO elements of the business case are typically updated during such a review?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Cost forecasts and benefit estimates must reflect the latest information.

n.0: Schedules and test cases belong to planning and execution artifacts.
n.2: Risk and communication plans are separate governance documents.
n.3: Office layout is unrelated to the business case.
n.4: Team charters and supplier lists aren’t core business case elements.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which two triggers necessitate a business case review?
o: Major scope changes and significant budget variances
Routine progress reports and team onboarding
Supplier invoice payments and timesheet approvals
Minor document revisions and meeting reschedules
Task re-sequencing within float and template updates
Project Success & Benefits.w: Significant changes in scope or cost alter the balance of benefits, costs and risks, so the business case must be re-assessed.

n.1: These are normal project activities that do not change the justification.
n.2: These are routine financial administration.
n.3: These are routine administrative changes.
n.4: Work moved within float does not affect cost, time or benefits; templates are administrative.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager finds that changing market conditions have materially altered the expected returns set out in the business case, and the revised justification needs formal sign-off before it can be adopted. Which pair of stakeholders is most likely responsible for approving the updated business case?
Project Success & Benefits.w: The sponsor and steering committee hold authority to approve major updates.

n.0: Procurement and development handle sourcing and build, not approvals.
n.1: End users and office managers aren’t governance bodies.
n.2: Day-to-day team members and auditors don’t formally approve business cases.
n.3: Test leads and communicators support the project but don’t approve the case.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Throughout delivery a project manager keeps the business case under formal configuration control so its agreed version stays the fixed point of comparison. When explaining the value of this discipline to the team, which pair of benefits best results from maintaining the business case baseline?
o: Delegated authority for the project manager to approve all changes
Guaranteed project success and the elimination of risk
A consistent reference for decisions and success measures
A fixed scope that no longer needs formal change control
Fewer decision gates and less frequent board reviews
Project Success & Benefits.w: A baselined business case is the fixed point against which changes and gate decisions are judged and against which success is measured.

n.0: Approval authority is set by delegation, not by having a baseline.
n.1: No baseline guarantees success or removes risk.
n.3: A baseline does not freeze scope; changes go through change control and are assessed against it.
n.4: Gates still re-check the business case; a baseline makes those reviews meaningful, not fewer.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Midway through a project the sponsor requests a structured review to confirm the business case remains viable. As the project manager prepares the session, which pair of activities would typically take place during a business case review?
o: Conduct user training and revise code style
Paint the office and rename files
Archive email threads and reorder desks
Assess assumption validity and update forecasts
Project Success & Benefits.w: Reviewing assumptions and updating forecasts are key review steps.

n.0: Training and code style are execution activities.
n.1: Office painting is not part of a business case review.
n.2: Archiving emails is administrative, not analytical.
n.3: Ignoring deviations contradicts the purpose of a review.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager completes a scheduled review of the business case at a stage boundary and must record for governance what the review has produced. Which pair of outputs would typically result from a regular business case review?
o: Additional meeting invites and office supplies
Revised business case and updated baseline
New test cases and code modules
Expired quality plans and archived schedules
Project Success & Benefits.w: A proper review yields a revised case and a formally updated baseline.

n.0: Invites and supplies are logistical, not review outputs.
n.2: Gossip is not an official output.
n.3: Technical artifacts aren’t outputs of a business case review.
n.4: Expired plans indicate neglect, not review outputs.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A newly appointed project manager asks why the business case is reviewed periodically rather than fixed once at approval. Considering the governance purpose of such reviews, which of the following is NOT a legitimate reason to review the business case?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Celebrations are not a governance activity for reviewing the business case.

n.0: Cost reforecasting is a core review activity.
n.1: Assumption evaluation is essential.
n.2: Identifying risks keeps the case current.
n.3: Benefit shortfalls must be assessed in a review.

Project Success & Benefits.q: While conducting a business case review, a project manager is careful to respect governance and configuration management rules. In line with good practice, which of the following actions should NOT occur during a business case review?
o: Documenting the assessed impact of changes
Engaging affected stakeholders in the review
Changing the baseline without proper approval
Project Success & Benefits.w: Baselines require formal approval before any changes are made.

n.0: Impact documentation is standard practice.
n.1: Benefit revisions ensure accuracy.
n.2: Cost updates reflect current information.
n.3: Stakeholder engagement is critical.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is drawing up the agenda for a business case review meeting with the sponsor and steering group. Checking the proposed items, which one is NOT typically part of a business case review meeting?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Walking through test scripts is a detailed quality control activity; a business case review looks at whether benefits still outweigh costs and risks.

n.1: Changes in risk affect the justification.
n.2: Benefit forecasts are central to the business case.
n.3: Cost variances affect viability.
n.4: Checking assumptions confirms the case is still valid.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager watches the environment for events that could undermine the project's continued justification and prompt a fresh look at the business case. Of the following, which would NOT typically trigger a business case review?
o: A critical quality failure in testing
Float used on a non-critical task
A major overrun against the budget
Project Success & Benefits.w: Using float on a non-critical task does not affect the end date, cost or benefits, so it does not threaten the project's justification.

n.0: A critical quality failure can change costs, timescales and benefits.
n.1: Significant scope creep changes costs and benefits.
n.2: New regulation can change assumptions, costs and risks.
n.4: A major overrun affects viability.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is shaping the delivery approach at the very start of a project that will hand a new solution over to an operations team. She wants the eventual handover built into her thinking from day one rather than treated as an afterthought. What is a key requirement for planning transition from the outset of a project?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Identifying transition requirements and stakeholders up front ensures the plan addresses all needs for a smooth handover.

n.0: Social events do not drive transition success.
n.1: Office layout is a logistical detail, not a transition driver.
n.2: Task automation is unrelated to transition planning.
n.3: Marketing materials are outside the core transition scope.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which activity supports business-as-usual throughout the project?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Regular check-ins with the operations team keep BAU processes visible and uninterrupted during the project.

n.0: Skipping BAU planning risks service disruption.
n.1: Budget focus alone doesn’t preserve daily operations.
n.3: External hires without handover disrupt BAU.
n.4: Removing support staff undermines operational continuity.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which best describes transition management?
o: Measuring and reporting the benefits realised after the project has closed
Coordinating the move of deliverables into the operational environment
Controlling changes to the agreed scope baseline through change control
Developing and testing new product features during the deployment phase
Managing the project budget, cost reporting and contingency drawdown
Project Success & Benefits.w: Transition management integrates the project's outputs into business as usual: preparing operations, handing over, and providing training and support, so that the benefits can then be realised.

n.0: Measuring realised benefits is benefits management, which continues after transition and often after the project has closed.
n.2: Controlling scope changes is change control, which runs throughout the project.
n.3: Developing and testing features is delivery work in deployment, before outputs are transitioned.
n.4: Budget, cost reporting and contingency are cost control, not the move of outputs into operations.

Project Success & Benefits.q: While a project introduces a major new customer system, the operational teams must keep serving existing customers without interruption throughout delivery. The project manager makes a point of accounting for these ongoing operational needs when planning. What is the purpose of considering business-as-usual during a project?
o: Reduces the need for project governance
Project Success & Benefits.w: Considering BAU ensures critical services remain stable and uninterrupted while the project runs.

n.1: BAU planning complements, not eliminates, change management.
n.2: Marketing reach is unrelated to operational stability.
n.3: Defect elimination cannot be guaranteed by BAU considerations.
n.4: BAU planning does not replace governance requirements.

Project Success & Benefits.q: As a project approaches completion, the project manager needs a single reference that sets out how the finished deliverables will be moved from the project into live operational use, with the tasks, roles and timing captured in one place. Which document outlines the strategy for moving deliverables into operations?
Project Success & Benefits.w: The transition plan details tasks, roles, and schedules needed for a smooth operational handover.

n.0: Communications plan focuses on stakeholder messaging, not full transition sequencing.
n.1: A risk register tracks threats, not the overall transition strategy.
n.2: Procurement strategy relates to buying goods/services.
n.4: A quality plan covers standards, not handover tasks.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Transition planning should begin at ______ of the project.
Project Success & Benefits.w: The initiation (outset) phase is when transition requirements should be identified and integrated into planning.

n.0: Monitoring phase focuses on control, not initial planning.
n.2: The closing phase is too late to influence handover design.
n.3: Execution phase is after key transition requirements should already be set.
n.4: Post-project is after the transition has occurred.

Project Success & Benefits.q: As a new solution is being introduced, the operations team must continue running core services so that customers experience no disruption while the change beds in. Complete the following statement about how this continuity is preserved. Maintaining ______ processes ensures continuity during transition.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Business-as-usual processes keep core operations stable as new changes are introduced.

n.0: Emergency processes are for incident response only.
n.1: Prototype processes are for testing, not daily operations.
n.2: Theoretical processes are not applied practice.
n.3: Ad hoc processes lack standardisation needed for BAU.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is drafting a thorough transition plan for handing a new service to operations. She has already set out how stakeholders will be engaged and how staff will be trained, and now wants everyone kept informed of timing and responsibilities. Complete the statement: a robust transition plan defines stakeholder engagement, training, and ______.
Project Success & Benefits.w: The stem describes keeping everyone informed of timing and responsibilities, which is the communication element of a transition plan, alongside stakeholder engagement and training.

n.0: Budgeting sets the cost of the transition and does not inform people of timing and roles.
n.1: Procurement obtains goods and services from suppliers and is unrelated to informing stakeholders.
n.3: Transition plans do transfer risks to BAU owners, but keeping people informed of timing and responsibilities is communication, not risk mitigation.
n.4: Resource allocation assigns people to work; it does not keep stakeholders informed.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is coaching a junior colleague on the principles that underpin a successful handover of deliverables into operational use. The colleague lists several behaviours they believe support good transition management, but one of them would actually undermine it. Which of the following is NOT a principle of successful transition management?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Ignoring stakeholder input undermines buy-in and risks failure during handover.

n.0: Clear role definitions prevent confusion post-handover.
n.1: Maintaining BAU processes avoids service disruption.
n.2: Engaging operations early is essential for smooth transition.
n.3: Planning from the outset ensures transition needs are built in.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which is NOT typically included in a transition plan?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Lessons learned are captured after project closure, not in the transition plan itself.

n.0: Communication plans keep stakeholders informed during transition.
n.1: Training schedules prepare users for the new environment.
n.2: Cutover activities define the actual handover steps.
n.3: Go-live criteria ensure readiness for launch.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which factor is NOT necessary to sustain business-as-usual?
o: Complete budget isolation from the project
Project Success & Benefits.w: Isolating budgets from the project can prevent funding for daily operations, so it’s not required.

n.0: Documentation guides operators in day-to-day work.
n.2: Monitoring performance ensures BAU quality remains acceptable.
n.3: Resources must be allocated to both project and BAU tasks.
n.4: Involving stakeholders secures support for BAU continuity.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project is about to hand a new IT service over to a live support environment, and the project manager is most concerned that customers experience no break in service during the changeover. She wants to focus on the elements that most directly protect continuity of service. Which two components best ensure continuity of service during transition?
o: Risk closure reports and design prototypes
User training sessions and support documentation
Quality audit schedule and performance appraisals
Marketing campaign launch and press releases
Operations team involvement and detailed SLAs
Project Success & Benefits.w: Involving operations and having clear SLAs ensure services continue without interruption during handover.

n.0: Closure reports and prototypes do not directly support live service continuity.
n.1: Training and documentation help, but without ops involvement/SLAs continuity isn’t guaranteed.
n.2: Audits assess quality but don’t manage day-to-day handover operations.
n.3: Marketing activities do not directly ensure service continuity.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which two activities combined support effective transition planning?
o: Earned value analysis and cost forecasting
Critical path analysis and resource levelling
Code refactoring and user interface prototyping
Project Success & Benefits.w: Transition planning is about preparing the business to receive the outputs: understanding who is affected (stakeholder analysis) and how their operations will change (impact assessment) shapes readiness, training, support and risk transfer.

n.0: Tendering and negotiation are procurement activities for securing suppliers.
n.1: Earned value and cost forecasting are cost control techniques, not transition planning activities.
n.2: Critical path analysis and levelling are scheduling techniques for delivery work, not the core of planning the handover into BAU.
n.3: Refactoring and prototyping are solution development tasks in deployment.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which two deliverables should a transition plan include?
Project Success & Benefits.w: A transition plan sets out how the move into live operation will happen: a cutover checklist sequences and confirms each step of the switch, and rollback procedures define how to revert safely if it fails.

n.0: The business case and benefits profiles justify the project and describe benefits; they are not transition deliverables.
n.1: The stakeholder map and grid come from stakeholder analysis and inform engagement, not cutover.
n.3: The WBS and CBS break down work and cost during planning, not the handover into operations.
n.4: The procurement strategy and tender documents are used to appoint suppliers earlier in the project.

Project Success & Benefits.q: As a project prepares to move a new solution into day-to-day running, the project manager is deciding who must take part in the transition discussions so that ongoing support is ready. She wants the people accountable for live services and front-line user support at the table. Which two stakeholders are essential to involve in transition discussions?
o: Operations manager and service desk lead
Project Success & Benefits.w: The operations manager and service desk lead ensure that support and day-to-day services are prepared for the new delivery.

n.1: ECM admins/designers are technical, not high‐level operational owners.
n.2: HR or union reps may be involved but aren’t primary for operational handover.
n.3: Finance and marketing have roles but aren’t the core day-to-day operators.
n.4: Competitors are not stakeholder participants in your transition.

Project Success & Benefits.q: In a software deployment project, the operations team was not consulted until after go-live, causing support delays. Which transition planning step should have been taken earlier?
o: Engaging operations team in requirements gathering
Project Success & Benefits.w: Early engagement of the operations team ensures support processes are designed alongside the solution.

n.1: Backups are technical; support readiness requires ops involvement.
n.2: Adding developers doesn’t address operations readiness.
n.3: Communication planning is important but secondary to involving the operations team.
n.4: Marketing is not a primary factor in support readiness.

Project Success & Benefits.q: After a handover, the operations team was unsure who was accountable for various support tasks, and duties were either duplicated or overlooked. Reviewing the transition plan, the project manager realises a key element was not defined clearly enough. Complete the statement: the transition plan lacked clear ________, leading to confusion about role responsibilities.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Defining responsibilities clearly prevents overlap, gaps, and confusion during handover.

n.0: Budget clarity is important but not the root cause of role confusion.
n.1: Governance structure supports decision making but isn’t the same as individual roles.
n.2: Risk clarity is separate from role definitions.
n.3: Metrics track performance; they do not assign roles.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project team updates all data sources but forgets to communicate process changes to operations. Which is NOT an effective mitigation in this scenario?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Skipping the operations handover would ignore the core issue and lead to further delays.

n.0: End-user training ensures operations understand new processes.
n.1: Cutover updates can include handover steps for operations.
n.3: A communication plan directly addresses the lack of messaging.
n.4: Documenting support processes clarifies how operations should proceed.

Project Success & Benefits.q: During the transition of a new system, a readiness assessment reveals that the receiving support team does not fully understand how to operate it. The project manager wants to close this knowledge gap using practical, complementary measures. Which two actions together would best address a knowledge gap identified during transition?
o: Conducting performance appraisals and salary reviews
Issuing press releases and updating brand guidelines
Creating quick reference guides and hosting Q&A workshops
Ordering new hardware and software licences
Scheduling daily standups and weekend retreats
Project Success & Benefits.w: Quick reference guides paired with Q&A workshops build practical knowledge and address questions in real time.

n.0: Appraisals and salaries are unrelated to operational know-how.
n.1: Press releases focus on public messaging, not internal knowledge transfer.
n.3: Hardware orders do not fill procedural knowledge gaps.
n.4: Standups and retreats do not target specific knowledge gaps.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Midway through moving a new solution into live service, the operations team finds that one critical business process cannot be supported because the necessary documentation was never produced. The project manager must decide how to respond. What is the priority action?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Creating the required documentation enables operations to support the process after handover.

n.0: Reducing support desk capacity worsens the situation.
n.1: Cancellation ignores the core planning need.
n.2: Marketing is unrelated to process support.
n.3: An auditor may find non-conformities but won’t create the missing docs.

Project Success & Benefits.q: When a new way of working was rolled out to a business area, staff pushed back because they had not been involved or consulted during planning. Reviewing what went wrong, the project manager identifies the missing element. Complete the statement: without proper stakeholder ________, resistance to new processes increased.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Engagement ensures stakeholders understand and buy into changes, reducing resistance.

n.1: Budget alone doesn’t address resistance.
n.2: Testing does not manage stakeholder buy-in.
n.3: Design is a technical activity, not stakeholder management.
n.4: Metrics track performance but don’t directly engage stakeholders.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is explaining to a sponsor why business-as-usual must be protected while the project delivers change. The sponsor asks her to list the legitimate reasons for doing so, but one suggested reason runs contrary to good governance. Which of the following is NOT a reason to maintain business-as-usual during project delivery?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Business-as-usual aims for transparency and continuity; hiding issues undermines trust and should be avoided.

n.0: BAU prevents interruption of daily services.
n.1: Customer satisfaction is maintained by uninterrupted service.
n.2: Compliance often relies on stable BAU processes.
n.4: Revenue continuity depends on BAU stability.

Project Success & Benefits.q: After deployment, the service desk reports a surge in incident tickets. Which two transition plan components could have mitigated this?
o: Supplier selection criteria and tender evaluation
Daily stand-ups and quarterly status reviews
Benefits profiles and a benefits review schedule
Project Success & Benefits.w: A surge in incident tickets after go-live usually means users were not ready to use the new service. User training and support materials, part of business readiness in the transition plan, would have reduced it.

n.0: A cutover checklist and rollback protect the technical switchover, but tickets from users who do not know how to use the service call for training and support.
n.1: Supplier selection happens much earlier and does not prepare users for the new service.
n.3: Stand-ups and status reviews are internal team and governance routines; they do not equip users.
n.4: Benefits profiles and reviews track benefits; they do not prepare users to operate the service.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Shortly before go-live, a transition readiness assessment finds that several key members of the support team do not yet have the system access they will need to keep the service running after handover. The project manager must decide what to do. What should be done?
o: Remove support staff from transition plan
Provision system access to support staff
Project Success & Benefits.w: Ensuring support staff have access is critical for post-go-live support and should be addressed immediately.

n.0: Change control maintains stability; it should not be disabled.
n.1: Indefinite delays are impractical; targeted fixes are preferable.
n.2: Removing staff undermines support readiness.
n.3: QA scope reduction risks undiscovered defects.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Throughout the transition of a new service, fresh issues and threats continue to surface as go-live approaches. The project manager wants the transition risk register to stay a reliable reflection of the current situation. Complete the statement: transition risk registers should be regularly ________ to capture emerging issues.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Regular updates ensure the transition risk register reflects the current risk landscape and supports mitigation actions.

n.0: Archiving is for closed projects, not active risk management.
n.1: Uploading alone does not guarantee current content.
n.2: Freezing it prevents new risks from being captured.
n.3: Deleting the register removes visibility of risks.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is persuading a sceptical sponsor of the value of holding transition readiness reviews before handover. The sponsor lists several outcomes he expects such reviews to deliver, but one of them overstates what a review can realistically achieve. Which is NOT a benefit of conducting transition readiness reviews?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Readiness reviews cannot guarantee zero incidents but they do help identify and mitigate risks beforehand.

n.0: They improve risk awareness and management.
n.1: They highlight gaps that need addressing.
n.2: Reviews secure buy-in and preparedness from stakeholders.
n.3: They confirm that resources are in place.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is preparing a cutover plan for switching customers from a legacy system to a new one over a single weekend, and she is determined to keep any downtime to an absolute minimum and recoverable. She wants to include the elements that most directly serve those aims. Which two factors should be included in a cutover plan to minimise downtime?
o: Change request backlog and issue logs
Sequenced task list and rollback procedures
Benefits profiles and the realisation timeline
User satisfaction survey and training feedback
Project Success & Benefits.w: Minimising downtime needs a tightly sequenced, timed list of cutover tasks; keeping it recoverable needs tested rollback procedures to restore the legacy system if go-live fails.

n.0: Change and issue logs are project control records, not the elements that run and protect the cutover weekend.
n.2: Lessons learned are captured after the event; they do not minimise downtime on the night.
n.3: Benefits profiles describe benefits realised after transition; they do not reduce or recover downtime during cutover.
n.4: Satisfaction surveys and training feedback are gathered from users, not used to control cutover downtime.

Project Success & Benefits.q: During transition, a critical defect was discovered in the new system. What is the immediate next step according to good transition practices?
Project Success & Benefits.w: If a critical defect arises, rollback to the last stable state prevents major service disruption.

n.0: Deleting the plan removes guidance in a crisis.
n.1: Marketing updates do not address system defects.
n.2: Proceeding with a critical defect risks operational failure.
n.3: Celebrating success ignores the defect issue.

Project Success & Benefits.q: As several teams prepare to switch a live service across to a new platform, the project manager needs a means of coordinating the timing, dependencies and activities so everyone acts in step. Complete the statement: effective transition management requires clear cutover ________ to coordinate activities.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Detailed cutover plans align teams, timing, and dependencies for a coordinated transition.

n.0: Documents support plans but the plan itself is the core guide.
n.1: Metrics track outcomes, not execution sequencing.
n.2: Budgets are managed separately from cutover sequencing.
n.4: Dashboards display data but don’t replace execution plans.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is walking her team through the activities they will carry out while executing the transition plan for a new solution. One team member proposes a shortcut that would actually put the handover at risk. Which action is NOT recommended when executing a transition plan?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Skipping testing phases risks introducing defects and undermines transition success.

n.0: Verifying support readiness ensures ongoing operations post-go-live.
n.1: User communication is critical for awareness and adoption.
n.2: Documenting handover actions provides an audit trail for accountability.
n.3: Monitoring metrics ensures the transition meets performance targets.

Project Success & Benefits.q: As a new operational system is handed over, the project manager arranges structured knowledge transfer between the project team and the operations staff who will run it. A colleague asks what this activity is fundamentally intended to achieve. What is the primary purpose of knowledge transfer during transition?
o: To reassign the project team to new initiatives
To ensure operational teams can support new processes
To document lessons learned for the closure report
To sign off deliverables against the acceptance criteria
To confirm the business case benefits are realised
Project Success & Benefits.w: Knowledge transfer equips operations with the know-how to maintain and support new solutions post-handover.

n.0: Automation is a technical solution, not the transfer of know-how.
n.2: Budget finalisation is a financial activity, not knowledge transfer.
n.3: System retirement may follow transition, but KT focuses on people.
n.4: Sponsor recruitment is unrelated to operational readiness.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Having completed the transition of a new service into operations, a project manager wants to capture what the team learned so the organisation improves how it handles future handovers. She is choosing structured approaches to draw out that experience. Which two methods best support learning from experience in transition?
o: Earned value reports and cumulative cost S-curves
Daily stand-up meetings and weekly progress reports
Configuration status accounting and change control audits
Informal ad hoc chats and corridor conversations
Project Success & Benefits.w: Post-implementation reviews and lessons-learned workshops are structured ways to draw out what worked and what did not, so the organisation improves future handovers.

n.0: Earned value reports and S-curves track cost and schedule performance, not lessons from the transition.
n.1: Stand-ups and progress reports manage current work; they are not structured reflection on the completed transition.
n.3: Configuration status accounting and audits control and verify items and versions; they do not capture learning from experience.
n.4: Informal chats are unstructured and leave no reliable record, so learning is easily lost.

Project Success & Benefits.q: After go-live, the team holds a workshop to identify what went well and what didn’t. This is an example of ________.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Reviewing successes and failures post-transition drives ongoing enhancements in processes and plans.

n.0: Risk management addresses threats, not experiential learning per se.
n.2: Technical design is a development activity.
n.3: Budget forecasting is a financial projection.
n.4: Stakeholder mapping identifies stakeholders, not lessons.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project sponsor asks a project manager to explain the value of formally capturing lessons learned as part of transition. The project manager lists several genuine benefits, but wants to correct one claim the sponsor makes that overstates what lessons learned can deliver. Which is NOT a benefit of capturing lessons learned during transition?
o: Informing refinements to future transition processes
Enhancing the knowledge held across the team
Guaranteeing all future transitions are flawless
Reducing the recurrence of past mistakes
Supporting the organisation's continuous improvement efforts
Project Success & Benefits.w: Lessons learned cannot guarantee flawless outcomes but do improve future practices.

n.0: They inform refinements to processes.
n.1: They build collective team expertise.
n.3: They help avoid repeating errors.
n.4: They underpin ongoing improvements.

Project Success & Benefits.q: After a new system went live, the receiving support team struggled to diagnose and resolve recurring incidents because they lacked hands-on familiarity with how it behaved. The project manager wants a practical way to close this operational knowledge gap. Which action addresses this knowledge gap?
o: Outsourcing the entire support function to a provider
Lowering the severity rating of recurring support incidents
Developing detailed run-books and conducting shadowing sessions
Escalating every incident directly to the project manager
Reverting the new system back to the legacy platform
Project Success & Benefits.w: Run-books and shadowing transfer operational details and practical know-how to support staff.

n.0: Outsourcing shifts responsibility but doesn’t build internal capability.
n.1: Thresholds don’t teach troubleshooting.
n.3: Replacing staff ignores the root cause: missing knowledge.
n.4: Canceling the plan avoids the problem without solving it.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which two outputs are typical from a post-transition review?
o: Baselined schedule and work breakdown structure for the next phase
Revised business case and a new funding request for the next phase
Supplier tender documents and weighted bid evaluation criteria
Approved change requests and a re-baselined schedule for operations
Process improvement actions and an updated knowledge repository
Project Success & Benefits.w: A post-transition review looks back on the handover and produces improvement actions and updated knowledge (documentation, lessons learned) so the organisation learns and support improves.

n.0: Baselining a schedule and WBS is planning for future work, not an output of reviewing a completed transition.
n.1: A revised business case and funding request belong to a decision gate, not a review of a completed transition.
n.2: Tender documents and evaluation criteria are procurement outputs.
n.3: Change requests and re-baselining arise from change control during delivery, not from a post-transition review.

Project Success & Benefits.q: An organisation wants its store of transition lessons and operational guidance to genuinely feed continuous improvement, so that teams actually reuse past experience on future handovers. A project manager is reviewing what quality the repository most needs to make that possible. Which characteristic is essential for a knowledge repository to support continuous improvement?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Accessible repositories ensure teams can easily find and apply past lessons to new transitions.

n.0: Obscure information isn’t useful.
n.1: Unnecessary redundancy can cause confusion.
n.2: Complexity hinders quick retrieval.
n.3: Excess volume can overwhelm users.

Project Success & Benefits.q: During a handover, a project manager needs to pass on the hard-won, experience-based know-how that support staff cannot easily pick up from written material alone. She is weighing up several methods and wants to rule out the one that is least suited to conveying this kind of knowledge. Which is NOT an effective method for transferring tacit knowledge?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Slides alone fail to convey nuance; tacit knowledge requires interactive, experiential methods.

n.0: Mentoring helps share hands-on insights.
n.1: Knowledge cafés foster open dialogue.
n.3: Coaching embeds learning in real tasks.
n.4: Workshops encourage two-way exchange.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which two practices enhance continuous improvement in transition processes?
o: Regular retrospective meetings and process performance metrics
Extended vacation periods and office redecorations
One-time training only and static documentation
Ad hoc decision making and reactive fixes
Project Success & Benefits.w: Retrospectives identify improvement opportunities and metrics track process effectiveness over time.

n.1: Non-work activities don’t drive process enhancements.
n.2: Arbitrary actions lack systematic rationale.
n.3: Single training events won’t sustain ongoing improvement.
n.4: Reactive fixes lack structured learning.

Project Success & Benefits.q: After completing a significant transition, a project manager schedules a session to record what went well and what did not, so the same problems do not resurface on the next handover. Complete the statement: organisations should capture lessons learned after each major transition to avoid repeating ________.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Lessons learned are captured so the organisation repeats what worked and avoids repeating mistakes on future transitions.

n.1: Benefits are what the project is trying to realise, not something to avoid repeating.
n.2: Milestones are planned key events; capturing lessons does not aim to avoid them.
n.3: Organisations want to repeat successes; that is part of why lessons are captured.
n.4: Baselines are agreed reference points for control; lessons learned are not about avoiding them.

Project Success & Benefits.q: In a scenario where a new system roll-out failed due to lack of user training, which improvement action should the team implement?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Mandatory practical training ensures users gain competence before go-live, preventing similar failures.

n.0: Indefinite delays avoid learning, not improvement.
n.1: Unnotified updates create confusion and risk.
n.2: Removing manuals reduces support options.
n.4: Governance ensures process adherence, not reduces it.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager is planning a session to draw out lessons from a recently completed transition and wants it to be genuinely productive. A colleague suggests several features for the session, but one of them belongs to a different activity altogether. Which is NOT a characteristic of an effective lessons-learned session?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Financial auditing is a separate activity; sessions focus on process insights and improvements.

n.0: Tracking agreed actions ensures lessons are applied.
n.2: A blame-free environment encourages honest feedback.
n.3: Active participation captures diverse perspectives.
n.4: An agenda keeps the session focused.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Following a handover, a support lead keeps adding new material to the knowledge base but never asks the operations users whether the content is actually helping them do their jobs. A project manager reviewing this identifies a continuous improvement practice that is absent. Which continuous improvement practice is missing?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Continuous improvement needs feedback loops: asking users whether the knowledge base helps them and using the answers to improve it. The support lead adds content but never checks its usefulness.

n.0: Configuration audits check items match their records, not whether users find the content useful.
n.1: Version control manages changes to documents but does not tell you whether they help users.
n.3: Risk avoidance is a threat response, not a continuous improvement practice for the knowledge base.
n.4: Knowledge capture is already happening (material keeps being added); what is missing is feedback on its value.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which two tools facilitate effective continuous improvement?
o: Gantt charts and critical path networks
Work breakdown structures and responsibility assignment matrices
Root cause analysis and process performance dashboards
Project Success & Benefits.w: Continuous improvement needs to understand why problems happen (root cause analysis) and to measure process performance over time to see whether changes work (dashboards).

n.0: Gantt charts and network diagrams are scheduling tools, not improvement tools.
n.1: Stakeholder grids and communication plans support engagement, not process improvement.
n.2: Tender evaluations and contracts are procurement tools.
n.3: WBS and RAM/RACI define work and responsibilities; they do not analyse or measure process performance.

Project Success & Benefits.q: After a new solution went live, support staff followed the handover documentation but repeatedly applied steps and settings that no longer matched the current system, causing errors. Reviewing why the knowledge transfer failed, the project manager identifies the root cause. Complete the statement: knowledge transfer failure is most likely when documentation is ________.
Project Success & Benefits.w: Outdated documentation misleads users and fails to convey current processes or configurations.

n.0: Good structure enhances clarity.
n.1: Accessibility improves knowledge use.
n.3: Comprehensive docs aid, not hinder, transfer.
n.4: Validation ensures accuracy and reliability.

Project Success & Benefits.q: At the very start of transition planning, a project manager decides to bring the affected operational teams and other stakeholders into the conversation early rather than presenting them with a finished plan. A colleague asks what she is mainly hoping to gain from this. What is the key benefit of engaging stakeholders early in transition planning?
o: Eliminating the need for any technical reviews
Avoiding the need for any budget discussions
Removing the need for a formal transition plan
Securing buy-in and commitment to the transition plan
Guaranteeing there will be no post-live issues
Project Success & Benefits.w: Early engagement builds stakeholder ownership and commitment to the transition plan.

n.0: Technical reviews remain necessary for system readiness.
n.1: Budget discussions remain essential to plan viability.
n.2: You still need a transition plan regardless of engagement timing.
n.4: Zero issues cannot be guaranteed by engagement alone.

Project Success & Benefits.q: In a scenario where the operations team resists taking on support for a new system, which activity would best secure their agreement?
o: Sending operations a detailed briefing pack on the new system
Facilitating a risk transfer workshop to clarify responsibilities
Escalating to the sponsor to instruct operations to accept handover
Issuing the finalised transition plan to operations for sign-off
Keeping all support within the project team after go-live
Project Success & Benefits.w: Agreement comes from engagement and consultation. A workshop that clarifies which risks and responsibilities transfer, and how, addresses operations' concerns and gains genuine ownership.

n.0: A briefing pack only informs; one-way communication does not resolve operations' concerns about responsibility.
n.2: Instruction from the sponsor may force compliance but does not secure agreement; it is a last resort, not the best first step.
n.3: Issuing a finished plan without consulting operations seeks sign-off rather than agreement and is likely to deepen resistance.
n.4: The project team is temporary; retaining support avoids the issue and leaves nothing properly owned by BAU.

Project Success & Benefits.q: While finalising a transition plan, a project manager needs to agree who will take ownership of the risks being transferred to the receiving organisation as the new service goes live. She wants the right people around the table to reach that agreement. Which two stakeholders should be involved to agree risk transfer in a transition plan?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Operations managers and risk owners jointly agree on who will assume specific transition risks.

n.1: Facilities staff support logistics but don’t own transition risks.
n.2: Marketing and design roles are unrelated to risk ownership in transition.
n.3: Competitors are not internal decision-makers for risk transfer.
n.4: Shareholders/customers are recipients of value but not day-to-day risk owners.

Project Success & Benefits.q: As a project moves into transition, the project manager relies on a particular record to keep track of how involved and supportive each stakeholder is as the handover progresses. Complete the statement: the stakeholder register is used to track stakeholder ________ during transition.
Project Success & Benefits.w: The stakeholder register records stakeholders' interest, influence, attitude and current versus desired engagement, so it is used to track engagement levels through transition.

n.0: Acceptance criteria belong in the quality and acceptance documentation, not the stakeholder register.
n.1: Risk ratings are held in the risk register.
n.2: Issue status is tracked in the issue log.
n.3: Change requests are recorded in the change log.

Project Success & Benefits.q: Which technique is NOT effective for engaging stakeholders in agreeing a transition plan?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Imposition without dialogue alienates stakeholders and fails to secure agreement.

n.0: Risk matrices clarify responsibilities and build confidence.
n.1: Workshops foster two-way communication and consensus.
n.2: Impact assessments show stakeholders what's changing and why.
n.3: Training ensures stakeholders understand their roles in transition.

Project Success & Benefits.q: While preparing a transition plan, a project manager wants each stakeholder to see clearly how the pending changes and risks will affect them, so that ownership of those risks can be aligned and agreed. Complete the statement: a transition plan must include a stakeholder ________ to align risk ownership.
Project Success & Benefits.w: A stakeholder impact assessment shows each stakeholder how the changes and risks will affect them, which is the basis for agreeing who will own each transferred risk.

n.0: An attendance log records presence at sessions, not impact or ownership.
n.1: A contact directory lists who to reach, not how they are affected or which risks they own.
n.2: A satisfaction survey measures opinion after the event; it does not show how risks will affect each stakeholder.
n.3: A training record shows who has been trained, not impacts or risk ownership.

Project Success & Benefits.q: As a project prepares to hand a new service to operations, the project manager is compiling the risks that will pass to the receiving organisation at go-live. A colleague proposes several items for that list, but one of them relates to an earlier phase and should already have been closed. Which of the following is NOT a risk typically transferred in a transition plan?
Project Success & Benefits.w: Tender evaluation happens early in the life cycle, so any risk of delay there has passed and should be closed long before go-live. Risks that continue into live operation are the ones transferred to BAU owners.

n.1: Service level breaches are an ongoing operational risk that BAU must own after go-live.
n.2: Data quality problems can surface after migration and must be owned by the receiving organisation.
n.3: Support gaps affect live operations, so operations must own them.
n.4: Defects found in live use are an operational risk passed to support teams.

Project Success & Benefits.q: During a transition, the legal team confirms it will retain ownership of the risk of any data compliance breaches rather than passing it to operations. The project manager wants to make sure this arrangement is properly agreed and cannot later be disputed. Which activity ensures stakeholder agreement?
o: Postponing all legal sign-off until after go-live
Excluding legal from all transition planning discussions
Documenting legal’s risk responsibilities in the transition plan
Reassigning the compliance risk to the marketing team
Disregarding the relevant data protection regulations
Project Success & Benefits.w: Documenting responsibilities formalises agreement and avoids ambiguity about compliance ownership.

n.0: Delays in sign-off stall the entire transition process.
n.1: Exclusion leads to misunderstandings and legal exposure.
n.3: Marketing lacks the mandate to manage compliance risk.
n.4: Ignoring regulations exposes the organisation to penalties.

Project Success & Benefits.q: A project manager wants the stakeholders receiving a new service to reach a shared understanding of who owns which transferred risks. She is selecting activities that will both clarify the allocation and secure collective agreement to it. Which two activities support stakeholder alignment on risk transfer?
o: Finalising the procurement schedule and payment milestone dates
Publishing the marketing plan and the communications calendar
Drafting the closure report and archiving project records

o: Select the lowest-cost supplier to preserve budget
Split procurement evenly across all available suppliers
Prioritise supplier reliability and lead-time certainty over cost
Delay procurement until internal capability improves
Procure only after detailed design is fully complete
Procurement.w: For critical, long-lead items, reliability and certainty reduce schedule risk more than cost savings.

n.0: Lowest cost may increase delivery risk.
n.1: Splitting may introduce coordination issues.
n.3: Delaying procurement increases schedule risk.
n.4: Waiting may worsen lead-time constraints.

Procurement.q: A project manager is deciding between a fixed-price contract and a cost-reimbursable contract for uncertain scope work. What is the most appropriate driver of this decision?
o: The preferred contracting approach of the supplier
The number of suppliers available in the market
The frequency of required progress reporting
Level of scope definition and risk allocation
The project's internal governance and reporting structure
Procurement.w: Contract type should reflect how risk is shared based on scope certainty.

n.0: Supplier preference is secondary.
n.1: Availability does not determine contract type.
n.2: Reporting frequency is irrelevant.
n.4: Governance is not the main factor.

Procurement.q: A project team responsible for a specialist control system is considering single sourcing a critical deliverable from one preferred supplier to speed up delivery. As the procurement lead evaluates this approach, what is the primary risk of this strategy?
o: Reduced supplier competition and dependency risk
Greater complexity in the contract terms
Higher internal workload for the project team
Increased contract administration and paperwork effort
Procurement.w: Single sourcing increases dependency and reduces competitive pressure.

n.0: This is a potential benefit, not a risk.
n.2: Complexity is not the key issue.
n.3: Internal workload is unrelated.
n.4: Admin effort is not the primary risk.

Procurement.q: A supplier offers a low bid but has a history of late delivery. What is the most appropriate procurement decision?
o: Evaluate total risk impact including schedule and quality
Reject the supplier without further analysis
Delay the decision until later in the project
Select the supplier due to cost savings
Split the contract to reduce cost exposure
Procurement.w: Procurement decisions should consider total impact, not just price.

n.1: Rejection without analysis is premature.
n.2: Delaying increases risk.
n.3: Cost alone ignores delivery risk.
n.4: Splitting may not resolve reliability issues.

Procurement.q: A project manager is developing the procurement strategy for a major infrastructure project and wants to ensure it clearly reflects the wider aims of the work. In this context, what is the main purpose of aligning procurement strategy with project objectives?
o: To minimise stakeholder involvement in procurement decisions
To simplify and speed up supplier selection
To ensure sourcing decisions support delivery outcomes
To standardise contract formats across all suppliers
To reduce the project's documentation and reporting burden
Procurement.w: Procurement strategy must support project success criteria.

n.0: Stakeholder involvement is still required.
n.1: Simplification is not the main goal.
n.3: Standardisation is not the primary objective.
n.4: Documentation is secondary.

Procurement.q: To avoid over-reliance on any one organisation, a project manager decides to award work packages across several suppliers rather than a single provider. As they plan the delivery approach, what is the main trade-off of this decision?
Procurement.w: Multiple suppliers increase coordination complexity.

n.0: Quality control may become harder.
n.2: Costs may increase.
n.3: Contracts become more complex.
n.4: Complexity increases, not decreases.

Procurement.q: An organisation is preparing to procure services for a new project and is weighing up how best to approach the market. The procurement lead is asked to justify running a competitive tender. In procurement strategy, what is the primary benefit of competitive tendering?
o: Complete transfer of delivery risk to suppliers
Improved cost efficiency and value for money
Reduced need for formal contract terms
Guaranteed performance from the chosen supplier
Faster selection of a preferred supplier
Procurement.w: Competition drives better pricing and value.

n.0: Risk remains.
n.2: Contracts are still required.
n.3: Performance is not guaranteed.
n.4: Tendering can take time.

Procurement.q: A project manager is procuring for a software development initiative where the requirements are expected to change considerably as work progresses and user needs become clearer. Given this uncertainty, which procurement approach is most suitable?
o: Single supplier with no contractual flexibility
Outsourcing all work regardless of uncertainty
Procurement.w: Flexible contracts accommodate uncertainty in scope.

n.0: Lack of flexibility increases risk.
n.1: Delaying procurement is impractical.
n.2: Fixed price is risky with uncertainty.
n.4: Blanket outsourcing ignores strategy.

Procurement.q: During supplier selection for a technically demanding project, an evaluation panel is tempted to choose the bidder with the strongest technical solution and give little weight to other factors. What is the key risk of selecting suppliers based solely on technical capability?
Procurement.w: Ignoring cost can make the project commercially unviable.

n.0: Scope is unaffected.
n.2: Decisions are not necessarily simpler.
n.3: Not directly related.
n.4: Capability improves quality.
