Procurement.q: Which TWO factors should influence supplier selection decisions?
o: Rapport with the supplier's sales team
The order in which bids were received
Length of the supplier's tender document
Procurement.w: Supplier selection weighs value for money (cost and commercial terms) against the ability to deliver (technical capability and relevant experience), usually through weighted evaluation criteria.

n.1: Rapport is not an objective criterion and would undermine a fair, auditable evaluation.
n.2: The order in which bids arrive has no bearing on value or capability; all compliant bids received by the deadline are evaluated equally.
n.4: A longer tender document is not evidence of better value or capability; bids are judged against the evaluation criteria, not their length.

Procurement.q: Which TWO risks are associated with poor procurement strategy?
o: Cost overruns due to poor contract terms
Procurement.w: Poor procurement increases risk and cost exposure.

n.2: Not a risk.
n.3: Certainty decreases.
n.4: Planning is still required.

Procurement.q: Which TWO approaches can reduce supplier dependency risk?
Procurement.w: Diversification and contracts reduce dependency risk.

n.0: Communication is essential.
n.1: History is critical.
n.2: Cost focus increases risk.

Procurement.q: A newly appointed project manager is drafting the procurement strategy for a project and needs to be clear about what such a document should contain. Which TWO elements are typically defined within a procurement strategy?
Procurement.w: Procurement strategy defines sourcing and contracts.

n.0: Not procurement-related.
n.1: Irrelevant.
n.4: Operational detail.

Procurement.q: While shaping a procurement strategy, a project manager must decide whether certain components will be delivered using the organisation's own resources or sourced from external suppliers. Which of the following best describes a make-or-buy analysis in procurement strategy?
o: Selection of the most appropriate contract pricing type
Analysis of schedule risk within the supply chain
Evaluation of whether to produce internally or purchase externally
Mapping the influence of external procurement stakeholders
Pre-qualification and shortlisting of potential suppliers
Procurement.w: Make-or-buy analysis determines if goods or services should be produced in-house or procured externally.

n.0: Quality processes are managed elsewhere in project plans.
n.1: Schedule risk analysis is part of risk management.
n.3: Stakeholder mapping is part of communications planning.
n.4: Team hierarchy is defined in the org breakdown structure.

Procurement.q: A project manager is procuring specialised steel for a construction project and wants the greatest possible certainty over the final price the organisation will pay the supplier. Which contract type best optimises cost certainty?
Procurement.w: Fixed-price contracts provide a set total cost, offering maximum cost certainty.

n.0: Unit price depends on quantities, not a single total amount.
n.1: Time-and-materials varies with effort, not cost certainty.
n.3: Blanket agreements cover multiple orders but may have variable pricing.
n.4: Cost-plus reimburses costs plus markup, so total is uncertain.

Procurement.q: As part of the procurement strategy, a project manager needs to set out when key sourcing activities such as tendering, award and delivery will take place. Which typical element of a procurement strategy outlines the timeline for procurement activities?
Procurement.w: The procurement schedule defines when sourcing tasks occur through the project.

n.0: Risk registers list risks, not schedules.
n.2: Checklists support quality but don’t set timelines.
n.3: Stakeholder matrices map roles, not timelines.
n.4: Communication planning covers messaging, not procurement timing.

Procurement.q: A software implementation project is under considerable schedule pressure, and the project manager is tailoring the procurement strategy to help meet the tight deadlines. Which of the following should the procurement strategy emphasise?
o: Full open tender for every item
Procurement.w: When deadlines are tight, the procurement strategy should focus on securing goods and services quickly, for example by using existing frameworks, ordering long-lead items early and choosing suppliers who can deliver fast.

n.0: A full open tender for every item adds time to procurement, the opposite of what a tight schedule needs.
n.2: Choosing purely on lowest price ignores delivery speed and can add delay; schedule pressure needs timely supply.
n.3: A post-implementation review happens after delivery, so it does nothing to help meet the current deadline.
n.4: Buying only once a year delays supply and cannot respond to the project's immediate needs.

Procurement.q: A project manager is drafting a procurement strategy and wants it to make clear how suppliers will be chosen and how the resulting relationships will be governed. Which pair of aspects is typically included within the contents of a procurement strategy?
o: Project scope statement and resource plan
Supplier selection criteria and contract management approach
Procurement.w: Supplier criteria and contract management outline how vendors are chosen and governed.

n.0: Scope and resources are part of project planning, not procurement strategy.
n.1: Lessons learned and issue logs are post-delivery artifacts.
n.2: Marketing and sales belong to business strategy, not procurement.
n.4: Test strategies belong in quality plans.

Procurement.q: Preparing a procurement strategy for an upcoming marketing campaign, a project manager wants to set clear sourcing goals and a means of judging how well vendors deliver against them. Which pair of items should you document?
o: Team RACI chart and resource histogram
Stakeholder register and board risk tolerance
Procurement.w: Objectives set what the procurement must achieve, and supplier performance indicators provide the means of judging how well vendors deliver against them.

n.0: These cover internal responsibilities and resource demand, not supplier performance.
n.1: These belong to stakeholder management and governance, not sourcing goals.
n.2: These belong to quality control.
n.3: These are iterative delivery tools.

Procurement.q: A project manager explains to a new team member that the procurement strategy sets out how the project's goods and services will be obtained. It defines the ______ and process for obtaining project goods and services.
Procurement.w: The approach describes the overall sourcing method and process flow.

n.0: Timelines are part of the schedule section.
n.1: Quality is managed separately in quality strategies.
n.2: Budgets are detailed in cost plans.
n.4: Governance is a section but not the blank described.

Procurement.q: A project's key materials are subject to volatile market prices, so the project manager tailors the procurement strategy to guard against cost uncertainty. In this situation the strategy must include a ______ strategy to mitigate cost risk.
Procurement.w: Risk management plans address how to handle price volatility and its impacts.

n.0: Communication plans handle messaging, not cost volatility.
n.2: Resource allocation is staffing-focused.
n.3: Quality assurance covers product/service standards, not price risk.
n.4: Stakeholder engagement covers relationships, not market risk.

Procurement.q: A project manager is checking that a draft procurement strategy contains only relevant material before submitting it for approval. Of the following, which is NOT a typical content of a procurement strategy?
Procurement.w: Team performance reviews are internal HR activities, not procurement contents.

n.0: Payment terms establish invoicing and settlement.
n.1: Contract types define commercial agreements.
n.3: Supplier criteria guide vendor selection.
n.4: Schedules set procurement timelines.

Procurement.q: During a review meeting, stakeholders query whether every listed item belongs in the procurement strategy. Which of these should NOT be part of the procurement strategy?
Procurement.w: The benefits realisation plan sets out how and when benefits will be measured and realised; it is a separate document, not part of how goods and services are sourced.

n.0: Evaluation criteria are core to supplier selection.
n.1: Payment arrangements are part of the reimbursement approach.
n.3: The contract type and terms are a key strategy decision.
n.4: Roles give clear accountability for procurement.

Procurement.q: Before finalising the sourcing approach, a project manager researches the supply market to understand what vendors can offer and how prices are moving. What is the role of supplier market analysis in procurement strategy?
o: Assessing market capabilities and pricing trends
Procurement.w: Market analysis identifies potential vendors, capabilities, and expected costs.

n.0: Team structure belongs to organisational planning.
n.1: Stand-ups are an agile execution practice.
n.2: Communication channels are defined in communications planning.
n.3: Meeting minutes are recording artifacts.

Procurement.q: A pharmaceutical project must source highly specialised manufacturing equipment within a tightly regulated environment. As the project manager sets the procurement objectives, which is most critical to include in the strategy?
o: Minimise the number of suppliers invited
Put delivery speed ahead of validation
Define software coding standards for the team
Procurement.w: In a tightly regulated pharmaceutical setting, equipment that does not meet regulatory standards cannot be used, so compliance must be a central procurement objective and evaluation criterion.

n.0: Limiting the field may reduce effort, but it is not the critical objective here; compliance is.
n.1: Rushing or skipping validation risks a regulatory breach; speed must not override compliance.
n.2: Lowest cost does not guarantee compliant equipment; non-compliant equipment would be unusable whatever it cost.
n.4: Coding standards relate to software development, not to sourcing regulated manufacturing equipment.

Procurement.q: A stakeholder asks the project manager where the project's procurement strategy is formally held alongside the other subsidiary plans. Which document typically contains the procurement strategy in project management?
Procurement.w: The procurement strategy is a subsidiary plan within the overall Project Management Plan.

n.0: Quality plans focus on standards, not procurement.
n.2: The business case justifies the project, not the detailed strategy.
n.3: Risk registers list risks, not procurement approach.
n.4: Communication matrices map stakeholder information flows.

Procurement.q: A project is being delivered across several widely separated sites, adding complexity to how goods physically reach each location. As the project manager tailors the procurement strategy, which should it prioritise?
Procurement.w: When goods must reach several widely separated sites, the strategy must plan how, when and where items are delivered, including transport, storage and site access, so each location is supplied on time.

n.0: Using one supplier may simplify contracting, but it does not solve the physical challenge of delivering to many sites.
n.2: Version control applies to software and documents, not the physical delivery of goods.
n.3: Debriefing unsuccessful bidders is part of the award stage, not a response to multi-site delivery complexity.
n.4: Payment milestones manage cash flow and supplier incentives, not getting goods to each site.

Procurement.q: What metric in a procurement strategy measures supplier reliability?
Procurement.w: On-time delivery directly reflects a supplier’s ability to meet schedule commitments.

n.0: Meeting attendance is administrative, not performance.
n.1: Stakeholder satisfaction is broader than supplier reliability.
n.3: Defect density measures product quality, not delivery reliability.
n.4: Staff turnover is internal to the supplier, not a direct strategy metric.

Procurement.q: A project depends on suppliers paid in foreign currencies, and the project manager is concerned about the organisation's exposure to exchange-rate movements. Which mitigation should the procurement strategy include?
Procurement.w: Hedging protects against adverse currency movements in international contracts.

n.0: Cleaning schedules are unrelated.
n.1: Morale surveys don’t address financial risk.
n.2: Scrum timings are agile execution details.
n.4: Brand planning is marketing-focused.

Procurement.q: A project manager is setting out within the procurement strategy how uncertainties affecting sourcing will be handled. Which pair of elements forms part of procurement risk management in a strategy?
Procurement.w: Identifying risks and planning mitigations are core to procurement risk management.

n.0: Logs and minutes document events, not risk management.
n.1: Scope and milestones belong in project planning.
n.3: Training/reviews are HR activities.
n.4: Budget summaries/changes are cost management artifacts.

Procurement.q: Drafting a procurement strategy to source IT hardware, the project manager wants to be explicit about after-delivery support and the performance expected from the vendor. Which pair of items should be detailed?
o: Warranty conditions and service level agreements
Bid evaluation weightings and the tender timetable
Procurement.w: Warranties and service level agreements define the support and performance expected from the vendor after delivery.

n.1: These inform who to invite to tender, not after-delivery support.
n.2: These are development records, not contract terms.
n.3: These decide whether and how to buy, not what support follows delivery.
n.4: These govern selection before award, not support after delivery.

Procurement.q: Explaining the procurement strategy, a project manager notes that it must set out how bidders will be judged against the defined requirements. The strategy should specify the ______ criteria for selecting suppliers.
Procurement.w: The procurement strategy sets the evaluation criteria (for example quality, price, capability and risk, often weighted) against which bids are judged and suppliers selected.

n.0: Communication covers how information is shared, not how bidders are judged.
n.1: Delegation concerns authority within the organisation, not supplier selection.
n.3: Implementation criteria are not used to select suppliers; bids are judged against evaluation criteria.
n.4: Acceptance criteria define when a deliverable is accepted; they are not the criteria for choosing a supplier.

Procurement.q: On a project where the failure of a key supplier would cause serious disruption, a project manager builds resilience into the procurement strategy. Given this high supply risk, the strategy must include a detailed ______ plan.
Procurement.w: Where supplier failure would cause serious disruption, the strategy needs a contingency plan: a planned fallback, such as an alternative supplier or buffer stock, ready to use if the risk occurs.

n.1: A communication plan sets out who receives what information; it does not provide resilience if a supplier fails.
n.2: A transition plan covers handover into business as usual, not supply failure during the project.
n.3: A quality plan defines standards and checks for outputs, not what to do if a supplier fails.
n.4: A procurement plan sets out how goods and services will be bought; it does not provide the fallback needed if a key supplier fails.

Procurement.q: Reviewing a draft procurement strategy, a project manager wants to remove anything that does not belong among its sections. Which of the following is NOT a typical section in a procurement strategy?
Procurement.w: Meal plans are unrelated to procurement strategy content.

n.1: Contract strategy details how agreements will be structured.
n.2: Process flows map procurement steps.
n.3: Metrics track vendor and process performance.
n.4: Supplier segmentation groups vendors by criticality and capability.

Procurement.q: During a review, stakeholders flag that one item in the procurement strategy is clearly out of place. Which of the following should NOT appear in the procurement strategy?
o: Belbin role profiles of the project team
Supplier onboarding and contract management process
Procurement.w: A procurement strategy covers how goods and services will be obtained from external suppliers. The Belbin team roles of the internal project team are a team management matter and do not belong in it.

n.1: Payment milestones relate to the reimbursement method and contract terms, which the strategy covers.
n.2: How suppliers will be onboarded and managed is part of the contract management approach in the strategy.
n.3: Bid evaluation criteria are a core part of the procurement strategy.
n.4: The governance model, including roles and approvals for procurement decisions, is typical strategy content.

Procurement.q: How does a procurement strategy contribute to cost control?
o: By setting the reimbursement method and pricing terms
By transferring all cost risk to the buyer
By removing the need for a contingency budget
By guaranteeing that the lowest tender price is accepted
By defining internal team roles and reporting lines
Procurement.w: The reimbursement method (fixed price, cost plus fee, per unit quantity or target cost) and pricing terms decide who carries cost risk and how costs are controlled.

n.1: A strategy allocates cost risk deliberately; transferring all of it to the buyer weakens cost control.
n.2: Contingency is still needed for risk; a strategy does not remove it.
n.3: Value for money matters more than the lowest price, which can raise whole-life cost.
n.4: Roles support accountability but do not set financial mechanisms.

Procurement.q: A defence project involves handling sensitive material and must meet stringent security requirements. As the project manager develops the procurement strategy, which should it emphasise?
Procurement.w: Where sensitive material is handled, the procurement strategy must make sure suppliers hold the required security clearances.

n.1: The payment method does not address security.
n.2: Opening the tender widely could expose sensitive material; security needs restricted access.
n.3: Speed of mobilisation does not address security.
n.4: Price alone ignores the security requirement.

Procurement.q: A project manager anticipates that contracts and sourcing arrangements may need adjusting as the project progresses. Which section of a procurement strategy details how such changes are handled?
Procurement.w: Change control procedures define how amendments to contracts and sourcing plans are approved.

n.0: Sponsor lists identify leadership, not process details.
n.1: Risk registers log risks, not change protocols.
n.3: Matrices map communication channels.
n.4: Metrics measure performance, not control change.

Procurement.q: After issuing a tender, a project manager receives bids that differ widely in price and approach and needs a consistent, objective basis for comparing them. Which should the procurement strategy guide?
Procurement.w: An evaluation methodology with weighted criteria gives a consistent, objective basis for comparing bids that differ in price and approach.

n.0: Change control manages changes after the baseline is set.
n.2: Make-or-buy decides whether to procure at all, before tenders are issued.
n.3: Close-out happens at the end of the contract, not when comparing bids.
n.4: Debriefing follows the award decision; it does not compare bids.

Procurement.q: Which two contents define contract administration in procurement strategy?
Procurement.w: Contract administration manages the contract once it has been awarded: monitoring the supplier's performance against the agreed terms and managing changes to the contract in a controlled way.

n.0: Stakeholder engagement and communication logs belong to communication management, not contract administration.
n.2: Budget summaries and risk prioritisation are wider project control activities, not the content of contract administration.
n.3: Market analysis and shortlisting happen before a contract is awarded, during supplier selection.
n.4: Quality control checks outputs and team training builds capability; neither defines how the contract is administered.

Procurement.q: A project manager is arranging a turnkey contract in which a single supplier delivers a complete, ready-to-use solution. In shaping this strategy, which pair of items should you include?
o: End-to-end scope and acceptance criteria for delivery
Defect logs and code refactoring plans
Daily stand-up timings and sprint review dates
Internal resource histograms and team rotas
Separate contracts for each component and its interfaces
Procurement.w: In a turnkey contract one supplier delivers a complete solution, so the strategy needs the full end-to-end scope and clear acceptance criteria for the finished result.

n.1: These are software delivery records.
n.2: These are delivery team arrangements, not procurement strategy.
n.3: These manage internal resources, not the supplier contract.
n.4: Separate contracts contradict the single-supplier turnkey approach.

Procurement.q: To keep quality on track after contracts are awarded, a project manager builds ongoing oversight of vendors into the procurement strategy. It must include a plan for supplier ______ to ensure quality.
Procurement.w: Performance monitoring tracks adherence to quality and delivery requirements.

n.0: Colour selection is design-related, not procurement.
n.1: Task assignment refers to project staffing.
n.3: Lobbying is an advocacy activity.
n.4: Events are HR/PR activities.

Procurement.q: On a project with critical, non-negotiable deadlines, a project manager wants orders placed early enough that materials always arrive in time. The procurement strategy should therefore specify ______ lead times.
Procurement.w: Minimum lead times ensure orders are placed early enough to meet deadlines.

n.0: Averages may underestimate worst-case delivery.
n.1: Maximum lead times are less useful for urgency planning.
n.2: Variable times require further definition.
n.3: Optional lead times lack commitment.

Procurement.q: A project manager is explaining to sponsors the value a well-defined procurement strategy brings to the project. Of the following, which is NOT a benefit of a well-defined procurement strategy?
Procurement.w: A strategy reduces and allocates supply chain risk but cannot eliminate it, so elimination is not a realistic benefit.

n.0: Managing supply chain risk is a core purpose.
n.1: Clear processes improve consistency and efficiency.
n.2: Alignment makes sure sourcing meets project needs.
n.3: A clear strategy supports stronger supplier relationships.

Procurement.q: During a strategy review, the team checks whether each listed item belongs in the procurement strategy. Which of the following should be excluded?
o: The contract renewal and review schedule
Procurement.w: The lessons learned log is a project-wide record of experience; it is not part of the procurement strategy.

n.0: Renewal and review schedules manage the contract life cycle.
n.1: Risk assessment documents procurement risks and their allocation.
n.2: Qualification criteria are core to supplier selection.
n.3: Payment terms define the financial arrangements.

Procurement.q: As part of supplier selection, a project manager wants prospective vendors to submit detailed proposals showing how they would meet the requirement. Which stage of the supplier selection process involves gathering this detailed information from potential suppliers?
Procurement.w: The RFP stage involves soliciting detailed proposals and information from potential suppliers.

n.0: Close-out is the final stage of contract management.
n.1: Risk management is an ongoing process, not the information-gathering stage.
n.2: Onboarding happens after contract award.
n.4: Contract negotiation occurs after evaluation.

Procurement.q: In procurement negotiation, what does BATNA stand for?
o: Basic Agreement for Trade and Negotiation Actions
Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement
Procurement.w: BATNA stands for Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement, referring to the fallback position.

n.0: This phrase is incorrect and not used in negotiations.
n.1: This is not a recognised procurement term.
n.2: This is not the correct expansion of BATNA.
n.4: This option does not reflect the true meaning of BATNA.

Procurement.q: What does ZOPA represent in negotiation planning?
Procurement.w: ZOPA is the Zone of Possible Agreement where both parties can find acceptable terms.

n.0: This phrase is not used in negotiation theory.
n.2: This is not the correct term for ZOPA.
n.3: This is not a recognised negotiation concept.
n.4: This suggests a zero-sum scenario, not ZOPA.

Procurement.q: Which document outlines project procurement requirements for suppliers?
Procurement.w: The Statement of Work details objectives, deliverables, and requirements for procurement.

n.0: The stakeholder register lists stakeholders and roles.
n.1: Quality plans focus on standards, not procurement.
n.3: The communications matrix maps information flows.
n.4: The risk register logs project risks.

Procurement.q: Which stage follows supplier evaluation in the selection process?
Procurement.w: After evaluating proposals, the next stage is negotiation to finalise terms.

n.1: Onboarding happens post-award.
n.2: Planning occurs before evaluation.
n.3: Closure is after contract management.
n.4: Re-evaluation is not a formal stage.

Procurement.q: A project manager is mapping out the sequence of stages that make up the supplier selection process. Of the following, which is NOT a stage of the supplier selection process?
Procurement.w: Performance audits occur after contract award, not during supplier selection.

n.0: Contract negotiation follows evaluation.
n.1: Shortlisting happens after initial screening.
n.2: Proposal evaluation is a key selection step.
n.4: Needs assessment is the initial stage.

Procurement.q: Which is NOT a valid negotiation approach?
Procurement.w: "Zero-sum conflict" is not a recommended approach as it assumes one side wins only at the other's expense.

n.0: Win–win seeks mutual benefits.
n.2: Collaborative focuses on joint solutions.
n.3: Principled negotiation uses objective criteria.
n.4: Interest-based addresses underlying needs.

Procurement.q: Which is NOT part of procurement planning?
Procurement.w: Performance reviews occur in contract management, not planning.

n.0: Requirement definition is a planning step.
n.1: Supplier identification is part of planning.
n.2: Developing strategy is central to planning.
n.4: Selecting contract types belongs to planning.

Procurement.q: Which is NOT a factor when evaluating suppliers?
Procurement.w: A personal relationship with the sponsor is a conflict of interest, not a legitimate evaluation factor; selection must be objective and fair.

n.0: Stability indicates the supplier can sustain delivery.
n.1: Distance influences lead times, logistics and cost.
n.2: Technical capability is crucial for performance.
n.3: Cultural fit affects how well the parties collaborate.

Procurement.q: Which is NOT an objective of negotiation in procurement?
o: Defeat the supplier on every point
Procurement.w: Negotiation aims for an agreement that meets objectives and protects the relationship; winning every point at the other party's expense damages trust and long-term value.

n.0: Terms and conditions form the negotiated agreement.
n.1: Controlling whole-life cost is a common objective.
n.2: Creating mutual value is the aim of principled negotiation.
n.3: Deliverables must be clearly defined.

Procurement.q: Having gathered initial responses from interested vendors, a project manager works to narrow the field to those best suited to the requirement. Which pair of activities occurs during the supplier shortlisting stage?
o: Review RFI responses and conduct initial supplier screenings
Develop risk mitigation plan and audit suppliers
Evaluate performance data and close contracts
Issue purchase order and arrange logistics
Procurement.w: Shortlisting involves screening RFI responses to identify qualified suppliers.

n.1: Risk plans are broader governance documents.
n.2: Negotiations happen later.
n.3: Performance evaluation occurs during contract management.
n.4: PO issuance is post-selection.

Procurement.q: Which two elements should a Request for Proposal include?
o: Project risk register and sponsor names
Scope of work and evaluation criteria
Team contact list and communication plan
Internal budget limit and walk-away price
Procurement.w: An RFP tells bidders what is needed (the scope of work and requirements) and how their proposals will be judged (the evaluation criteria), so they can submit relevant, comparable bids.

n.0: The full risk register and sponsor names are internal; at most, key risks relevant to the work are summarised for bidders.
n.1: The internal schedule and resource plan are working documents for the buyer's team; bidders need the scope and key dates, not the full plan.
n.3: The team contact list and communication plan are internal; an RFP gives bidders a single point of contact.
n.4: The buyer's budget limit and walk-away price are kept confidential to protect its negotiating position.

Procurement.q: Which two negotiation planning steps are essential?
o: Draft the project charter and baseline scope
Book the venue and circulate the agenda
Set quality metrics and write test cases
Sign the contract and issue purchase orders
Procurement.w: Planning a negotiation means setting objectives, priorities and a walk-away point, and knowing your best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA).

n.1: These are project initiation and planning activities.
n.2: These are logistics, not substantive planning.
n.3: These belong to quality planning.
n.4: These come after the negotiation has concluded.

Procurement.q: Which two criteria are commonly used for supplier evaluation?
o: Project float and critical path length
Number of internal stakeholders and team size
Earned value and schedule performance index
Bid document length and the quality of its formatting
Procurement.w: Suppliers are commonly evaluated on value for money (price competitiveness) and their ability to deliver on time and to standard (delivery reliability), usually alongside quality and capability criteria.

n.0: Float and critical path length describe the project schedule, not a supplier's merits.
n.1: Internal stakeholder numbers and team size are features of the buyer's project, not supplier evaluation criteria.
n.2: Earned value and SPI measure the buyer's own project performance, not a supplier's suitability.
n.3: The presentation of a bid is not a measure of value or capability; its content is judged against the criteria.

Procurement.q: A project manager is comparing contract options and is concerned about which arrangements leave the buyer bearing the greatest exposure to cost overruns. Which pair of contract types exposes the buyer to the highest cost risk?
o: Memorandum of understanding and framework agreement
Procurement.w: T&M and cost-plus reimburse actual costs, placing risk on the buyer.

n.0: Unit-price caps per-unit cost but not total quantities.
n.2: Incentive contracts share risk with performance targets.
n.3: Fixed-price moves cost risk to the supplier.
n.4: MOUs and frameworks do not define final costs.

Procurement.q: Which two negotiation outcomes reflect a win–win approach?
o: Splitting the difference so both concede equally
Agreement reached quickly by avoiding hard issues
Mutual gains and a lasting working relationship
Buyer secures lowest price, supplier absorbs risk
Supplier accepts all terms to keep the account
Procurement.w: A win-win (principled) outcome creates gains for both parties by focusing on interests, and protects the long-term relationship.

n.0: Splitting the difference is compromise: both give something up rather than both gaining.
n.1: Avoiding hard issues leaves them unresolved; it is not a win-win outcome.
n.3: One side gains at the other's expense, a win-lose outcome.
n.4: One side gives way to the other, an accommodating rather than win-win outcome.

Procurement.q: During contract negotiations, a project manager works out what the organisation will do if no agreement is reached with this supplier, such as turning to the second-ranked bidder. What is this fallback option called?
Procurement.w: BATNA (Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement) is what you will do if no deal is reached. Knowing it strengthens your negotiating position and informs your walk-away point.

n.0: ZOPA is the overlap between both sides' acceptable ranges, where a deal is possible.
n.1: An SLA defines service levels once a contract is in place.
n.3: Win-win describes an integrative negotiation where both sides gain, not the fallback if talks fail.
n.4: An RFP is a document inviting suppliers to propose a solution.

Procurement.q: The zone of possible agreement is abbreviated as ______.
Procurement.w: ZOPA stands for Zone of Possible Agreement where deals are mutually acceptable.

n.0: SLA refers to service levels.
n.1: POA is not used in negotiation theory.
n.2: BATNA is the fallback alternative.
n.4: MOQ is minimum order quantity.

Procurement.q: Supplier evaluation typically follows the shortlisting and ______ stages.
Procurement.w: After suppliers submit proposals, the evaluation stage assesses those submissions.

n.0: Award happens after negotiations.
n.1: Negotiation comes after evaluation.
n.2: Planning is done before shortlisting.
n.4: Sourcing strategy is broader than the evaluation sequence.

Procurement.q: Ready to go to market, a project manager needs the formal document that invites suppliers to submit their bids for the work. The document that formally invites vendors to submit bids is an ______.
Procurement.w: An Invitation to Tender (ITT) is the formal request for bidders to submit offers.

n.1: The SOW defines deliverables, not the invitation format.
n.2: Notice to Proceed is issued post-award.
n.3: Change Orders modify existing contracts.
n.4: Requisitions are internal purchase requests.

Procurement.q: In procurement planning, ______ analysis identifies potential suppliers' capabilities.
Procurement.w: Market analysis surveys supplier capabilities, offerings, and pricing trends.

n.0: Cost-benefit evaluates project value, not suppliers.
n.1: PESTLE examines macro-environmental factors.
n.2: Risk analysis focuses on threats and mitigations.
n.3: SWOT assesses organisational factors.

Procurement.q: A project manager is preparing to negotiate a supply contract and wants to understand where the buyer's acceptable terms and the supplier's acceptable terms overlap so that a deal can realistically be struck. Which negotiation concept represents the range in which agreement is possible?
Procurement.w: ZOPA defines the overlapping area where both parties’ acceptable terms meet.

n.0: MOQ is minimum order quantity.
n.1: SLA is service level agreement.
n.2: BATNA is the fallback option, not the overlapping range.
n.4: RFQ is request for quotation.

Procurement.q: What does SLA stand for in supplier contracts?
Procurement.w: SLA stands for Service Level Agreement governing performance standards.

n.0: This phrase does not match the acronym.
n.1: This is not the standard meaning of SLA.
n.2: There is no Supplier License Act in this context.
n.4: Liability agreements are separate documents.

Procurement.q: Which document contains the procurement strategy in project management?
Procurement.w: The procurement strategy is included as a subsidiary plan within the Project Management Plan.

n.0: The business case justifies the project, not the detailed strategy.
n.1: Risk registers list risks, not strategy details.
n.2: Quality plans cover standards, not procurement approach.
n.4: Communication matrices map stakeholder interactions.

Procurement.q: During the procurement phase, a project manager explains to a new team member why the organisation runs a structured supplier selection process before awarding any work. Considering the aims of that process, which of the following is NOT a purpose of the supplier selection process?
o: To guarantee the lowest bid wins
Procurement.w: Supplier selection seeks best value against weighted criteria such as quality, price, capability and risk; it does not automatically award to the lowest bid.

n.0: Risk assessment helps judge reliability.
n.1: Comparing proposals is essential for selection.
n.3: Identifying qualified vendors is a core purpose.
n.4: Shortlisting narrows the field to credible suppliers.

Procurement.q: As part of solicitation, a procurement team approaches the market to gather background information and then invite formal proposals from potential suppliers for an upcoming package of work. Which two documents are typically issued to suppliers during this solicitation stage?
Procurement.w: RFIs and RFPs are formal solicitations issued to gather information and proposals.

n.0: SLAs and contracts are post-award documents.
n.2: Budgets and schedules are internal plans.
n.3: Purchase orders come after selection.
n.4: Change orders modify existing contracts.

Procurement.q: A project requires quick deployment of servers. During procurement planning, the team is preparing evaluation criteria. Which stage are they in?
Procurement.w: Developing evaluation criteria occurs during the solicitation planning stage.

n.0: Evaluation follows solicitation planning.
n.2: Negotiation happens after evaluation.
n.3: Closure is the final contract management step.
n.4: Award comes after negotiation.

Procurement.q: Having received several bids for a construction package, the project team scores and ranks each vendor against cost and quality before making an award recommendation to the sponsor. Which procurement process are they carrying out?
Procurement.w: Ranking proposals is part of the proposal evaluation process.

n.0: Market research is preliminary to solicitation.
n.1: Closure finalises completed contracts.
n.3: Onboarding occurs after contract award.
n.4: Negotiation refines terms post-evaluation.

Procurement.q: Before entering supplier talks for a critical system, the negotiation team carefully identifies its best alternative to a negotiated agreement in case discussions fail. In practical terms, what does establishing this best alternative help the team determine?
Procurement.w: BATNA is what the team will do if no deal is reached. Comparing any offer against it shows the point at which walking away is better than agreeing, so it informs the walk-away point and strengthens the team's position.

n.0: Quality thresholds come from requirements and quality planning.
n.1: Scope comes from requirements management, not from the fallback option.
n.2: The stakeholder register comes from stakeholder analysis, not from negotiation planning.
n.4: The budget is set through planning and the business case, not by the fallback option.

Procurement.q: Pricing bids exceed the project's budget. The team seeks the range where both parties can agree. Which concept guides this effort?
Procurement.w: ZOPA defines the range in which buyer and supplier expectations overlap.

n.0: POs are purchase orders issued after agreements.
n.1: WBS is a work breakdown structure, not negotiation-related.
n.2: RFQs request pricing but don't define agreement zones.
n.3: SLAs set post-award performance commitments.

Procurement.q: A supplier providing ongoing IT support commits to financial penalties if agreed response and delivery times are missed during the contract. In which document is this type of performance and penalty clause typically found?
Procurement.w: SLAs include performance penalties and service commitments post-award.

n.1: The SOW defines deliverables but not penalty clauses.
n.2: Risk registers log potential issues, not contractual terms.
n.3: RFIs are preliminary information requests.
n.4: Requisitions are internal documents.

Procurement.q: Early in the procurement process, the project team drafts a document defining the deliverables, standards and requirements against which suppliers will later bid. During which procurement stage does drafting this Statement of Work occur?
Procurement.w: Drafting the SOW is part of planning the solicitation requirements.

n.1: Evaluation happens after the SOW is complete.
n.2: Negotiation follows evaluation.
n.3: Award is post-negotiation.
n.4: Close-out finalises contracts.

Procurement.q: A project team is preparing to negotiate a major hardware supply agreement and wants to plan the negotiation thoroughly before ever meeting the suppliers. Which two steps should they perform during negotiation planning?
o: Agree the final price and close the deal
Draft risk register and update charter
Send purchase orders and schedule shipments
Set QA metrics and write test plans
Procurement.w: Effective negotiation planning needs clear objectives and an understanding of the best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA).

n.0: Agreeing and closing happen during the negotiation itself, not in the planning stage.
n.1: These are separate project management activities.
n.3: Purchase orders follow the negotiation.
n.4: QA planning is distinct from negotiation.

Procurement.q: During supplier evaluation, the procurement team studies each candidate's audited financial statements and its pricing against comparable offers in the market. Which two evaluation criteria does examining this financial information primarily reflect?
o: Health and safety record and industry accreditations
Procurement.w: Audited accounts show whether a supplier is financially stable, and comparing its pricing with the market shows how competitive it is.

n.0: These are assessed from method statements, references and demonstrations, not financial information.
n.1: These are judged from policies, evidence and interviews.
n.3: These are judged from safety records and certificates, not accounts or price.
n.4: These are judged from track record and references.

Procurement.q: A negotiator wants the supplier relationship to be sustainable and mutually beneficial over the life of the contract rather than one-sided, aiming for a win–win outcome. Which two actions best reflect this collaborative approach?
o: Ignore supplier concerns and set fixed terms
Demand lowest price and use ultimatums
Share information and propose joint problem solving
Procurement.w: Win–win approaches involve transparency and collaborative problem solving.

n.0: Threats create adversarial dynamics.
n.1: Ignoring concerns undermines collaboration.
n.2: Ultimatums harm long-term relationships.
n.4: Locking terms without dialogue is inflexible.

Procurement.q: A large project sources critical components from suppliers based in several different countries, adding significant complexity to its procurement approach. Which two procurement strategy elements most directly address this international sourcing complexity?
o: Logistics planning and currency risk management
Earned value analysis and S-curve reporting
Stakeholder mapping and stakeholder communication planning
Procurement.w: Sourcing from several countries adds physical complexity (shipping, customs, lead times) and financial exposure to exchange rate movements, so logistics planning and currency risk management address it most directly.

n.0: Levelling and float management are scheduling techniques for resources, not responses to international supply.
n.2: Earned value and S-curves report cost and schedule performance; they do not manage cross-border supply risk.
n.3: Framework agreements allow call-off over time, but they do not address shipping, customs or exchange rate exposure.
n.4: Stakeholder mapping and communication planning support engagement, not international sourcing.

Procurement.q: To compare competing supplier proposals objectively rather than relying on individual judgement, the selection team applies a weighted scoring model. Which two factors are typically weighted within such a model?
o: Quality of solution and whole-life cost
Internal team size and project float
Bidder's order of submission and page count
Test pass rates and code coverage
Procurement.w: Weighted scoring models typically weight quality and cost so proposals can be compared objectively.

n.1: These describe the buyer's project, not the bids.
n.2: The order or length of a bid says nothing about its value.
n.3: These measure software quality during delivery, not bid quality.
n.4: Personal preference and contacts are not objective criteria.

Procurement.q: Work must start almost immediately, before the scope can be properly defined. Which reimbursement method best suits this situation, and why?
o: Target cost, as overruns fall on the supplier alone
Fixed price, as the supplier will carry the cost risk
Cost plus fee, as it does not need a defined scope
Cost plus fee, as the supplier carries the cost risk
Per unit quantity, as the total quantity is known
Procurement.w: Cost plus fee reimburses actual costs plus a fee, so work can start without a fully defined scope. The trade-off is that the buyer carries the cost risk and needs strong cost control.

n.0: Target cost shares overruns and savings through pain/gain and needs a target agreed from a defined scope.
n.1: Fixed price needs a well-defined scope to price; without one, agreeing it takes time and later changes are costly.
n.3: Under cost plus fee the buyer, not the supplier, carries the cost risk.
n.4: Per unit quantity suits measurable work where quantities are uncertain, so the reason given is wrong, and here the scope itself is undefined.

Procurement.q: Once a supplier agreement has been signed and delivery is under way, the project moves beyond selection into the ongoing management of that supplier relationship. Which two activities typically occur during this contract management stage?
o: Issue RFP and conduct market analysis
Finalise SOW and set up stakeholder workshops
Develop procurement strategy and define scope
Monitor performance and process change requests
Procurement.w: Contract management involves tracking supplier performance and handling contract amendments.

n.0: RFP issuance occurs in solicitation, not post-award.
n.1: SOW finalisation occurs before contract signing.
n.2: Strategy development is done before awarding.
n.3: Evaluation/shortlisting happen prior to award.

Procurement.q: Ahead of meeting suppliers for a key package, the negotiation team agrees the course of action it will take if the talks break down entirely. The team identifies its ______ (the best alternative if negotiation fails) before meeting suppliers.
Procurement.w: BATNA defines the fallback option if negotiations do not reach agreement.

n.0: RFQ is a request for quotation.
n.1: MOQ is the minimum order quantity.
n.2: SLA refers to service level terms.
n.3: ZOPA defines the range of possible agreement, not the fallback.

Procurement.q: When preparing for supplier talks, the buyer's team maps the overlap between the terms they will accept and the terms the supplier is likely to accept. To find a mutually acceptable agreement range, negotiators look at the ______.
Procurement.w: Negotiators examine the Zone of Possible Agreement (ZOPA) to identify overlapping acceptable terms.

n.0: RFQs gather price quotes.
n.2: POs are purchase orders issued later.
n.3: SLAs set performance requirements after contract award.
n.4: WBS is a work breakdown structure for project tasks.

Procurement.q: When an organisation first decides to source goods and services externally, the project team must define requirements and the sourcing approach before approaching any supplier. The procurement process begins with ______, defining what needs to be sourced.
Procurement.w: Procurement planning defines requirements and approach before sourcing suppliers.

n.1: Closing finalises contracts.
n.2: Execution follows planning.
n.3: Monitoring tracks performance post-award.
n.4: Negotiation occurs after evaluation.

Procurement.q: After a supplier agreement has been signed, the project team turns its attention to ensuring the supplier delivers against every obligation it has taken on. After signing, the contract moves into ______ management to ensure compliance.
Procurement.w: Contract management tracks deliverables and supplier performance under the contract.

n.0: Schedule management oversees timelines.
n.1: Communication management addresses information flow.
n.2: Risk management identifies and mitigates threats.
n.4: Quality management controls standards.

Procurement.q: As part of preparing for a supplier negotiation, the buyer's negotiator sets the least favourable terms at which they would still be willing to close a deal. The negotiator prepares their ______, detailing the worst acceptable outcome.
Procurement.w: The reservation price is the least favourable point at which a negotiator will accept a deal.

n.1: Target price represents the desired outcome.
n.2: BATNA is the fallback alternative, not the minimum price.
n.3: Aspiration price is the ideal target.
n.4: ZOPA is the agreement range.

Procurement.q: A procurement lead is deciding which solicitation document to issue for a purchase whose specifications, quantities and standards are already fixed and unambiguous. The request for quotation (RFQ) is used when requirements are ______.
Procurement.w: RFQs are issued when scope and specifications are clearly defined.

n.0: Subjective criteria require proposal evaluation, not fixed quotes.
n.1: Ambiguous requirements need an RFI first.
n.2: Changing requirements need further planning.
n.3: Flexible requirements suit an RFP, not RFQ.

Procurement.q: After evaluation, the team values cultural alignment with the supplier. Which of the following is NOT a typical evaluation criterion?
Procurement.w: The order in which bids arrive has no bearing on a supplier's ability to deliver value, so it is not an evaluation criterion.

n.0: Reliability affects project timelines.
n.1: Financial stability indicates supplier viability.
n.2: Technical capability is essential for performance.
n.4: Competitive pricing affects cost objectives.

Procurement.q: In preparing for an upcoming supplier negotiation, a buyer works methodically through the activities that make up thorough negotiation planning. Which of the following is NOT part of effective negotiation planning?
Procurement.w: Ignoring stakeholder interests undermines comprehensive preparation.

n.1: Clear objectives guide negotiation strategy.
n.2: Defining roles ensures accountability.
n.3: Market research informs realistic targets.
n.4: BATNA analysis identifies fallback position.

Procurement.q: A supplier has repeatedly failed to meet the service levels agreed in its contract, and the project manager must respond appropriately to protect the project. Which of the following is NOT a recommended contract management activity in this situation?
Procurement.w: Celebrating failures is counterproductive; contract management addresses them.

n.0: Term reviews clarify obligations.
n.1: Metrics monitoring tracks compliance.
n.3: Corrective actions address performance gaps.
n.4: Communication keeps stakeholders informed.

Procurement.q: A procurement strategy for an internationally sourced project must address the risk that exchange rates move unfavourably during the life of the contract. Which of the following options is NOT a valid currency risk strategy?
Procurement.w: Ignoring exchange rates leaves the project exposed to currency volatility.

n.0: Escalation clauses adjust for rate changes.
n.1: Hedging contracts lock in rates.
n.2: Stable currency pricing reduces fluctuations.
n.3: Diversifying can spread currency risk.

Procurement.q: While shortlisting suppliers for a package of work, the evaluation team weighs a range of non-financial factors alongside price. Which of the following is NOT a genuine non-financial evaluation criterion?
Procurement.w: Tendered price is a genuine evaluation criterion but it is financial, so it is not a non-financial criterion.

n.1: Culture fit influences collaboration.
n.2: Expertise is a key non-financial criterion.
n.3: Sustainability practices reflect responsibility and are increasingly weighted.
n.4: Past performance predicts reliability.

Procurement.q: As a supplier contract reaches the award stage, the procurement team assembles the documentation needed to formally conclude the award. Which of the following documents is NOT typically required at this stage?
Procurement.w: A close-out report is produced when the contract ends, not when it is awarded. At award you need the signed contract, the agreed scope, the evaluation evidence and the approval record.

n.0: The final scope statement confirms exactly what the supplier has been contracted to deliver.
n.1: A record of approval by the appropriate authority shows the award was made within delegated limits.
n.2: The bid evaluation report records how bids were scored against the weighted criteria and justifies the choice of supplier.
n.3: A signed contract is the formal instrument that concludes the award.

Procurement.q: A project manager is selecting a contract type and wants the supplier, rather than the buyer, to bear the consequences of any cost overrun on the work. Which contract type places the highest cost risk on the supplier?
Procurement.w: In a fixed-price contract, the supplier bears cost overruns.

n.1: Cost-plus reimburses supplier costs, shifting risk to the buyer.
n.2: Per-unit contracts reimburse per item, with quantity risk shared.
n.3: Time-and-materials reimburses actual time and expense, risk to buyer.
n.4: Target cost shares overruns or underruns between parties.

Procurement.q: In a cost-plus fee contract, the buyer reimburses:
o: Actual costs plus a fixed fee
Procurement.w: Cost-plus fee reimburses actual costs and pays an agreed fee on top.

n.0: Target cost may include incentives, not fixed fee.
n.2: Per-unit contracts reimburse per deliverable count.
n.3: Cost-plus includes both costs and fee.
n.4: Fixed price is a different contract type.

Procurement.q: For a project buying a large volume of an identical item over time, the buyer wants an agreement that fixes the price paid for every item delivered. A ______ contract sets a predetermined rate for each unit supplied.
Procurement.w: Per-unit quantity contracts specify a rate per unit delivered.

n.0: Target cost includes shared incentives over a cap.
n.1: Time-and-materials reimburses time and expenses.
n.2: Cost-plus covers actual costs plus a fee.
n.3: Fixed-price sets a total sum for the entire scope.

Procurement.q: A buyer and supplier agree a cost baseline for the work and want a mechanism that divides any savings or overruns against that baseline between them. Which contract type includes such a shared savings or overrun mechanism?
Procurement.w: Target cost contracts share savings or overruns against a target baseline.

n.1: Per-unit does not include incentive sharing.
n.2: Fixed-price has no sharing mechanism.
n.3: Unit-rate is another term for per-unit contract without sharing.
n.4: Cost-plus fee pays a fixed mark-up, no sharing.

Procurement.q: Which is NOT a feature of a fixed-price contract?
o: Total cost adjustment for actual hours
Procurement.w: Fixed-price contracts do not adjust total cost based on actual hours spent.

n.0: Scope is defined upfront in fixed-price contracts.
n.1: Supplier carries risk of cost overruns.
n.3: Change control is essential to manage scope changes.
n.4: Buyers enjoy price certainty.

Procurement.q: A risk-averse buyer with a well-defined scope wants the greatest possible certainty over the total price before committing to a supplier. Which reimbursement method gives the buyer the most cost certainty?
Procurement.w: A fixed price is a lump sum agreed up front, so the supplier carries the cost risk and the buyer knows the total (subject to agreed changes). Per unit quantity fixes only the rate; the buyer still carries the quantity risk.

n.0: Target cost shares overruns and savings through pain/gain, so the final cost can still vary.
n.2: Cost plus fee reimburses actual costs, so the buyer carries the cost risk.
n.3: Per unit quantity fixes the rate per unit, but the total depends on quantities, which the buyer bears.
n.4: Time and materials pays for time and materials used, so the total is open-ended.

Procurement.q: A project's scope of work cannot yet be clearly defined, and the buyer accepts they will pay the supplier's actual costs plus an agreed fee as the work unfolds. Which contract type is most appropriate when project scope is highly uncertain?
Procurement.w: Cost-plus allows flexibility in scope with buyer covering actual costs plus fee.

n.0: Target cost needs an initial target for sharing savings.
n.1: Fixed-price requires well-defined scope.
n.2: Lump-sum is another fixed-price term requiring defined scope.
n.4: Per-unit depends on clear unit definitions.

Procurement.q: Which clause is essential in a target cost contract?
Procurement.w: Incentive fees reward savings or penalise overruns against the target cost.

n.0: Overhead rates relate to cost-plus contracts.
n.1: Unit prices apply to per-unit contracts.
n.2: Time charges are for time-and-materials contracts.
n.3: Termination fees may exist but are not unique to target cost.

Procurement.q: A project requires a large quantity of identical, repetitive deliverables where the total cost is driven mainly by how many units are supplied. Which reimbursement method should be used in this situation?
Procurement.w: Per-unit contracts suit repetitive, identical deliverables where quantity drives cost.

n.0: Fixed-price may overcomplicate unit pricing.
n.1: Target cost is for complex projects with incentives.
n.2: Time-and-materials is for services, not unit goods.
n.4: Cost-plus is complex for repetitive items.

Procurement.q: A project manager is weighing the advantages of a cost-plus fee arrangement for a piece of work whose effort is hard to predict. Which of the following is NOT a genuine benefit of a cost-plus fee contract?
Procurement.w: Cost-plus fee does not guarantee a fixed total cost—buyer covers actual costs.

n.0: Actual costs are visible to the buyer.
n.1: Buyers can adjust scope without renegotiating price.
n.2: Fewer pricing debates are needed since costs are reimbursed.
n.3: Suppliers can be engaged early on detailed costing.

Procurement.q: Which two contract types require rigorous scope definition?
Procurement.w: Both fixed-price and target cost depend on clear scope to set prices or targets.

n.0: Cost-plus and per-unit allow some scope flexibility.
n.1: Per-unit depends on quantity but less on full scope.
n.2: Time-and-materials and cost-plus accommodate scope changes.
n.3: Target cost requires scope clarity, but cost-plus less so.

Procurement.q: A project involves highly specialised, bespoke work where the effort required is difficult to estimate reliably in advance. Which contract type is most suitable for this kind of custom work?
Procurement.w: Custom work with uncertain effort suits cost-plus fee to cover actual expenses.

n.0: Fixed-price may misestimate custom work cost.
n.1: Per-unit applies to mass-produced items.
n.2: Target cost needs an agreed target, hard for unique work.
n.4: Unit-rate is analogous to per-unit contracts.

Procurement.q: A project manager reviews a draft reimbursement clause to confirm it captures the financial terms of how the supplier will actually be paid. Which of the following elements is NOT typically included in a reimbursement clause?
Procurement.w: Evaluation weightings are used to select the supplier before award; they are not part of how the supplier is paid.

n.0: Overhead rates set how indirect costs are recovered.
n.1: Invoice procedures govern how payment is claimed.
n.2: The clause defines which costs are reimbursable.
n.4: The fee sets the supplier's profit.

Procurement.q: A buyer wants a contract under which the supplier is paid an agreed total sum and is not required to justify a detailed breakdown of its underlying costs. Which contract type eliminates the need for a detailed cost breakdown?
Procurement.w: Fixed-price contracts require only a total sum, not cost details.

n.0: Cost-plus requires detailed cost records.
n.1: Per-unit needs unit cost details.
n.3: Time-and-materials needs time and expense logs.
n.4: Target cost needs cost breakdown for target setting.

Procurement.q: A supplier is paid under a per unit quantity arrangement, and meeting strict quality standards matters more than the number of units produced. What should the buyer do to stop volume being prioritised over quality?
o: Leave quality checks to the supplier's discretion
Raise the unit rate so the supplier takes care
Inspect only the final batch before handover
Switch to paying for the hours worked instead
Pay only for units that meet acceptance criteria
Procurement.w: Under per unit quantity the supplier is paid for each unit delivered, which can reward volume. Linking payment to units that pass agreed acceptance criteria, checked through quality control, protects quality.

n.0: The buyer needs its own checks against the acceptance criteria.
n.1: A higher rate costs more but does not tie payment to meeting the standard.
n.2: Checking only at the end detects defects too late and lets poor units be paid for.
n.3: Paying for hours removes the volume incentive but leaves cost open-ended and still does not link payment to quality.

Procurement.q: A supplier is working out how carefully it must record its actual expenditure in order to be paid correctly under different types of agreement. Which two contract types require the supplier to track actual costs meticulously?
Procurement.w: Both cost-plus fee and target cost depend on actual cost tracking for reimbursement and sharing.

n.0: Unit-rate/per-unit are similar, not cost tracking focused.
n.1: Fixed-price and per-unit charge predetermined rates.
n.2: Per-unit depends on quantities, not actual cost detail.
n.3: Target cost needs cost tracking but fixed-price does not.

Procurement.q: A buyer wants an arrangement where, if the supplier delivers below the agreed cost baseline, the resulting savings are shared between the two parties. Which contract type gives the buyer the option to share cost savings?
Procurement.w: Target cost contracts include provisions to share cost underruns as savings.

n.0: Fixed-price locks in price with no savings sharing.
n.1: Cost-plus fee pays a fixed fee regardless of savings.
n.3: Time-and-materials pays actual effort without savings share.
n.4: Per-unit does not include savings sharing.

Procurement.q: Which reimbursement method typically requires the least administrative overhead?
Procurement.w: Fixed-price contracts need minimal tracking of individual costs or hours.

n.0: Time-and-materials needs timesheets and expense reports.
n.2: Per-unit requires counting and verifying quantities.
n.3: Cost-plus requires detailed cost documentation.
n.4: Target cost needs tracking and reporting of costs and incentives.

Procurement.q: A project manager is confirming their understanding of exactly how a target cost contract is meant to operate before recommending it. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a target cost contract?
o: Incentive fee based on performance against target
Buyer reimburses actual expenses without any fee
Procurement.w: Target cost contracts include a fee, not just reimbursement without fee.

n.0: Incentives drive performance against the target.
n.2: Joint management ensures transparency and control.
n.3: Overruns and underruns are shared per agreement.
n.4: A baseline target cost is foundational to the contract.

Procurement.q: During procurement training, a project manager notes that one common contract type is often referred to by an alternative name meaning a single agreed total sum. Which contract type is also known as a lump-sum contract?
Procurement.w: Lump-sum is another term for fixed-price contracts.

n.0: Per-unit is based on unit counts, not lump-sum.
n.1: Cost-plus is distinct and not lump-sum.
n.2: Time-and-materials vary with effort, not lump-sum.
n.3: Target cost includes incentives, not lump-sum.

Procurement.q: A project engages a supplier for support services whose volume will vary over time, and the buyer wants to be billed according to the hours and resources actually used. Which reimbursement method is most suitable for scalable services billed by usage?
Procurement.w: Time-and-materials allows billing based on hours or units of service used.

n.0: Per-unit is for discrete physical units, not service hours.
n.1: Target cost sets a baseline, not usage billing.
n.2: Fixed-price is a total sum, not usage-based.
n.4: Cost-plus is cost reimbursement, not usage billing.

Procurement.q: A buyer with an uncertain scope agrees to reimburse a supplier's actual costs plus an agreed fee. Which reimbursement method is this, and who carries the cost risk?
o: Cost plus fee; the supplier carries the cost risk
Fixed price; the supplier carries the cost risk
Cost plus fee; the buyer carries the cost risk
Target cost; the supplier carries all the risk
Per unit quantity; the supplier carries all risk
Procurement.w: Cost plus fee reimburses actual costs plus a fixed or percentage fee. Because the buyer pays whatever the costs turn out to be, the buyer carries the cost risk and needs strong cost control. It suits uncertain scope.

n.0: The buyer reimburses whatever the actual costs are, so the buyer, not the supplier, carries the cost risk.
n.1: Paying actual costs plus a fee is not a lump sum, so it is not fixed price.
n.3: Target cost shares overruns and savings; it does not put all the risk on the supplier.
n.4: Per unit quantity pays an agreed rate per unit; it does not reimburse actual costs.

Procurement.q: A finance team notes that some supplier agreements can only be paid once the supplier submits itemised records of the costs and hours it has incurred. Which two contract types require a detailed invoice and cost breakdown for payment?
Procurement.w: Both cost-plus fee and time-and-materials rely on detailed cost and time records.

n.1: Fixed-price doesn’t need cost breakdown.
n.2: Per-unit invoicing counts units, but no cost breakdown needed.
n.3: Target cost shares costs, but invoicing may be aggregated.
n.4: Fixed-price payments are milestone-based, not detailed costs.

Procurement.q: A project manager is engaging a supplier for complex development work where actual costs will be reimbursed, but the buyer also wants to motivate efficient delivery by rewarding the supplier for beating an agreed cost baseline. Which contract type supports both cost reimbursement and incentive fees?
Procurement.w: Target cost contracts reimburse costs and include incentive or disincentive fees.

n.0: Lump-sum is a fixed-price term.
n.1: T&M usually has no incentive fees.
n.2: Per-unit contracts focus on unit rates.
n.3: Fixed-price pays a single sum, no incentives.

Procurement.q: Which reimbursement method is appropriate for low-risk, well-defined deliverables?
Procurement.w: Well-defined, low-risk work is best suited to fixed-price agreements.

n.1: Cost-plus suits undefined or high-risk work.
n.2: Per-unit suits volume-based, not well-defined scope.
n.3: T&M suits uncertain effort, not low-risk defined work.
n.4: Target cost is for moderate risk with shared incentives.

Procurement.q: Which reimbursement method sets an agreed target cost, with any overrun or saving against it shared between buyer and supplier through a pain/gain mechanism?
Procurement.w: A target cost contract sets an agreed target; if the actual cost is above or below it, the difference is shared through a pain/gain mechanism, which incentivises collaboration and efficiency.

n.0: Time and materials pays for time and materials used, with no shared target.
n.1: Cost plus fee reimburses actual cost plus a fee; overruns fall on the buyer with no sharing.
n.2: Under fixed price the supplier keeps any saving and bears any overrun alone.
n.3: Per unit quantity pays an agreed rate for each unit delivered.

Procurement.q: An organisation is buying repeatable components under an arrangement that prices each item and bills by the volume delivered. As the project manager weighs its merits, which of the following is NOT a genuine advantage of a per-unit quantity contract?
Procurement.w: A per-unit contract fixes the rate, not the total quantity, so it does not stop scope creep; the overall scope and total cost can still grow.

n.0: Quantities can be increased or reduced without renegotiating the rate, which suits work where volumes are uncertain.
n.1: The buyer pays the agreed rate only for units actually delivered, not for an estimated total.
n.2: Invoices are simply the agreed rate multiplied by the units delivered.
n.4: The rate per unit is agreed in advance, so unit cost is predictable.

Procurement.q: Which reimbursement method minimises the buyer’s administrative burden?
Procurement.w: Fixed-price requires minimal oversight of individual costs or timesheets.

n.0: T&M needs timesheet and expense review.
n.1: Cost-plus requires detailed cost tracking.
n.3: Per-unit needs quantity verification.
n.4: Target cost also demands cost reporting.

Procurement.q: A programme is running over several years and the finance team is worried that rising input prices will erode the supplier's margins and disrupt delivery. When drafting agreements, which two contract types can readily include provisions for cost escalation due to inflation?
Procurement.w: Both cost-plus fee and target cost agreements often include escalation clauses to adjust for inflation.

n.1: Per-unit alone may not adjust for inflation.
n.2: Lump-sum is fixed and doesn’t adjust automatically.
n.3: Fixed-price and per-unit typically lock prices unless explicitly negotiated.
n.4: Time-and-materials may adjust rates but not always inflation-specific.

Procurement.q: A project manager is comparing terms across different supplier agreements and reviewing which clauses must be defined for each. Which clause is critical in a cost-plus contract, where the buyer reimburses the supplier's spend, yet only optional in a fixed-price contract?
Procurement.w: Cost-plus contracts must define which costs are reimbursable, whereas fixed-price does not require this detail.

n.0: Change control applies to both contract types.
n.1: Payment schedules are standard in all contracts.
n.2: Confidentiality clauses can be in any contract.
n.3: Acceptance criteria are needed regardless of pricing method.

Procurement.q: On completion of a work package, the supplier and buyer must compare the actual outturn cost against the agreed baseline so the shared savings or overruns can be calculated. Which contract type typically requires such a target cost reconciliation report?
Procurement.w: Target cost contracts include reconciliation of actual versus target costs for incentive calculation.

n.0: Fixed-price does not compare actual costs to a target.
n.2: Cost-plus may report costs but not target reconciliations.
n.3: T&M reports hours and expenses, not target comparisons.
n.4: Per-unit focuses on delivered quantities, not targets.

Procurement.q: A procurement lead is assessing where financial exposure will sit before selecting a payment approach for a high-uncertainty package. Which two reimbursement methods shift the most financial risk onto the buyer, who ends up funding actual costs incurred?
Procurement.w: Both cost-plus fee and time-and-materials reimburse actual expenses, exposing the buyer to cost overruns.

n.0: Lump-sum is another fixed-price arrangement.
n.1: Fixed-price shifts risk to the supplier.
n.3: Target cost shares risk with incentive mechanisms.
n.4: Per-unit shares cost with buyer but caps per unit.

Procurement.q: A project manager is preparing tender documents for a well-defined package where the supplier commits to a single agreed price. To limit ambiguity and disputes over what is included, which contract type most relies on a detailed statement of work (SOW)?
Procurement.w: Fixed-price contracts rely on a clear SOW to define scope and boundaries for the set price.

n.0: T&M allows flexibility in scope definition.
n.1: Per-unit relies on unit definitions, not full SOW.
n.2: Target cost benefits from clarity but is less rigid than fixed-price.
n.4: Cost-plus can tolerate some scope ambiguity due to cost reimbursement.

Procurement.q: Under an agreement priced by the item, the buyer wants to be certain that each delivered unit meets requirements before releasing payment for it. Which clause in a per-unit contract defines the conditions under which units are accepted for payment?
Procurement.w: Acceptance criteria specify how the buyer verifies and accepts each unit before payment.

n.0: Incentives apply in target cost or other incentive contracts.
n.1: Fee schedule sets the price, not acceptance conditions.
n.3: Termination conditions govern contract end, not acceptance.
n.4: Audit rights allow review of records.

Procurement.q: Which two contract types are classified as cost-reimbursement agreements?
Procurement.w: Both cost-plus fee and target cost reimburse actual costs, with differing fee structures.

n.0: Fixed-price and per-unit do not reimburse actual costs.
n.1: Target cost is cost-reimbursement but per-unit is unit-rate.
n.2: Lump-sum is a fixed-price variant.
n.4: Per-unit focuses on quantity, not cost reimbursement.

Procurement.q: A project manager faces uncertain demand and wants a supplier agreement that commits to a floor of orders while capping the buyer's total exposure to volume. Which contract type frequently includes a minimum and maximum quantity range?
Procurement.w: Per-unit contracts frequently specify quantity ranges to manage volume uncertainty.

n.0: Target cost sets a total, not unit limits.
n.2: T&M pertains to services, not unit volumes.
n.3: Fixed-price covers total scope, not unit ranges.
n.4: Cost-plus focuses on costs, not unit counts.

Procurement.q: A buyer reimbursing a supplier's actual expenditure wants the contractual right to inspect the supplier's books and verify that claimed costs are genuine and allowable. Which clause in a cost-reimbursement contract secures this access to cost records?
Procurement.w: Audit rights give the buyer access to cost and expense records for verification.

n.0: Scope definition sets deliverable boundaries.
n.1: Force majeure covers unforeseen events.
n.2: Termination for convenience allows contract cancellation.
n.4: Acceptance criteria govern deliverable approval.

Procurement.q: A sponsor is deciding whether a cost-plus fee arrangement fits a project with evolving requirements and specialist technical work. When justifying that choice, which of the following is NOT a valid reason to select a cost-plus fee contract?
o: A high level of technical complexity
Procurement.w: Cost-plus fee does not guarantee total cost certainty—costs vary.

n.0: Uncertain scope is suited to cost-plus arrangements.
n.1: Evolving requirements are easier under cost-plus contracts.
n.2: Early engagement benefits from cost-plus’s flexibility.
n.3: Complex technical work often uses cost-plus to cover risks.

Procurement.q: A project manager and supplier agree an expected cost up front and set out how any underspend or overspend against it will be divided between the two parties. Which contract type typically involves negotiating a target price and a sharing formula?
Procurement.w: Target cost contracts negotiate a target and define how savings or overruns are shared.

n.0: Time-and-materials does not specify target sharing.
n.1: Fixed-price does not share costs or savings.
n.2: Cost-plus sets fees, not sharing formulas.
n.3: Per-unit fixes unit rates without sharing.

Procurement.q: A buyer reimbursing the supplier's actual costs is anxious about open-ended exposure and wants a hard limit on the total it can ever be required to pay. Which clause sets the maximum amount payable under a cost-plus arrangement?
Procurement.w: A ceiling price limits the buyer’s exposure under a cost-plus contract.

n.0: Escalation adjusts for cost changes, not cap total.
n.1: Incentive clause sets fees based on performance.
n.2: Renewal governs contract extensions.
n.3: Acceptance clause defines deliverable approval.

Procurement.q: Which contract type often uses a bill of quantities?
Procurement.w: A bill of quantities lists items and unit rates for per-unit contracts.

n.0: Cost-plus is cost-reimbursement, not unit-based billing.
n.1: Target cost may reference costs, not unit bills.
n.3: Fixed-price uses a total sum, not a bill of quantities.
n.4: Time-and-materials bills time and expenses, not quantities.

Procurement.q: Midway through a per-unit contract, changing conditions mean the agreed rates per item may need revising. The project manager wants a defined mechanism for this rather than renegotiating the whole deal. Which clause specifies how changes to unit rates are handled mid-contract?
Procurement.w: Price adjustment clauses allow unit rates to be revised for defined circumstances.

n.1: Force majeure covers unforeseeable events.
n.2: Termination outlines how to end the contract.
n.3: Dispute resolution covers conflicts, not price.
n.4: Scope definition sets deliverable boundaries.

Procurement.q: A project team is commissioning exploratory pilot and prototype work where the effort required cannot be reliably estimated in advance. To ensure the supplier's genuine costs are covered, which two contract types are most suitable for such work?
Procurement.w: Pilot work with uncertain effort suits cost-plus or time-and-materials to cover real costs.

n.0: Lump-sum is a fixed-price model inappropriate for piloting.
n.2: Fixed-price requires well-known scope.
n.3: Target cost needs a reliable baseline.
n.4: Per-unit needs clear unit definitions.

Procurement.q: A buyer reimbursing a supplier's costs wants confidence that delivery quality and progress are being tracked against agreed measures throughout the engagement. Which clause in a cost-plus contract defines how the supplier's performance is measured?
Procurement.w: Performance monitoring clauses set metrics and processes for tracking supplier performance.

n.0: Termination outlines exit procedures.
n.1: Scope defines deliverables, not performance measurement.
n.3: Warranty addresses post-delivery defects.
n.4: Force majeure covers unforeseen events.

Procurement.q: Which reimbursement method encourages supplier efficiency through shared savings?
Procurement.w: Target cost contracts share cost underruns as savings, incentivising efficiency.

n.0: Cost-plus fee pays fixed fee, no savings sharing.
n.1: Fixed-price does not share savings explicitly.
n.2: Per-unit rewards quantity, not efficiency.
n.4: T&M pays actual effort, no shared savings.

Procurement.q: In a contract priced per item, both parties want clarity on who bears the impact if input costs rise over the delivery period. The project manager reviews the terms to confirm this. Which clause allocates responsibility for price escalation in a per-unit contract?
Procurement.w: An escalation clause defines how unit rates adjust for inflation or cost changes.

n.0: Incentive clauses reward performance, not price escalation.
n.2: Scope clauses define deliverables.
n.3: Audit clauses allow record inspection.
n.4: Termination covers contract end procedures.
