Procurement.q: A sponsor wants supplier agreements that reward beating an agreed cost or performance target with an additional fee, motivating efficiency. When advising the sponsor, which two contract types typically include such a performance incentive mechanism?
Procurement.w: Both target cost (cost-plus incentive) and cost-plus incentive contracts include performance fees.

n.0: Lump-sum is fixed price without incentives.
n.1: Time-and-materials reimburses effort, no incentives.
n.3: Per-unit is unit-rate only.
n.4: Fixed-price has no fee incentives.

Procurement.q: A buyer for a novel, high-risk package insists on full visibility of every element of the supplier's expenditure and the ability to scrutinise each cost before reimbursing it. Which contract type is most appropriate when the buyer wants to audit every cost detail?
Procurement.w: Cost-plus fee contracts require detailed cost auditing to reimburse actual expenses.

n.0: Fixed-price does not involve cost audits.
n.1: Time-and-materials may audit effort but not every cost detail.
n.3: Per-unit audits focus on quantities, not costs.
n.4: Target cost audits are needed only for incentives.

Procurement.q: Under a target cost arrangement, the actual outturn cost has exceeded the agreed baseline, and the project manager must apply the agreed formula for apportioning the excess. Which clause in a target cost contract addresses how cost overruns are handled?
Procurement.w: Overrun sharing clauses define how cost overruns are split between buyer and supplier.

n.0: Insurance clauses specify risk coverage arrangements.
n.1: Force majeure addresses unforeseeable events.
n.3: Termination for convenience covers contract cancellation.
n.4: Liquidated damages cover delays or performance failures.

Procurement.q: A buyer reimbursing a supplier's costs is concerned that indirect charges such as administration could inflate the bill, so wants a defined cap on them. Which clause limits the supplier's allowable indirect cost for reimbursement?
Procurement.w: Overhead rate clauses cap the percentage of indirect costs billed by the supplier.

n.0: Acceptance sets approval criteria.
n.1: Escalation adjusts prices for inflation.
n.3: Audit allows inspection of records.
n.4: Scope defines deliverables.

Procurement.q: A project has a firm deadline and the sponsor wants a supplier agreement that financially rewards finishing ahead of the agreed baseline while still sharing efficiency gains. Which contract type is best suited to incentivising early completion?
Procurement.w: Target cost contracts can include incentives for early delivery against the target baseline.

n.0: Time-and-materials doesn’t reward early completion.
n.1: Cost-plus may include incentives, but target cost is designed for shared incentives.
n.3: Per-unit focuses on quantity, not schedule incentives.
n.4: Fixed-price has no formal incentive clauses unless negotiated separately.

Procurement.q: Which clause determines payment timing in a fixed-price contract?
Procurement.w: Milestone payment clauses specify dates or deliverables that trigger payments in fixed-price contracts.

n.0: Audit clauses provide record access, not payment timing.
n.1: Indirect cost clauses limit overhead reimbursement.
n.2: Overrun sharing applies to target cost, not fixed-price.
n.3: Incentive clauses reward performance, not baseline payments.

Procurement.q: Which contract type often requires a performance security bond?
Procurement.w: Fixed-price contracts often require performance bonds to guarantee completion at the set price.

n.1: Time-and-materials seldom use performance bonds.
n.2: Cost-plus fee may not require bonds since buyer covers costs.
n.3: Target cost may include bonds but less common.
n.4: Per-unit contracts rely on unit delivery, not bonds.

Procurement.q: Whatever the pricing model, a project manager wants every proposed change to scope to be raised, assessed, approved and documented through a defined process rather than agreed informally. Which clause ensures scope changes are formally managed in any contract type?
Procurement.w: Change control clauses mandate formal procedures for approving and documenting scope changes.

n.0: Audit covers record access, not scope management.
n.1: Termination covers contract end processes.
n.2: Overrun sharing is specific to target cost.
n.4: Escalation addresses price changes due to cost factors.

Procurement.q: A finance director reviewing a cost-reimbursement agreement wants assurance that the organisation's total liability is bounded, no matter how the supplier's actual spend develops. Which provision in a cost-plus contract caps the buyer's liability?
Procurement.w: A cost ceiling caps the maximum reimbursable amount to limit buyer exposure.

n.0: Unit pricing applies to per-unit contracts.
n.2: Scope defines deliverables, not liability caps.
n.3: Audit covers record inspection, not payment limits.
n.4: Incentive provisions reward performance beyond reimbursement.

Procurement.q: A construction-style package will be paid by measuring the quantities delivered and applying agreed prices to each item of work. Which contract type requires both a Schedule of Rates and a Schedule of Quantities to calculate payments?
Procurement.w: Per-unit contracts use rates per unit and quantities to calculate payments.

n.0: Target cost uses cost baselines, not rates/quantities.
n.1: T&M bills time, not unit quantities.
n.2: Fixed-price uses a total sum, not unit schedules.
n.3: Cost-plus relies on actual costs, not unit schedules.

Procurement.q: In a long-running item-priced contract, the buyer wants protection so that if market prices for the goods fall, the rates it pays can be revised downwards accordingly. Which clause gives the buyer the right to require lower unit rates when market prices fall?
Procurement.w: Price adjustment clauses can include downward adjustments if market rates decrease.

n.0: Warranty covers defects, not price changes.
n.1: Escalation typically allows upward adjustments, not downward.
n.3: Termination ends the contract.
n.4: Audit grants record access.

Procurement.q: Which two contract types commonly include performance bond requirements?
Procurement.w: Both fixed-price and target cost contracts often require performance bonds to secure completion.

n.0: Per-unit and cost-plus usually don’t use bonds.
n.1: T&M bills time, not typically bonded.
n.3: Cost-plus and T&M reimburse actuals, less need for bonds.
n.4: Fixed-price often uses bonds, per-unit less so.

Procurement.q: For a package with highly uncertain costs, the buyer wants full transparency and agrees the supplier will share detailed, verifiable records of actual expenditure. Which contract model is most likely to include an open-book accounting requirement?
Procurement.w: Open-book accounting gives the buyer transparency into the supplier’s actual costs in cost-plus fee contracts.

n.0: Fixed-price has no need for cost transparency.
n.2: T&M tracks time and expenses, but open-book is not always specified.
n.3: Target cost may include transparency but open-book is most common in cost-plus.
n.4: Per-unit only requires quantity verification.

Procurement.q: A supplier has delivered a work package below the agreed target cost, and both parties now need to divide the resulting underspend according to the terms set out at the start. Which clause in a target cost contract governs how savings are split?
Procurement.w: The incentive sharing clause defines percentages or formulas for splitting cost underruns or overruns.

n.0: Escalation adjusts prices for cost changes, not sharing.
n.2: Scope defines project boundaries.
n.3: Acceptance criteria govern deliverable approval.
n.4: Audit allows record inspection, not sharing terms.

Procurement.q: Which reimbursement method suits repeated, measurable work where the total quantity is uncertain, paying the supplier an agreed rate for each unit delivered?
Procurement.w: Per unit quantity (a schedule of rates or remeasurement) pays an agreed rate for each unit delivered. It suits repeated, measurable work where quantities are uncertain; the rate is fixed, but the buyer carries the quantity risk.

n.0: Fixed price is a single lump sum for a defined scope, not a rate per unit.
n.1: Target cost shares overruns and savings against an agreed target.
n.2: Time and materials pays for hours worked and materials used, not a rate per completed unit.
n.4: Cost plus fee reimburses actual costs plus a fee, not an agreed unit rate.

Procurement.q: A buyer reimbursing a supplier's actual costs plus a fee wants to prevent that fee from escalating without limit as the work grows. Which clause in a cost-plus contract limits the supplier's fee percentage?
Procurement.w: A fee ceiling clause caps the maximum allowable supplier fee percentage.

n.0: Overrun sharing applies to target cost contracts.
n.2: Audit covers record inspections.
n.3: Escalation addresses price changes due to cost factors.
n.4: Termination covers contract end provisions.

Procurement.q: Because the buyer is reimbursing the supplier's genuine expenditure, invoices must itemise spend so it can be verified line by line. Which contract type most often uses a price breakdown by labour, materials and overhead?
Procurement.w: Cost-plus fee contracts require detailed cost breakdowns to reimburse actual expenses.

n.0: T&M bills hours and expenses, but not always a formal breakdown.
n.1: Fixed-price may not disclose internal cost breakdowns.
n.2: Per-unit focuses on unit rates, not cost components.
n.4: Target cost may include a breakdown, but less detailed than cost-plus.

Planning.q: A project passes an initial approval but is not reassessed at stage boundaries. What is the most significant governance risk?
o: The business case may no longer reflect current viability
Stakeholder communication becomes excessive and difficult to manage
The project timeline becomes permanently fixed and inflexible
The project manager gradually loses control of delivery tasks
The suppliers gradually gain too much delivery authority
Planning.w: Without review points, the business case is not updated, risking continuation of a non-viable project.

Planning.q: At a stage gate review, a project's costs have clearly risen and its benefits have fallen, yet the project is allowed to continue exactly as before with no reassessment. What has failed here?
o: The accuracy of the original cost estimates
The use of the business case for decision-making
The frequency of stakeholder progress reporting
The initial approval of the project scope
The project manager's control of delivery tasks
Planning.w: Stage gates should use the business case to reassess viability and inform continuation decisions.

Planning.q: After significant replanning, a project manager updates the delivery schedule to reflect the new approach but leaves the business case entirely untouched. What is the main issue with doing this?
o: The stakeholders may receive too much reporting detail
The delivery team may lose motivation over changes
The governance structure may become largely redundant
The business case may not reflect current assumptions
The project manager may have exceeded their authority
Planning.w: Changes in delivery assumptions must be reflected in the business case.

Planning.q: At a review point, a project is forecast to exceed cost tolerances but still deliver strong benefits. What should the business case support?
o: A reassessment of viability before deciding to continue
Automatic continuation because the benefits remain strong
Immediate termination because cost tolerances will be breached
Adjusting cost tolerances to absorb the overspend
Delegation of the decision to the delivery team
Planning.w: Review points require reassessment of all components before continuation decisions.

Planning.q: A project moves from one phase to the next without any formal approval ever being sought at its key milestones. What does this indicate about the way its business case lifecycle is being managed?
o: Improved autonomy for the delivery team
Planning.w: Continuation decisions should be formally reviewed and approved at defined points.

Planning.q: A project is reviewed on schedule at every stage, but even as its risk profile shifts markedly, nothing about the plan or approach is ever changed as a result. What is the main issue?
o: Producing reports containing excessive technical detail
Failure to act on updated business case information
Scheduling far too many formal review points
Lacking the technical expertise to assess risks
Over-communicating minor risks to all stakeholders
Planning.w: Review without action undermines the purpose of updating the business case.

Planning.q: A newly qualified project manager wants to apply business case reviews well as their project progresses through its stages. Which scenario best demonstrates effective use of business case lifecycle reviews?
o: Continuing the project unchanged regardless of shifting circumstances
Avoiding formal reviews to save time and effort
Delegating all continuation decisions to the delivery team
Focusing reviews only on updated cost information
Updating the business case and reassessing viability at each stage
Planning.w: Effective lifecycle management involves updating and reassessing the business case regularly.

Planning.q: Following a review showing that the expected benefits have fallen substantially, the governance board decides to pause the project rather than continue. What does this decision demonstrate?
o: Effective governance decision-making based on the business case
An overreaction to relatively minor benefit changes
A sign of inadequate planning at initiation
A clear failure of project delivery performance
A fundamental lack of stakeholder support for delivery
Planning.w: Pausing based on updated viability reflects effective governance.

Planning.q: A project moves smoothly from stage to stage, but the assumptions set out at initiation are never revisited even though the operating environment has since changed. What is the key risk?
Planning.w: Failure to revisit assumptions leads to decisions based on outdated data.

Planning.q: As a project reaches a defined business case review point, the governance board wants to focus its limited time on what genuinely matters. Which TWO activities are essential at business case review points?
o: Evaluating whether the project remains viable
Planning.w: Review points focus on viability reassessment.

Planning.q: A project manager is maintaining a live business case and needs to know which developments genuinely warrant updating it rather than simply noting them. Which TWO factors should trigger an update to the business case?
Planning.w: Changes in benefits or risk require updates.

Planning.q: Across a project's life, the business case is revisited at defined points to inform certain governance choices about the work. Which TWO decisions are typically made using the business case lifecycle?
o: Whether to modify project scope or approach
Which team member completes a task
Planning.w: Continuation and modification decisions rely on the business case.

Planning.q: Which TWO outcomes indicate poor business case lifecycle management?
Planning.w: Poor lifecycle management leads to continuation of non-viable projects and outdated decisions.

Planning.q: A project manager defines multiple milestones but notices they are not being used in reporting or decision-making. What is the most likely issue?
o: Milestones should only be used at the end of the project
Milestones are not aligned to meaningful control points in the project
Milestones are only relevant for large projects
Stakeholders are not interested in milestone tracking
Milestones are too detailed and should be removed
Planning.w: Milestones must represent meaningful control points to support decision-making and progress tracking.

Planning.q: A project plan records that a key milestone has been reached, yet when the project manager checks, several of the deliverables that the milestone was meant to represent are still incomplete. What does reaching the milestone under these circumstances most clearly indicate?
o: Milestones do not need associated deliverables to close
The milestone was incorrectly defined or poorly controlled
The schedule is flexible and inherently accommodates this
The milestone should now be removed from the plan
The project is running comfortably ahead of schedule
Planning.w: Milestones should represent clear completion points; reaching one without deliverables indicates poor definition or control.

Planning.q: A sponsor prefers a light-touch view of a project and treats the achievement of scheduled milestones as the primary way of judging whether progress is on track. What risk does relying on milestone achievement in this manner introduce?
o: The critical path will effectively manage itself through milestones
Stakeholder engagement will inevitably improve across the project
Over-reliance on milestones may mask underlying delays between them
Overall project timelines will shorten as a direct result
Milestone forecasts will steadily become more accurate over time
Planning.w: Milestones provide snapshots; relying solely on them can hide issues between control points.

Planning.q: Which characteristic best defines an effective project milestone?
o: Represents a significant point with no duration
Must be on the critical path
Planning.w: Milestones are zero-duration events marking significant points or achievements.

Planning.q: In an effort to keep a close watch on delivery, a project manager builds a schedule in which milestones are packed very tightly together, only short intervals apart. What is the most likely consequence of scheduling the milestones so closely?
o: Improved control over detailed project progress
Reduced visibility of progress for stakeholders
Greatly simplified scheduling of the work
Excessive reporting overhead with limited additional insight
Faster overall completion of the project
Planning.w: Too many milestones create administrative burden without improving meaningful control.

Planning.q: A planned milestone that was intended to act as a control point is missed, but the project manager decides not to raise or escalate the slippage to the sponsor or steering group. What risk does this failure to escalate create for the project?
o: Governance controls will absorb the slippage without any action
The delay remains contained within the current stage only
Contingency reserves will offset the miss without formal reporting
Stakeholders may lose confidence due to lack of transparency
The critical path recalculates automatically to hide the delay
Planning.w: Milestones act as control points; failure to escalate undermines governance and trust.

Planning.q: An organisation wants milestones in its projects to function genuinely as control points rather than as mere reporting markers. Which of the following situations best demonstrates milestones being used in this way?
o: Monitoring resource usage continuously throughout each stage
Updating the project schedule at the end of each week
Reviewing individual team member performance against targets
Reviewing progress at key decision points before proceeding
Recording task completion percentages on a daily basis
Planning.w: Milestones provide structured points for review and decision-making.

Planning.q: A project manager sets a milestone in the plan to mark the completion of a significant piece of work but does not define any acceptance criteria against which it will be judged complete. What is the most likely outcome of defining the milestone in this way?
o: More consistent reporting across the project stages
Reduced effort needed to validate the milestone output
Stronger stakeholder confidence in the milestone status
Faster agreement on when the milestone is complete
Ambiguity in determining whether the milestone is achieved
Planning.w: Without criteria, milestone completion becomes subjective and difficult to validate.

Planning.q: A delivery team concentrates almost entirely on hitting each scheduled milestone and pays little attention to the day-to-day progress of the individual tasks that lie between those milestones. What is the key risk of managing progress in this manner?
o: Delays between milestones may go unnoticed
Critical activities will be completed faster
Planning.w: Milestones provide checkpoints, but ignoring detailed progress risks hidden delays.

Planning.q: Which TWO characteristics make milestones effective for progress tracking?
Planning.w: Effective milestones are clear and aligned with meaningful outputs.

Planning.q: Which TWO uses of milestones support governance?
o: Monitoring overall progress at key stages
Planning.w: Milestones support governance through structured reviews and progress tracking.

Planning.q: Which TWO outcomes result from effective milestone management?
Planning.w: Milestones enhance visibility and decision quality.

Planning.q: A project manager reports that the project is ‘on track’ based on overall percentage completion, despite several critical activities being delayed. What is the key issue with this approach?
o: Percentage completion provides too much detail for stakeholders
Stakeholders prefer qualitative updates over quantitative data
Critical activities are less important than overall progress
Progress reporting should focus only on completed tasks
Aggregated progress can mask issues affecting critical activities
Planning.w: High-level metrics like percentage completion can hide critical delays, leading to misleading status reporting.

Planning.q: A project manager issues thorough written progress reports to stakeholders every week, yet those same stakeholders continue to complain that they feel poorly informed about the project. What is the most likely reason for this disconnect?
o: The stakeholders have chosen to disengage from the project
The weekly reporting cycle occurs far too frequently now
The project manager is communicating far too much overall
The reports simply do not contain enough underlying detail
The reports are not aligned with stakeholder information needs
Planning.w: Effective reporting must be tailored to stakeholder needs, not just frequency or detail.

Planning.q: A project manager produces a status report that carefully lists all the activities completed during the period but makes no mention of new risks that have started to emerge. What is the main consequence of reporting in this way?
o: Delayed identification and response to potential issues
Planning.w: Omitting risks prevents proactive management and can lead to larger issues later.

Planning.q: To save time, a project manager adopts a single fixed report format and issues an identical report to every stakeholder, from the executive board through to the delivery team. What risk does using one standard format for all stakeholders create?
o: Reduced ability to standardise future project reporting
Increased time spent producing each individual report
Failure to meet different stakeholder information needs
Greater difficulty in archiving the completed reports
Loss of consistency across the reports issued
Planning.w: Different stakeholders require different levels and types of information for effective decision-making.

Planning.q: A steering group receives a project report in which every activity is shown as 'green', despite the fact that several delays are already well known to the delivery team. What does this discrepancy most clearly indicate?
o: The project manager is reducing unnecessary detail
The project is performing well overall
The reporting system is highly efficient
Status reporting is not accurately reflecting project reality
Planning.w: Misleading status indicators undermine transparency and decision-making.

Planning.q: Which approach best improves the effectiveness of progress reporting?
o: Aligning reporting content with stakeholder decision needs
Increasing the volume of data in reports
Planning.w: Effective reporting focuses on relevant information that supports stakeholder decisions.

Planning.q: Worried about how the sponsor will react, a project manager chooses to hold back reporting some negative progress in the hope that the situation will recover before it needs to be disclosed. What is the most significant risk arising from this decision?
o: Issues may escalate without timely intervention
Planning.w: Delayed reporting prevents timely corrective action and increases risk of escalation.

Planning.q: A stakeholder requests more frequent updates, but the project manager believes current reporting is sufficient. What should guide the decision?
o: Stakeholder information needs and decision requirements
Planning.w: Reporting frequency should align with stakeholder needs and decision-making requirements.

Planning.q: A quality reviewer is examining several examples of project progress reporting in order to identify poor practice. Which of the following scenarios best demonstrates ineffective progress reporting?
o: Reporting key milestones achieved and upcoming risks
Using visual indicators for status updates
Providing concise summaries tailored to stakeholders
Including both qualitative and quantitative data
Planning.w: Reporting deviations without impact lacks context and limits decision-making.

Planning.q: Which TWO elements are essential for effective progress reporting?
o: Clear communication of risks and issues
Planning.w: Effective reporting requires accuracy and transparency about risks and issues.

Planning.q: Which TWO risks arise from poor progress reporting?
o: Misalignment between stakeholders and project team
Planning.w: Poor reporting leads to delays in decisions and misalignment.

Planning.q: Which TWO practices improve communication in progress reporting?
o: Using consistent reporting formats for all audiences
Planning.w: Tailoring and providing context enhance communication effectiveness.

Planning.q: Which TWO characteristics indicate effective status reporting?
Planning.w: Transparency and alignment with objectives are key to effective reporting.

Planning.q: A project reaches a decision gate where outputs have been delivered, but revised forecasts show benefits are now marginal. What is the most appropriate basis for the decision?
o: Proceed and review benefits after closure
Continue because delivery is nearly complete
Delay the gate until benefits improve
Reassess viability against the updated business case
Planning.w: Decision gates are based on ongoing business justification, not sunk cost or stakeholder pressure.

n.0: Post-project review cannot replace a decision gate.
n.1: Near completion does not justify continuation if benefits are weak.
n.2: Delaying avoids the decision rather than addressing viability.
n.4: Stakeholder pressure is not a governance basis.

Planning.q: At a stage boundary, costs have increased but benefits remain achievable with minor delay. What should the decision gate focus on?
o: Team performance over the last stage
Planning.w: Decision gates assess whether the updated cost-benefit balance still justifies continuation.

n.0: Schedule variance alone does not determine viability.
n.1: Team performance is not the primary decision factor.
n.3: Tolerance does not replace structured justification.
n.4: Process compliance is secondary to business value.

Planning.q: A decision gate approves continuation despite marginal benefits because significant costs have already been incurred. What issue does this indicate?
Planning.w: Continuing due to sunk costs reflects escalation of commitment rather than rational decision-making.

n.0: Governance should challenge this bias.
n.2: This reflects poor decision-making, not effective risk management.
n.3: Forecasting is not the core issue here.
n.4: Alignment does not justify poor decisions.

Planning.q: On a change programme, a key decision gate is postponed several times because stakeholders remain unsure whether the promised benefits will actually materialise, so no formal go or no-go decision is taken. What risk does this repeated delay create for the project?
Planning.w: Delaying decisions undermines governance and allows uncertainty to persist without control.

n.0: Delays do not guarantee better decisions.
n.1: Motivation is not directly improved.
n.3: Risk exposure may increase, not reduce.
n.4: Engagement is not the primary outcome.

Planning.q: A project successfully passed every scheduled decision gate and was formally closed on time, yet months later the organisation finds the expected benefits have not been delivered. What does this outcome MOST strongly suggest about the project's governance arrangements?
o: Gates focused on outputs not outcomes
Planning.w: If gates only assess outputs, they fail to ensure benefits are realised.

n.1: Team capability does not explain governance failure.
n.2: Number of reviews is not the core issue.
n.3: Reporting frequency is irrelevant here.
n.4: Stakeholder involvement is not the problem.

Planning.q: A project board approves continuation despite weak benefits justification because termination would damage reputation. What is the primary governance failure?
Planning.w: Decisions should be based on business justification, not reputation concerns.

n.0: Risk planning is not the central issue.
n.1: Reporting structure is not the issue.
n.2: Leadership is not the main factor here.
n.4: Communication is not the root problem.

Planning.q: Midway through a project, market conditions and internal priorities have shifted significantly, and the sponsor has convened a decision gate to confirm whether the project should continue. Which TWO factors should be reassessed at this gate to confirm ongoing viability?
Planning.w: Decision gates reassess costs and benefits to confirm ongoing viability.

n.0: Location is irrelevant.
n.2: Morale is not a primary decision factor.
n.4: Communication frequency is not central.

Planning.q: Which TWO issues indicate weak decision gate governance?
Planning.w: Sunk cost bias and ignoring benefits both indicate poor governance.

n.2: Documentation supports governance.
n.3: Escalation routes strengthen governance.
n.4: Updated forecasts are good practice.

Planning.q: A steering board meets at the end of each life cycle phase to decide whether the project should be authorised to continue, be amended, or be stopped. What is the primary benefit of conducting these decision gate reviews during a project life cycle?
o: Improving day-to-day team morale and motivation
Ensuring alignment with business objectives before proceeding
Accelerating the onboarding of new stakeholders
Reducing the costs charged by suppliers
Planning.w: Decision gate reviews ensure the project remains aligned with business objectives before committing further resources.

n.0: Decision gate reviews are more comprehensive than just simplifying reporting.
n.1: Team morale may be influenced but is not the primary purpose of decision gate reviews.
n.3: Stakeholder onboarding speed is not directly addressed through decision gate reviews.
n.4: Supplier cost reduction is a potential benefit but not the main focus of decision gates.

Planning.q: A construction project is approaching a decision gate at the end of its design phase. Which benefit does this review primarily provide?
o: Confirmation that design deliverables meet approval criteria
Planning.w: Design-phase decision gates confirm that deliverables meet predefined approval criteria before moving forward.

n.0: Marketing materials are unrelated to the design review.
n.1: Workforce productivity is managed operationally, not via decision gates.
n.2: Financial account closure happens at project closure, not a design gate.
n.4: Subcontractor selection is a separate procurement activity.

Planning.q: After deployment, a project manager schedules periodic reviews to check whether the value the project promised is actually materialising for the organisation. Which benefit is most directly associated with conducting such regular benefits reviews?
o: Tracking actual versus forecasted benefits realisation
Improving collaboration between project team members
Planning.w: Regular benefits reviews focus on tracking actual benefits against forecasts to ensure value realisation.

n.0: Legal liability reduction is outside the scope of benefits reviews.
n.1: Automation of tasks is not a direct outcome of benefits reviews.
n.3: Vendor relationships may be indirectly affected but are not the main focus.
n.4: Collaboration may improve but is not the primary objective of benefits reviews.

Planning.q: On a software upgrade project, an independent audit examines the team's work and uncovers several deviations from the organisation's mandated standards. Which of the following best describes the key benefit that this audit delivers?
Planning.w: An independent audit checks compliance with mandated standards. Its key benefit is finding deviations early, while they can still be corrected, which gives assurance to the sponsor and board.

n.0: An audit examines compliance; it does not speed up development work.
n.1: Checking whether benefits are being realised is the purpose of a benefits review, not a compliance audit.
n.2: Licensing costs are a commercial matter and are not reduced by an audit.
n.4: Approving next-phase funding is the purpose of a decision gate, not an audit.

Planning.q: A sponsor and senior stakeholders want reassurance that the project is being formally scrutinised at defined points before further funding is committed. Which benefit of decision gate reviews most helps stakeholders feel confident in project progress?
o: Ensuring personal recognition for team members
Planning.w: Structured decision gate checkpoints give stakeholders visibility and confidence in progress.

n.0: Zero errors cannot be guaranteed by reviews alone.
n.2: Personal recognition is not an inherent deliverable of reviews.
n.3: Throughput is a productivity metric, not a primary gate benefit.
n.4: Reviews mitigate but cannot eliminate all risks.

Planning.q: At a benefits review meeting held during delivery, the data reveals that several expected benefits are falling short of their forecast targets. What advantage does holding this review provide to the project?
o: Opportunity to implement corrective actions early
Planning.w: Identifying shortfalls in benefits reviews enables early corrective actions to steer the project back on track.

n.0: Product launch timing is not dictated by benefits reviews.
n.1: Stakeholder engagement remains active, not closed.
n.2: Risks cannot be entirely terminated by a review.
n.3: Reviews do not guarantee budget increases.

Planning.q: During a mid-project audit, the reviewer identifies discrepancies between the deliverables produced and the agreed quality standards. Which benefit does conducting this audit deliver to the project manager?
Planning.w: Audits highlight non-conformities so that corrective actions can be planned and implemented.

n.0: Procurement speed is not the audit’s primary concern.
n.2: Audits do not directly change resource allocation.
n.3: No review can eliminate every defect instantly.
n.4: Reducing meetings is not a direct audit outcome.

Planning.q: An assurance function schedules independent audits at several points across a project's life cycle to check how the work is being carried out. Which of the following is a key benefit of conducting these audits throughout the life cycle?
o: Ensuring adherence to standards and procedures
Planning.w: Audits ensure the project adheres to required standards and procedures at each stage.

n.1: Team social events are unrelated to audits.
n.2: Marketing reach is not influenced by compliance audits.
n.3: Aesthetics are not the focus of procedural audits.
n.4: Audits help manage risk, but cannot guarantee halving duration.

Planning.q: A project manager is explaining to the sponsor why benefits reviews are held after outputs are delivered into operational use. Which two outcomes, taken together, best illustrate the main advantages of conducting a benefits review?
o: Monitoring realised benefits and identifying corrective actions
Organising a launch event and procuring office supplies
Updating team vacation schedules and sending newsletters
Designing product features and closing accounts
Hiring new staff and renewing licences
Planning.w: Benefits reviews monitor actual benefits and trigger corrective actions when needed.

n.1: Event planning and supply procurement are not core review functions.
n.2: Vacation scheduling and newsletters are unrelated to benefits reviews.
n.3: Feature design and account closure are separate processes.
n.4: Staff hiring and licence renewal are administrative tasks, not benefits review outcomes.

Planning.q: A newly appointed project manager is asked to justify the decision gates built into the governance plan for a major change initiative. Which two of the following, combined, best represent the benefits that decision gate reviews provide?
o: Managing risk early and confirming resources are ready
Moving accountability to the PM and ending all assurance
Approving every change request and adding budget
Guaranteeing delivery dates and eliminating risk
Removing progress reporting and freezing all scope
Planning.w: Decision gates let the board check readiness, including risk and resources, before committing to the next phase, so problems are dealt with early.

n.1: The sponsor stays accountable; gates strengthen assurance rather than end it.
n.2: Gates are go/no-go decisions, not blanket approval of changes or extra funds.
n.3: Gates support informed decisions but cannot guarantee dates or remove risk.
n.4: Gates do not replace progress reporting or freeze scope.

Planning.q: The finance department wants to understand what value benefits reviews add to its own planning and forecasting work on a live project. Which two things do benefits reviews deliver together that would most interest finance?
o: Validating benefit forecasts and informing budget updates
Approving supplier invoices and paying retentions
Calculating earned value and the project's schedule variance
Auditing timesheets and closing cost codes
Planning.w: Benefits reviews check whether forecast benefits are being realised, which informs updates to financial plans and forecasts.

n.1: These are scheduling techniques.
n.2: These are contract payment activities.
n.3: These are earned value analyses, not benefits reviews.
n.4: These are financial control and close-down tasks.

Planning.q: Which two combined benefits result from regular project audits?
o: Approving change requests and releasing contingency
Setting the scope baseline and writing the schedule
Finding compliance gaps and recommending improvements
Guaranteeing compliance and removing all project risk
Replacing the project manager and directing the team
Planning.w: Audits independently check compliance with standards and processes and recommend improvements.

n.0: These are decisions for the appropriate authority, not audit outcomes.
n.1: These are planning activities by the project manager and team.
n.3: Audits give assurance, not guarantees, and cannot remove all risk.
n.4: Auditors are independent; they do not take over management.

Planning.q: A programme office is briefing sponsors on why benefits reviews are conducted at intervals after delivery rather than only at closure. Which two of these outcomes best illustrate the advantages of holding benefits reviews?
o: Confirming compliance with standards and issuing audit findings
Re-estimating the remaining work and updating the project schedule baseline
Comparing actual benefits with targets and prompting corrective action
Approving next-phase funding and confirming readiness at a gate
Recording lessons learned and closing the project's cost codes
Planning.w: Benefits reviews compare the benefits actually being realised with the targets in the business case and benefits plan, and trigger corrective action where they fall short, which is why they continue after delivery.

n.0: Compliance checks and audit findings are the output of an audit, not a benefits review.
n.1: Re-estimating and updating the schedule baseline are re-planning activities during delivery, not benefits reviews.
n.3: Funding approval and readiness checks happen at decision gates during the life cycle.
n.4: Lessons learned and closing cost codes are part of project closure, not reviews of benefits after delivery.

Planning.q: Which combination best describes decision gate review benefits?
o: Validating deliverables and authorising next-phase funding
Checking compliance and issuing formal audit findings
Smoothing resource demand and levelling the overall schedule
Logging issues and assigning actions to their owners
Measuring realised benefits and tracking dis-benefits
Planning.w: A decision gate is a go/no-go point at the end of a phase: it confirms the phase's deliverables are complete and acceptable, re-checks the business case and readiness, and releases funding for the next phase.

n.1: Independent compliance checking with formal findings describes an audit.
n.2: Smoothing and levelling are resource optimisation techniques used in scheduling.
n.3: Logging issues and assigning actions is the issue management process, which runs continuously rather than at gates.
n.4: Measuring realised benefits and dis-benefits is the job of benefits reviews, mostly after delivery.

Planning.q: A governance board convenes at the boundary between two life cycle phases to decide whether the project should proceed, be redirected, or be halted. Completing the statement: the primary purpose of a decision gate review is to ________.
o: ensure that the project remains aligned with its objectives
boost the morale of individual team members
Planning.w: Decision gates are checkpoints to confirm alignment with project objectives.

n.0: Procurement speed is not the main focus of decision gates.
n.2: Organisational charts are defined elsewhere.
n.3: While morale may benefit, it’s not the primary purpose.
n.4: Task automation is unrelated to gate objectives.

Planning.q: As a project moves into its operational phase, the sponsor commissions a benefits review to establish whether the investment is delivering the value set out in the business case. In this context, the main goal of the benefits review is to do what?
o: measure actual benefits against planned targets
organise team social and networking events
resolve interpersonal conflicts within the team
Planning.w: Benefits reviews measure realised benefits versus planned targets to track value delivery.

n.0: Vendor negotiations happen separately.
n.2: License updates are administrative tasks.
n.3: Social events are unrelated to benefits reviews.
n.4: Conflict resolution is not the primary goal.

Planning.q: An organisation runs a series of audit activities at regular points across the life cycle of a large infrastructure project. Considering the purpose of such audits, they primarily help the project team to do what?
Planning.w: Audits identify deviations from required standards so corrective actions can be taken.

n.0: Product launch timing is not controlled by audits.
n.2: Staff hiring is HR’s responsibility.
n.3: Marketing exposure is not an audit function.
n.4: Stakeholder communications remain open after audits.

Planning.q: A project board is concerned about maintaining control and governance as a multi-phase programme progresses. It decides to hold regular decision gate reviews between phases. In terms of governance, these reviews primarily do what?
o: eliminate the need for risk management
Planning.w: Decision gates create formal approval checkpoints to maintain governance.

n.0: Changes can still occur if approved.
n.1: Budget variances must be monitored, not ignored.
n.2: Risk management remains necessary throughout.
n.4: Benefit measurement isn’t automated by gates.

Planning.q: A project manager is explaining to a new team member the value that regular benefits reviews add throughout and beyond a project. Which of the following is NOT a genuine benefit of conducting benefits reviews?
o: Providing insight into benefit realisation progress
Supporting ongoing alignment with strategic goals
Enabling corrective actions if targets are missed
Guaranteeing the elimination of all project risks
Planning.w: Benefits reviews cannot guarantee elimination of all project risks.

n.0: Reviews do provide insight into benefit progress.
n.1: Reviews support alignment with strategic goals.
n.2: Corrective actions are enabled when targets are missed.
n.3: Stakeholders are informed of actual outcomes.

Planning.q: Following an internal audit of a delivery programme, a sponsor asks the project manager what such audit reviews can realistically be expected to produce. Which of the following is NOT a typical outcome of audit reviews?
o: Recommending corrective actions to address findings
Issuing a guarantee that no future issues will occur
Planning.w: No audit can guarantee that no future issues will occur.

n.0: Corrective actions are recommended based on findings.
n.1: Audits identify areas for process improvement.
n.2: Findings are documented for accountability.
n.4: Compliance gaps are highlighted by audits.

Planning.q: Regular decision gate reviews do NOT ________.
o: eliminate the need for ongoing risk management
Planning.w: Gates do not remove the requirement for continuous risk management.

n.0: They help identify issues early.
n.1: They ensure alignment with objectives.
n.2: They do provide formal approval points.
n.4: They facilitate governance.

Planning.q: During a scenario where a project has missed several milestones, which benefit of a decision gate review would be most valuable?
o: Eliminating the need to report to sponsors
Enabling a go/no-go decision to realign resources
Planning.w: In such a scenario, the gate allows stakeholders to decide whether to continue, pause, or stop to reallocate resources.

n.0: Reporting remains essential even after a gate.
n.1: Gate reviews do not reduce meeting frequency.
n.3: Success cannot be guaranteed by a gate.
n.4: Risk management cannot be fully outsourced.

Planning.q: The primary benefit of benefits reviews is to ________.
o: track realised benefits against expected outcomes
Planning.w: Benefits reviews focus on comparing actual benefits to expected results.

n.0: Deliverable creation is part of execution, not benefits review.
n.2: Contractor hiring is separate from benefits reviews.
n.3: Immediate closure is not driven by benefits reviews.
n.4: Designing prototypes is not a review outcome.

Planning.q: Audits throughout the life cycle help to ________.
Planning.w: Audits verify that processes are being followed as defined.

n.0: Marketing is unrelated to audit activities.
n.1: Contract negotiation is outside audit scope.
n.2: No audit can guarantee total defect removal.
n.4: Team resizing is an operational decision.

Planning.q: A project has completed its definition phase and is seeking approval to begin execution. Before work starts, the project board convenes a decision gate. What key benefit does this decision gate provide before the project moves into execution?
Planning.w: Gates formally authorise the allocation of resources for the next phase.

n.0: Unplanned changes still require approval.
n.1: Satisfaction must be managed continuously.
n.2: Completion timing isn’t guaranteed by a gate.
n.4: Defects aren’t resolved automatically by gates.

Planning.q: Which advantage does a benefits review NOT offer?
o: Guaranteeing elimination of all project risks
Planning.w: Benefits reviews cannot guarantee that all risks are eliminated.

n.0: They do highlight shortfalls early.
n.1: They track target progress.
n.2: They recommend plan adjustments.
n.3: They keep stakeholders informed.

Planning.q: A primary goal of an audit is to ________.
o: prioritise the backlog of requirements for the next release
re-estimate the remaining work and update the baseline
approve the funding and resources for the next phase
measure the benefits realised against the business case
Planning.w: An audit is an independent check of compliance. Its primary goal is to identify where the project departs from established standards, policies or regulations so that corrective action can be taken.

n.0: Backlog prioritisation is done by the product owner in iterative delivery, not by auditors.
n.1: Re-estimating and rebaselining are planning activities carried out by the project manager.
n.2: Approving funding for the next phase is a decision gate function, not an audit goal.
n.4: Measuring benefits against the business case is the purpose of a benefits review.

Planning.q: At the end of a phase, a project manager prepares the deliverables for scrutiny by the project board at a decision gate before the next phase is authorised. In governance terms, the decision gate review helps to do what before approving the next phase?
o: confirm that deliverables meet acceptance criteria
Planning.w: Gates confirm that deliverables satisfy defined acceptance criteria before progression.

n.0: Card printing is administrative.
n.1: Donor funding closure is not part of gate reviews.
n.2: Brochure publication is unrelated.
n.4: Consultant hiring is not the gate’s main purpose.

Planning.q: A key benefit of benefits reviews is to ________.
o: authorise funding for the next phase of the project
verify that each deliverable meets its acceptance criteria
capture lessons about how the project was managed
identify whether expected benefits are on track
confirm compliance with organisational standards and policies
Planning.w: Benefits reviews check whether the benefits set out in the business case are being realised as planned, so corrective action can be taken if they are not.

n.0: Authorising next-phase funding happens at a decision gate.
n.1: Checking deliverables against acceptance criteria is quality control, not a benefits review.
n.2: Lessons about how the project was managed are captured in post-project and lessons learned reviews.
n.4: Confirming compliance with standards and policies is the purpose of an audit.

Planning.q: A programme office is promoting the use of regular project audits across its portfolio and lists the advantages they bring. Which of the following is NOT a genuine benefit of conducting regular project audits?
o: Providing a basis for corrective action plans
Guaranteeing that no future audit findings will occur
Detecting process gaps at an early stage
Planning.w: No audit can guarantee that future findings will never occur.

n.0: They provide corrective action bases.
n.2: Audits do enhance compliance confidence.
n.3: They detect gaps early.
n.4: They document accountability.

Planning.q: On a completed change project, the realised benefits have significantly exceeded the forecasts set out in the business case. Given that regular benefits reviews were carried out, what is a key advantage the organisation gains from having conducted them?
o: Removing the need for any future reviews
Automatically increasing the approved project budget
Reducing the project team size immediately
Understanding the drivers of success for replication
Planning.w: When benefits exceed forecasts, reviews help identify success factors to replicate.

n.0: Future reviews remain valuable.
n.1: Budgets are not automatically changed.
n.2: Team size isn’t reduced based on benefit results alone.
n.3: Communication continues even after positive results.

Planning.q: The purpose of an audit review is to ________.
o: verify adherence to defined procedures and standards
Planning.w: Audit reviews verify that procedures and standards are being followed correctly.

n.0: Marketing planning is not an audit task.
n.1: Firewall configuration is IT’s domain.
n.2: Hiring is HR’s responsibility.
n.3: Promotional design is marketing work.

Planning.q: Midway through the operational phase, a benefits review reveals that several target benefits are falling short of the levels forecast in the business case. In this situation, a benefits review primarily helps the organisation to do what?
o: identify corrective measures to improve outcomes
Planning.w: Benefits reviews identify corrective measures if targets are not being met.

n.1: Staff termination is not a review outcome.
n.2: Press releases are unrelated.
n.3: Risk assignment remains the risk manager’s role.
n.4: Stakeholder communication continues throughout.

Planning.q: A project manager is briefing stakeholders on why decision gate reviews are built into the project's governance framework. Which of the following is NOT a genuine advantage of decision gate reviews?
o: Confirming readiness to enter the next phase
Ensuring resources are available for continuation
Removing the need for any future risk assessments
Planning.w: Decision gates do not remove the need for ongoing risk assessments.

n.0: They do provide clear decision points.
n.1: They confirm readiness.
n.2: They ensure resources are available.
n.4: They facilitate alignment.

Planning.q: An assurance team is asked to audit a project that has been running for several months against the organisation's approved procedures. Considering its purpose, the main benefit of such a project audit is to do what?
o: highlight discrepancies between practice and policy
Planning.w: Audits highlight where actual practice diverges from established policy or procedure.

n.0: Profitability cannot be guaranteed by audits.
n.2: Budgets aren’t reallocated automatically by audits.
n.3: UI design is not an audit function.
n.4: Retreat planning is unrelated.

Planning.q: During an audit review of a regulated project, the assurance team discovers that a critical compliance standard was missed during the previous phase. In this scenario, what does the audit review process enable the project to do?
o: Rapid identification and correction of the non-compliant area
Immediate cancellation of the project without review
Automatic distribution of performance rewards to staff
Disregarding the concerns raised by stakeholders
Halting all further compliance monitoring efforts
Planning.w: Audits enable rapid detection and correction of compliance failures.

n.1: Cancellation without review is not a standard process.

n.4: Complexity may decrease usability.

Planning.q: A project manager is assessing whether each report actually addresses what its particular readers require. The term ______ refers to the relevance of information to stakeholders' needs.
Planning.w: Pertinence indicates how well information matches stakeholder requirements.

n.1: Opacity prevents clarity.
n.2: Magnitude refers to size or amount, not relevance.
n.3: Volatility refers to change frequency, not relevance.
n.4: Redundancy means duplication, not relevance.

Planning.q: When preparing an executive summary for a time-poor project board, the project manager must decide which figures to include. Selecting the most ______ metrics prevents information overload.
Planning.w: Critical metrics focus on key indicators that drive decisions without overwhelming stakeholders.

n.1: Excessive metrics cause overload.
n.2: Obscure metrics lack clarity.
n.3: Verbose metrics add unnecessary detail.
n.4: Irrelevant metrics do not inform decisions.

Planning.q: On a project where stakeholders receive daily progress emails, the project manager is evaluating the effects of updating them this often. Which of the following is NOT a benefit of this reporting frequency?
o: Maintaining engagement through frequent regular updates
Allowing important insights to be overlooked due to information overload
Enabling faster feedback on newly emerging issues
Supporting timely and well-informed decision making
Increasing stakeholder visibility into current project status
Planning.w: Daily emails can overload stakeholders, causing important insights to be missed.

n.0: Regular updates help maintain engagement.
n.2: They enable quicker feedback.
n.3: Timely information supports decisions.
n.4: Daily updates do increase visibility.

Planning.q: A project manager is explaining to a new team member why the project routinely produces information and reports for its stakeholders. Which of the following is NOT a key purpose of producing project information?
Planning.w: Project information aims to be transparent, not to conceal performance issues.

n.0: It communicates what actions and who is responsible.
n.1: Risk management relies on accurate information.
n.2: Progress tracking is a core purpose.
n.4: Information should directly inform decisions.

Planning.q: A sponsor complains that the monthly report includes too much detail. Which is NOT a reason to include only high-level information?
o: It focuses on key metrics that drive decisions
It ensures stakeholders miss critical detailed issues
It aligns content with audience needs
Planning.w: Excluding too much detail risks stakeholders not seeing important issues, which is not desirable.

n.0: Conciseness is a key report quality.
n.1: High-level focus does highlight decision drivers.
n.2: Reducing overload prevents overwhelm.
n.4: Audience alignment is essential.

Planning.q: A project manager is designing a survey to gather stakeholder feedback on a recently delivered release. Which of the following practices is NOT recommended when collecting this feedback data?
o: Defining clear objectives for the survey
Using leading questions to bias responses
Planning.w: Leading questions bias feedback, undermining data quality and credibility.

n.0: Clear objectives guide relevant questions.
n.2: Systematic analysis yields actionable insights.
n.3: Representative sampling improves validity.
n.4: Anonymity can increase honesty.

Planning.q: During a design review, the team is debating whether to adopt a standardised report template for all future project reports. Which of the following is NOT a benefit of using such a template?
o: Inconsistencies between sections due to varied formats
Easier comparison across successive project phases
Planning.w: A standard template reduces inconsistencies; inconsistent formats are a drawback, not a benefit.

n.0: They enhance clarity for stakeholders.
n.2: Templates speed up preparation.
n.3: They help enforce data quality standards.
n.4: They allow phase-to-phase comparisons.

Planning.q: A project team has moved to capturing progress metrics continuously as the work happens, rather than compiling a batch of figures at the end of each week. The project manager reviews the effects of this real-time data collection. Which of the following is NOT a benefit of collecting data in this way?
o: Enhancing the team's responsiveness to change
Allowing decisions based on outdated information
Identifying issues as they actually occur
Planning.w: Real-time collection prevents outdated information; using outdated data is not a benefit.

n.0: Responsiveness improves with immediacy.
n.2: Lag in reporting is reduced.
n.3: Real-time data helps spot problems instantly.
n.4: Transparency is enhanced with current data.

Planning.q: On a project where all key decisions are recorded in a log that is visible to stakeholders, the project manager reviews the effects of this openness. Which of the following is NOT an advantage of this practice?
o: Discouraging accountability by hiding action records
Planning.w: Public logs enhance accountability; hiding records would have the opposite effect and is not advantageous.

n.1: Pending items tracking relies on logs.
n.2: Logs serve as historical reference.
n.3: Transparency builds trust.
n.4: Logs provide an audit trail for review.

Planning.q: A project manager must communicate a set of recent decisions to a stakeholder group whose members have widely varying backgrounds and technical knowledge. Which practice is NOT effective for communicating decisions to such a diverse group?
o: Using overly technical jargon without explanation
Planning.w: Technical jargon without context alienates non-technical stakeholders and undermines communication.

n.0: Multiple channels ensure broader reach.
n.2: Clarity and conciseness are communication best practices.
n.3: Summaries and appendices meet different depth needs.
n.4: Audience-tailored messaging improves understanding.

Planning.q: Following a scheduled project review that has produced new information, the project manager is considering whether to revise the plan. What is a common reason to re-plan activities after a review?
Planning.w: Re-planning incorporates new risk information to keep the plan realistic and achievable.

n.0: Communication reduction is unrelated to plan accuracy.
n.1: Team meetings aren’t eliminated by re-planning.
n.2: Close-down deliverables occur at project end, not during re-planning.
n.3: Celebrations don’t drive plan changes.

Planning.q: A resource review reveals that a key developer is overallocated across several concurrent tasks. Why should the project manager re-plan the affected activities in response?
o: To rebalance workloads and avoid burnout
To hide the issue from sponsors
Planning.w: Re-planning reallocates tasks so no one is overloaded, maintaining productivity and morale.

n.0: Budget reporting is separate from resource allocation.
n.2: Indefinite extension is unrealistic and unhelpful.
n.3: Ignoring constraints leads to missed deadlines.
n.4: Transparency builds trust; hiding issues is poor practice.

Planning.q: A review highlights that the agreed scope has grown while the availability of several team members has changed. Which combined reasons justify re-planning the project's activities?
o: To fully automate reporting and remove the need for management oversight
To adjust timelines due to scope changes and rebalance tasks based on resource shifts
To reduce the frequency of stakeholder updates and conceal resource shortfalls
To remove the risk register entirely and shorten quality assurance checks
To schedule additional informal meetings and postpone all outstanding project decisions
Planning.w: Re-planning aligns the schedule with the new scope and resources to keep the project on track.

n.0: Automation without oversight risks data errors and misalignment.
n.2: Reducing updates and hiding gaps undermines governance.
n.3: Removing risk and quality practices increases exposure.
n.4: Informal meetings and decision delays don’t address the root issues.

Planning.q: Following a schedule review that exposed bottlenecks delaying dependent work, the project manager considers revising the plan. Activities may be re-planned to address ______ issues identified during the review.
Planning.w: Adjusting the critical path addresses schedule bottlenecks revealed in the review.

n.0: Morale is managed through engagement, not schedule re-planning.
n.1: Preferences aren’t typically the driver for re-planning.
n.2: Office layout doesn’t impact the project schedule.
n.3: Marketing trends are outside immediate project activity plans.

Planning.q: A project manager is deciding whether a recent project review warrants revising the activity plan at all. Which of the following is NOT a valid reason to re-plan activities after a review?
Planning.w: Early celebration doesn’t require adjusting the activity plan.

n.0: Priority shifts necessitate plan adjustments.
n.2: New risk responses may alter timelines or resources.
n.3: Approved scope additions must be reflected in the plan.
n.4: Performance variances often trigger schedule changes.

Planning.q: A benefits review concludes that an approved deliverable must be expanded in order to realise the intended outcomes. Why might the team re-plan the affected activities?
o: To disregard the approved change request entirely
To reduce communication with affected stakeholders
To integrate the additional work into the schedule
To skip the remaining testing and review phases
To close the project earlier than planned
Planning.w: Re-planning ensures the expanded deliverable is scheduled and resourced appropriately.

n.0: Ignoring change requests breaches governance.
n.1: Communication should increase, not reduce.
n.3: Skipping tests risks quality failures.
n.4: Early closure ignores the needed work.

Planning.q: At a gate review, quality audit findings reveal that some completed work requires rework before the project can proceed. Why should the schedule be re-planned in response?
o: To hide defects from the team
To allocate time for corrective actions
To push all tasks to sponsors
Planning.w: Scheduling corrective work prevents future defects and maintains quality standards.

n.0: Skipping rework risks non-conformance.
n.1: Hiding defects undermines transparency.
n.2: Audit frequency is separate from re-planning tasks.
n.4: Sponsors don’t perform project tasks.

Planning.q: A review highlights both a shift in business priorities and a shortage of currently available resources. Which combined reasons justify re-planning the project's activities?
o: To automate all tasks and minimise oversight
To ignore stakeholder input and reduce documentation
To double the team size and eliminate risk registers
To delay every deliverable by a fixed margin
To reschedule lower-priority tasks and reallocate limited resources
Planning.w: Rescheduling tasks and reallocating resources align the plan with current priorities and availability.

n.0: Automation and no oversight increase risk.
n.1: Ignoring input and reducing docs undermines governance.
n.2: Team doubling and registry removal are impractical fixes.
n.3: Uniform delays ignore task criticality and dependencies.

Planning.q: Unexpected vendor delays mean that key materials will now arrive later than planned. The project schedule must therefore be updated to reflect the new ______ constraints.
Planning.w: Late arrival of materials changes when work can start, so the schedule must be re-planned around the new delivery constraints (dates when materials will actually be available).

n.1: The vendor delay does not alter what is being designed; it alters when materials arrive.
n.2: The deliverables required have not changed, so scope is not the constraint being updated.
n.3: The standard the materials must meet is unchanged; only their arrival date has moved.
n.4: Nothing in the scenario changes who must approve the work; the constraint is material delivery timing.

Planning.q: A mid-project audit finds that the initial estimates were overly optimistic when compared with actual performance to date. Which of the following is NOT an appropriate trigger to re-plan activities?
o: Incorporating audit recommendations into the schedule
Believing the original estimates were infallible
Revising the critical path to reflect reality
Adjusting durations based on actual performance
Planning.w: Assuming estimates are perfect prevents necessary corrections; it’s not a valid trigger for re-planning.

n.0: Resource changes address bottlenecks.
n.1: Audit recommendations often require schedule updates.
n.3: Updating the critical path reflects the true sequence of tasks.
n.4: Adjusting durations aligns estimates with reality.

Planning.q: A newly appointed project manager is asked by the sponsor to produce an integrated project management plan for an upcoming programme of work. Which of the following BEST describes what such a plan is?
o: A set of separate plans each owned by a different function
A detailed schedule listing only the project's start and end dates
A register capturing the lessons learned from previously completed projects
A high-level summary intended mainly for communicating with external stakeholders
A single, coordinated document that combines all key project elements and controls
Planning.w: An integrated plan brings together all controls, objectives, and management information in one place.

n.0: Personal goals are not project management content.
n.1: Schedules are just one component of the plan.
n.2: Lessons learned inform plans but are not the plan itself.
n.3: Marketing materials are not project plans.

Planning.q: A project manager is assembling the contents of the integrated project management plan and reviewing which items genuinely belong within it. Which of the following would NOT typically be included in an integrated project management plan?
Planning.w: Performance appraisals are confidential line-management records; they are not part of the integrated project management plan.

n.0: The scope statement defines what will be delivered and is a core part of the plan.
n.2: The plan sets out the risk management approach.
n.3: The quality management plan is a subsidiary plan brought into the integrated plan.
n.4: The schedule baseline is a core element of the plan.

Planning.q: A project sponsor asks the project manager to confirm that the integrated project management plan will cover the full range of management areas needed to control delivery. A well-structured plan of this kind will typically include which of the following?
o: The risk register and the project issue log exclusively
The communication plan and the stakeholder register only
Objectives, scope, schedule, resources, risks, and quality management
Procurement contracts and supplier payment schedules on their own
Financial budgets and profit targets set for the shareholders
Planning.w: A comprehensive plan covers all critical management areas for the project.

n.0: Risk is just one part.
n.1: Communication is important but not the only section.
n.3: Holiday schedules are not relevant.
n.4: Financials are just one aspect.

Planning.q: A project team is debating whether to maintain a single coordinated plan or to let each function run its own separate documents. As project manager, you argue for an integrated approach. Why is integration important in a project management plan?
o: It enables each team member to plan and work in isolation
It ensures all elements of the project work together towards common objectives
It provides a guarantee that the project will encounter no risks
It replaces the requirement for a separate project business case
It removes the need to maintain any formal project documentation
Planning.w: Integration aligns objectives, controls and processes for project success.

n.0: Teamwork is essential.
n.2: Risk cannot be eliminated.
n.3: Business cases are still needed.
n.4: Documentation is still required.

Planning.q: An organisation has decided to consolidate its various project documents into one integrated project management plan for a major initiative. What is the main benefit of adopting a single, integrated plan?
o: It removes the need for any formal change management process
It provides a guarantee that the project is delivered on time
It provides a clear and consistent reference for all stakeholders
It lowers the amount of communication the project actually requires
It concentrates attention solely on the project's technical requirements
Planning.w: An integrated plan gives everyone a unified view of how the project will be managed.

n.0: Change management is always needed.
n.1: Plans support delivery but don’t guarantee it.
n.3: Communication remains important.
n.4: Non-technical areas are also covered.

Planning.q: While drafting the integrated project management plan, a project manager is identifying the sections that establish the time framework and other core controls for delivery. Which of the following is a typical content section of such a plan?
Planning.w: The schedule baseline is the agreed time framework against which progress is controlled, and it is a standard section of the integrated plan.

n.1: Market share analysis is business strategy information, not a project control.
n.2: Competitor products are market information, not part of the plan.
n.3: Personal development plans are individual HR records.
n.4: Corporate accounts are organisational financial statements, not part of a project plan.

Planning.q: A project management plan brings the project's risk, quality and communication strategies together within a single integrated document rather than treating them separately. What is the advantage of this approach?
o: Risk and quality can be ignored
All project aspects are coordinated and aligned
Planning.w: Integration ensures all management disciplines support each other.

n.0: Documentation remains essential.
n.1: All areas should still be addressed.
n.3: Both technical and non-technical issues are considered.
n.4: Stakeholder feedback is always important.

Planning.q: A project manager is reviewing a draft integrated project management plan and removing any content that does not properly belong in it. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be found in such a plan?
o: The allocation of resources across tasks
The strategy for managing project risks
The definition of the project scope
The procedures for controlling any agreed changes
A record of individual staff appraisal ratings
Planning.w: Appraisal ratings are confidential HR records and have no place in the integrated project management plan.

n.0: Resource allocation is part of the plan's resource management content.
n.1: The risk management strategy is included in the plan.
n.2: Scope definition is a core part of the plan.
n.3: Change control procedures are included in the plan.

Planning.q: Within the integrated project management plan for a change initiative, one section is dedicated to how uncertainty affecting the project will be handled. What is the primary function of the risk management approach in this plan?
o: To outline how risks will be identified, assessed, and managed
To record issues that have occurred and the actions to resolve them
To set out how changes to the baseline will be assessed and approved
To define the acceptance criteria and quality checks for outputs
To schedule the decision gates at which the business case is reviewed
Planning.w: The risk management approach in the plan sets out how uncertainty will be handled: how risks will be identified, analysed, responded to, monitored, escalated and closed, and by whom.

n.1: Recording issues that have already happened is the role of the issue log and issue management process.
n.2: Assessing and approving changes to the baseline is the change control approach.
n.3: Acceptance criteria and quality checks belong to the quality management approach.
n.4: Decision gates are part of the governance and life cycle arrangements, not the risk approach.

Planning.q: A project manager is briefing the team on how the integrated project management plan will be used to guide and control delivery throughout the project. Which statement about the integrated project management plan is TRUE?
o: It should be withheld from external stakeholders to protect confidentiality
It is produced only after the project has formally closed
It serves as the master document guiding all aspects of project delivery
It removes the need to maintain a separate risk register
It is required exclusively for large information technology delivery projects
Planning.w: The integrated plan is the main reference for managing and controlling the project.

n.0: Plans should be accessible to stakeholders as appropriate.
n.1: Planning happens before work starts.
n.3: Registers support, not replace, plans.
n.4: All project types require plans.

Planning.q: As the project manager finalises the schedule baseline section of the integrated project management plan, they consider what information this part of the document should capture. What is typically included in the schedule baseline section?
o: The approved budget and cost breakdown structure
Key milestones and timelines for deliverables
Risk register and named risk owners
Planning.w: The schedule baseline is the approved timeline against which progress is measured, so it records the key milestones and the planned dates for activities and deliverables.

n.0: The budget and CBS form the cost baseline, a separate section of the plan.
n.2: Risks and their owners are recorded in the risk register and risk approach, not the schedule baseline.
n.3: Communication frequency is set out in the communication management plan.
n.4: Acceptance criteria belong to quality planning, defining when deliverables are acceptable.

Planning.q: A project board wants assurance that the integrated project management plan makes clear who is accountable for what across delivery. Which element is ESSENTIAL to include for the plan to be effective?
o: A full register of configuration items and versions
The time-phased budget and cash-flow profile
Defined roles and responsibilities for project delivery
A detailed log of lessons learned from previous projects
Planning.w: The board wants to know who is accountable for what. The plan shows this by defining roles and responsibilities, often through the OBS and a RACI chart with one accountable person for each work package.

n.0: A register of configuration items controls products and versions, not delivery accountability.
n.1: The budget and cash-flow profile show cost over time, not who is accountable.
n.3: The communication schedule shows who receives information and when, not who is accountable for the work.
n.4: Lessons from earlier projects inform planning, but they do not show who is accountable on this project.

Planning.q: A section of the integrated project management plan sets out how any proposed alterations to scope, schedule and cost will be raised, assessed and approved during delivery. This section is known as which of the following?
Planning.w: Change control procedures outline how project changes will be approved and tracked.

n.0: Stakeholder analysis reviews project influence.
n.2: Competitor review is a business analysis task.
n.3: Market analysis is outside plan content.
n.4: Reward strategy is a HR function.

Planning.q: A project manager is explaining to stakeholders the genuine benefits that an integrated project management plan brings to delivery, and wants to correct a common misunderstanding. Which of the following is NOT a typical benefit of such a plan?
o: Ensuring alignment of all project management processes
Removing the need for change control once approved
Providing a unified source of project information
Planning.w: The approved plan is the baseline that change control protects; it does not remove the need for change control. Changes still need formal assessment and the plan must be updated.

n.0: The plan provides the baseline for monitoring and decision-making.
n.1: Integration aligns all the subsidiary plans and processes.
n.3: The plan clarifies who does what.
n.4: A unified source of information is a key benefit.

Planning.q: Within an integrated project management plan, the project manager is drafting the section that deals with the threats and opportunities the project may face. What would a typical risk management section of this plan include?
o: The reimbursement terms agreed with external suppliers
How risks will be identified, assessed and responded to
The detailed log of issues that are already affecting delivery
The acceptance criteria for each project deliverable
The procedure for raising and approving change requests
Planning.w: The risk management section sets out how risks will be identified, analysed, responded to, monitored and escalated, including roles and tolerances.

n.0: Reimbursement terms belong to the procurement strategy and contracts.
n.2: Issues already affecting delivery are managed in the issue log, not the risk management approach.
n.3: Acceptance criteria belong to the quality section.
n.4: Change request procedures belong to the change control section.

Planning.q: A project manager is justifying to the sponsor why a communication plan should form part of the integrated project management plan rather than be handled informally. Why should communication plans be included in the plan?
