o: To hold confidential personal data about each individual project team member
To transfer the project manager's reporting duties onto the wider team
To ensure the right information reaches the right people at the right time
To guarantee every stakeholder will support the project's objectives
To remove the need for any formal stakeholder analysis activities entirely
Planning.w: A planned communication approach delivers timely, targeted information to each stakeholder, manages expectations and is aligned with the rest of the plan.

n.0: The plan is not a store for personal data; that would raise data protection concerns.
n.1: The project manager remains responsible for reporting.
n.3: Good communication builds support but cannot guarantee it.
n.4: Stakeholder analysis is what drives the communication plan, so it is still needed.

Planning.q: During delivery, a project manager is deciding under what circumstances the integrated project management plan should be formally revised and reissued to the team. A project management plan should be updated when which of the following occurs?
o: A weekly progress report is issued to the project sponsor
A task finishes a day early but within its available float
There are significant changes to scope, schedule, cost, or risk
A risk owner revises the probability score of a minor risk
A team member reports minor progress slippage that is within tolerance
Planning.w: The plan is a controlled baseline document, revised through change control when there are significant changes to scope, schedule, cost or risk.

n.0: Routine reporting compares progress with the plan; it does not change the plan.
n.1: A task finishing early within float does not alter the baseline.
n.3: A minor change to a risk score is recorded in the risk register, not by reissuing the plan.
n.4: Minor progress within tolerance is managed day to day and does not require the plan to be reissued.

Planning.q: A project manager is describing to a colleague what the quality management plan contributes when it sits within the wider integrated project management plan. What is the role of the quality management plan within the integrated plan?
o: It allocates the contingency budget for correcting any defects
It lists each benefit and when it is expected to be realised
It defines standards, processes, and responsibilities for delivering quality outputs
It records the detailed inspection and test results for every single completed deliverable
It replaces the need for independent quality assurance reviews
Planning.w: The quality management plan sets out the standards, acceptance criteria, methods, quality activities and responsibilities that will show the outputs are fit for purpose.

n.0: Contingency is a budget matter controlled through governance, not the quality plan's role.
n.1: Benefits and their timing are set out in the benefits management plan.
n.3: Test and inspection results are quality records produced by quality control, not the plan itself.
n.4: The plan defines how assurance will happen; it does not replace it.

Planning.q: At the start of a new project, the organisation needs to confirm who will lead the preparation of the integrated project management plan and coordinate the necessary contributions. Who is typically responsible for preparing this plan?
o: The finance director acting alone without any wider input
The project manager with input from the team and stakeholders
Individual team members each planning their own work separately
The marketing department working on behalf of the sponsor
External suppliers contracted to deliver the project's outputs
Planning.w: The project manager leads the process, gathering input from all relevant parties.

n.0: Finance leads budgeting, not planning overall.
n.2: Team input is essential, but integration is managed centrally.
n.3: Marketing may contribute, but does not lead planning.
n.4: Suppliers may be consulted, but not responsible.

Planning.q: A project manager is arguing for a dedicated resource management section within the integrated project management plan to support smooth delivery. What is the benefit of including such a section in the plan?
o: It removes the need for regular project progress reporting
It replaces the need for a work breakdown structure
It guarantees that no scheduled activity will ever need to be moved or delayed
It ensures that people, equipment and materials are allocated effectively
It defines the acceptance criteria for each project deliverable
Planning.w: A resource management section identifies the resources needed, matches them to availability and plans their allocation, so people, equipment and materials are used effectively.

n.0: Progress reporting is still needed to monitor delivery.
n.1: Resource needs are derived from the WBS, so it is still required.
n.2: Resource planning reduces conflicts but cannot guarantee that no activity will move.
n.4: Acceptance criteria belong to quality planning.

Planning.q: A sponsor questions whether the effort of producing a full integrated project management plan is really worthwhile for the success of an upcoming project. Why is producing such a plan important for project success?
o: It lets team members work independently without any coordination between them
It replaces the requirement to produce a project business case
It aligns objectives, processes and controls across all areas of the project
It provides a guarantee that the project will have no risks
It removes the need for communication between the project team members
Planning.w: Integration ensures all project elements work together toward common objectives.

n.0: Coordination is required for success.
n.1: A business case is still needed.
n.3: Risks cannot be fully eliminated.
n.4: Communication remains essential for project success.

Planning.q: A project manager on a large IT transformation programme is consolidating separate team documents into one governing document before delivery begins. When explaining the value of this approach to the sponsor, which is a key benefit of having a single integrated project management plan?
o: It removes the need for a formal change control process
It avoids having to define the project's objectives clearly upfront
It supports a separate management plan for each department involved
It provides a clear reference point for all team members and stakeholders
It makes detailed project budgeting an entirely unnecessary planning activity
Planning.w: A single plan ensures everyone is working from the same information.

n.0: Change control is still needed.
n.1: Objectives must be defined clearly.
n.2: Integrated planning combines all departments.
n.4: Budgets are always necessary.

Planning.q: An integrated project management plan helps project managers by:
o: Reducing the need for monitoring project performance
Planning.w: A comprehensive plan enables informed, effective management decisions.

n.0: Resources must be planned and managed.
n.2: All project areas, not just technical, are included.
n.3: Activities should be coordinated, not isolated.
n.4: Performance monitoring is still required.

Planning.q: A project affecting several departments has many stakeholders with differing expectations of what will be delivered and when. The project manager relies on the integrated project management plan to keep everyone aligned. How does an integrated project management plan support stakeholder engagement?
o: By providing consistent information and setting clear expectations
By only sharing information with the project manager
By guaranteeing no changes will occur
By removing the need for progress reporting
By focusing only on internal communications
Planning.w: Consistent information keeps all stakeholders aligned and informed.

n.1: Communication should reach all relevant parties.
n.2: Change is a normal part of projects.
n.3: Reporting progress is still needed.
n.4: Both internal and external communications matter.

Planning.q: During the definition phase of an organisational change project, the project manager is drawing together scope, schedule, cost and quality into one coherent document. In this context, a key reason to produce an integrated project management plan is to:
o: Ensure every team member sets their own objectives
Allow separate teams to develop their own processes in isolation
Align all project activities and objectives to deliver value
Replace the need for quality assurance
Planning.w: Alignment maximises the project’s ability to deliver planned value.

n.0: Objectives should be agreed for the whole project.
n.1: Processes should be coordinated, not isolated.
n.3: Quality assurance remains necessary.
n.4: Schedules must be updated as needed.

Planning.q: A construction project faces threats spread across design, procurement and delivery, and the project manager wants a coordinated way of handling them rather than treating each in isolation. Integrated project management planning helps to reduce project risks by:
o: Replacing the risk register with a single milestone schedule
Ensuring all risks are identified, assessed and managed in one place
Focusing risk effort only on the project's critical path
Transferring every identified risk to the project sponsor to own
Delegating all risk decisions to a separate risk committee
Planning.w: A single plan helps spot and manage risks more effectively.

n.0: Risk management should involve the whole team.
n.2: All significant risks must be assessed.
n.3: Risk registers are still needed.
n.4: Documentation, not just verbal updates, is vital.

Planning.q: A company runs a project through several functional teams that each maintain their own separate plans, with no single overarching document tying the work together. Which outcome is most likely if a project does NOT use an integrated management plan?
o: Clear and consistent direction for the project
Increased confusion, duplication of effort and misalignment
Planning.w: Without integration, teams may lack alignment and efficiency.

n.0: Direction can become unclear.
n.1: Benefits are less likely to be delivered.
n.3: Performance monitoring is harder without one plan.
n.4: Communication often breaks down without a single plan.

Planning.q: On a systems upgrade project, requests to alter scope arrive regularly from different stakeholders, and the project manager has embedded the change process within the wider plan. What is a benefit of integrating change control into the project management plan?
o: Schedule and budget baselines stay fixed once changes are approved
Change requests are logged separately from the management plan
Only the project manager needs to authorise significant changes
Approved changes are applied before their impact has been assessed
All changes are documented and evaluated for impact on the entire project
Planning.w: Integrated change control maintains project alignment and records impacts.

n.0: Stakeholder approval is usually essential.
n.1: All changes, not just technical, must be managed.
n.2: Budgets and schedules may still change.
n.3: Ignoring changes can cause problems.

Planning.q: An integrated project management plan helps ensure that:
o: Project objectives can change at random
All team members are working towards the same project goals
Each department can operate without regard to others
Planning.w: A single plan focuses the team on common, clearly defined goals.

n.0: Objectives should be stable.
n.2: Performance should always be monitored.
n.3: Success criteria must be clear and agreed.
n.4: Coordination is required across the whole team.

Planning.q: Before releasing funding for the delivery phase of a major infrastructure project, a sponsor insists on seeing a fully integrated project management plan. Why is it valuable for project sponsors to require an integrated project management plan before authorising delivery?
o: It confirms that the detailed technical design is fully complete before any planning begins
It replaces the need for holding regular stage-gate reviews throughout the delivery phase
It locks the project scope completely so that no further changes can ever occur
It gives assurance that all aspects of the project are coordinated and risks are managed
It transfers full accountability for all delivery outcomes onto the project manager alone
Planning.w: Sponsors want assurance the project is well planned, controlled and coordinated.

n.0: Change is a normal part of projects.
n.1: The business case remains important.
n.2: Stakeholder input is vital throughout.
n.4: Progress should still be reviewed regularly.

Scope Management.q: A project team begins development based on high-level requirements, but stakeholders later dispute what was agreed. What is the most likely root cause?
o: Stakeholders were not involved in progress reporting
Scope boundaries and deliverables were not clearly defined and agreed
The project manager failed to control changes during execution
The project schedule was unrealistic from the outset
Requirements were too detailed for early stages
Scope Management.w: Unclear scope definition, including boundaries and deliverables, leads to misalignment and disputes.

Scope Management.q: A project scope statement sets out the deliverables in considerable detail, but says nothing about what falls outside the project's boundaries. As delivery proceeds, what risk does this omission most directly create?
o: Scope creep due to undefined boundaries
Scope Management.w: Without defined exclusions, stakeholders may assume additional work is included, leading to scope creep.

Scope Management.q: While defining the scope of a new project, a project manager finds that two influential stakeholder groups have submitted requirements that directly contradict one another. What is the most appropriate initial action for the project manager to take?
o: Delay scope definition until consensus is reached externally
Select the requirements that align with project constraints
Facilitate clarification to reconcile and prioritise requirements
Escalate the conflict to senior management immediately
Scope Management.w: Reconciling and prioritising requirements ensures clarity and alignment before proceeding.

Scope Management.q: A deliverable is produced and submitted for review, but the stakeholders reject it on the grounds that it does not meet their expectations of what they were going to receive. What does this rejection most clearly indicate about how the work was set up?
o: The deliverable was produced too early
Requirements were not clearly defined or agreed
Scope Management.w: Rejection indicates a gap between defined requirements and stakeholder expectations.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is reviewing how scope was established at the start of a workplace refurbishment project. Reflecting on the definition documentation and how boundaries were communicated, which of the following scenarios best demonstrates poor scope boundary definition?
o: Comprehensive and detailed requirements documentation maintained
Stakeholders assuming additional features are included without agreement
Deliverables defined precisely with agreed acceptance criteria
Explicit statements of what is included and excluded
Regular scope reviews conducted throughout the project
Scope Management.w: Assumptions about inclusions indicate unclear boundaries.

Scope Management.q: A project manager defines scope in detail but fails to validate it with stakeholders. What is the most likely outcome?
o: Reduced need for any formal change control
Simplified governance with fewer reporting requirements needed
Improved efficiency across the whole delivery phase
Misalignment between delivered outputs and stakeholder expectations
Faster stakeholder agreement on the final deliverables
Scope Management.w: Without validation, scope may not reflect stakeholder needs, leading to misalignment.

Scope Management.q: Which factor is most critical when defining project deliverables?
Scope Management.w: Deliverables must directly reflect agreed requirements to ensure alignment.

Scope Management.q: On a software development project, the team repeatedly returns to renegotiate what is in and out of scope, and work is often reopened after it was thought complete. Considering the pattern of behaviour described, what is the primary issue?
o: Poor scope definition and requirement clarity
Excessive and overly detailed project documentation
Inadequate resource allocation across the project
Deliverables that are technically far too complex
Ineffective scheduling of the project activities
Scope Management.w: Unclear requirements lead to repeated revisions and instability in scope.

Scope Management.q: Which approach best ensures clear scope boundaries?
Scope Management.w: Explicit inclusions and exclusions define boundaries clearly.

Scope Management.q: Which TWO elements are essential for effective scope definition?
Scope Management.w: Scope definition relies on clear requirements and boundaries.

Scope Management.q: Which TWO risks arise from poorly defined deliverables?
Scope Management.w: Unclear deliverables lead to misalignment and rework.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is defining scope for a new product introduction and wants to strengthen how requirements are captured and agreed with those affected. Which TWO practices would most improve requirement clarity during scope definition?
Scope Management.w: Engagement and clarity of assumptions improve requirement quality.

Scope Management.q: Which TWO consequences result from unclear scope boundaries?
Scope Management.w: Unclear boundaries lead to scope creep and disputes.

Scope Management.q: A project team creates a detailed task list but struggles to ensure all deliverables are covered. What is the most likely issue?
o: The schedule was built before resources were assigned to each of the tasks
The team did not identify a defined critical path through the network diagram
The team focused on activities instead of structuring deliverables using a product breakdown
Stakeholders were not consulted when the progress reports were being prepared and issued
The individual tasks in the list were not sequenced in the correct logical order
Scope Management.w: Without a product-based structure (PBS), teams risk missing deliverables because they focus on activities rather than outputs.

Scope Management.q: A Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) is created, but stakeholders still question whether all required outputs are included. What is the most likely cause?
o: The WBS was developed without a preceding Product Breakdown Structure
The project schedule was left incomplete at the planning stage
The WBS was aligned to deliverables rather than to activities
The dependencies between the work packages were not fully identified
The WBS was decomposed into too many detailed lower levels
Scope Management.w: A PBS ensures all products are identified before decomposing into work. Skipping it risks incomplete scope coverage.

Scope Management.q: A project manager preparing scope documentation for a facilities upgrade wants to select the technique that captures everything the project must produce. Which scenario best demonstrates appropriate use of a Product Breakdown Structure (PBS)?
o: Assigning the required resources to each individual project task
Sequencing the project activities according to their logical dependencies
Identifying all deliverables and sub-products required to meet objectives
Tracking delivery progress against the agreed project milestones
Listing every project activity in its planned execution order
Scope Management.w: PBS focuses on defining all products and deliverables required by the project.

Scope Management.q: On a large transformation programme, a project manager finds that the Work Breakdown Structure has been organised around the business departments involved rather than around the outputs to be produced. What risk does structuring the WBS in this way create?
o: Misalignment between work packages and project outputs
Improved accountability across the departmental teams
Simplified scheduling across the work packages
Reduced need for ongoing stakeholder engagement
Faster overall delivery of the project outputs
Scope Management.w: WBS should be deliverable-oriented; structuring by departments risks losing alignment with outputs.

Scope Management.q: Midway through delivery, a project manager observes that several teams are producing overlapping outputs and effort is being duplicated across different work packages. Examining how the work was originally broken down, what is the most likely cause?
o: The PBS includes too many products
The project schedule is too detailed
The WBS lacks clear structure and decomposition
Scope Management.w: Poor WBS structure can lead to overlapping or duplicated work packages.

Scope Management.q: Which characteristic best defines a well-structured WBS?
o: Hierarchical decomposition of deliverables into manageable work packages
Scope Management.w: A WBS breaks down deliverables hierarchically into manageable components.

Scope Management.q: A project manager has produced a complete Product Breakdown Structure, but the Work Breakdown Structure derived from it does not consistently reflect the products it should deliver. Given the relationship between these two structures, what is the most likely issue?
o: The stakeholders were never properly aligned on the project objectives
The project schedule remained incomplete right through the planning stage
The required resources were all assigned before defining the work
The overall project scope was originally defined far too broadly
The transition from product structure to work structure is poorly managed
Scope Management.w: The WBS must logically derive from the PBS; inconsistency indicates poor translation from products to work.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is planning a new office relocation and wants to demonstrate that products and work have been structured in the correct logical order. Which scenario indicates effective use of both a PBS and a WBS?
o: Resources are allocated before the project scope is defined
Activities are sequenced before any deliverables have been defined
Deliverables are defined first, then decomposed into structured work packages
Dependencies are identified before the work has been structured
Milestones are set before the required outputs are defined
Scope Management.w: PBS defines outputs first, then WBS structures the work needed to produce them.

Scope Management.q: While reviewing the Work Breakdown Structure for an IT rollout, a project manager finds several tasks that cannot be traced to any of the defined deliverables. Considering how work should relate to outputs, what does the presence of these tasks indicate?
o: Scope has expanded beyond defined deliverables
Scope Management.w: All work in the WBS should link to deliverables; otherwise, scope creep or misalignment exists.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is explaining to a new sponsor why a Product Breakdown Structure has been prepared before detailed planning begins on a construction project. Which TWO benefits result from using a Product Breakdown Structure?
Scope Management.w: PBS ensures completeness of deliverables and clarifies scope through defined outputs.

Scope Management.q: Which TWO risks arise from a poorly structured WBS?
Scope Management.w: Poor structure leads to duplication and missing elements.

Scope Management.q: Which TWO practices improve the effectiveness of a WBS?
o: Breaking down deliverables into manageable components
Ensuring all work packages link to deliverables
Scope Management.w: Effective WBS ensures traceability to deliverables and appropriate decomposition.

Scope Management.q: On a systems integration project, a project manager reviews how the Product Breakdown Structure and Work Breakdown Structure have been developed together. Which TWO outcomes would demonstrate that the two structures have been effectively integrated?
o: Clear linkage between outputs and work packages
Scope Management.w: Integration ensures completeness and traceability from deliverables to work.

Scope Management.q: A stakeholder informally requests a change to a deliverable, and the project team implements it immediately to maintain goodwill. What is the most significant risk of this approach?
o: Uncontrolled scope change without assessing impact
Scope Management.w: Implementing changes without formal control bypasses impact analysis, leading to uncontrolled scope, cost, and schedule risk.

Scope Management.q: A project manager receives a formal change request but delays analysis due to workload. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Delayed decision-making and potential project disruption
Automatic rejection of the change request
Scope Management.w: Delaying impact analysis postpones decisions and can disrupt planning and execution.

Scope Management.q: Which action best represents effective change control?
o: Rejecting all changes to maintain scope stability
Assessing the impact of changes before approval
Allowing the team to decide on changes informally
Scope Management.w: Effective change control requires impact analysis before decisions are made.

Scope Management.q: Under pressure from a sponsor, a project manager approves a significant change request before any assessment of its effect on the budget or timeline has been carried out. What is the most likely outcome of proceeding in this way?
Scope Management.w: Without impact analysis, changes can introduce unanticipated cost and schedule implications.

Scope Management.q: A project assurance reviewer is examining how changes are handled on a delivery project and looking for signs that control is weak. Which of the following scenarios indicates ineffective change control?
o: Changes are implemented without formal approval processes
Stakeholders are informed of change impacts
Decisions are aligned with project objectives
All changes are documented and assessed before approval
Impact analysis includes cost, time, and scope
Scope Management.w: Implementing changes without formal approval undermines control and governance.

Scope Management.q: To keep the plan stable, a project team has decided to reject every change request that arises, regardless of its merit. Considering the purpose of change control, what is the key limitation of adopting this approach?
o: It transfers scope authority away from the sponsor
It reduces the accuracy of progress reporting data
It weakens the reliability of project cost estimates
It prevents necessary changes that could improve outcomes
It removes the requirement for stakeholder sign-off
Scope Management.w: Change control should enable informed decisions, not block beneficial changes.

Scope Management.q: A change control board is reviewing a proposed change to a live project and must decide how to judge it. When evaluating a change request, which factor is most critical to consider?
o: The project manager's own personal view of the change
How many stakeholders have asked for the change
How quickly and easily it could be implemented
The life cycle phase in which the change arises
Its impact on the baseline, risks and business case
Scope Management.w: A change request is judged on its full impact: scope, time, cost and quality, plus risks, benefits and the business case, resources, stakeholders, other projects and BAU. The recommendation is then justified against the business case and objectives.

n.0: Decisions rest on evidence and the right authority, not personal preference.
n.1: The number of requesters says nothing about the change's value or impact.
n.2: Ease of implementation matters only once impact and value are understood.
n.3: Timing affects the cost of change, but the impact on the baseline and business case is decisive.

Scope Management.q: On a project with several engaged stakeholders, a submitted change request is turned down without any reason being given to those who raised it. What risk does rejecting the request in this way create?
o: Unmanaged expansion of the project scope
Weaker traceability between deliverables and requirements
Reduced accuracy of the cost forecast
Increased duplication of work across teams
Scope Management.w: Lack of transparency undermines stakeholder confidence and trust.

Scope Management.q: Which outcome best demonstrates effective change approval processes?
o: Decisions are made informally by the team
Changes are approved based on their alignment with project objectives
All changes are accepted to satisfy stakeholders
Changes are delayed until project completion
Scope Management.w: Approval decisions should align with project objectives and constraints.

Scope Management.q: A newly appointed project manager finds that changes are being made to the project frequently, with very little supporting documentation recorded for any of them. Considering how change should be governed, what is the most likely issue?
Scope Management.w: Lack of documentation indicates poor control and governance.

Scope Management.q: Which situation best demonstrates proper impact analysis?
o: Implementing changes strictly in order of stakeholder urgency
Skipping any assessment for changes that seem minor
Assessing only the cost implications of a change
Assessing effects on baseline, risks, benefits and BAU
Weighing only the short-term benefits of the change
Scope Management.w: Proper impact analysis looks beyond scope, time, cost and quality to risks, benefits and the business case, resources, stakeholders, other projects, BAU and contracts, so the decision-maker sees the whole effect of the change.

n.0: Urgency does not replace an assessment of impact.
n.1: Apparently minor changes can have significant knock-on effects.
n.2: Cost is only one dimension of impact.
n.4: Short-term gains can hide longer-term effects on benefits and risk.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is setting up a formal change control process for a regulated project and wants to ensure the essentials are in place. Which TWO elements are essential in a formal change control process?
Scope Management.w: Formal processes require documentation and impact assessment.

Scope Management.q: Which TWO risks arise from poor change control?
Scope Management.w: Poor control leads to uncontrolled scope and cost increases.

Scope Management.q: Which TWO outcomes demonstrate effective change approval?
o: Impacts are clearly understood before decisions
Scope Management.w: Effective approval requires alignment and understanding of impacts.

Scope Management.q: Which TWO practices improve change control effectiveness?
Scope Management.w: Documentation and structured approvals improve control.

Scope Management.q: A project team is preparing to capture what the client wants before defining the project scope. What is the first activity they should undertake?
Scope Management.w: Gathering requirements is the initial step in defining scope, as it identifies what stakeholders need from the project.

n.0: The business case supports justification, not initial gathering.
n.1: Change control is relevant once requirements may change.
n.3: Project charters are approved after requirements are known.
n.4: The WBS is created after requirements are established.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is preparing to begin delivery and wants to ensure the scope is accurately defined and documented before any work starts. Which process is primarily responsible for achieving this outcome?
Scope Management.w: Requirements analysis helps clarify and document what the project must deliver.

n.1: Risk management deals with threats and opportunities.
n.2: Cost estimating follows scope definition.
n.3: Issue logs track problems, not requirements.
n.4: Resource allocation happens after scope is defined.

Scope Management.q: A business analyst is working with a project team during the early stages of a project to establish what the solution must deliver. During requirements gathering, which two activities are most likely to occur together?
o: Completing risk assessments and writing a business case
Updating lessons learned and auditing the project
Drafting contracts and issuing purchase orders
Scope Management.w: Interviewing and analysing are both core parts of gathering requirements.

n.0: Risk assessments and business cases are not primary to requirements gathering.
n.1: Lessons learned and audits are after implementation.
n.3: Contracts and purchase orders relate to procurement.
n.4: Budgeting follows requirements gathering.

Scope Management.q: A project team is challenged by the sponsor to explain why a particular set of requirements has been included in the project. To be properly justified, the requirements should be based on which of the following?
o: the needs and objectives of stakeholders
Scope Management.w: Requirements are justified by aligning them with stakeholder needs and project objectives.

n.0: Resource availability alone is insufficient for justification.
n.2: Decisions shouldn't be based on volume but on value.
n.3: Contingency funds are financial reserves, not justification.
n.4: Supplier preferences may not align with project needs.

Scope Management.q: During scope definition, a project team is debating whether a proposed feature should be included in the project. To justify this requirement, what must the team confirm about it?
o: It is the easiest to deliver
Scope Management.w: A requirement must support the project’s business objectives to be justified.

n.0: Cost is important, but objectives take priority.
n.1: Risk avoidance is part of planning, not justification.
n.2: Ease of delivery alone doesn't justify inclusion.
n.4: Trends are not sufficient justification.

Scope Management.q: A new project manager is learning which activities belong to the requirements management process. Which of the following is NOT an activity carried out within requirements management?
Scope Management.w: Lessons learned workshops are part of project closure, not requirements management.

n.0: Stakeholder needs must be gathered for requirements.
n.2: Validation ensures requirements are accurate.
n.3: Analysing is core to requirements management.
n.4: Baseline needs are documented as part of requirements.

Scope Management.q: Project manager Sam is leading a new software project. She must make sure requirements are clear and agreed. Which step should she complete before starting design?
Scope Management.w: Requirements analysis must be done before design to ensure clarity and agreement.

n.0: Asset disposal is unrelated.
n.1: Audits happen later in the project.
n.3: Vendor negotiation is part of procurement.
n.4: Performance reviews are HR-related.

Scope Management.q: Having gathered and agreed the project's requirements, the project manager establishes a baseline for them before delivery begins. Creating this requirements baseline primarily helps the project to do what?
Scope Management.w: Baselining requirements helps control changes by setting a reference point.

n.0: Stakeholder meetings remain necessary.
n.1: Training speed is not affected by baselining requirements.
n.2: Procurement speed is not related to requirements baselining.
n.3: Risks cannot be eliminated entirely by baselining.

Scope Management.q: While reviewing the project's requirements, the team identifies one that cannot be justified against the project's objectives. What is the best course of action for this requirement?
o: Remove it from the project scope
Move it to the risk register
Add it to the lessons learned
Scope Management.w: Unjustified requirements should be removed to prevent scope creep.

n.1: Requirements not justified do not belong in the risk register.
n.2: Unjustified requirements should not be approved.
n.3: Lessons learned are for project closure.
n.4: Contingency budgets are for risk, not unjustified requirements.

Scope Management.q: A project team has just finished collecting the needs and expectations of its stakeholders. Within the requirements management process, which activity directly follows the gathering of requirements?
Scope Management.w: Analysis of requirements follows their gathering, to clarify and prioritise.

n.0: Contract issuance is a procurement activity.
n.1: Project closure happens after delivery.
n.2: Resource assignment follows after requirements are set.
n.3: Disengagement is post-delivery.

Scope Management.q: A project team needs to ensure all stakeholders’ needs are met in the project scope. What tool can help them document and track these needs?
Scope Management.w: A requirements register captures, documents and tracks stakeholder needs.

n.1: Risk matrix is for assessing risk.
n.2: A project log is a general record, not specific to requirements.
n.3: Audit reports are not for ongoing requirements tracking.
n.4: Change log tracks changes, not requirements.

Scope Management.q: Which statement is TRUE about establishing baseline needs?
o: It creates a point of reference for future changes
It removes the need for scope management
It sets the project’s risk appetite
Scope Management.w: A baseline provides a reference point against which changes can be measured.

n.0: Project closure involves other processes.
n.1: Uncertainty can only be managed, not eliminated.
n.3: Scope management is still required after baseline is set.
n.4: Risk appetite is set separately.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is concerned about the risk of scope creep as requests continue to arrive during delivery. During requirements management, which principle should be followed to help avoid scope creep?
o: Complete the project as quickly as possible
Only include justified and approved requirements
Scope Management.w: Including only justified and approved requirements keeps the project scope controlled.

n.0: Accepting all requests leads to uncontrolled scope.
n.1: Speed alone cannot justify requirements.
n.2: Stakeholder engagement is essential.
n.3: Budget is important, but not the only factor.

Scope Management.q: After the project's requirements have been formally baselined, a stakeholder asks for a change to one of them. As the project manager, what is the first action you should take?
o: Assess the impact before considering the change
Assign the request to the finance team
Add it directly to the risk register
Scope Management.w: Impact assessment must happen before accepting or rejecting any change.

n.1: Immediate implementation could destabilise the project.
n.2: Requests should be properly considered, not dismissed outright.
n.3: Finance is not responsible for requirement evaluation.
n.4: Not all change requests represent risks.

Scope Management.q: When analysing requirements, what is the main aim?
o: Reduce project duration at all costs
Scope Management.w: The aim is to clarify and prioritise needs so the project delivers value.

n.1: Increased spend is not an objective of analysis.
n.2: Sponsor replacement is unrelated.
n.3: Duration must be balanced with quality.
n.4: Risks are managed, not entirely avoided.

Scope Management.q: Which of these best describes 'requirements validation'?
o: Confirming that requirements are feasible and meet objectives
Scope Management.w: Validation ensures requirements are realistic and meet the project's goals.

n.1: Gantt charts are scheduling tools.
n.2: Resource allocation comes after requirements.
n.3: Handover is project closure, not validation.
n.4: Stakeholder numbers are not part of validation.

Scope Management.q: A project sponsor asks the project manager why the scope of a recent project became confused and difficult to control. A project's scope is most likely to become unclear if which of the following occurs?
Scope Management.w: Without clear requirements, the project scope cannot be accurately established.

n.1: Meetings alone don't cause unclear scope.
n.2: Standard templates help consistency.
n.3: Cost estimates do not define scope.
n.4: Detailed risk assessments can be helpful, not harmful.

Scope Management.q: A junior project team member is listing the activities they expect to carry out while gathering requirements from stakeholders. Which of the following activities is LEAST likely to occur during requirements gathering?
Scope Management.w: Procurement negotiations are related to acquiring goods/services, not gathering requirements.

n.1: Existing documentation supports requirement analysis.
n.2: Workshops are used for clarification.
n.3: Interviews are commonly used to gather requirements.
n.4: Surveys help collect stakeholder needs.

Scope Management.q: During requirements analysis, a stakeholder raises a need that cannot be justified when tested against the project's objectives. To keep the scope relevant and controlled, what should happen to this need?
o: The need should be excluded from project scope
It should be added to project baseline anyway
The team should allocate extra budget for it
It should become a high-priority risk
It should be escalated to project sponsors without review
Scope Management.w: Unjustified requirements should be excluded to keep the scope relevant and controlled.

n.1: Only justified needs should enter the baseline.
n.2: Budget should be allocated to agreed requirements.
n.3: Unjustified requirements are not automatically risks.
n.4: Escalation should follow analysis, not be automatic.

Scope Management.q: A project team has now gathered and analysed all of the project's requirements and is deciding what to do before delivery work begins. What should be the next step in the requirements management process?
Scope Management.w: Requirements should be documented and baselined before project work begins.

n.1: Contracts come after requirements definition.
n.2: Marketing is not part of requirements management.
n.3: Project closure happens much later.
n.4: Issue logs are maintained throughout.

Scope Management.q: A project board is reviewing the case for a set of proposed requirements before approving them. When justifying these requirements, which of the following is most important?
Scope Management.w: Requirements should always align with business needs to be justified.

n.0: Sponsor preference should not override business needs.
n.2: The number of stakeholders is not a key factor.
n.3: Location is not relevant for justification.
n.4: Cost is secondary to alignment.

Scope Management.q: A major stakeholder joins the project late and asks for several new features to be added. What should the project manager do first?
o: Review the requests against the project baseline
Add all features to the project plan
Scope Management.w: Requests should be reviewed against the agreed baseline before any action.

n.0: Stakeholder analysis is essential and cannot be skipped.
n.2: Not all new features should be automatically added.
n.3: Resources are planned based on agreed requirements.
n.4: Budget changes come after impact analysis.

Scope Management.q: Project manager Nia is facilitating a workshop with stakeholders to clarify several ambiguous requirements before they are baselined. What is the main benefit of taking this approach?
o: It eliminates the need for documentation
It replaces all risk management activities
It increases stakeholder engagement and clarity
It removes the need for a business case
It ensures the lowest possible project cost
Scope Management.w: Workshops improve clarity and stakeholder engagement, leading to better requirements.

n.0: Documentation is still needed.
n.1: Risk management remains necessary.
n.3: A business case is still required.
n.4: Cost is influenced by several factors.

Scope Management.q: The process of documenting requirements helps to _____.
o: reduce the number of team meetings to zero
create a shared understanding among stakeholders
Scope Management.w: Documenting requirements ensures all stakeholders understand and agree on what is needed.

n.0: Quality management is a separate discipline.
n.1: Meetings may still be required for clarification.
n.2: Communication cannot be fully automated.
n.4: Reporting is still needed.

Scope Management.q: A project manager wants to establish a robust baseline for the project's requirements so that future changes can be controlled. Which combination of actions BEST establishes such a baseline?
o: Hire new staff and conduct audits
Allocate contingency funds and issue contracts
Scope Management.w: Baseline should be built by documenting, validating and gaining agreement on requirements.

n.0: Staffing and audits do not set a baseline.
n.1: Contingency funds and contracts are unrelated to baselining.
n.3: Risk mitigation is important, but not the core activity here.
n.4: Procurement is a separate process.

Scope Management.q: During delivery, a project team realises that a number of stakeholder requirements were never formally written down. What is the MOST likely risk arising from these undocumented requirements?
Scope Management.w: Undocumented requirements can lead to scope creep and misunderstandings.

n.0: Documentation is typically insufficient, not excessive.
n.2: Budgets can be exceeded, not reduced.
n.3: Undocumented requirements rarely reduce timelines.
n.4: Risks are increased, not eliminated.

Scope Management.q: A sponsor lists several outcomes they expect from investing effort in thorough requirements management. Which of the following is NOT a direct benefit that requirements management can be relied upon to deliver?
Scope Management.w: Risks can only be managed, not eliminated automatically by requirements management.

n.0: Accurate requirements enable better planning.
n.1: Stakeholders are more satisfied when needs are met.
n.2: Scope creep is reduced with good requirements management.
n.4: Clear objectives result from thorough requirements.

Scope Management.q: Shortly after handover, several stakeholders complain that their needs were overlooked in the delivered solution. In a review of what went wrong, which element of the project was most likely NOT followed properly?
o: Detailed cost estimation and budgeting analysis
Formal change control and configuration procedures
Technical documentation and version control standards
Structured procurement and supplier selection policies
Scope Management.w: Incomplete gathering and analysis can result in missed stakeholder needs.

n.0: Market research is less relevant for internal stakeholders.
n.2: Change control is important, but not the direct cause here.
n.3: Technical documentation is not the core issue.
n.4: Procurement policies are unrelated.

Scope Management.q: A project manager wants to ensure every product version is tracked throughout the project lifecycle. Which configuration management process best supports this?
Scope Management.w: Configuration identification ensures all products and versions are uniquely tracked.

n.0: Risk escalation is a risk management process.
n.2: Issue logging relates to problems, not configuration items.
n.3: Procurement is about acquiring resources, not tracking versions.
n.4: Resource smoothing is a scheduling activity.

Scope Management.q: A project is running a formal configuration management process, and a proposed change to a controlled product has been submitted. Which activity within configuration management is responsible for authorising such changes to products?
Scope Management.w: Configuration control is responsible for authorising and managing changes to products.

n.0: Identification is about defining items, not controlling changes.
n.2: Status accounting tracks changes, but doesn't authorise them.
n.3: Lessons learned summarises knowledge, not changes.
n.4: Procurement is unrelated to configuration control.

Scope Management.q: A project team is systematically recording the current state, version and history of every deliverable and its components so this information can be reported on. Which configuration management process are they performing?
Scope Management.w: Status accounting involves recording the current state and history of configuration items.

n.0: Quality assurance focuses on meeting standards.
n.1: Risk assessment evaluates potential threats, not item status.
n.2: Stakeholder engagement is about communication, not tracking items.
n.4: Resource allocation assigns resources, not records status.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is defining which activities fall within the scope of the project's configuration management process. Which of the following is NOT part of configuration management?
Scope Management.w: Communication planning is not a process within configuration management.

n.0: Planning is a fundamental step of configuration management.
n.1: Status accounting records changes and versions.
n.2: Change control is part of configuration management.
n.4: Identification is a key configuration management activity.

Scope Management.q: A project team completes a formal review to confirm that all project outputs match the documented configuration. What is this process called?
Scope Management.w: Verification audits confirm that outputs match their documented configuration.

n.0: Issue escalation moves problems up the chain.
n.2: Milestone planning is scheduling.
n.3: Risk analysis looks at threats and opportunities.
n.4: Budget reforecast is financial.

Scope Management.q: On a construction project, the project manager wants confidence that any amendment to a baselined deliverable is only made once it has been formally approved and properly recorded. Which configuration management activity provides this assurance?
Scope Management.w: Configuration control ensures that all changes are approved and documented.

n.0: Lessons learned is post-project review.
n.1: Procurement is about acquiring goods and services.
n.2: Initiation starts the project but doesn't manage change.
n.3: Quality inspection verifies product quality, not change approval.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is planning how configuration management will be carried out, including roles, tools, and processes. What is this activity called?
Scope Management.w: Configuration management planning defines how the process will be managed throughout the project.

n.0: Procurement is unrelated to configuration management planning.
n.2: Logging is part of control, not planning.
n.3: Quality assurance ensures standards, not configuration.
n.4: Status accounting records the status, not the planning.

Scope Management.q: Which statement is TRUE about configuration identification?
o: It eliminates the need for change control
It guarantees project delivery on time
It is the same as quality inspection
It defines and labels every configuration item
Scope Management.w: Configuration identification defines and uniquely labels every configuration item.

n.0: Change control is still needed after identification.
n.1: Expenditure tracking is part of financial management.
n.2: Identification does not guarantee delivery times.
n.3: Quality inspection checks standards, not identification.

Scope Management.q: A formal check is being conducted to ensure that only approved changes have been made to configuration items. Which process is being performed?
Scope Management.w: Verification audit checks that only approved changes are present in configuration items.

n.0: Risk identification addresses potential threats, not configuration.
n.1: Stakeholder engagement is not part of configuration audits.
n.2: Procurement review is about contracts and suppliers.
n.3: Status accounting tracks status, not verifies changes.

Scope Management.q: A newly appointed project manager is setting up configuration management for a product-development project and wants to base it on the recognised core activities. Which combination of activities forms the core of configuration management?
o: Risk analysis, stakeholder engagement, lessons learned
Quality control, health and safety inspection
Planning, identification, control, status accounting, verification audit
Scope Management.w: These five activities make up the configuration management process.

n.0: These are important, but not configuration management activities.
n.1: Quality and safety are managed separately.
n.2: These relate to other aspects of project management.
n.3: Resource levelling and scheduling are about time and resource management.

Scope Management.q: A project team is unsure which components make up the final product. Which configuration management process should they use to clarify this?
Scope Management.w: Configuration identification ensures all components are defined and documented.

n.0: Communication planning focuses on information flow.
n.1: Risk mitigation addresses threats, not product structure.
n.2: Change enablement is part of change control, not identification.
n.3: Stakeholder mapping relates to people, not items.

Scope Management.q: On a software project, the sponsor is concerned that developers are altering approved deliverables without going through any formal route. Which of the following would BEST help prevent unauthorised changes to those deliverables?
Scope Management.w: Configuration control authorises and tracks all changes to deliverables.

n.0: Budget monitoring focuses on financials, not product changes.
n.2: Status accounting records status but does not control change.
n.3: Issue management addresses problems, not product changes.
n.4: Schedule compression is related to timelines, not change control.

Scope Management.q: Towards the end of a delivery phase, the project manager arranges a verification audit as part of the project's configuration management process. In configuration management, a verification audit is performed to _____.
o: authorise proposed changes to baselined products
record the current status of all configuration items
confirm products match their approved configuration
establish the initial configuration item baseline
identify and assess newly emerging project risks
Scope Management.w: Verification audits ensure products conform to their documented configuration.

n.0: Resource scheduling is unrelated.
n.1: Budget approval is outside configuration management.
n.3: Stakeholder engagement is not a core aim of verification audits.
n.4: Risk identification is not the audit's purpose.

Scope Management.q: A project manager needs a single reference that shows every approved change and the current version of each product on an engineering project. Which document is essential for recording all approved changes and current versions of configuration items?
Scope Management.w: Status accounting records all approved changes and current item versions.

n.0: Stakeholder register lists stakeholders.
n.1: Issue log deals with project problems.
n.2: The risk register is for tracking risks.
n.4: Lessons learned log is for capturing knowledge.

Scope Management.q: During delivery, a team member discovers that one of the project's products has been altered without any authorisation being sought. In line with configuration management, what should be the first action taken?
o: Report the change via the configuration control process
Assess the technical impact before informing anyone
Revert the product to its previous approved version
Escalate the change straight to the project sponsor
Record the change in the project status account
Scope Management.w: Unapproved changes must be reported using the configuration control process.

n.1: Budget changes may result from, but not replace, proper control.
n.2: Ignoring it could lead to confusion and errors.
n.3: Procurement planning is unrelated.
n.4: Only authorised personnel should approve changes.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is briefing the team on why configuration status accounting is carried out throughout a project. Which of the following is NOT a main purpose of configuration status accounting?
o: To track the history of approved changes
To record the current state of configuration items
To provide information about item versions
Scope Management.w: Status accounting is not focused on risk identification.

n.0: Tracking change history is a main purpose.
n.1: Recording state is a main purpose of status accounting.
n.3: Providing version information is a main purpose.
n.4: Audit support is a main purpose.

Scope Management.q: A project manager needs to ensure that every change to project scope is fully traceable. Which process best achieves this?
Scope Management.w: Configuration control tracks and authorises all changes, ensuring traceability.

n.0: Market research is unrelated to configuration management.
n.1: Stakeholder analysis relates to people, not changes.
n.2: Issue management focuses on problems, not traceability.
n.3: Schedule management is about time, not configuration items.

Scope Management.q: An assurance reviewer asks the project manager to explain what a verification audit achieves within configuration management. Which statement is TRUE about verification audits in configuration management?
o: They confirm products conform to their approved configuration
They are only needed for IT projects
They replace the need for change control
Scope Management.w: Verification audits confirm that products match the agreed configuration documentation.

n.0: Audits do not automatically reduce costs.
n.2: Verification audits apply to all projects, not just IT.
n.3: Project risks can be managed, not eliminated.
n.4: Change control is still needed after audits.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is planning how configuration management will operate on a new programme and is deciding what to focus on. When planning configuration management, which aspect is LEAST important?
o: Methods for verification audit and status accounting
Scope Management.w: Configuration management planning sets out which items will be controlled, who is responsible, the processes and tools, and how status accounting and audits will work. The reimbursement method is a procurement decision, so it is least relevant.

n.0: Clear roles, such as who may approve or release a new version, are essential to control.
n.1: Planning for verification audit and status accounting is part of configuration management.
n.3: Deciding which types of item will be controlled is the starting point of configuration planning.
n.4: Processes and tools are needed to identify, control and record items consistently.

Scope Management.q: Before handover of a complex deliverable, the project manager schedules a configuration management verification audit. A key reason for conducting such an audit is to _____.
o: ensure deliverables match the documented configuration
Scope Management.w: Verification audits are conducted to confirm deliverables match their approved configuration.

n.1: Stakeholder numbers are not affected by audits.
n.2: Planning is still required.
n.3: Procurement speed is unrelated to verification audits.
n.4: Performance reviews are managed separately.

Scope Management.q: A project’s configuration management plan specifies regular reviews of all configuration items. What is the MAIN purpose of these reviews?
o: To confirm that items remain consistent with their approved versions
To record every access made to the configuration items
To reallocate resources across the configuration items
To identify configuration items that need new baselines
To approve outstanding change requests against each item
Scope Management.w: Regular reviews ensure configuration items remain unchanged except through approved processes.

n.1: Contingency funds are managed through risk processes.
n.2: Scheduling is handled elsewhere in the project.
n.3: Training needs are identified separately.
n.4: Market analysis is not a configuration activity.

Scope Management.q: A project team under time pressure decides to bypass configuration identification and move straight into producing deliverables. If configuration identification is skipped, what is the MOST likely risk?
o: Delayed sign-off of the project business case
Inaccurate forecasting of the remaining project budget
Higher procurement costs across the project supply chain
Uncontrolled changes and confusion about product versions
Scope Management.w: Without identification, changes can't be controlled and versions become unclear.

n.0: Resource allocation may become harder.
n.1: Stakeholder numbers are unrelated.
n.2: Costs can rise due to rework and errors.
n.3: Delivery is more likely to be delayed by confusion.

Scope Management.q: On a project generating many interdependent outputs, the project manager wants each product and its versions to be clearly defined and traceable throughout the life cycle. Which process provides this?
Scope Management.w: Configuration identification defines and uniquely tracks outputs and their versions.

n.0: Lessons learned are captured post-delivery.
n.2: WBS is for scope, not configuration tracking.
n.3: Risk management addresses threats and opportunities.
n.4: Procurement planning concerns resource acquisition.

Scope Management.q: A verification audit on a key deliverable has revealed several changes that were made without being documented or approved. What is the best course of action for the project manager?
o: Rework the entire project scope to accommodate them
Re-baseline the deliverable to include the new changes
Update the configuration records to match the current state
Investigate and return the deliverable to its approved configuration
Approve the undocumented changes retrospectively without assessment
Scope Management.w: Undocumented changes must be investigated and reversed to maintain control.

n.0: Rebaselining is a significant step not always necessary.
n.1: Replacing personnel is not the first step.
n.2: Quality is important, but undocumented changes undermine control.
n.4: Changes should not be approved without proper process.

Scope Management.q: Which is NOT a direct responsibility of configuration management?
Scope Management.w: Contract negotiations are a procurement function, not configuration management.

n.0: Identification is a configuration management responsibility.
n.1: Change control is central to configuration management.
n.2: Status accounting is key to configuration management.
n.3: Verification audits are part of configuration management.

Scope Management.q: A project has experienced confusion over which documents are the latest versions. What is the BEST way to address this?
o: Reduce the number of project documents
Increase the frequency of project audits only
Let team members choose their own version
Scope Management.w: Status accounting keeps records of latest versions and approved changes.

n.0: Reducing documents doesn't solve version control.
n.1: Audits alone do not prevent version issues.
n.2: Allowing personal choice undermines control.
n.3: Verbal communication can increase confusion.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is worried that gradual, unmanaged changes are expanding the scope of the deliverables. Which combination of configuration management activities helps to prevent scope creep?
Scope Management.w: Identification, control, and verification ensure changes are managed and scope is maintained.

n.0: Scheduling and budgeting are not part of configuration management.
n.1: Risk and procurement processes are separate.
n.2: Stakeholder analysis and lessons learned are not configuration controls.
n.3: Quality and recruitment are not configuration activities.

Scope Management.q: As part of routine configuration management, a project team completes a status accounting exercise across all products. What is the main output of this exercise?
o: A definition of the naming convention for each configuration item
A schedule showing when each configuration item will be delivered
A register of unauthorised changes made to each configuration item
A record of the current state and history of each configuration item
A list of the reviewers who approve each configuration change
Scope Management.w: Status accounting provides a clear record of item status and change history.

n.0: Resource histograms are part of resource management.
n.1: Marketing is unrelated.
n.2: Risk lists are generated by risk management, not configuration.
n.4: Milestones are tracked in scheduling.

Scope Management.q: On a fast-moving project, configuration control is not being enforced when changes are requested to deliverables. Which is the MOST likely consequence of this?
o: Unapproved changes are made to project deliverables
Scope Management.w: Without control, unauthorised changes may occur, compromising project quality and scope.

n.0: Risks cannot be eliminated.
n.1: Costs may increase due to rework.
n.2: Stakeholder satisfaction is likely to drop.
n.4: Audit needs could actually increase.

Scope Management.q: Ahead of formal acceptance, the project manager commissions a verification audit within the configuration management process. A key outcome of such a verification audit is _____.
o: updating the deliverables to reflect requested changes
ensuring all deliverables match their approved configuration
identifying which configuration items to place under control
confirming the configuration items are correctly named
recording the change history of each configuration item
Scope Management.w: Verification audits confirm deliverables conform to the documented and approved configuration.

n.0: Documentation may actually increase for compliance.
n.2: Supplier selection is unrelated.
n.3: Business cases are separate from configuration audits.
n.4: Project vision is set at initiation, not in audits.

Scope Management.q: A project team must select which features to deliver first to meet urgent business needs. What is the primary factor they should consider when prioritising requirements?
o: The length of the requirements list
Which features are easiest to code
Scope Management.w: Requirements should be prioritised by business value and impact on stakeholders.

n.1: List length is not a prioritisation factor.
n.2: Team size may affect delivery, but not prioritisation.
n.3: Ease of coding is less important than value.
n.4: Trends can inform, but are not a core prioritisation factor.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is comparing several proposed options and must judge which will deliver the best solution for the organisation. Which two actions are most important when evaluating requirements for an optimal project solution?
o: Baselining every requirement before any analysis
Tendering for suppliers and awarding contracts
Documenting lessons learned and updating the issue log
Scope Management.w: Finding the optimal solution means evaluating whether each option is feasible and how well it aligns with the business case and objectives (with prioritisation such as MoSCoW or value versus effort).

n.0: Levelling and fast-tracking are scheduling techniques used after the solution is chosen.
n.1: Requirements are baselined after they have been analysed and justified, not before.
n.2: Tendering and award are procurement steps that follow the choice of solution.
n.4: Lessons and issue logs are control and learning records, not ways of evaluating requirements.

Scope Management.q: A project manager needs to select the minimum set of features that will deliver value early in an iterative life cycle. What is this approach called?
Scope Management.w: MVP refers to the smallest set of features that delivers value and allows feedback.

n.0: Testing is not a life cycle approach.
n.2: Waterfall is a linear life cycle.
n.3: Critical path is for scheduling.
n.4: Comprehensive analysis is not an iterative delivery approach.

Scope Management.q: Which statement about prioritising requirements is TRUE?
o: It guarantees all requirements are delivered at once
It only applies to IT projects
It helps ensure that resources focus on the most valuable outcomes
It prevents the need for stakeholder engagement
It is the sole responsibility of the project sponsor
Scope Management.w: Prioritisation ensures focus on the requirements with greatest value.

n.0: Not all requirements are delivered together.
n.1: Prioritisation is important for all project types.
n.3: Stakeholder engagement is still required.
n.4: It requires input from multiple roles.

Scope Management.q: A project using an iterative life cycle wants to deliver a Minimum Marketable Product (MMP). What is the primary aim of this approach?
o: To deliver the smallest version that still yields useful user feedback
To prove technical feasibility before committing to further investment
To build every planned feature before releasing to any customer
To reduce quality assurance so the product ships more quickly
To deliver enough value that the product can be sold to customers
Scope Management.w: MMP aims to deliver a usable and saleable product with the minimum feature set.

n.0: Delivering every feature is not the aim.
n.1: Quality assurance is still necessary.
n.2: Stakeholder input remains vital.
n.3: The business case is prepared earlier.

Scope Management.q: At the start of solution development, a project manager has gathered a long list of requirements from stakeholders. When evaluating these requirements, what should be done before assigning priorities to them?
o: Document each requirement in the technical specification
Begin building the highest-profile requirements immediately
Baseline the full requirements list for formal sign-off
Confirm the delivery order with the development team
Assess the feasibility and value of each requirement
Scope Management.w: Feasibility and value assessment is essential before prioritisation.

n.0: Scheduling comes after prioritisation.
n.1: Project closure is the final phase.
n.2: Testing follows design and build.
n.3: Procurement is not the first step.

Scope Management.q: A product manager must choose between two features: one delivers high business value but is costly; the other is cheap but has limited value. What is the best course of action?
o: Select the cheaper feature because it minimises project expenditure
Postpone the decision until the project is closing
Prioritise the high-value feature if it aligns with project objectives
Deliver both features to satisfy every stakeholder request
Delegate the choice entirely to the development team
Scope Management.w: High-value features aligned with objectives should be prioritised, even if more costly.

n.0: Lowest cost does not always mean greatest value.
n.1: Deferring decisions can delay project benefits.
n.3: Both features should be analysed first.
n.4: Stakeholders should be involved in decisions.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is guiding the team through selecting features for an optimal solution using sound, objective methods. Which of the following is NOT a step in developing an optimal project solution?
o: Assessing the business value delivered by each requirement
Evaluating the technical feasibility of each proposed option
Analysing the risks associated with each solution option
Ranking each feature by the order in which it was first requested
Prioritising stakeholder needs against the available time and cost
Scope Management.w: An optimal solution comes from objectively evaluating options and requirements by feasibility, value, constraints and risk. Ranking features by when they were requested ignores all of these, so it is not part of the process.

n.0: Assessing business value links each requirement to benefits, so the most valuable are delivered.
n.1: Checking technical feasibility makes sure each option can actually be delivered.
n.2: Analysing risk for each option helps choose a solution that is likely to succeed.
n.4: Prioritising against time and cost, for example with MoSCoW, is central to finding the optimal solution.

Scope Management.q: A project team is delivering a digital product using an iterative life cycle and applying MVP and MMP concepts. A key benefit of using MVP and MMP approaches in iterative life cycles is that _____.
o: the project budget can be treated as effectively unlimited
only the technical team needs to contribute to delivery
products can be delivered and improved quickly based on feedback
risk management becomes unnecessary once early delivery begins
all requirements are guaranteed to be delivered at project start
Scope Management.w: MVP and MMP allow early delivery and continual improvement based on feedback.

n.0: Budgets are still managed.
n.1: A broad team contributes to solutions.
n.3: Risk management is still vital.
n.4: Incremental delivery, not all at once, is the goal.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is deciding which factors should influence the ranking of competing requirements. Which activity is LEAST likely to support prioritising project requirements?
o: Ranking requirements by the date they were logged
Evaluating the cost against expected benefit
Assessing the project constraints and dependencies
Analysing the risk of delivery delay
Consulting stakeholders about their key priorities
Scope Management.w: Prioritisation should reflect value, cost, constraints, dependencies and risk, informed by stakeholders. The date a requirement was logged says nothing about its importance.

n.1: Comparing cost with expected benefit is a standard prioritisation approach.
n.2: Constraints and dependencies affect what can be delivered and in what order.
n.3: The risk of delay shows the consequence of not delivering on time, which helps prioritise.
n.4: Consulting stakeholders about their priorities is a key input to ranking requirements.

Scope Management.q: A project team is working in short cycles, delivering small increments of functionality and adapting based on user feedback. Which life cycle approach are they using?
Scope Management.w: Iterative life cycles involve repeated cycles of delivery and feedback.

n.1: Predictive approaches plan and deliver everything up front.
n.2: Linear life cycles deliver all outputs at once.
n.3: Waterfall is a type of linear/predictive cycle.
n.4: Programme management covers multiple projects.

Scope Management.q: A start-up wants to get an early version of its product in front of real users to test its assumptions before investing further. Which is the BEST reason to use the Minimum Viable Product (MVP) approach in project delivery?
o: To limit the number of stakeholders involved in the delivery
To complete every feature before the product is launched
To guarantee that no changes are required after release
To remove the need for any project planning entirely
To launch a basic version quickly and learn from user feedback
Scope Management.w: MVP enables early learning and allows changes based on real feedback.

n.0: Stakeholder involvement is still required.
n.1: Not all features are delivered at first.
n.2: Change may be required after MVP release.
n.3: Planning is always needed.

Scope Management.q: When prioritising requirements, which factor is LEAST important?
o: Seniority of the person who raised it
Risk of not delivering a requirement
Scope Management.w: Requirements are ranked on business need, impact on objectives, resources and risk. Who raised a requirement does not change its value, so the requester's seniority is the least important factor.

n.0: Requirements with greater impact on objectives and benefits should rank higher.
n.1: Available resources limit what can be delivered, so they shape the priority order.
n.2: Urgent business needs usually rank higher because delay has a real cost.
n.4: The risk of not delivering a requirement shows how important it is to the project.

Scope Management.q: A project manager working in an iterative life cycle is explaining to stakeholders how a Minimum Viable Product differs from a Minimum Marketable Product. A key difference between MVP and MMP is that:
o: MVP delivers just enough for feedback, MMP delivers enough for market launch
MVP includes every possible feature, whereas MMP includes only a few
MVP requires no stakeholder involvement at all, unlike the MMP
MMP deliberately aims to deliver lower quality outputs to the market
MMP can only ever be used within a linear life cycle
Scope Management.w: MVP is for early feedback; MMP is ready for the market.

n.1: MVP delivers the minimum, not all features.
n.2: Stakeholder input is always needed.
n.3: Quality should be maintained for both.
n.4: MMP is relevant to iterative cycles.

Scope Management.q: A team needs to decide which requirements should be delivered first in a constrained timeline. Which technique will help them?
Scope Management.w: A prioritisation matrix enables systematic selection based on agreed criteria.

n.1: Random choice does not ensure value.
n.2: All requirements rarely fit constraints.
n.3: Stakeholder input is vital.
n.4: Popularity may not reflect value.

Scope Management.q: Before any build work begins, a project manager reviews all captured requirements against the business need. What is the main purpose of evaluating requirements before starting solution development?
o: To finalise the entire project budget straight away at once
To reduce the overall volume of project documentation being produced
To ensure resources focus on the most valuable and feasible outcomes
To satisfy each and every stakeholder request that is received
To remove every possible risk from the project entirely
Scope Management.w: Evaluation helps ensure value, feasibility and alignment with objectives.

n.0: Budgeting comes after requirements are clear.
n.1: Documentation should be appropriate but is not the main purpose.
n.3: Not all requests are valuable or feasible.
n.4: Risks cannot be eliminated entirely.

Scope Management.q: After a product's MVP is released, users begin reporting additional needs that were not part of the original scope. What should the project team do next?
o: Deliver only the original requirements and ignore new needs
Stop iterative development and switch to a linear approach
Assess the feedback and reprioritise requirements for the next release
Store the feedback for review only at project closure
Release the final version without making any further changes
Scope Management.w: MVP feedback should be used to adjust future priorities and iterations.

n.0: Focusing solely on initial needs misses improvements.
n.1: All requirements should be regularly reviewed.
n.3: Feedback is valuable at all stages.
n.4: Iterative cycles continue after MVP.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is explaining to the sponsor how requirements are handled when using an iterative life cycle. Which statement about requirements prioritisation in iterative life cycles is TRUE?
o: Prioritisation is ongoing and can change with each cycle
All requirements must be fully agreed before any work starts
Prioritisation is not needed by teams working in agile
Only technical constraints are considered when ranking requirements
Once priorities are set they must remain permanently fixed
Scope Management.w: Prioritisation is dynamic and adapts to new feedback in iterative cycles.

n.1: Requirements can be revisited each cycle.
n.2: Prioritisation is vital for agile teams.
n.3: Business, user and risk factors also matter.
n.4: Priorities change as value and context shift.

Scope Management.q: A commercial project is releasing a Minimum Marketable Product to customers early in an iterative delivery. A benefit of using an MMP in this way is that:
o: It reduces the need for change management
It allows early revenue and real-world validation
It delays user involvement until project closure
It guarantees all requirements will be met immediately
Scope Management.w: MMP enables market launch and testing of real-world value early.

n.0: Change management is still required.
n.1: Stakeholder sign-off is always important.
n.3: User involvement should be early and ongoing.
n.4: All requirements are not delivered at once.
