Scope Management.q: A project manager must decide how to shape a solution so that it delivers genuine benefit within the project's constraints. When developing an optimal solution, which combination is most important?
o: Delivering all requested features within a single release
Prioritising by value, feasibility, and alignment with objectives
Disregarding risk analysis to speed up the delivery
Basing selection decisions on individual personal interests
Allowing only the sponsor to make every decision
Scope Management.w: Value, feasibility and alignment ensure the solution delivers benefits.

n.0: Not all features can be delivered at once.
n.2: Risk analysis is crucial.
n.3: Personal interests should not drive solutions.
n.4: Group decision-making is better.

Scope Management.q: A project team receives conflicting requests from different stakeholders. What is the best way to resolve this when prioritising requirements?
o: Defer the decision to the end of the project
Let the development team decide without consulting stakeholders
Implement both requests regardless of impact
Choose whichever is easiest to deliver
Facilitate a discussion to align priorities with business objectives
Scope Management.w: Stakeholder alignment and business objectives should guide requirement prioritisation.

n.0: Delaying can create project risk.
n.1: Stakeholder consultation is essential.
n.2: Not all requests can or should be implemented.
n.3: Ease of delivery is less important than value.

Scope Management.q: Following the release of an MVP, user feedback shows that one particular feature is rarely being used. What should the team do next?
o: Remove the feature immediately without analysis
Hand over to the project sponsor
Re-evaluate the feature’s priority for future releases
Scope Management.w: User feedback should drive reprioritisation and further analysis.

n.0: Adding features without considering value is wasteful.
n.1: Feedback should not be ignored.
n.2: Analysis should occur before removal.
n.3: Decision making should remain with the project team.

Scope Management.q: On an iterative project, requirements are re-assessed at the end of each cycle before the next one begins. What is the main benefit of this approach?
o: It reduces the need for any ongoing stakeholder engagement at all
It allows the solution to be refined based on new information
It removes every possible risk from the project entirely
It means that all testing activities can simply be skipped
It guarantees all requirements will ship in the very first release
Scope Management.w: Iterative reassessment enables continuous improvement.

n.0: Stakeholder engagement remains crucial.
n.2: Risks are managed, not eliminated.
n.3: Testing is always required.
n.4: Incremental delivery is expected.

Scope Management.q: To rank a large set of competing requirements fairly, a project manager introduces a prioritisation matrix. Which is a key advantage of using a prioritisation matrix for requirements?
o: It ensures every requirement will be delivered in the time box
It removes the need to baseline requirements under change control
It guarantees that the cheapest requirements are delivered first
It provides an objective method to evaluate and rank requirements
It replaces the need to consult stakeholders on priorities
Scope Management.w: A prioritisation matrix scores requirements against agreed criteria, such as value, cost, risk and feasibility, giving a transparent, objective basis for ranking them.

n.0: Prioritising accepts that lower-ranked requirements may not be delivered; it does not guarantee all of them.
n.1: Requirements still need to be baselined and changes controlled; the matrix only ranks them.
n.2: The matrix ranks on several weighted criteria; cost alone does not decide the order.
n.4: Stakeholders still need to agree the criteria and weightings; the matrix structures their input rather than replacing it.

Scope Management.q: A project is preparing a Minimum Marketable Product for release to paying customers. What distinguishes the MMP from the MVP?
o: MMP removes the need for any further product testing whatsoever
MVP is used only for internal projects and never externally
MVP must always include every single possible product feature at launch
MMP is always much cheaper to produce than an equivalent MVP
MMP is ready for full market launch; MVP is for learning and feedback
Scope Management.w: MMP delivers enough value for sale; MVP focuses on minimum learning.

n.0: Testing remains essential for both.
n.1: Both approaches apply in different contexts.
n.2: MVPs deliberately avoid feature bloat.
n.3: Cost depends on scope, not model.

Scope Management.q: A project sponsor insists that every requirement on the list is delivered straight away, with nothing left out. What should the project manager advise?
o: Begin procurement for every single feature to satisfy the sponsor quickly
Agree to deliver all of the requirements immediately without any impact analysis
Ignore the sponsor's request entirely and set your own priorities instead
Delivering all requirements at once may not be feasible or optimal; prioritisation is essential
Delegate the entire prioritisation decision to the technical delivery team alone
Scope Management.w: Not all requirements can be delivered immediately—prioritisation ensures the best use of resources.

n.0: Procurement should match priority and feasibility.
n.1: Analysis should always precede agreement.
n.2: Requests from sponsors should be discussed, not ignored.
n.4: Collaboration, not delegation, is best.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is defining the criteria to be used in a requirements prioritisation matrix. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be an appropriate criterion in such a matrix?
Scope Management.w: Prioritisation criteria should reflect value, feasibility, risk and mandatory needs. The date a requirement was logged has no bearing on its importance, so it is not an appropriate criterion.

n.0: Regulatory requirements are mandatory and normally rank as Must Haves.
n.1: Risk impact helps rank requirements whose omission or delay would threaten objectives.
n.3: Business value is a core criterion because requirements should deliver benefits.
n.4: Technical feasibility shows whether a requirement can realistically be delivered.

Scope Management.q: During a requirements workshop, stakeholders are asked to rank the proposed features in order of importance. What is the main benefit of this exercise?
o: It helps ensure the most valued features are delivered first
It guarantees that all requested features will be included
It speeds up the procurement of every requested feature
It removes the need for any further stakeholder engagement
It lets the team disregard the agreed budget constraints
Scope Management.w: Stakeholder ranking supports value-driven prioritisation.

n.1: All features may not be feasible or needed.
n.2: Procurement planning is separate.
n.3: Ongoing engagement is usually required.
n.4: Budget constraints must still be considered.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is determined that the solution developed will be as close to optimal as possible for the organisation. Which combination of actions should they prioritise?
o: Rely solely on the original requirements list throughout
Evaluate requirements for value, prioritise delivery, and incorporate feedback iteratively
Let the team self-organise without any stakeholder input
Complete all technical tasks first and weigh value later
Deliver every requested feature regardless of its value
Scope Management.w: An optimal solution is built by evaluating, prioritising and adapting based on feedback.

n.0: Requirements can change as more is learned.
n.2: Leadership and input improve outcomes.
n.3: Value should inform all technical decisions.
n.4: Value analysis prevents waste.

Scope Management.q: A project team facing evolving stakeholder needs chooses an iterative life cycle for developing its solution. A benefit of using iterative life cycles for solution development is that:
o: The project plan is fixed and never has to change
There is no need to document any requirements at all
Every feature is delivered within the very first release
Stakeholder feedback is gathered only at the very end
Requirements and priorities can be adapted as the project progresses
Scope Management.w: Iterative cycles encourage adaptation and ongoing improvement.

n.0: Plans are updated as the project evolves.
n.1: Requirements documentation is still needed.
n.2: Features are released incrementally.
n.3: Feedback is considered at every stage.

Scope Management.q: A project is being planned to deliver a new customer management system. The project manager wants to clarify the difference between outputs, outcomes, and benefits when defining the project scope. Which of the following best represents an output in this context?
Scope Management.w: An output is the immediate deliverable produced by the project, such as the completed software.

n.0: Increased sales revenue is a benefit achieved after the outcome.
n.1: Improved customer satisfaction is an outcome resulting from using the output.
n.3: Higher employee retention is an unrelated benefit.
n.4: Reduction in customer complaints is an outcome, not the direct output.

Scope Management.q: A retailer is investing in a project to streamline its warehouse operations, and the project team is defining scope by distinguishing deliverables from the improvements the business expects to gain. In this situation, which of the following best describes a benefit when defining project scope?
o: Enhanced business efficiency resulting from project changes
The creation of a cost baseline
Scope Management.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from project outcomes, such as business efficiency.

n.0: A project status report is a deliverable, not a benefit.
n.2: A breakdown of project tasks is part of planning, not a benefit.
n.3: Meetings are a project activity, not a benefit.
n.4: A cost baseline is a planning tool.

Scope Management.q: A project manager leading a complex office relocation needs a way to divide the entire body of work into smaller, more governable pieces before estimating and assigning it. In project management, the work breakdown structure (WBS) is primarily used to:
o: Assign individual team members to specific project roles
Organise the total scope of work into manageable sections
Sequence the project activities into a logical delivery order
Define the acceptance criteria for each project deliverable
Allocate the project budget across each defined cost centre
Scope Management.w: The WBS breaks down the total scope of work into smaller, more manageable sections.

n.0: Stakeholder satisfaction is managed through communication and engagement plans.
n.2: Cost estimation may use the WBS, but it is not its primary purpose.
n.3: Quality standards are defined elsewhere in the project plan.
n.4: Resource scheduling is done separately from WBS creation.

Scope Management.q: A project team uses a cost breakdown structure (CBS) to help manage its budget. What does the CBS mainly illustrate?
o: The timeline for each project phase
The risks associated with each work package
The allocation of project costs across deliverables
The hierarchy of the project team
Scope Management.w: The CBS allocates costs to different project deliverables or components.

n.0: The timeline is shown on a schedule, not a CBS.
n.1: Risks are managed in a risk register.
n.2: Stakeholder engagement is not depicted in the CBS.
n.4: Team hierarchy is represented in an OBS, not CBS.

Scope Management.q: When defining scope, a project manager distinguishes between a product breakdown structure (PBS) and a work breakdown structure (WBS). What is the key difference?
o: PBS and WBS are identical in purpose
PBS focuses on deliverables; WBS focuses on activities
WBS defines only the project schedule
WBS is only used in agile projects
PBS includes project costs; WBS does not
Scope Management.w: PBS identifies the deliverables, while WBS breaks down the work needed to produce them.

n.0: PBS and WBS serve different purposes.
n.2: WBS defines work, not the schedule.
n.3: WBS can be used in any project approach, not just agile.
n.4: Cost allocation is the focus of the CBS, not PBS.

Scope Management.q: A project is at the planning stage. The project manager is reviewing the outputs, outcomes and benefits. Which of the following is NOT an example of an outcome or a benefit?
o: Staff routinely using a new process
Improved response times for customer enquiries
The delivery of a project report
Scope Management.w: The delivery of a project report is an output (a deliverable); outcomes are the changed circumstances when outputs are used, and benefits are the measurable improvements that follow.

n.0: Faster processing is a changed circumstance resulting from the outputs.
n.1: Staff working differently with the new process is an outcome.
n.2: Improved response times are a result of using the outputs.
n.3: Increased customer retention is a measurable benefit.

Scope Management.q: Your team has completed the product breakdown structure for a construction project. What is the next logical step to ensure all elements are delivered?
Scope Management.w: Once the PBS is complete, the WBS is developed to plan the work required to deliver all elements.

n.0: Stakeholder identification is important but not the next step after PBS.
n.1: Project sponsor assignment typically happens before detailed planning.
n.2: Cost estimation follows the definition of scope and work.
n.4: Procurement is addressed later in the planning process.

Scope Management.q: A software upgrade project has listed the following: 1) Updated software installed, 2) Faster system performance, 3) Reduced IT support costs. How should these be classified when defining project scope?
o: 1 is an outcome, 2 is a benefit, 3 is an output
1 is an output, 2 is an outcome, 3 is a benefit
1 is an outcome, 2 is an output, 3 is a benefit
1 is a benefit, 2 is an outcome, 3 is an output
1 is a benefit, 2 is an output, 3 is an outcome
Scope Management.w: Output: installed software; outcome: faster performance; benefit: reduced IT support costs.

n.0: Faster performance is an outcome, not a benefit or output.
n.2: The updated software is the output, not the outcome.
n.3: Reduced costs are a benefit, not an output.
n.4: The benefit is reduced IT support costs, not software installation.

Scope Management.q: At the start of a new product development project, the team is concerned that some required work might be overlooked, and they want a tool that organises all the activities and confirms nothing is missing. Which of the following structures is best used to organise project activities and ensure all required work is identified?
Scope Management.w: A work breakdown structure (WBS) organises and identifies all work needed in a project.

n.0: CBS is used for budgeting.
n.1: OBS shows team structure.
n.2: Risk breakdown structure identifies risks, not work.
n.4: PBS is focused on deliverables, not activities.

Scope Management.q: A project sponsor wants to see how project costs are distributed across deliverables. Which tool should the project manager use to show this information?
Scope Management.w: The cost breakdown structure (CBS) allocates and visualises costs for each project deliverable.

n.0: Milestone charts show key events, not costs.
n.1: WBS focuses on work, not cost distribution.
n.3: Network diagrams are used for scheduling, not cost allocation.
n.4: PBS shows deliverables, not costs.

Scope Management.q: A project is approaching the delivery stage. Which document will show the relationship between project deliverables and the required work to produce them?
o: Product breakdown structure and work breakdown structure together
Cost breakdown structure and organisational breakdown structure together
Communication plan aligned with the stakeholder engagement matrix
Organisational breakdown structure mapped against the resource plan
Risk register combined with the project issue log
Scope Management.w: The PBS lists deliverables, and the WBS maps the work needed for each deliverable.

n.1: The CBS only deals with costs, not deliverables and work.
n.2: The communication plan sets out communication activities, not deliverables or work.
n.3: OBS shows project team structure, not work or deliverables.
n.4: The risk register identifies risks, not project work or deliverables.

Scope Management.q: A newly qualified project manager is reviewing how the work breakdown structure will be used across the planning of a facilities project. Which of the following is NOT a purpose of the work breakdown structure in project management?
o: To identify all tasks required to complete the project
To provide a basis for estimating costs and durations
To allocate work to team members
To define the project’s communication plan
Scope Management.w: The communication plan is a separate project management document, not a WBS function.

n.0: Identifying tasks is a key use of the WBS.
n.1: The WBS supports estimating by breaking work into smaller tasks.
n.2: The WBS is used for allocating work.
n.4: Managing scope is one of the WBS’s primary purposes.

Scope Management.q: A company is replacing its manual payroll process with a new automated payroll system, and the project team is careful to distinguish the change the project brings about from what it physically produces. In this context, the outcome they expect is:
o: Payroll processed more quickly and accurately
The business case for the project
Scope Management.w: An outcome is the change brought about by the output—in this case, improved payroll processing.

n.0: A list of employees is data, not an outcome.
n.2: A business case justifies the project, not its result.
n.3: System testing records are supporting documents.
n.4: A Gantt chart is a schedule, not an outcome.

Scope Management.q: A project team delivering a new visitor centre wants to organise and control its expenditure by grouping costs against the different components of the work. When would a project team typically use a cost breakdown structure (CBS)?
o: To assign quality criteria to deliverables
To allocate and manage project expenses
Scope Management.w: The CBS is used to allocate costs across project components and manage the budget.

n.0: Stakeholder strategies belong in the stakeholder management plan.
n.1: Quality criteria are addressed separately in the quality plan.
n.2: Communication planning is handled elsewhere.
n.3: Lessons learned are recorded during closure, not in the CBS.

Scope Management.q: While defining the scope of a marketing project, the team is careful to separate the tangible things it will produce from the wider improvements the organisation hopes to gain. In the context of scope definition, what does the term 'output' refer to?
o: A tangible deliverable produced by the project
The summary of project lessons learned
A risk that could impact the project
A financial benefit realised by the organisation
Scope Management.w: An output is a tangible deliverable, such as a new product or report.

n.1: Lessons learned are part of project closure, not outputs.
n.2: Risks are managed separately and are not outputs.
n.3: Stakeholder numbers do not define outputs.
n.4: Benefits are achieved after outputs are realised.

Scope Management.q: A client wants to ensure all aspects of scope are fully covered. Which combination of structures is most useful for this?
o: Risk management plan and project brief
Product, work, and cost breakdown structures
Change control log and issue register
Scope Management.w: These three structures together help ensure scope, work, and cost are comprehensively covered.

n.0: Risk planning and project briefs support but do not fully define scope.
n.1: These documents do not collectively address all aspects of scope.
n.2: Stakeholder and time charts are not used for full scope coverage.
n.4: Change and issue logs are important but do not define scope.

Scope Management.q: A sponsor questions why the expected improvements from a new customer portal cannot be reported until some time after the portal itself goes live. Considering the link between what a project produces and the value it enables, which statement is true regarding the relationship between benefits and outputs?
o: Outputs must be delivered before benefits can be realised
Outputs and benefits are the same thing
Outputs are optional in project management
Benefits define the work breakdown structure
Benefits always occur at the same time as outputs
Scope Management.w: Benefits are realised only after the output has been delivered and used.

n.1: Outputs and benefits are distinct concepts.
n.2: Outputs are required deliverables, not optional.
n.3: The WBS is based on scope, not benefits directly.
n.4: Benefits typically occur after outputs are in use.

Scope Management.q: A project manager preparing to build a new road bridge wants a structured view of the physical parts that make up the finished structure, such as the deck, piers and foundations. Which structure should they use?
Scope Management.w: A PBS shows all the physical components that make up the end product, such as a bridge.

n.0: CBS deals with cost allocation, not components.
n.1: A WBS details work, not physical parts.
n.3: An org chart shows people, not products.
n.4: A risk register manages risks, not physical components.

Scope Management.q: While defining the scope of a data centre project, the project manager wants to make sure every element of work identified in the breakdown of activities is properly costed. When defining project scope, why is it important to link the work breakdown structure with the cost breakdown structure?
o: To ensure compliance with procurement law
To assign responsibilities for risk management
To enable accurate budgeting for all project activities
Scope Management.w: Linking WBS and CBS ensures each work package is budgeted for, supporting accurate cost control.

n.0: Legal compliance is not a purpose of linking WBS and CBS.
n.1: Risk responsibilities are handled elsewhere.
n.2: Communication requirements are a separate consideration.
n.3: Meeting schedules are not set through WBS and CBS links.

Scope Management.q: A client has commissioned a project to upgrade its ageing IT infrastructure and replace outdated systems across the business. Distinguishing the value the organisation gains from what is physically delivered, the main benefit expected by the client is:
o: The appointment of a new project team
The network diagram for the project
Improved organisational performance due to enhanced IT systems
Scope Management.w: Benefits are the measurable improvements gained, such as improved organisational performance.

n.0: Team appointments are part of project setup.
n.1: Network diagrams are project management tools.
n.2: Technical specifications are outputs, not benefits.
n.4: Meeting minutes are supporting documents.

Scope Management.q: During a project, a change request is submitted to alter the design of a key deliverable. What is the immediate next step in the change control process after the request is received?
o: Initial evaluation of the change request
Scope Management.w: After a change request is submitted, the first step is to carry out an initial evaluation before any further actions.

n.1: Stakeholder communication is important but not the immediate next step.
n.2: A detailed evaluation happens after the initial screening.
n.3: Implementation only occurs after evaluations and approvals.
n.4: Plans are updated only after approval and decisions are made.

Scope Management.q: A project manager on an agile (iterative) project receives frequent minor change requests. How is change control typically managed differently in iterative projects compared to linear projects?
o: All changes are rejected by default in iterative projects
Plans are never updated after changes in iterative projects
Changes require a formal review board for each request in iterative projects
Changes are expected and managed continuously in iterative life cycles
Change requests are not allowed in iterative projects
Scope Management.w: Iterative projects integrate change control continuously, as changes are expected throughout the life cycle.

n.0: Minor changes are not automatically rejected in iterative projects.
n.1: Plans are updated as necessary in response to changes.
n.2: Not every change in iterative projects goes through a formal board.
n.4: Change requests are allowed and expected.

Scope Management.q: What stage of the change control process involves considering potential impacts, costs, and benefits in depth before making a recommendation?
Scope Management.w: A detailed evaluation explores all potential impacts, costs, and benefits before any recommendation.

n.0: Implementation occurs after evaluation and approval.
n.1: Initial evaluation is a high-level review, not in-depth.
n.3: Submission is just the initial raising of the change.
n.4: Plans are only updated once a decision has been made.

Scope Management.q: A construction project team has completed the detailed evaluation of a change to building materials. What should happen next according to the change control process?
o: A recommendation is made based on the evaluation
A new business case is created
Stakeholders are informed and the change is logged
Scope Management.w: Once a detailed evaluation is completed, a recommendation is made regarding whether to proceed with the change.

n.0: Implementation must follow formal decision-making, not immediately after evaluation.
n.2: A new business case is not always required for every change.
n.3: Only relevant plans are updated after a change is approved.
n.4: Informing stakeholders is important but follows the decision process.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is documenting the recognised sequence of steps that a formal change control process follows from the point a change is raised through to a decision. Which of the following is NOT typically a stage in the standard change control process?
Scope Management.w: "Risk closure" is not a stage in the standard change control process.

n.0: Recommendation is a defined stage in change control.
n.2: Submitting the change request is the first step.
n.3: Detailed evaluation occurs before recommendations.
n.4: Initial evaluation is a key early stage.

Scope Management.q: On a linear project, the change advisory board has just approved a scope change and the project manager is deciding what to do next. In a linear project, why is it important to update the project plans after a change has been approved?
o: To reduce the need for further stakeholder communication about scope
To capture and record the requester's original reason for the change
To ensure all aspects of the project are aligned with the new scope
To keep the original scope unchanged while adding the new work
To notify the change advisory board that implementation has now begun
Scope Management.w: Updating plans aligns project delivery with the approved changes, keeping everyone on track.

n.0: Future changes may still be required.
n.1: Documentation should not be made complex without purpose.
n.3: Stakeholder engagement should not be delayed.
n.4: Team size changes are separate decisions.

Scope Management.q: A software development project receives multiple change requests each week. What is a key advantage of iterative life cycles when managing change control?
o: They use only annual change control reviews
They accommodate frequent changes without disrupting the project flow
They ignore change requests to maintain stability
They eliminate the need for change logs
They delay all changes until the end of the project
Scope Management.w: Iterative life cycles are flexible and can accommodate ongoing change without major disruption.

n.0: Frequent reviews occur in iterative, not just annual.
n.2: Ignoring change requests is not best practice.
n.3: Change logs are still required for accountability.
n.4: Delaying all changes is not how iterative projects operate.

Scope Management.q: Having assessed a change request's impact and feasibility, a project manager reaches the 'recommendation' stage of the change control process before the board makes its final decision. What does the 'recommendation' stage in the change control process typically involve?
o: Gathering the initial details of the change from the requester
Recording the raw change request in the change register
Providing a decision or course of action based on evaluations
Implementing the approved change across all of the project plans
Assessing the impact and feasibility of the proposed change
Scope Management.w: The recommendation stage provides a suggested course of action, whether to proceed with the change or not.

n.0: A new request is not part of the recommendation stage.
n.1: Plan updates occur after recommendations are agreed.
n.3: Notification to clients comes later in the process.
n.4: Project scope is only altered as needed.

Scope Management.q: After a change has been successfully implemented on a project, the project manager wants to make sure the experience improves how future changes are handled. Which action ensures lessons are captured for future change control improvements?
o: Postponing any reflection on the change process
Starting a new project phase immediately
Deleting all documentation related to the change
Scope Management.w: Recording outcomes and lessons supports continuous improvement of the change control process.

n.0: Immediate reflection is important for improvement.
n.1: A new phase can start, but lessons should be captured first.
n.2: Documentation should be retained for accountability.
n.4: Team feedback is valuable and should not be ignored.

Scope Management.q: A project manager who works across both linear and iterative delivery is mapping the change control steps that appear in each approach, looking for common ground. Which pair of stages is common to both linear and iterative change control processes?
o: Product backlog refinement and change approval
Iteration planning and risk register update
Scope Management.w: Both linear and iterative processes include initial and detailed evaluations as part of change control.

n.0: Stakeholder mapping is a separate process.
n.1: Risk closure is not a defined stage in change control.
n.2: Sprint review is not part of standard change control stages.
n.3: Backlog refinement and iteration planning are agile concepts but not specific to change control.

Scope Management.q: A project team submits a request to alter the project schedule due to new client requirements. What is the first formal stage in the change control process?
Scope Management.w: The initial evaluation is the first formal stage after a change request is received.

n.1: Resource reallocation is not the first step in the process.
n.2: Detailed evaluation comes after the initial review.
n.3: Plans are updated only if the change is approved.
n.4: Implementation follows approval and plan updates.

Scope Management.q: During change control, a proposed change reaches the point where the project team must thoroughly analyse its consequences before any recommendation is made. Which of the following BEST describes the role of 'detailed evaluation' in the change control process?
o: Communicating the agreed change to all affected stakeholders
Analysing the impact, feasibility, and risks of the proposed change
Formally submitting the change request into the control process
Recording the outcome of the change board's final decision
Updating the project baseline once the change is approved
Scope Management.w: Detailed evaluation assesses all potential impacts, risks, and feasibility before a decision.

n.0: Lessons learned are reviewed after change implementation.
n.2: Supplier notification occurs if the change affects them, not in every evaluation.
n.3: Contact details are not the focus of detailed evaluation.
n.4: Closure reports are not linked to the evaluation stage.

Scope Management.q: A project manager moving from a traditional waterfall project to an agile delivery team notices that changes are handled quite differently. In an agile project, how does the change control process differ from that of a traditional linear project?
o: All changes must be approved at the project board level
Changes are reviewed and incorporated continuously
Change requests are only considered at project closure
No changes are allowed during delivery
Scope Management.w: Agile and iterative projects expect and integrate changes throughout the process.

n.0: Approval is typically less hierarchical in agile approaches.
n.2: Waiting until closure defeats the purpose of iterative delivery.
n.3: Change is a fundamental part of agile and iterative approaches.
n.4: Iterative processes do not reject changes by default.

Scope Management.q: A project sponsor asks for a cost-benefit analysis before deciding on a change. At which stage in change control is this MOST likely to happen?
Scope Management.w: The detailed evaluation includes cost-benefit and impact analyses before recommendation.

n.0: Reviews happen after project completion, not during change control.
n.1: Implementation follows evaluation and decision-making.
n.2: Plans are updated only after approval.
n.4: Initial evaluation is high-level, not in-depth.

Scope Management.q: Once a change has been approved, a project manager reaches the 'update plans' stage and begins revising the affected project documents. Which of the following is NOT a typical activity within the 'update plans' stage of the change control process?
Scope Management.w: A new project charter is not normally created during the update plans stage.

n.0: Budgets are updated to reflect new costs or savings.
n.1: Resources may need to be reassigned.
n.2: The schedule is often amended to reflect changes.
n.3: Timelines are revised if required by the change.

Scope Management.q: Following the evaluation of a change request, a project manager prepares a formal recommendation for the change authority ahead of its decision. What is the main purpose of making a formal recommendation during change control?
o: To implement the approved change across all project plans at once
To notify affected stakeholders that the change has been rejected
To capture the original details of the requested change formally
To assess the technical feasibility and risks of the change
To provide an informed decision on whether to proceed with the change
Scope Management.w: The recommendation stage guides decision-makers with an informed course of action.

n.0: Risk registers are maintained throughout the project.
n.1: Procurement activities are separate from change control recommendations.
n.2: Documentation updates occur after a decision is made.
n.3: Team changes are not the focus of recommendations.

Scope Management.q: During a project, the client repeatedly requests small changes to features after sprints. Which stage of the change control process is most critical in an iterative project to ensure these changes do not disrupt delivery?
Scope Management.w: Continuous initial evaluation helps manage ongoing change requests efficiently in iterative projects.

n.1: Formal closure happens after all work is done, not during change control.
n.2: Rejecting all changes is not a feature of iterative approaches.
n.3: Risk closure is not a stage in change control.
n.4: Plan updates occur as needed, but not only annually.

Scope Management.q: A trainee is comparing how changes are handled on both linear and iterative projects and is asked to identify a principle that holds true in each. Which statement about change implementation in both linear and iterative projects is TRUE?
o: Implementation can start before evaluation in iterative projects
Changes are never implemented in iterative projects
Implementation is optional in linear projects
Implementation should only proceed after proper evaluation and approval
Implementation occurs automatically after a request
Scope Management.w: Both approaches require that changes are evaluated and approved before implementation.

n.0: Evaluation is always needed before proceeding, regardless of life cycle.
n.1: Iterative projects implement approved changes.
n.2: Implementation is not optional if a change is approved.
n.4: Implementation is not automatic and must be controlled.

Scope Management.q: A stakeholder identifies a needed alteration to a deliverable and the project manager formally logs it to set the change control process in motion. What is a common purpose of the 'request' stage in change control?
o: To formally document the need for a change and begin the process
To update the project schedule to reflect the requested change
To record the lessons learned from the completed change
To secure the change board's approval ahead of any evaluation
To analyse the full impact of the change before deciding
Scope Management.w: The request stage formally records and initiates the change process.

n.1: Risks are managed separately from change control.
n.2: The project is not closed during change control.
n.3: Changes are not approved at the request stage.
n.4: Financial records are only updated if a change is approved.

Scope Management.q: A stakeholder disagrees with a change that has already been implemented. What is the BEST action the project manager should take to maintain good change control practice?
o: Update the change register to remove the disputed decision
Review the change control records and communicate the rationale for the decision
Escalate the disagreement to the sponsor for a fresh ruling
Submit a new change request to formally overturn the decision
Reverse the implemented change and restore the previous project baseline
Scope Management.w: Good practice includes transparency and clear communication, referencing decision records as needed.

n.0: Responsibility should not be shifted without cause.
n.2: Documentation should always be maintained.
n.3: Stakeholder concerns should not be ignored.
n.4: Reversing changes should only be considered if justified and approved.

Scope Management.q: On a linear project, a change authority has considered the recommendation for a proposed change and reached its decision. Which activity typically follows the 'recommendation' stage in the change control process?
o: Carrying out a detailed evaluation of impact
Raising the request and logging it in the change log
Carrying out an initial evaluation of the request
Scope Management.w: In the change control process, the recommendation (approve, reject or defer) is followed by updating plans: the baseline, project management plan and configuration records are revised before the change is implemented.

n.0: Detailed evaluation of impact happens before the recommendation, not after it.
n.2: Raising and logging the request is the first stage of the process.
n.3: Initial evaluation is an early screening step, well before the recommendation.
n.4: Implementation comes after the plans have been updated, so everyone works to the revised baseline.

Scope Management.q: A product owner suggests a new feature late in an agile project iteration. What makes change control more flexible in iterative life cycles compared to linear ones?
o: Changes are logged but implemented only after the project closes
Changes require sign-off from the full governance board each time
Changes are deferred to the final iteration before the release
Changes bypass the evaluation step because the iterations are short
Changes can be evaluated and incorporated within short cycles or sprints
Scope Management.w: Iterative projects are structured to allow changes to be considered and implemented within short cycles.

n.0: Postponing changes contradicts the agile philosophy.
n.1: Stakeholder approval is still important.
n.2: Documentation remains essential in all projects.
n.3: Automatic acceptance is not good practice.

Scope Management.q: A project manager insists that every change request, whether approved or rejected, along with its outcome, is entered into the change register. What is the main reason for recording all change requests and their outcomes?
o: To limit the number of changes stakeholders request
To satisfy the supplier's contractual reporting duties
To transfer responsibility for changes to the sponsor
To speed up approval of future change requests
To maintain a clear audit trail and accountability
Scope Management.w: A clear audit trail ensures accountability and supports future reviews of decisions.

n.0: Visibility of changes is increased, not decreased.
n.1: Engagement is improved by transparency.
n.2: Documentation supports timely decision making, not delays.
n.3: Paperwork is not the primary reason; it's about governance.

Scope Management.q: When a change request first arrives, the project manager carries out a quick initial evaluation to screen it before any in-depth work is done. Which of these is NOT usually considered when performing an initial evaluation of a change request?
o: Possible risks introduced by the change
Scope Management.w: A detailed cost-benefit analysis is typically reserved for the detailed evaluation stage.

n.0: Impact on objectives is reviewed even at the initial evaluation.
n.1: Scope alignment is considered early on.
n.2: Urgency helps prioritise evaluation.
n.3: Risks are reviewed even at a high level initially.

Scope Management.q: A change has been approved and implemented, but was not logged in the change register. What risk does this pose?
o: Overspend against the approved change budget
Duplicate approval by the change board

n.2: Quality impact concerns standards and acceptance criteria, not dates.
n.4: Budget impact concerns cost; the project manager here is judging the effect on delivery dates.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is preparing a high-level impact summary for a change before deciding whether a detailed evaluation is justified. In that summary, the high-level impact of a proposed change covers the classic project constraints: its effect on ______________, cost and quality.
Scope Management.w: The classic project constraints are time, cost and quality, so the high-level impact summary covers the change's effect on the schedule alongside cost and quality.

n.0: Stakeholders are considered in a full assessment, but they are not one of the classic time, cost and quality constraints.
n.2: Procurement may be affected by a change, but it is not one of the three classic constraints.
n.3: Communicating the change follows the decision; it is not one of the three constraints.
n.4: Governance decides who approves the change; it is not a constraint the change affects.

Scope Management.q: Having evaluated a proposed change, a project manager is deciding how to respond and lists the recognised courses of action open to them. Which of the following is NOT a typical option when assessing ways to address a proposed change?
o: Deferring the change to a later phase
Modifying the change to reduce impact
Scope Management.w: Ignoring a change is not a valid or responsible assessment option.

n.0: Accepting, modifying, rejecting, or deferring are valid options.

Scope Management.q: Faced with several alternative ways of accommodating a proposed change, the project manager wants a structured tool that scores each option against benefit and risk criteria. Which technique uses a matrix to compare the benefits and risks of different change options?
Scope Management.w: Decision matrices weigh different factors to support option selection.

n.0: Fishbone diagrams analyse causes of problems.
n.1: Pareto charts prioritise causes by frequency.
n.2: Critical path identifies longest project duration.
n.3: Gantt charts show schedules.

Scope Management.q: A proposed change could affect whether a deliverable still satisfies the quality standards and regulations the project is obliged to meet. When reviewing a change's impact on project quality, which of the following is a common factor to assess?
Scope Management.w: Assessing a change's impact on quality means checking whether the deliverables would still comply with the standards and regulations the project must meet.

n.0: Contract terms are a commercial impact; they do not show whether deliverables still meet standards.
n.1: Communication effects concern stakeholders, not whether the deliverable meets quality standards.
n.2: The critical path is a schedule measure, not a quality factor.
n.3: The cost baseline relates to budget impact, not quality.

Scope Management.q: When more than one way of accommodating a change exists, the project manager needs a structured method to weigh each alternative before recommending one. In change control, the process of ______________ helps evaluate different change options based on criteria like cost, risk, and benefit.
Scope Management.w: Option analysis compares alternatives to identify the best approach.

n.0: Stakeholder mapping identifies key stakeholders.
n.1: Resource leveling is a scheduling technique.
n.3: Scope creep is uncontrolled scope growth.
n.4: Risk avoidance is a risk strategy, not option analysis.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is carrying out a high-level impact assessment of a proposed change to decide whether detailed evaluation is warranted. Which of the following is NOT usually assessed when considering the high-level impact of a proposed change?
Scope Management.w: The CEO’s opinion is not a formal factor in high-level impact assessment.

n.0: Schedule, cost, resource, and quality are all core assessment areas.

Scope Management.q: A proposed change to the project's approach is expected to push the completion date back by around two weeks, though it adds no extra cost. In a high-level impact assessment, what high-level impact does this delay best represent?
Scope Management.w: Delay directly affects the project schedule.

n.0: Cost may also be affected, but delay specifically refers to schedule.
n.2: Quality relates to standards, not schedule.
n.3: Risk is a broader concept.
n.4: Resources may be related but delay is primarily scheduling.

Scope Management.q: A project manager must choose between several competing responses to a change, each strong on different measures such as cost, risk and benefit. Which option is typically used to compare multiple change options based on weighted criteria?
Scope Management.w: Multi-criteria decision analysis ranks options using weighted factors.

n.0: Pareto analysis prioritises causes or effects.
n.1: Brainstorming is an idea generation technique.
n.2: CPM focuses on scheduling.
n.4: WBS breaks down project scope.

Scope Management.q: A proposed change may require different people or specialist skills than the project currently has available, and the project manager wants this reflected in the evaluation. When assessing the impact of a proposed change, the ______________ considers potential changes in available personnel and skills.
Scope Management.w: Resource assessment examines changes in workforce or skills needed.

n.0: Stakeholder analysis examines influence and interests.
n.2: Quality review examines standards.
n.3: Cost analysis examines financial impacts.
n.4: Risk assessment focuses on uncertainties.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is drafting a high-level impact assessment for a proposed change and wants it to show how far the change would push back the project's key delivery points. Which element of the assessment would show this?
Scope Management.w: To show how far the change would push back key delivery points, the assessment needs the expected delay to milestones (the schedule impact).

n.0: Cost impact matters but does not show the delay to delivery points.
n.1: Risk exposure does not show the delay to milestones.
n.3: Quality impact concerns standards, not timing.
n.4: Benefits impact concerns value, not how far milestones move.

Scope Management.q: After a change request is logged, the project manager reviews the legitimate ways of responding to it under the change control process. Which of these is NOT a valid option when assessing how to respond to a proposed change?
Scope Management.w: Rejecting without evaluation risks missing important information and is not best practice.

n.0: Acceptance is a valid response.
n.1: Deferring allows time for planning.
n.2: Further analysis improves decision quality.
n.4: Modifying is often a compromise.

Scope Management.q: With several viable options for handling a change, the project manager wants a simple scoring tool to rank them objectively before recommending one. In change control, the ______________ helps prioritise change options by scoring criteria such as cost, risk, and benefit.
Scope Management.w: Decision matrices score options across multiple criteria to aid selection.

n.0: Gantt charts show schedules.
n.1: WBS breaks down scope, not decisions.
n.3: Risk registers track risks, not decision criteria.
n.4: Stakeholder registers list stakeholders.

Scope Management.q: A project manager on a construction project receives a request to alter the design of a key deliverable. Under pressure from the sponsor to move quickly, they consider progressing it without first evaluating its high-level impact. Which of the following is a key risk of taking this approach?
Scope Management.w: Without proper assessment, projects face surprises that can derail plans.

n.1: It can actually increase scope creep.
n.2: Poor assessment tends to hurt morale.
n.3: Stakeholder satisfaction may decline.
n.4: Delivery usually slows with unmanaged changes.

Scope Management.q: During the delivery phase of an IT programme, a change request is raised to add new functionality. Before it goes to the change control board, the project manager wants to appraise how much the change would add to the approved budget. Which of the following high-level impacts is being assessed?
Scope Management.w: Assessing how much the change adds to the approved budget is the cost impact.

n.0: Schedule impact concerns timing, not budget.
n.1: Quality impact concerns standards and acceptance criteria.
n.3: Benefits impact concerns the value delivered, not the budget increase.
n.4: Resource impact concerns the people and equipment needed; the stem asks about the budget.

Scope Management.q: While appraising the options for a proposed change to a product's specification, the project manager wants to understand how robust each option remains if the underlying estimates and assumptions turn out to be inaccurate. What is the purpose of carrying out sensitivity analysis in this situation?
o: To allocate the budget across the work packages
To identify and record all new project risks
To define team roles and responsibilities in full
To rank stakeholders by their level of influence
To understand how changes in assumptions affect outcomes
Scope Management.w: Sensitivity analysis evaluates how varying inputs influence results, supporting robust decisions.

n.0: Risk registers are created independently.
n.1: Stakeholder roles are managed separately.
n.2: Budget allocation is separate from sensitivity analysis.
n.3: It is not intended to cause delays.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is preparing a recommendation to the change control board on a proposed change to the scope of a business transformation project. What is the primary reason that would justify recommending that the change be approved?
o: It adds value to the project and aligns with objectives
It pushes costs beyond the approved budget
It introduces significant delays to the schedule
It proceeds despite limited stakeholder support
It expands the project scope with no added benefit
Scope Management.w: Recommendations to approve focus on value addition and alignment with goals.

n.1: Budget overruns typically oppose approval.
n.2: Delays usually argue against approval.
n.3: Lack of support is a concern.
n.4: Unjustified scope increase is not a reason to approve.

Scope Management.q: Having assessed a change request during the delivery phase, the project manager intends to recommend that it is rejected, largely because of the effect it would have on the project timeline. Which of the following factors supports this recommendation to reject the change?
Scope Management.w: A recommendation must be justified against the business case and objectives. A significant negative impact on the schedule, the main concern here, is a valid reason to reject a change.

n.0: Being within delegated authority affects who decides, not whether the change should be rejected.
n.1: Stakeholder support argues for the change; it does not support rejecting it.
n.2: Strong alignment with objectives is a reason to approve a change, not reject it.
n.4: Benefits that outweigh costs support approval, not rejection.

Scope Management.q: One reason to defer a change might be:
o: The change is minor and irrelevant
The current project phase is not suitable for implementation
Scope Management.w: Deferment often occurs when timing is inappropriate despite potential value.

n.0: Minor irrelevant changes are usually rejected, not deferred.
n.1: Unanimous approval supports immediate action.
n.3: Full engagement favours proceeding.
n.4: Surplus funds encourage approval, not deferment.

Scope Management.q: A change has been proposed on a manufacturing project and the project manager is evaluating whether to put it forward for approval. Which of the following would justify a recommendation to approve the change?
o: The change is outside project scope
The change reduces overall project risk
The change increases project complexity unnecessarily
Scope Management.w: Risk reduction is a valid reason to approve a change.

n.0: Out-of-scope changes require rejection or redefinition.
n.2: Unnecessary complexity argues against approval.
n.3: Lack of benefits is a reason to reject.
n.4: Delays generally oppose approval.

Scope Management.q: A change request has been submitted, but the project manager does not yet have enough information about its effects to make a firm recommendation to approve or reject it. Which of the following would support a decision to defer the change to a later point?
o: Insufficient information to fully assess the change
Scope Management.w: Lack of information and current resource limits justify deferment.

n.1: Urgent risk mitigation calls for prompt action.
n.2: Cost savings encourage approval, not deferment.
n.4: Stakeholder demand favours approval or prioritisation.

Scope Management.q: During the delivery of a fast-moving project, the project manager reviews a proposed change and prepares to recommend that the change control board rejects it. What is a common justification for rejecting a proposed change?
o: The change is supported by stakeholders
The change negatively impacts critical project milestones
The change aligns well with the business case
Scope Management.w: Negative impact on key milestones is a valid reason for rejection.

n.0: Stakeholder support helps approval chances.
n.1: Quality improvement supports approval.
n.3: Cost reduction favours approval.
n.4: Good alignment supports approval.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is documenting the justification for a recommendation on a proposed change so that the change control board can reach an informed decision. Which of the following aspects is the LEAST relevant when justifying the recommendation?
o: The change's impact on the project schedule
Alignment of the change with project objectives
The level of risk introduced by the change
The cost implications of the proposed change
Personal opinions of project team members
Scope Management.w: Personal opinions are subjective and less relevant than objective factors.

n.0: Schedule impact is critical.
n.1: Alignment ensures strategic fit.
n.2: Risk affects project success.
n.3: Cost implications affect feasibility.

Scope Management.q: On a product development project, a proposed change is expected to increase costs but to improve the quality of the deliverable significantly. As the project manager preparing a recommendation for the sponsor, how should this recommendation be justified?
o: Approve if benefits outweigh additional costs
Scope Management.w: Justification balances cost increase against quality benefits to decide approval.

n.0: Deferring without analysis is not responsible.
n.1: Changes need evaluation before acceptance.
n.3: Ignoring benefits overlooks project value.
n.4: Rejecting without considering benefits may lose value.

Scope Management.q: A change is proposed midway through a project at a time when the delivery team is fully committed to other critical work. Which of the following is a valid reason to defer the change on the grounds of resource availability?
o: Key personnel are fully allocated to other tasks
The change is small, simple and low-effort
The change is urgent and business-critical
The project is currently ahead of schedule
Scope Management.w: Resource constraints justify delaying implementation.

n.1: Small changes usually can be done promptly.
n.2: Urgent changes should not be deferred.
n.3: Stakeholder demand favours prioritisation.
n.4: Ahead-of-schedule projects can handle changes faster.

Scope Management.q: When recommending rejection, what impact should be emphasized?
o: Negative effects on cost, schedule, or quality
Scope Management.w: Objective negative impacts provide sound grounds for rejection.

n.0: Documentation clarity should be improved but doesn’t justify rejection alone.
n.1: Subjective dislike is not a sufficient reason.
n.2: Minor challenges are expected and manageable.
n.4: Stakeholder enthusiasm alone does not determine approval.

Scope Management.q: When preparing a recommendation on a proposed change, the project manager carries out a risk assessment as part of the appraisal before advising the change control board. What role does this risk assessment play in justifying the recommendation?
o: Removes all uncertainty from the decision
Transfers risk ownership entirely to stakeholders
Speeds approval by skipping detailed analysis
Replaces the need for stakeholder consultation
Scope Management.w: Risk assessment informs decision-makers of potential downsides.

n.0: Risk assessment does not guarantee approval.
n.1: Stakeholder input remains important.
n.2: Risk management controls scope growth.
n.3: Communication should be enhanced, not limited.

Scope Management.q: If a change aligns with strategic objectives but causes a slight schedule delay, what is a balanced justification for approval?
o: Reject because of any schedule impact
Defer the change indefinitely to be safe
Scope Management.w: Strategic benefits can justify small delays when properly managed.

n.0: Schedule impact must be weighed against benefits.
n.2: Approval requires balanced consideration.
n.3: Ignoring alignment risks losing value.
n.4: Indefinite deferment may harm value delivery.

Scope Management.q: A project manager reviews a newly submitted change request but is not yet confident about its full effect on the project's cost, schedule and objectives. Which of the following is an appropriate reason to defer the change?
o: Project is behind schedule and needs speeding up
Lack of sufficient data to assess impact
All required resources are available now
Scope Management.w: Deferring allows time to gather more information for a sound decision.

n.0: Speeding up needs prioritising changes, not deferring.
n.1: Consensus suggests proceeding, not deferring.
n.3: Availability of resources supports proceeding.
n.4: Urgency calls for immediate action.

Scope Management.q: A proposed change on a fixed-budget project would require additional funding that the project simply does not have available. As the project manager, which of the following justifications supports rejecting the change on budget grounds?
o: The change would shorten the overall project schedule
The cost exceeds available funding and threatens project viability
The change is popular and widely supported by stakeholders
The change would improve deliverable quality significantly
The change carries very low risk to delivery
Scope Management.w: Exceeding budget limits without offsetting benefits supports rejection.

n.0: Schedule reduction is beneficial but not guaranteed.
n.2: Popularity does not override budget issues.
n.3: Quality improvements are positive but may not offset costs.
n.4: Low risk alone does not justify budget overspend.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is drafting a recommendation to approve a change for consideration by the sponsor and the change control board. When justifying a recommendation to approve a change, which of the following factors is the most important?
o: Length of time taken to submit the change
Alignment with business objectives and benefits realisation
Scope Management.w: Business alignment and benefits are primary reasons to approve changes.

n.0: Colour coding is irrelevant.
n.1: Submission time is procedural, not justification.
n.3: Stakeholder count does not determine approval.
n.4: Past delays do not justify or reject changes alone.

Scope Management.q: Late in a project, a change is proposed while the delivery team is already stretched across several critical tasks. Which of the following reasons would justify deferring the change because resources are currently limited?
o: The change has strong support from key stakeholders
The change would reduce overall delivery risk
The project is currently running under budget
The change is simple and quick to implement
Implementing now would overextend the team and risk delivery
Scope Management.w: Resource limitations can necessitate delaying changes to maintain quality and schedule.

n.0: Support encourages proceeding, not deferring.
n.1: Risk reduction supports approval.
n.2: Budget status alone does not justify deferral.
n.3: Simple changes typically proceed immediately.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is assessing a proposed change and is concerned about the effect it could have on the likelihood of the project succeeding. Which of the following would support a recommendation to reject the change on the grounds of risk?
o: The change introduces significant uncertainty threatening success
The change has minimal impact on deliverables
The change has a clear implementation plan
Scope Management.w: High risks to success justify rejection despite other factors.

n.0: Cost reduction encourages approval.
n.2: Minimal impact favours approval.
n.3: Clear plans aid approval.
n.4: Improved engagement supports change.

Scope Management.q: A change has just been approved through the formal change control process on a live project. Why is it important for the project manager to update the affected project plans following this approval?
o: To ensure all team members work with the latest information
To satisfy documentation requirements set by external auditors
To justify a later request for additional project funding
To reset the project baseline right back to its origin
To transfer schedule ownership over to the project sponsor
Scope Management.w: Updating plans keeps the team aligned and informed on current project scope and timelines.

n.1: The goal is not to add unnecessary paperwork.
n.2: Communication should be enhanced, not reduced.
n.3: Confusing stakeholders is counterproductive.
n.4: Proper updates aim to keep delivery on track.

Scope Management.q: Following approval of a change that alters the delivery dates of several milestones, the project manager sets about revising the project documentation. Which of the following documents would most directly be updated to reflect the revised timing?
Scope Management.w: The schedule holds the dates of activities and milestones, so it is the document most directly updated when approved timings change.

n.0: The OBS shows who is in the project organisation, not timings.
n.1: The quality plan sets standards and methods, not milestone dates.
n.3: The PBS shows the products to be delivered, not when.
n.4: The stakeholder register holds stakeholder information, not timings.

Scope Management.q: A change has been approved on a project, but the project manager neglects to revise the project schedule to reflect its impact on the timeline. What is a likely consequence of failing to update the schedule?
Scope Management.w: Outdated schedules cause confusion and can delay progress.

n.0: Costs may increase due to inefficiencies.
n.1: Risks often increase.
n.3: Trust may decline if communication is poor.
n.4: Completion is usually delayed.

Scope Management.q: Updating plans after a change helps in:
o: Communicating expectations clearly to all stakeholders
Scope Management.w: Clear communication via updated plans ensures alignment and sets expectations.

n.0: Documentation usually increases.
n.1: Meetings are often still necessary.
n.2: Procurement timing depends on plan updates.
n.3: Risks should be actively managed.

Scope Management.q: After a change is approved that affects the delivery dates of several work packages, the project manager needs to record the revised timeline for the team to work to. Which of the following plans specifically sets out the revised timeline following the change?
Scope Management.w: The project schedule reflects timing and milestone adjustments.

n.0: Quality plan focuses on standards.
n.2: Risk plan manages risks.
n.3: Communication plan handles information flows.
n.4: Procurement plan covers purchasing.

Scope Management.q: Immediately after a change is approved, the project manager circulates the updated plans to the team and to key stakeholders rather than waiting until the next progress meeting. What is a key benefit of communicating the updated plans promptly?
Scope Management.w: Timely communication reduces misunderstandings and helps maintain progress.

n.0: Responsibility should be clear and shared.
n.2: Costs generally increase if communication is poor.
n.3: Engagement improves with good communication.
n.4: Decisions should be timely, not delayed.

Scope Management.q: An approved change alters the way people will be deployed across the remaining work packages of a project. Which plan should the project manager update to record the new deployment of people?
Scope Management.w: The resource allocation plan records which people are assigned to which work and when, so it must be updated when an approved change alters how people are deployed.

n.0: The benefits realisation plan tracks benefits, not who works on which work package.
n.1: The quality management plan sets standards and checks for outputs, not resource assignments.
n.2: The communication plan sets out who receives information; it does not record resource deployment.
n.4: The procurement strategy covers buying from external suppliers, not deploying internal people.

Scope Management.q: A significant change has been approved that alters aspects of the deliverable being produced on a construction project. Why should the project manager review the quality management plan following such a change?
o: To ensure deliverables continue to meet standards
To speed up delivery regardless of quality
Scope Management.w: Quality plans must reflect changes to maintain expected standards.

n.0: Stakeholders remain important.
n.1: Closure occurs after delivery.
n.3: Documentation should be adequate.
n.4: Quality should not be sacrificed for speed.

Scope Management.q: A change has been approved and the schedule revised, but the project manager does not pass the updated schedule on to the delivery team. What can failing to communicate the schedule updates cause on the project?
o: Conflicts in task execution and delays
Faster progress across the remaining tasks
Lower overall costs for the project
Reduced scope of the project deliverables
Scope Management.w: Lack of communication often leads to confusion and schedule conflicts.

n.1: Progress usually slows with confusion.
n.2: Costs may increase due to inefficiencies.
n.3: Satisfaction declines without clear updates.
n.4: Scope is determined by the change, not communication.

Scope Management.q: Following a series of approved changes on a programme, the project manager wants to ensure that everyone continues to be kept informed in a structured and consistent way. Which of the following plans outlines how project information, including change updates, will be communicated?
Scope Management.w: Communication plans detail how and when information is shared with stakeholders.

n.0: Resource plans manage personnel and materials.
n.1: Quality plans focus on standards.
n.2: Procurement plans manage purchases.
n.4: Risk plans focus on managing risks.

Scope Management.q: Updating project plans after changes is important because:
o: It maintains project control and ensures accurate tracking
Scope Management.w: Accurate plans enable effective management and oversight.

n.0: Risks are better managed with updates.
n.1: Motivation often increases with clarity.
n.3: Updates streamline control, not bureaucracy.
n.4: Timely updates speed decisions.

Scope Management.q: A change that alters the project timeline has just been approved by the change control board. Which of the following should the project manager communicate to the team immediately after the change is approved?
Scope Management.w: Once a timeline change is approved, the team must work to the revised schedule, so it should be communicated immediately.

n.0: The whole change log is not what the team needs; they need the new schedule.
n.1: Previous milestones are out of date.
n.3: Draft options were working material before the decision and are no longer relevant.
n.4: The superseded baseline is no longer valid and would cause confusion.

Scope Management.q: During a large programme, the project manager fails to update the communication plan after a significant change is approved and rolled out. What is a likely consequence of this omission for the project?
o: Stakeholders receive inconsistent or delayed information
Project costs immediately begin to decrease
The project finishes ahead of its schedule
The project scope expands beyond its baseline
Scope Management.w: An outdated communication plan leads to poor information flow and stakeholder confusion.

n.1: Costs may increase with miscommunication.
n.2: Finishing early is unlikely.
n.3: Scope changes depend on other factors.
n.4: Quality is not necessarily improved.

Scope Management.q: A change has been approved that alters the scope of several work packages on a project. Why should the project manager review and update the risk register following the approval of this change?
o: Because changes may introduce new risks or affect existing ones
Because all previous risk assessments become instantly invalid
Because the change automatically cancels all existing risks
Because every risk must now transfer to the supplier
Because it removes the need for stakeholder risk meetings
Scope Management.w: Changes often affect project risks and require updated management strategies.

n.1: Previous assessments remain valid unless updated.
n.2: Closure happens after project delivery.
n.3: Issues must be documented for control.
n.4: Stakeholder meetings remain important.

Scope Management.q: As changes are approved and the plans are revised, the project manager continues to measure performance against the agreed project baseline. What is the role of the baseline when updating plans after changes have been made?
o: It fixes scope so that no further changes are permitted
It removes the need for a change control process
It updates itself automatically whenever changes are approved
It records only the financial aspects of the project
It provides a reference point to measure deviations
Scope Management.w: Baselines help track variances and manage changes effectively.

n.0: Baselines simplify control by providing clear reference.
n.1: Baseline use supports timely decisions.
n.2: Baselines remain important despite changes.
n.3: Stakeholder involvement should be maintained.

Scope Management.q: Shortly after a change is approved on a project, the project manager prioritises revising the project schedule ahead of other tasks. Which of the following is a key reason for promptly updating the schedule following the change?
Scope Management.w: Accurate schedules support effective tracking and management of progress.

n.0: Cost control requires accurate plans.
n.1: Delays should be reported timely.
n.2: Hiding delays undermines transparency.
n.4: Meetings are necessary for coordination.

Scope Management.q: Whenever changes are approved on a project, the project manager makes a point of updating the plans and sharing the revised versions openly with those affected. How does updating plans after changes affect stakeholder confidence?
o: It causes further delays to project delivery
It reduces confidence, as frequent updates suggest poor planning
It increases trust through transparency and control
It reduces accountability within the project team
It has little effect, as stakeholders judge only the final outputs
Scope Management.w: Updating and openly sharing plans after approved changes shows that change is controlled and that everyone works from the same version, which builds trust.

n.0: Updating plans keeps work aligned; it does not cause delay.
n.1: Controlled, transparent updates show good control; hidden or uncontrolled change damages confidence.
n.3: Clear, updated plans strengthen accountability.
n.4: Stakeholders also judge how the project is managed, and expectations are shaped throughout.

Scope Management.q: A project manager wants to set out in advance exactly how and when the impacts of any approved changes will be shared with the project's stakeholders. Which of the following plans details how and when changes and their impacts will be communicated?
Scope Management.w: Communication plans specify information distribution related to changes.

n.0: Procurement plans address purchasing.
n.1: Quality plans manage standards.
n.3: Resource plans focus on allocation.
n.4: Risk plans focus on risk identification and mitigation.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is presenting early cost estimates derived from limited scope definition. Stakeholders challenge the wide range and ask for a single definitive figure to approve funding. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refuse to provide any estimate until detailed design is complete
Select the highest estimate to minimise risk of overrun
Provide a single figure based on optimistic assumptions to secure approval
Explain the estimating funnel and present a range with assumptions and confidence levels
Average the high and low estimates and present that as the final cost
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Early estimates carry high uncertainty. The estimating funnel justifies a range with explicit assumptions and confidence, enabling informed decision-making without false precision.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: During an infrastructure project, successive estimates are narrowing but still diverge significantly between engineering and procurement teams. What is the most likely underlying issue?
o: Procurement has insufficient authority to influence cost estimates
Differences in estimating techniques are creating inconsistent assumptions
Engineering estimates are always more reliable than procurement estimates
The estimating funnel requires all estimates to converge at the same rate
The project has moved beyond the estimating phase
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Divergence often reflects inconsistent assumptions or methods rather than process failure. Alignment of assumptions is critical as estimates mature.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A sponsor requests cost certainty before approving the next phase, despite the project being in early concept stages. Which approach best balances governance and uncertainty?
o: Provide a detailed bottom-up estimate regardless of available information
Commit to a fixed cost and manage deviations later
Present staged estimates linked to decision gates with defined tolerances
Delay approval until cost certainty is achievable
Escalate the request as unrealistic and refuse to proceed
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Linking estimates to decision gates aligns with the estimating funnel and governance, enabling progressive refinement rather than premature certainty.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In a project with evolving requirements, a project manager continues to refine estimates without revisiting initial assumptions. What risk does this create?
o: The project will automatically reduce its overall uncertainty
The estimating funnel will cease to apply to the project
Estimates will converge far faster than the funnel predicts
Underlying assumptions may no longer reflect reality, reducing estimate credibility
Stakeholders will automatically gain greater confidence in the estimates
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: If assumptions are not updated, estimates may appear precise but are based on outdated context, undermining reliability.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project team uses analogous estimating based on a previous project, but fails to adjust for scale and complexity differences. What is the most likely outcome?
o: Systematic underestimation or overestimation due to invalid assumptions
Improved stakeholder confidence in the estimate
Faster convergence within the estimating funnel
Accurate estimates due to historical data
Elimination of uncertainty in early stages
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Analogous estimates require adjustment for context; failing to do so introduces bias and inaccurate assumptions.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is preparing cost estimates and wants to handle contingency in a way that reflects the concept of the estimating funnel as the project moves through successive phases. Which of the following scenarios best demonstrates an appropriate use of contingency in this context?
o: Adjusting contingency levels as uncertainty reduces across phases
Applying a fixed percentage contingency regardless of project stage
Adding contingency only after final estimates are agreed
Removing contingency once estimates are reviewed
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Contingency should reduce as uncertainty decreases, reflecting increasing estimate confidence.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A stakeholder insists that narrowing estimate ranges indicate improved team performance rather than reduced uncertainty. What is the correct interpretation?
o: Narrowing ranges typically reflect reduced uncertainty as information improves
Narrowing ranges have no real bearing on uncertainty
Narrowing ranges always demonstrate genuinely improved team performance
Narrowing ranges usually indicate poor or manipulated estimating
Narrowing ranges should generally be avoided during planning
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The estimating funnel narrows as uncertainty reduces with better information, not necessarily due to team performance.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: At the very start of a novel research and development project, little detailed information is available and uncertainty is high. The organisation has never run a comparable project and holds no relevant historical data, but several experienced specialists are available. Which estimating approach is most appropriate for the initial concept-phase cost estimate?
o: Delphi estimating using anonymous expert rounds
Earned value forecasting from progress to date
Parametric estimating from historical unit rates
