Analogous estimating from a similar past project
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: With no comparable project or historical data, analogous and parametric methods have no basis, and there is no detailed WBS yet for bottom-up estimating. Delphi gathers anonymous expert judgement over several facilitated rounds to reach a consensus, avoiding dominant voices.

n.1: Earned value forecasts from progress against a baseline; no work has been done yet.
n.2: Parametric estimating needs reliable historical data, which this novel project lacks.
n.3: Bottom-up estimating needs a detailed WBS, which does not exist at concept.
n.4: Analogous estimating needs a genuinely comparable past project, and there is none.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is pressured to reduce the estimate range to satisfy stakeholders without additional information. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reduce the range arbitrarily to preserve stakeholder confidence now
Delay communication until the estimates naturally converge later
Increase the contingency reserve to compensate for the pressure
Explain that reducing range requires reducing uncertainty through additional information
Present the range midpoint as the single final estimate
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Estimate ranges reflect uncertainty; reducing them without new information misrepresents reality.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: As a construction project progresses from its early feasibility work through to detailed design, the range around its cost and schedule estimates gradually becomes tighter, consistent with the estimating funnel. Which factor most directly drives this narrowing of the estimating funnel over time?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The funnel narrows as uncertainty reduces due to improved information and clarity.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project has formally moved from the concept phase into the design phase, yet the cost and schedule estimates the project manager presents remain almost as wide as they were at the outset. Given the expectations of the estimating funnel, what is the most likely explanation for this?
o: Stakeholders are actively resisting the required changes
Uncertainty has not been sufficiently reduced through analysis
The estimating process has already been fully completed
The project has been significantly overestimated throughout
The estimating funnel does not apply to this project
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: If estimates remain wide, uncertainty has not been adequately addressed despite phase progression.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A newly appointed project manager is producing the first cost and duration estimates for a project where much of the detail is still unknown, and is relying heavily on a set of assumptions to bridge the gaps. Which statement best reflects the proper role of assumptions in these early estimates?
o: Assumptions should be avoided until estimates are precise
Assumptions underpin estimates and must be documented and validated
Assumptions reduce the need for contingency
Assumptions are only relevant in later project stages
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Assumptions are critical drivers of estimates and must be transparent and reviewed.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager notices that estimates from different teams converge but remain consistently inaccurate. What is the most likely cause?
o: The estimating funnel is incorrectly applied
Teams are using consistent but flawed assumptions
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Converging but inaccurate estimates indicate shared incorrect assumptions rather than improved accuracy.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is concerned that the current estimates for a project carry a wide margin of uncertainty and wants to improve their reliability before the plan is baselined. Which TWO actions would most effectively reduce the uncertainty in the estimates?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Reducing uncertainty requires better information and validation, not artificial adjustments.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO characteristics best describe early-stage estimates?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Early estimates are uncertain and assumption-driven.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Under pressure from senior stakeholders, a project manager considers presenting tightly specified cost and schedule figures very early in the lifecycle, even though the underlying information is still limited. Which TWO outcomes are the most likely risks of presenting such overly precise estimates at this stage?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: False precision leads to unrealistic expectations and poor decisions.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: As a project moves from its early concept work through detailed planning and into delivery, the project manager observes that the estimates become steadily more dependable. Which TWO factors most strongly influence this improvement in estimate accuracy as the project progresses?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Accuracy improves with better data and clearer scope.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO practices improve transparency in estimating?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Transparency comes from clarity around assumptions and uncertainty.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO consequences arise from poorly managed assumptions?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Poor assumptions distort estimates and conceal risks.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager identifies that several activities appear independent but later discovers delays due to hidden dependencies. What is the most likely cause?
o: The timeline was too aggressive for the project scope
The critical path was incorrectly calculated
Activities were incorrectly sequenced due to incomplete dependency identification
Resources were not allocated efficiently across tasks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Hidden dependencies typically arise from incomplete identification during planning, leading to sequencing issues and delays.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A sponsor challenges a project timeline that shows several activities running in parallel, arguing that the plan is overly optimistic. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Recalculate the schedule using only sequential activities
Demonstrate the logical dependencies that allow parallel sequencing
Remove parallel activities to reduce perceived risk
Delay the project start until sequencing is simplified
Extend all activity durations to create buffer
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Parallel activities are valid where dependencies allow. The key is to justify sequencing based on logical relationships rather than perception.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In a schedule review, two activities are shown as sequential, but the team argues they could overlap. What should determine whether overlap is appropriate?
o: The duration of the activities involved
The logical dependency type between the activities
The preference of the project manager
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Overlap depends on dependency type (e.g., finish-to-start vs start-to-start), not preference or pressure.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager reviews a schedule that clearly shows many dependencies between activities, yet delivery is repeatedly hampered by delays that were not anticipated. On closer inspection the logical order of the work does not match how the tasks can realistically be carried out. What is the most likely underlying issue?
o: Stakeholders are not sufficiently engaged in delivery
Individual activities have been estimated too short
Sequencing does not reflect actual execution constraints
Dependencies have been documented in excessive detail
The timeline contains too much granular detail
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: If sequencing does not reflect real-world constraints, dependencies may exist but not be accurate, causing delays.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: While building a network diagram, a project manager is defining the logical relationship between two activities, A and B. Which of the following scenarios best demonstrates a finish-to-start dependency between them?
o: Activity B can start once Activity A has finished
Activity B must finish before Activity A starts
Activity B can start once Activity A has started
Activity B overlaps fully with Activity A
Activity B runs independently of Activity A
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Finish-to-start means the successor begins only after the predecessor finishes.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is arranging the order in which the activities in a work package will be carried out and wants the sequence to be both logically sound and achievable in practice. Which TWO factors are most critical when determining the sequencing of these activities?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Sequencing depends on logical relationships and resource constraints, both of which influence execution order.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When constructing the schedule network for a project, a project manager is aware that the logical relationships between activities must be defined correctly. If some of these dependencies are set up incorrectly, which TWO consequences are the most likely to result?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Incorrect dependencies distort sequencing and critical path, leading to delays and rework.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager identifies that a non-critical activity has been delayed, but the overall project end date remains unchanged. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The activity has available float that absorbs the delay
The project schedule is inaccurate and needs to be rebuilt
The activity is on the critical path but has been incorrectly calculated
The critical path has shifted automatically
The delay has not yet been reflected in the timeline
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Non-critical activities have float, allowing delays without impacting the overall project timeline.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: While carrying out a network analysis, a project manager notices that, in addition to the critical path, several other paths through the schedule have durations that are only marginally shorter. What risk does the presence of these paths present to the project?
o: Elimination of float across the schedule
Multiple near-critical paths that could become critical
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Near-critical paths can easily become critical if minor delays occur, increasing overall schedule risk.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager creates a Work Breakdown Structure but struggles to assign clear accountability for each work package. What is the most appropriate tool to resolve this?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A RAM links work packages to responsible roles, ensuring accountability.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: On a multi-team project, members are frequently unsure who is responsible for particular pieces of work, and responsibilities appear to overlap. Looking at how the project has been organised, what is the most likely root cause of this confusion?
o: The milestones have not been scheduled at frequent enough intervals
The OBS is not clearly defined or aligned with the WBS
The project does not have a documented risk management plan
The project schedule has become far too complex to follow
The cost breakdown structure has been defined in excessive detail
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: An unclear OBS leads to ambiguity in roles and responsibilities.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is preparing to assign responsibilities across the work packages of an infrastructure project and wants to show accountability is unambiguous. Which scenario best demonstrates effective use of a Responsibility Assignment Matrix (RAM)?
o: Sequencing the project activities according to their logical dependencies
Tracking the accumulated project costs against each deliverable produced
Clearly linking each work package to a single accountable role
Assigning several people to each task with no clear accountability
Mapping deliverables to stakeholders without clearly defining their roles
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A RAM ensures clear accountability by linking work to roles.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is reviewing a Responsibility Assignment Matrix and notices that one work package has been given more than one accountable role. Considering how accountability should work, which issue is most likely to arise?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Multiple accountable roles create ambiguity and reduce ownership clarity.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: On a programme delivered across several business units, the Organisation Breakdown Structure has been developed separately from the Work Breakdown Structure, without cross-referencing the two. What risk does developing the OBS independently in this way create?
o: Loss of traceability between costs and deliverables
Misalignment between roles and work packages
Weaker definition of quality acceptance criteria
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: OBS must align with WBS to ensure responsibilities match work.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which combination best supports effective responsibility mapping?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: WBS defines work, RAM assigns responsibility.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is justifying to a governance board why a Responsibility Assignment Matrix has been introduced on a complex delivery. Which TWO benefits result from using a Responsibility Assignment Matrix?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: RAM clarifies roles and accountability.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO risks arise from poor OBS definition?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Poor OBS leads to unclear roles and duplicated work.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: On a cross-functional project, a project manager reviews how the Organisation Breakdown Structure and Responsibility Assignment Matrix work together. Which TWO outcomes would demonstrate that the OBS and RAM have been effectively integrated?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: OBS defines roles, RAM assigns them effectively.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project is entering detailed planning, but key specialist resources are only partially available due to ongoing operational commitments. Which approach best supports effective resource allocation under these constraints?
o: Delay planning until all resources are fully available
Prioritise critical activities and assign scarce resources to them first
Evenly distribute limited resources across all tasks
Increase overall project duration to match resource availability
Allocate resources based on initial estimates and adjust later
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Focusing scarce resources on critical activities ensures progress on tasks that directly impact project completion.

n.0: Waiting delays the project unnecessarily.
n.2: Spreading resources reduces effectiveness on key tasks.
n.3: Extending duration may not address priority constraints.
n.4: Reactive adjustment increases risk and inefficiency.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: During resource planning, a project manager identifies that two concurrent activities require the same specialist engineer. Both activities have similar durations but different downstream impacts. What is the most appropriate decision?
o: Delay both activities until extra specialist resources can be secured externally
Reassign both activities to less experienced staff to release the specialist engineer
Split the engineer's time equally between both of the two competing activities
Assign the engineer to whichever activity has the higher stakeholder visibility
Allocate the engineer to the activity with the greater impact on the critical path
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path impact determines which activity most affects overall delivery.

n.0: Delaying both increases project risk.
n.1: Skill mismatch may reduce quality.
n.2: Splitting time reduces efficiency and may delay both.
n.3: Visibility does not necessarily reflect schedule impact.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project team has access to sufficient resources overall, but availability fluctuates significantly week to week. What is the most appropriate planning response?
o: Develop a resource-loaded schedule reflecting availability constraints
Replace fluctuating resources with external contractors immediately
Increase resource allocation during peak periods only
Reduce the scope to match the lowest availability periods
Ignore variability and assume consistent availability
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A resource-loaded schedule accounts for varying availability and supports realistic planning.

n.1: Immediate replacement may be unnecessary and costly.
n.2: This does not address low availability periods.
n.3: Scope reduction may not be justified.
n.4: Ignoring variability leads to unrealistic plans.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager notices that resource constraints are causing repeated delays across multiple tasks. What is the most effective long-term response?
o: Ask stakeholders to accept delays as unavoidable
Level resources so demand stays within availability
Focus effort only on the high-priority tasks
Increase reporting frequency to track the delays
Keep reallocating resources between the tasks ad hoc
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling reschedules activities so that demand never exceeds the resources available. The end date may move, but the plan becomes realistic rather than slipping repeatedly. (Resource smoothing, by contrast, works only within float and keeps the end date.)

n.0: Accepting delays is not management of the resource constraint.
n.2: Neglecting other tasks ignores dependencies and creates new delays.
n.3: More reporting describes the delays but does not resolve their cause.
n.4: Ad hoc reallocation treats symptoms and does not fix the underlying over-allocation.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is developing the resource plan for a project with a fixed delivery deadline. When planning resources in this way, which factor most directly influences whether the proposed schedule is feasible?
o: The frequency of project progress reporting
The chosen project governance and reporting structure
The timing of budget and funding approvals
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Availability and capacity determine whether planned work can be executed.

n.0: Communication affects coordination, not feasibility.
n.2: Governance does not directly constrain execution.
n.3: Budget timing is indirect.
n.4: Preferences do not define feasibility.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: With limited resources available, a project manager must decide how to distribute them across several activities that all sit off the critical path. What is the most appropriate basis for allocating these resources?
o: Allocate based on the pressure applied by stakeholders
Allocate randomly to ensure a fair distribution
Allocate based on the duration of each task
Allocate equally across all remaining project tasks
Allocate based on risk exposure and potential impact
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Risk-based allocation ensures resources are used where they provide the greatest protection to outcomes.

n.0: Pressure is not a valid planning criterion.
n.1: Random allocation lacks rationale.
n.2: Duration alone does not reflect importance.
n.3: Equal allocation ignores priorities.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: During resource planning, a project manager realises the project depends on specialist skills that are in short supply within the organisation. What is the most appropriate initial action to take?
o: Assume internal resources will become available
Delay planning until resources are confirmed
Identify alternative sourcing strategies and assess feasibility
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Exploring sourcing options ensures realistic planning given constraints.

n.0: May reduce quality.
n.1: Assumptions increase risk.
n.2: May compromise project objectives.
n.3: Delays decision-making.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is finalising the resource plan and has scheduled several team members to work well beyond their available capacity. What is the primary risk of over-allocating resources in this way?
o: Reduced engagement from key project stakeholders
Higher upfront capital costs for the project
Increased communication overhead across the team
Reduced productivity and potential schedule slippage
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Over-allocation leads to inefficiencies and delays.

n.0: Governance impact is minimal.
n.1: Indirect effect.
n.2: Costs may increase but are secondary.
n.3: Not the primary impact.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager must choose between using highly skilled but limited resources or less skilled but available resources. What is the most appropriate consideration?
o: Consider impact on quality and schedule risk
Allocate both equally regardless of task complexity
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Balancing quality and schedule risk ensures optimal outcomes.

n.0: Availability ignores competence.
n.1: Preference is not a valid factor.
n.3: Equal allocation ignores task needs.
n.4: Cost alone is insufficient.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: At the outset of planning a delivery project, a project manager works to surface limitations on resources, funding and time as early as possible. In resource planning, what is the main purpose of identifying constraints early?
o: To enable realistic scheduling and decision-making
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Constraints inform feasible plans and trade-offs.

n.0: Documentation is not the focus.
n.1: Not the primary purpose.
n.3: Reporting is secondary.
n.4: Indirect outcome.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project is falling behind because key resources are becoming bottlenecks, with too much work converging on them at once. Before seeking more budget or people, what is the most appropriate immediate action for the project manager to take?
o: Re-sequence activities to reduce demand on constrained resources
Request additional budget to hire more resources
Escalate to stakeholders before analysing the problem
Pause the project until the bottleneck clears
Increase the frequency of project status reporting
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Re-sequencing can alleviate bottlenecks without requiring additional resources.

n.1: Budget may not solve availability.
n.2: Escalation without analysis is premature.
n.3: Pausing is excessive.
n.4: Monitoring does not resolve constraints.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is assessing whether particular team members will genuinely be available to deliver the planned work. When assessing resource availability during planning, which TWO factors should be considered?
o: Format of the project highlight report
Earned value of completed work packages
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Availability depends on what people are already committed to (other projects, BAU work, leave) and on whether the people who are free have the skills and competence the work needs. Both are checked against the resource requirements from the WBS and estimates.

n.0: The report format is a communication choice and has no bearing on resource availability.
n.1: Power and interest come from stakeholder analysis and shape engagement, not whether team members are free to do the work.
n.4: Earned value measures performance on work already done; it says nothing about whether people are available for planned work.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager prepares a schedule but does not account for known limits on the resources available to the project. Which TWO outcomes are most likely if resource constraints are ignored during planning?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Ignoring constraints leads to over-allocation and delays.

n.0: Complexity remains.
n.1: Performance may decline.
n.4: Accuracy decreases.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO approaches can improve resource allocation under uncertainty?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Flexibility and review improve responsiveness.

n.2: Engagement is unrelated.
n.3: Fixing schedules reduces adaptability.
n.4: Ignoring constraints increases risk.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO constraints most directly affect resource planning decisions?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time and budget directly limit resource use.

n.0: Not a constraint.
n.1: Irrelevant.
n.4: Indirect influence.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO actions help mitigate resource bottlenecks?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Re-sequencing and adding resources directly address bottlenecks.

n.0: Reduces effectiveness.
n.3: Increases pressure.
n.4: Irrelevant.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project schedule shows multiple periods where the same specialist resource is required across overlapping activities. What is the most appropriate application of resource levelling in this situation?
o: Keep the schedule and accept lower productivity
Extend all activities equally to spread the workload
Increase the working hours of the specialist
Delay activities until the specialist is available
Reassign the tasks regardless of required expertise
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling resolves over-allocation by delaying activities until the resource is free, even if this extends the end date (resource-limited scheduling). Moving work only within float so the end date does not change is resource smoothing.

n.0: Accepting inefficiency leaves the over-allocation unresolved.
n.1: Stretching every activity ignores where the clash actually is and the dependencies.
n.2: Overtime is a separate option, not levelling, and is rarely sustainable.
n.4: Ignoring skill requirements risks quality and rework.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: After applying resource levelling to a draft plan, a project manager finds that the overall project duration has been extended beyond the original finish date. What does this extension most likely indicate?
o: The project has too many stakeholders
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling extends duration when resource demand cannot be met within the original schedule.

n.0: Stakeholders are unrelated.
n.1: Budget is not the direct cause.
n.2: Sequencing may be correct.
n.3: Not necessarily inefficient, just constrained.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Despite a schedule that clearly shows several resources booked beyond their capacity, a project manager decides not to apply resource levelling. What is the most likely outcome of this decision?
o: Increased risk of delays and reduced productivity
Greater flexibility across the project schedule
Full resolution of all resource conflicts
Increased likelihood of uncontrolled scope creep
A naturally shortened project critical path
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Ignoring over-allocation leads to inefficiency and delays.

n.1: Efficiency decreases.
n.2: There are clear consequences.
n.3: Stakeholders may become dissatisfied.
n.4: Duration may increase due to inefficiencies.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is deciding between resource levelling and resource smoothing for a plan showing peaks in demand. Which scenario best justifies choosing resource levelling over smoothing?
o: When resource demand exceeds supply and schedule flexibility exists
When stakeholder expectations for scope are fixed
When resources are consistently underutilised across activities
When maintaining the original end date is critical
When project tasks are largely independent of each other
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling is used when demand exceeds supply and schedule changes are acceptable.

n.1: Expectations do not define technique choice.
n.2: Levelling is unnecessary.
n.3: This aligns with smoothing.
n.4: Independence is irrelevant.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: After resource levelling has been applied to the schedule, a project manager notices that an activity on the critical path has been pushed back. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this delay?
o: Critical activities should never be adjusted
The project schedule was unrealistic given resource constraints
Resource levelling should only affect non-critical tasks
The levelling process was incorrectly applied
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Delays to critical activities indicate constraints were not previously accounted for.

n.0: They may need adjustment under constraints.
n.2: Levelling can affect any task if required.
n.3: The process may be correct.
n.4: Cancellation is not justified.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the primary trade-off when applying resource levelling?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling trades schedule duration against resource constraints.

n.1: Not applicable.
n.2: Irrelevant.
n.3: Indirect relationship.
n.4: Not the core trade-off.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Having applied resource levelling to balance workloads, a project manager observes that some resources now have idle periods within the revised schedule. What does the appearance of these idle periods suggest?
o: Resources should be removed from the project
Demand has been balanced against supply constraints
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling smooths peaks, which can create idle periods.

n.0: Removal may not be necessary.
n.2: This is a normal outcome.
n.3: Alignment is not the issue.
n.4: Complexity is unrelated.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is trying to predict whether applying resource levelling will change the planned end date of the project. Which factor most strongly determines whether resource levelling will affect project duration?
o: Float on the activities being delayed
Method used to allocate the budget
Number of stakeholders who are involved
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling delays activities to fit resource availability. If the delays can be absorbed within the activities' float, the end date holds; if they exceed the float or fall on critical activities, the project duration extends.

n.0: How often the team communicates does not affect activity timing.
n.1: Governance sets decision rights, not the float available in the schedule.
n.3: How the budget is allocated does not decide whether delays fit within float.
n.4: Stakeholder numbers do not change the network logic or float.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In what situation would resource levelling be inappropriate?
o: When schedule deadlines are fixed and cannot change
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling typically changes the schedule, which is not acceptable if deadlines are fixed.

n.0: Irrelevant.
n.2: This is when levelling is needed.
n.3: Not a limiting factor.
n.4: Unrelated.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO outcomes are expected when applying resource levelling?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling balances demand but often extends duration.

n.1: Costs may increase.
n.3: Not directly affected.
n.4: Risks remain.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is explaining to the team what practical steps resource levelling involves when demand exceeds capacity. Which TWO actions are part of the resource levelling process?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling involves adjusting schedules and resource allocation.

n.1: Dependencies must be respected.
n.2: Deadlines may change.
n.4: Scope is unrelated.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO constraints directly influence resource levelling decisions?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling balances demand against availability and time flexibility.

n.1: Not a constraint.
n.2: Irrelevant.
n.3: Irrelevant.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO risks are associated with resource levelling?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling can introduce delays and inefficiencies.

n.0: Not guaranteed.
n.1: Dependencies remain.
n.4: Delivery is not guaranteed.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project is forecast to finish on time, but several resources are heavily overloaded in the middle of the schedule. The sponsor insists that the final delivery date must not move. Which approach best reflects resource smoothing?
o: Delay critical path activities until workload is balanced
Extend the project duration to remove all over-allocation
Add resources to every overloaded activity
Re-baseline the schedule around resource availability
Adjust activities within available float to reduce resource peaks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing reduces resource peaks within existing float while preserving the project end date.

n.0: Delaying critical path activities would normally move the end date, which smoothing avoids.
n.1: Extending duration describes resource levelling, not smoothing.
n.2: Adding resources is not the core mechanism of smoothing.
n.3: Re-baselining may be required later, but smoothing first works within the existing time constraint.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager has identified two non-critical activities that can be moved without affecting the planned completion date. Both use the same testing specialist currently overloaded in week four. What should the project manager do first?
o: Move one or both activities within their float
Escalate the resource conflict to the sponsor
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing uses available float on non-critical activities to reduce resource overload without changing the end date.

n.0: Removing testing risks quality and does not address resource planning properly.
n.1: Changing the completion date would move into levelling territory.
n.2: Extra hours may hide the planning issue and increase fatigue risk.
n.4: Escalation is premature when float can resolve the conflict.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which statement best distinguishes resource smoothing from resource levelling?
o: Smoothing ignores resource limits, whereas levelling applies them
Smoothing may change scope, whereas levelling changes cost
Smoothing removes all resource conflict, whereas levelling only reduces it
Smoothing preserves the end date, whereas levelling may extend it
Smoothing applies only to external contractors, whereas levelling applies internally
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The key distinction is that smoothing works within time constraints, while levelling may alter the finish date.

n.0: Smoothing still considers resource limits, but only within available scheduling flexibility.
n.1: Neither technique is primarily defined by changing scope.
n.2: Smoothing may not eliminate all overload if float is insufficient.
n.4: Both can apply to internal or external resources.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A resource histogram shows a short-term demand peak above available capacity, but all affected activities have some float. The client has fixed the delivery date contractually. What is the most appropriate scheduling response?
o: Apply resource levelling and inform the client of the delay
Transfer accountability for the overload to functional managers
Reduce quality assurance activity to protect the finish date
Apply resource smoothing before considering a change request
Accept the overload because the contract date is fixed
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Because float exists and the end date is fixed, smoothing is the first appropriate response.

n.0: Levelling may extend the schedule, which conflicts with the fixed date.
n.1: Accountability transfer does not resolve the planning constraint.
n.2: Cutting assurance may create quality and acceptance problems.
n.4: Accepting overload creates delivery risk.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: After smoothing a schedule, the project manager finds one specialist remains over-allocated during a critical activity. What does this most likely indicate?
o: Smoothing has been applied incorrectly in all areas
The project manager should ignore the remaining overload
The activity should be removed from the critical path
Resource smoothing always requires extra budget
There is insufficient float to remove every resource conflict
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing is limited by available float and may not fully resolve overloads on critical or near-critical work.

n.0: Residual overload does not prove the whole process was incorrect.
n.1: Remaining overload needs risk treatment or escalation.
n.2: Critical path status is an outcome of logic and duration, not something to remove arbitrarily.
n.3: Smoothing does not inherently require extra budget.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A team proposes smoothing the schedule by moving a task with zero float into the following week. What is the project manager’s strongest objection?
o: The change would likely affect the planned finish date
The project budget has not changed
The task duration has not been reduced
The task is not externally visible
The team has not requested extra resource
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A zero-float task cannot be moved without affecting successors or the finish date, so this is not smoothing in the strict sense.

n.1: Budget change is not the core concern.
n.2: Duration reduction is not required for smoothing.
n.3: Visibility does not determine whether smoothing is valid.
n.4: Extra resources are not the defining issue.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which condition makes resource smoothing most useful?
o: All resources are permanently assigned full-time
There is available float in non-critical activities
The project has unlimited resource supply
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing relies on available float to adjust work timing without changing the end date.

n.0: Full-time assignment may make smoothing harder, not easier.
n.2: Unlimited supply would reduce the need for smoothing.
n.3: Flexible deadlines are more associated with levelling.
n.4: Without flexibility, smoothing options are limited.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: On a construction programme, the project manager has applied resource smoothing to a labour histogram that showed several weeks of overload. The sponsor is surprised that some peaks of demand still remain and asks for an explanation. Which response is most accurate?
o: Smoothing always requires the agreed end date to be moved
Smoothing can only be applied once the project has failed
Smoothing resolves overload only by reducing the project scope
Smoothing can only use available float and may leave some overload unresolved
Smoothing is purely a progress reporting and control technique
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing reduces demand peaks where possible within existing time limits but cannot guarantee full resolution.

n.0: Preserving the end date is the defining feature of smoothing.
n.1: It is a planning and control tool, not a failure response.
n.2: Scope reduction is not smoothing.
n.4: Smoothing is a scheduling technique, not just reporting.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager reviewing a resource histogram is considering whether to smooth the schedule to ease periods of overload. Before proceeding, they want to establish whether smoothing is even feasible for this plan. Which question should be answered first?
o: Can all resource conflicts be transferred to external suppliers?
Can the project budget be increased to add more resources?
Can the overall project scope be reduced or simplified?
Can activity timing be adjusted without changing the final delivery date?
Can the frequency of stakeholder reporting be reduced significantly?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing depends on whether work can be moved within existing time constraints.

n.0: Transferring conflicts does not necessarily solve them.
n.1: Budget increase may be relevant later but is not the first smoothing question.
n.2: Scope simplification is a different trade-off.
n.4: Reporting frequency is unrelated to the scheduling technique.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO statements accurately describe resource smoothing?
o: It is only relevant after a project is in delivery
It uses available float to reduce resource demand peaks
It may extend the planned project completion date
It aims to keep the project end date unchanged
It removes the need for resource capacity planning
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing adjusts work within float while protecting the planned finish date.

n.0: Smoothing can be used during planning and control.
n.2: Extending completion is associated with levelling.
n.4: Capacity planning is still essential.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: During resource optimisation on a fixed-deadline programme, a scheduler finds that smoothing eases some demand peaks but cannot flatten the histogram completely. Considering how the technique works, which TWO factors limit how far resource smoothing can go?
o: The accuracy of the activity cost estimates
The earned value reported at the last review
The reimbursement method agreed with suppliers
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing only moves activities within their available float so that the end date does not change. Once the float is used up, the remaining peaks cannot be removed without moving the fixed completion date, which would be levelling.

n.0: Cost estimate accuracy affects the budget, not how far activities can be moved within float to even out resource demand.
n.1: Earned value reports past performance; it does not limit how activities can be rescheduled to smooth resource use.
n.4: The reimbursement method sets how suppliers are paid; it does not constrain the timing of activities in the schedule.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which TWO actions would be consistent with resource smoothing?
o: Extending the project end date to remove all overload
Removing acceptance testing to reduce resource demand
Moving a non-critical design review later within its float
Delaying a critical path activity beyond its latest finish date
Re-sequencing activities where logic and float allow it
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Both actions reduce resource pressure without necessarily changing the final completion date.

n.0: Extending the end date is levelling, not smoothing.
n.1: Removing testing changes quality/scope controls, not resource smoothing.
n.3: This is likely to affect the end date and does not fit smoothing.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project has a fixed completion date and a temporary shortage of business analysts. Which TWO responses best fit resource smoothing?
o: Shift non-critical workshops away from peak demand weeks
Assume analysts can work evenings until the peak passes
Remove requirements validation from the plan
Move lower-priority analysis tasks into unused float
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Both options smooth demand by adjusting non-critical work timing while preserving the end date.

n.0: Delaying handover changes the end date.
n.2: Overtime may create risk and is not smoothing.
n.3: Removing validation risks scope and quality control.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: During a project to upgrade office equipment, deliveries can only be accepted outside of business hours due to ongoing daily operations. What is the best description of this situation?
o: A dependency between project and business-as-usual activities
An issue with the project’s budget
A project risk with no mitigation
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: This is a direct example of a dependency between project work and normal business operations.

n.1: Budget is not the issue here.
n.2: A risk is potential, but this is a confirmed scheduling dependency.
n.3: Communication may be required but is not the dependency itself.
n.4: Quality is not at fault in this scenario.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager planning a systems rollout is considering the various ways the project could become tied to the organisation's ongoing operations. Which of the following could create a dependency between a project and business-as-usual activities?
o: Updates to the project risk register
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: When key resources are shared, both project and business-as-usual activities become interdependent.

n.0: Scope changes affect the project, not necessarily business-as-usual.
n.2: Audits are typically after completion, not concurrent dependencies.
n.3: Benefits reviews are usually post-project.
n.4: Stakeholder mapping is planning, not a dependency itself.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A manufacturing company is launching a new product while maintaining normal production levels. Which factor is most likely to impact the project schedule?
o: Availability of production equipment for both activities
The colour of the final product
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: If the same equipment is used for project and BAU, its availability creates a dependency and can cause delays.

n.0: Marketing is not central to the scheduling dependency described.
n.1: Paperwork volume does not create dependencies.
n.3: Team size may influence progress, but equipment sharing is a direct dependency.
n.4: Product colour is unrelated to scheduling dependencies.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is assessing how ongoing operational work in a busy organisation might affect the delivery timeline of a change project. Which of these is NOT a common impact of business-as-usual activities on a project schedule?
o: Requirement for project activities outside standard hours
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Business-as-usual often restricts resources, not guarantees uninterrupted access.

n.0: Scheduling project work outside normal hours is a common result.
n.1: Staff may be pulled away for BAU, delaying the project.
n.3: IT systems may need to be shared.
n.4: Physical space is often shared, creating dependencies.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A hospital is running a project to implement a new patient records system. The implementation must not disrupt normal patient care. What does this requirement create?
o: A scheduling dependency on business-as-usual activities
A financial benefit for the hospital
A project risk that cannot be managed
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Project work must be scheduled around normal operations, creating a direct dependency.

n.1: The benefit is not a dependency.
n.2: Procurement is unrelated in this case.
n.3: Quality assurance is important but not the dependency itself.
n.4: Risks can often be managed with proper planning.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project relies on an operational team whose routine work carries its own threats, such as system outages and seasonal workload spikes. How can risks in business-as-usual activities affect the schedule of a project?
o: By guaranteeing extra resources are assigned to the project
By causing delays to project tasks if BAU risks materialise
By transferring all BAU risks onto the project risk register
By automatically extending the project deadline to absorb them
By lowering the project's agreed quality requirements
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: BAU risks can disrupt project timelines if they materialise.

n.0: Staff availability may decrease if BAU is affected.
n.2: Scope changes are managed through formal change control, not BAU risks.
n.3: Contingency is needed precisely because risks exist.
n.4: Risks generally slow down progress, not speed it up.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is analysing how expenditure on a delivery project might become tied to the demands of the organisation's ongoing operations. Which scenario best demonstrates a dependency between project and business-as-usual costs?
o: Project manager attends a training course
BAU staff attend a project meeting once
Project requires overtime payments during BAU peak times
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Overtime required due to BAU demands links project costs directly to BAU activities.

n.0: Training is a staff development activity, not a cost dependency.
n.1: A single meeting does not indicate a cost dependency.
n.3: Reporting frequency is not related to cost dependencies.
n.4: Energy efficiency is not a cost dependency.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project’s quality requirements demand testing to be performed when BAU operations are lowest. What kind of relationship is this?
o: A communication gap between the project and operations teams
A procurement constraint linked to supplier delivery timing
A scheduling dependency based on quality and BAU activity levels
A resource conflict caused by competing project funding demands
A scope change arising from revised quality requirements
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Scheduling must be based on the relationship between BAU activity levels and quality requirements.

n.0: Communication is not the dependency here.
n.1: Procurement is not mentioned.
n.3: Funding is not the key dependency described.
n.4: Scope is not being changed, just the timing.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager preparing the schedule for a change initiative is mapping out where project tasks and routine operational work will interact. Why is it important to identify dependencies between project and BAU activities when planning the project schedule?
o: To reduce the size of the project team
To increase the number of meetings held
To avoid conflicts that can delay project delivery
To ensure all stakeholders receive status updates
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Identifying dependencies helps avoid scheduling conflicts and project delays.

n.0: Team size is not determined by BAU dependencies.
n.1: Meeting frequency is not directly related to schedule dependencies.
n.2: Procurement is not simplified by identifying dependencies.
n.4: Status updates are important but not the main purpose here.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When reviewing the links between a delivery project and the organisation's ongoing operations, a project manager considers a range of possible sources of dependency. Which factor is LEAST likely to create a dependency between a project and business-as-usual activities?
o: Need for change approvals from BAU managers
Sequencing between two internal project tasks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A link between two of the project's own tasks is an internal project dependency, not a dependency between the project and business-as-usual activities.

n.0: Finance staff serving both BAU and the project create a dependency.
n.1: BAU reporting deadlines constrain when the project can use people or systems.
n.2: Equipment shared with operations creates a project to BAU dependency.
n.3: Needing approvals from BAU managers links the schedule to BAU.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project team needs to schedule a major software upgrade. However, the IT department is also supporting month-end business processes at the same time. What should the project manager do?
o: Cancel the upgrade due to resource unavailability
Request more funding to bypass the IT department
Assign the upgrade task to business analysts
Coordinate the upgrade to avoid month-end business-as-usual peaks
Proceed with the upgrade as planned regardless of BAU activities
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Project managers must plan around BAU activities to avoid resource conflicts and delays.

n.0: Cancellation is unnecessary; better coordination is possible.
n.1: Funding alone does not resolve the resource dependency.
n.2: Business analysts may not have the technical expertise for upgrades.
n.4: Ignoring BAU activities risks schedule clashes and service disruption.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager developing a network diagram is explaining to a junior colleague how the logical links between scheduled activities work. Which of the following BEST describes a dependency in project scheduling?
o: A buffer of spare time added to protect the critical path
A relationship where one activity relies on another to start or finish
A resource assigned to complete a specific scheduled activity
A milestone marking the completion of a major project deliverable
A constraint that fixes the earliest date an activity can begin
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Dependencies occur when one activity cannot start or finish until another does.

n.0: Risk register updates may record dependencies, but are not dependencies themselves.
n.2: Budget changes do not define dependencies.
n.3: Meetings are activities, not dependencies.
n.4: Benefits are outcomes, not dependencies.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project is affected by an increase in business-as-usual demand during the holiday season. What is a likely impact on the project schedule?
o: Project risks transfer automatically to the operations team
Project activities may be delayed due to reduced resource availability
Project scope expands to cover the extra BAU workload
Project costs fall because the staff are already employed
Project quality standards must be raised to match the demand
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: BAU peaks can reduce resources for the project, resulting in potential schedule delays.

n.0: Scope is managed separately and isn't directly affected by BAU demand.
n.2: Risks remain and may increase.
n.3: Quality must still be met despite resource constraints.
n.4: Increased BAU demand generally causes delays, not acceleration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is reviewing several situations to decide which ones genuinely tie project costs to ongoing operational work when building the schedule. Which is NOT an example of how costs can link business-as-usual activities to a project schedule?
o: Business-as-usual overtime costs delaying project milestones
Temporary staff hired to cover BAU so project staff are released
Increased costs for shared equipment during BAU peaks
Shared costs for joint project and BAU training
Project budget tracking against a separate cost code
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Budget tracking with a separate cost code does not create a dependency between project and BAU.

n.0: Overtime costs may divert resources and cause project delays.
n.1: Hiring temporary staff is a direct response to the resource dependency.
n.2: Increased equipment costs during BAU peaks impact project scheduling.
n.3: Joint training links project and BAU cost scheduling.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: While building the schedule for a finance system upgrade, a project manager reviews the organisation's key operational reporting dates before fixing task timings. Why should a project manager assess business-as-usual deadlines when creating the project schedule?
o: To avoid conflicts that could delay project tasks
To set up more project meetings
To improve the company’s public image
To select a new project sponsor
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Assessing BAU deadlines helps avoid clashes that can cause project delays.

n.1: Scope reduction is a separate decision.
n.2: More meetings do not solve scheduling conflicts.
n.3: Public image is not directly affected by BAU deadlines.
n.4: Project sponsorship is unrelated to BAU deadlines.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager finds that the organisation's annual financial audit, which draws heavily on finance staff, falls during the project's planned testing phase. How could this impact the project?
o: All risks associated with testing are removed
The project will be exempt from documentation requirements
Project testing may be rescheduled to avoid resource clashes
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A major BAU event like an audit can limit available resources, requiring the project to adjust its schedule.

n.0: Risks may actually increase, not disappear.
n.1: Quality standards should remain consistent.
n.2: Audit timing may impact costs if resources are diverted.
n.3: Documentation is still required.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following is most likely to create a risk to the project schedule when there are links with business-as-usual activities?
o: A documented resource-sharing agreement with operations
Early engagement with the operations line managers
Regular joint project and BAU planning meetings
A shared calendar of upcoming BAU milestones
Unexpected staff shortages due to BAU demands
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Staff shortages caused by BAU create a risk that can delay project activities.

n.0: Good morale supports delivery rather than creates risk.
n.1: Escalation processes help manage, not create, risk.
n.2: Reporting does not directly create schedule risks.
n.3: A log update is not a risk in itself.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project to upgrade a contact centre's systems must be delivered without interrupting the hours during which customers are normally served. What does this requirement illustrate?
o: A benefit to be realised after project handover
A constraint imposed by the project's fixed budget
A risk arising from unclear stakeholder requirements
A quality standard defined within the project scope
A dependency between project activities and BAU operations
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Project tasks must be scheduled around BAU to avoid service disruption—a direct dependency.

n.0: This is not a benefit milestone.
n.1: Budget is not the main concern.
n.2: Quality should not be reduced.
n.3: Communication may be important, but the key is the dependency.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project is being implemented in a school during term time. Which is the most likely dependency to impact the schedule?
o: Design of the signage used around the site
The number of teachers attending progress meetings
Exam periods and term dates restricting noisy project work
Choice of contractor for the classroom refurbishment
Availability of the team's preferred project management software
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: In a school, BAU activity (term dates and exam periods) restricts when disruptive work can happen, which is the dependency most likely to affect the schedule.

n.0: Signage design is a minor deliverable detail, not a scheduling dependency.
n.1: Meeting attendance does not constrain when work can be done.
n.3: Contractor choice is a procurement decision, not a dependency on school operations.
n.4: Software availability is a minor tooling matter that does not drive the schedule.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager finds that many of the project's activities cannot proceed without input from teams running the organisation's day-to-day operations. If a project's activities are highly dependent on business-as-usual processes, what is the best action for the project manager?
o: Engage with BAU managers early and regularly to plan around key activities
Reduce the project scope until the dependencies no longer exist
Assume BAU activities will pause while the project is being delivered
Schedule every single project task during normal business operating hours
Delegate all BAU coordination entirely to the project sponsor alone
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Effective engagement with BAU managers ensures project activities can be planned around critical BAU events.

n.1: External consultants may not have the required organisational knowledge.
n.2: Contingency helps but is not a substitute for planning with BAU.
n.3: Ignoring BAU will likely result in scheduling conflicts and failure.
n.4: Reporting does not resolve schedule dependencies.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: During the refurbishment of a company's head office, the workforce must keep carrying out its normal duties in the same building throughout the works. What is a likely approach to manage this dependency?
o: Increase the project scope to include more offices
Schedule noisy activities outside standard working hours
Replace all office staff with temporary workers
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Adjusting work hours minimises disruption to ongoing operations—a key way to manage dependencies.

n.0: Meetings may need to be adapted, not eliminated.
n.1: Expanding scope increases disruption, not reduces it.
n.3: Replacing all staff is rarely justified and does not address the dependency directly.
n.4: Health and safety must not be reduced to accommodate scheduling.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is trying to identify the clearest case where the project's schedule is genuinely tied to the organisation's ongoing operations. Which is the best example of a schedule dependency between project and business-as-usual activities?
o: Project uses shared IT infrastructure needed for daily business tasks
Project sponsor also chairs the monthly operations steering group meeting
Project reuses a report template from an earlier project
Project team is located in the same building as operations
Project adopts the operations team's document naming rules
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A schedule dependency with BAU exists when project activities rely on something the business also needs. Shared IT infrastructure used for daily operations means project work such as testing or cutover must be timed around business use, for example in maintenance windows.

n.1: The sponsor's dual role is a governance link, not a dependency that constrains the schedule.
n.2: Reusing a report template saves effort but creates no timing link with operations.
n.3: Sharing a building does not in itself tie project activities to the timing of operational work.
n.4: Sharing naming rules is a standards choice; it does not constrain when project work can happen.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A business’s quarterly reporting cycle will limit staff availability for a key project deliverable. What is the most effective scheduling strategy?
o: Increase the project budget for overtime
Ignore the reporting cycle and proceed as planned
Assign reporting tasks to junior project staff
Plan the deliverable for after the reporting cycle ends
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Planning after the reporting cycle ensures necessary staff are available for the project.

n.0: Overtime is costly and may not always solve scheduling conflicts.
n.1: Ignoring the cycle risks project delays and staff overload.
n.2: Reporting is a BAU responsibility and may require experienced staff.
n.3: Quality must be maintained regardless of scheduling challenges.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When assessing how ongoing operational commitments might constrain the timing of a delivery project, a project manager weighs up several possible influences. Which factor is LEAST likely to impact a project's schedule when considering business-as-usual dependencies?
o: Key staff needed for both BAU and project
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: BAU affects a project's schedule where the two compete for the same people, equipment or time windows. The report format that operations prefers has no effect on when project work can be done.

n.1: Mandatory inspections fix dates that project work must fit around.
n.2: Equipment shared with operations can only be used by the project when BAU does not need it.
n.3: Staff needed by both BAU and the project limit when project tasks can be scheduled.
n.4: Peak trading periods often bring change freezes, so project activities must avoid them.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project has to push back several planned tasks after the operations team brings forward its own key reporting deadlines. What does this demonstrate?
o: A weakness in the project's overall procurement strategy
The need to escalate the delay to the project sponsor
The direct impact of BAU dependencies on project scheduling
A failure in the project's quality assurance process
The value of holding an early project closure review
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: When BAU deadlines change, project tasks often must be rescheduled, demonstrating dependency.

n.0: Project closure is not related to ongoing BAU dependencies.
n.1: Quality management relates to standards, not scheduling.
n.3: Communication plans help but are not the main dependency here.
n.4: Procurement risks are different from scheduling dependencies.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A public transport authority is upgrading track infrastructure and has restricted the work to weekends only, when services are far quieter. Why is this scheduling approach often necessary?
o: To allow staff longer rest periods
To reduce the total cost of the project
To ensure sponsors are always present
To minimise disruption to daily business-as-usual operations
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Weekend work reduces impact on regular services, managing BAU-project dependencies.

n.0: Rest periods are not the primary reason for scheduling choices.
n.1: Weekend work may actually cost more.
n.2: Risk registers should always be updated regardless of schedule.
n.3: Sponsor presence is not the reason for weekend work.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Midway through delivery, the operations team's priorities shift unexpectedly, affecting resources the project was relying on. When business-as-usual priorities change unexpectedly, what should a project manager do to manage dependencies?
o: Transfer the affected tasks straight to the operations team
Raise the quality targets to offset the disruption
Reassess the project schedule and update plans as needed
Escalate immediately to cancel the affected project tasks
Freeze the current schedule and absorb the changes later
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Schedules should be updated to reflect new BAU priorities, ensuring realistic planning.

n.0: Ignoring BAU will cause further conflicts.
n.1: Increasing quality does not resolve dependency issues.
n.3: Abandonment is rarely justified.
n.4: Team changes should be considered carefully and with input.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is putting in place practices to coordinate the project's schedule with the organisation's routine operational work. Which is NOT a typical action to manage schedule dependencies between project and BAU activities?
o: Holding planning meetings with BAU managers
Proceeding without regard for BAU constraints
Identifying shared resources and planning accordingly
Adjusting project timelines to fit business peaks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Ignoring BAU constraints risks project failure due to unaddressed dependencies.

n.0: Engagement with BAU managers is good practice.
n.2: Shared resource planning is crucial.
n.3: BAU is dynamic and should be monitored.
n.4: Timeline adjustments can prevent conflicts.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A new marketing campaign must not interfere with standard customer support hours. What is the best way to address this dependency?
o: Remove customer support from BAU temporarily
Limit marketing to online channels only
Schedule campaign activities outside core support hours
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Running campaign tasks outside support hours avoids conflict—a textbook scheduling dependency solution.

n.0: More budget does not remove the dependency.
n.1: Removing support is impractical and would harm the business.
n.2: Channel limitation does not guarantee no interference with support hours.
n.4: Scope reduction is unnecessary if scheduling can resolve the issue.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A sponsor asks a project manager to explain, in a single statement, why so much effort is spent coordinating the project's schedule with the organisation's ongoing operations. Which statement best summarises the need to manage dependencies between project and business-as-usual activities?
o: Project schedules should never influence live BAU operations
Managed dependencies remove the need for a project schedule
BAU activities take priority over project work at all times
Unmanaged dependencies can lead to project delays and operational disruption
Dependencies always shorten the overall project delivery time
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: If dependencies are ignored, both project and business operations can suffer, causing delays and disruption.

n.0: Good management can actually control or reduce costs.
n.1: Benefits are not guaranteed just by managing dependencies.
n.2: Project schedules should be tailored, not identical to BAU.
n.4: Some risks are always present, even if dependencies are managed.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project team discovers that a supplier will deliver components two weeks later than planned. Why should the schedule be re-estimated?
o: To recover the lost time by removing testing tasks
To pass the schedule impact directly to the sponsor
To reflect the new delivery date and assess project impact
To shift the delay onto the supplier's own schedule
To keep the original baseline dates unchanged for reporting
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Re-estimating updates the schedule based on new facts and helps assess the effect on project deadlines.

n.0: Scope is managed separately and not a reason to re-estimate the schedule.
n.1: The goal is accurate scheduling, not cosmetic reporting.
n.3: Profit margins may be affected, but the main purpose is accurate planning.
n.4: Risk management remains essential, not eliminated.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager reviewing a lengthy delivery schedule is looking at schedule optimisation as a way to improve how the project will be delivered. Which of the following is a key benefit of schedule optimisation in project management?
o: It transfers scheduling responsibility away from the project manager
It can reduce unnecessary delays and make better use of resources
It fixes the schedule so that no re-estimation is required
It shortens the project by cutting agreed quality checks
It removes the need to monitor the project's critical path
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Schedule optimisation aims to streamline delivery and resource use, reducing delays.

n.0: Not every project can finish early; optimisation just improves efficiency.
n.2: Stakeholder communication remains vital.
n.3: Scope changes still need to be considered.
n.4: Risks cannot be completely avoided, only managed.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When is it most appropriate to re-estimate project timescales?
o: Only at the project’s halfway point
Whenever significant changes occur that could affect the schedule
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Re-estimation is needed after any significant change that may affect timing.

n.0: Audits are not the only trigger for re-estimation.
n.1: Halfway reviews are useful, but changes can occur at any time.
n.2: Waiting until project closure is too late.
n.3: Not every meeting warrants re-estimation.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A construction project identifies a new regulatory requirement that will add several days to a key activity. What should the project manager do?
o: Re-estimate the schedule to reflect the new requirement
Remove a quality check to save time
Ignore the requirement to keep to the original timeline
Shorten all other activities by one day
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Schedules should be re-estimated to reflect new mandatory requirements.

n.1: Quality checks are essential and should not be arbitrarily removed.
n.2: Prompt communication is best practice.
n.3: Ignoring requirements risks project compliance and quality.
n.4: Reducing time on all other activities may compromise quality and is not a considered approach.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following statements best describes schedule optimisation?
o: Increasing the project scope without extra resources
Scheduling all tasks to start at the same time
Adjusting tasks and resources to achieve the best possible project delivery time
Reducing project quality to meet deadlines
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Schedule optimisation aims to deliver projects efficiently by adjusting tasks and resources.

n.0: Scope increases without resources cause delays.
n.1: Not all tasks can or should start at once due to dependencies.
n.2: Risks should be managed proactively.
n.4: Reducing quality is not an acceptable form of optimisation.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: During a project review, the team discovers that certain tasks have taken longer than expected. Why is schedule optimisation valuable in this situation?
o: It removes the need for stakeholder reporting
It helps the team adjust plans to avoid further delays
It guarantees that no tasks will ever run late again
It allows quality standards to be ignored
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Schedule optimisation allows the project to adapt and reduce the chance of further delays.

n.0: Reporting is still necessary.
n.2: Delays can be reduced, but not eliminated.
n.3: Quality must not be sacrificed.
n.4: Risks still need to be managed separately.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: As a project progresses through its life cycle, the project manager regularly revisits and refines the original estimates in light of new information. Which is NOT a benefit of re-estimating during the project life cycle?
o: Guaranteeing project closure ahead of schedule
Providing a more realistic project timeline
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Re-estimation does not guarantee early closure, it just improves schedule accuracy.

n.0: Stakeholders are more confident when the plan is realistic.
n.1: Timely re-estimation allows risks to be identified earlier.
n.3: It helps ensure timelines are up-to-date.
n.4: Re-estimation corrects old or wrong assumptions.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Under pressure to bring forward a critical delivery date, a project manager looks at schedule optimisation methods to shorten the overall duration. Which technique might they use?
o: Sequencing all tasks to run one after another
Extending the critical path to reduce daily workload
Fast-tracking tasks that can be completed in parallel
Adding float to every task on the critical path
Levelling resources evenly across the remaining activities
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Fast-tracking allows parallel work, reducing overall project duration.

n.0: Unnecessary deliverables will only add time and complexity.
n.1: Eliminating all contingency increases project risk.
n.3: Stakeholder updates are important for control and transparency.
n.4: Delaying non-critical activities does not optimise the schedule.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is regular re-estimation important in agile projects?
o: Because changing requirements can affect the project schedule at any time
Because team size always remains the same
Because scope is fixed from the start
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Agile projects are adaptive; regular re-estimation is needed as requirements change.

n.0: Budgets may change as priorities shift.
n.2: Team sizes may also change in agile approaches.
n.3: Risks should always be tracked.
n.4: Scope is typically flexible, not fixed.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Partway through a software project, the team adopts a new tool that automates a previously manual part of the workflow. How might schedule optimisation respond to this change?
o: By revising the schedule to reflect potential time savings
By increasing all task durations to be cautious
By locking the original schedule in place
By reducing the quality assurance steps
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Optimisation includes updating the schedule when productivity tools improve efficiency.

n.0: New tools must be considered for planning.
n.2: Durations should only increase if justified by evidence.
n.3: Schedules should be flexible and reflect reality.
n.4: Quality must always be maintained.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A construction project running through the winter has fallen behind after a prolonged spell of severe weather stopped site work for several days, and the original dates no longer look achievable. As the project manager reviews the plan, what should be done about the schedule?
o: Draw down contingency budget without revising the schedule
Crash every remaining activity to recover the lost days
Re-estimate remaining activities based on the new circumstances
Hold the original dates and ask the team to recover all the lost time
Assume no further weather disruption for the remaining work
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: When the original dates are no longer realistic, the remaining work should be re-estimated with the latest information so a realistic schedule can be agreed through change control.

n.0: Spending contingency without revising the schedule leaves an unrealistic plan in place.
n.1: Crashing should target critical activities only and adds cost; crashing everything is wasteful.
n.3: Holding unachievable dates gives a false picture and puts pressure on the team without addressing the delay.
n.4: Ignoring the risk of further bad weather in winter is unrealistic estimating.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is reviewing the situations that would justify updating the schedule and re-estimating the remaining work partway through delivery. Which of the following would NOT be a valid reason to re-estimate the project schedule?
o: A sponsor's wish for an earlier finish date
Delivery delays confirmed by a key supplier
A change in the availability of key resources
Unforeseen technical issues delaying the work
Discovery of new risks affecting the plan
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Re-estimating is triggered by new information that changes the expected work, such as new risks, resource changes, technical problems or supplier delays. A wish for an earlier date gives no new information; it calls for schedule optimisation or change control, not new estimates.

n.1: Confirmed supplier delays change dependent dates and require the schedule to be re-estimated.
n.2: A change in key resource availability alters how long the work will take.
n.3: Unforeseen technical problems change the remaining effort and justify re-estimating.
n.4: New risks may change the expected work or duration, so the estimates should be revisited.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Midway through a project, significant changes to scope and resource availability have occurred, yet the project manager continues to report against the original schedule without updating it. What is a potential consequence of failing to re-estimate the schedule after these changes?
o: Lower likelihood of stakeholder escalation and concern
Improved accuracy of the project's reported progress
Better alignment between the plan and reality
Reduced overall project risk exposure over time
Unrealistic deadlines and increased likelihood of project overruns
