Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Ignoring changes leads to deadlines that don’t match reality and increases risk of overrun.

n.0: Transparency may suffer, but overruns are the main risk.
n.1: Success cannot be guaranteed without accurate planning.
n.2: Stakeholders may lose confidence if deadlines slip.
n.3: Risks are always present.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager uses schedule optimisation to reassign resources from non-critical to critical path tasks. What is the benefit of this action?
o: It guarantees all deliverables are on time
It increases the risk of missing critical milestones
It reduces the need for project monitoring
It can shorten the overall project duration
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Moving resources to the critical path can reduce project length by addressing bottlenecks.

n.0: No technique can guarantee every deliverable is on time.
n.1: This action helps meet critical milestones, not miss them.
n.2: Non-critical work must still be managed, just less urgently.
n.3: Monitoring remains necessary.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager decides to keep refining and adjusting the schedule at regular points across the delivery phase rather than treating the baseline as fixed. Which of the following is a benefit of this continuous schedule optimisation throughout a project?
o: Rigid adherence to the initial plan
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Continuous optimisation makes the project flexible and responsive to changes.

n.0: Being rigid can cause problems if circumstances change.
n.1: Lessons learned are valuable and should not be ignored.
n.2: Stakeholders remain crucial throughout the project.
n.3: Quality should never be reduced to optimise schedule.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which statement about schedule re-estimation is TRUE?
o: It should be avoided to prevent confusion
It helps maintain project realism when assumptions or conditions change
It is only needed for large projects
It removes all uncertainty from the project
It allows ignoring critical path analysis
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Re-estimation ensures the project plan matches actual circumstances as they evolve.

n.0: Re-estimation increases clarity, not confusion.
n.2: Projects of all sizes benefit from re-estimation.
n.3: Uncertainty can be managed, but never eliminated.
n.4: Critical path analysis remains vital in scheduling.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager wants to understand when it is appropriate to revisit and improve the schedule during delivery rather than leaving it untouched. What should trigger schedule optimisation during the project life cycle?
o: Any minor variation that stays within agreed tolerances
Sign-off of the project's initial requirements document
Formal closure of the project after final handover
Routine completion of each weekly status report
Discovery of delays, new risks, or opportunities to improve efficiency
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Optimisation is prompted by significant events like delays, risks, or new efficiencies.

n.0: Lessons learned come after project closure.
n.1: The charter comes before detailed planning.
n.2: Not every minor issue justifies major schedule changes.
n.3: Budget approval is a milestone but not the sole trigger.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: On a software project, a development team completes a major task several days ahead of the planned date, freeing capacity earlier than expected. How should the project manager manage the schedule in response?
o: Ignore the early finish and keep the original dates
Add new unplanned tasks to fill the gap
Reduce quality standards to finish even earlier
Re-estimate and optimise the schedule to reflect early completion
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Schedules should be updated to reflect actual progress, improving accuracy.

n.0: Schedules should always reflect actual progress.
n.1: Unplanned tasks risk scope creep.
n.2: Scope should be managed separately.
n.3: Quality standards must always be maintained.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A large infrastructure programme has many linked activities where a change to one task ripples through to others. As delivery progresses and circumstances change, what is the primary reason for ongoing re-estimation in projects with complex interdependencies?
o: To transfer dependency management onto the project sponsor
To fix the baseline so that dependencies no longer change
To satisfy a mandatory weekly progress reporting requirement
To ensure dependencies and impacts are considered as circumstances evolve
To reduce the total number of dependencies in the plan
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Re-estimation ensures the impact of interdependencies is accounted for throughout the project.

n.0: Project management requires ongoing attention.
n.1: Administrative burden is not the main reason for re-estimation.
n.2: The team should remain involved in project planning.
n.4: Updates serve planning, not sponsor impression.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project benefits from schedule optimisation by completing tasks in parallel where possible. What is a risk of this approach?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Parallel tasks can save time but require greater coordination and communication.

n.0: Stakeholder engagement is always important.
n.1: Risks cannot be eliminated, only managed.
n.3: Resource savings are possible, but not guaranteed.
n.4: Dependencies must be carefully managed with parallel tasks.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is preparing for a new office relocation. Which step is most important in determining the resources needed for moving IT equipment?
o: Identify all items to be moved and required technical expertise
Agree the relocation date with the building landlord
Book the removal vehicles and crew needed for the actual move day
Send a progress update to all project stakeholders
Confirm the desk layout plan for the new office
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource requirements come from the work: first identify what IT equipment must be moved and what technical skills are needed to disconnect, move and reconnect it.

n.1: Agreeing the date sets timing but does not determine which resources are needed.
n.2: Booking vehicles comes after the requirement has been determined.
n.3: Progress updates are communication, not resource planning.
n.4: The desk layout is a design detail, not how IT resource needs are determined.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A newly appointed project manager is compiling a list of the resources needed to deliver an office relocation and wants to be sure each item genuinely counts as a project resource. Which of the following is NOT typically considered a project resource?
o: Specialist equipment required for the tasks
Members of the assigned project team
Raw materials consumed during project tasks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: An annual report is a document, not a resource used to deliver project activities.

n.1: Equipment is a tangible resource.
n.2: Budget is a financial resource.
n.3: Team members are human resources.
n.4: Materials are resources needed to carry out tasks.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: While planning a project that relies on a small pool of specialist engineers shared across the organisation, the project manager reviews when those engineers can be released to the work. During project planning, why is it important to check the availability of specialist staff?
o: To reduce the need for quality assurance
To avoid scheduling conflicts and potential delays
To increase the number of project meetings
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Specialist staff may have other commitments—checking their availability helps avoid bottlenecks.

n.0: Risks must be managed, not ignored.
n.1: Scope change is not related to resource checks.
n.2: Quality assurance is always needed.
n.4: Meetings should be purposeful.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project requires delivery vans for a marketing campaign, but another department is using them for a separate project. What should the project manager do?
o: Deliver the whole campaign using office-based staff only
Postpone every project activity until the vans are free
Proceed with the campaign without any transport arranged
Cancel the other department’s booking to take the vans
Negotiate a schedule to share the vans or seek alternatives
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Negotiation or finding alternatives ensures that required resources are available when needed.

n.0: Office-based staff may not meet delivery requirements.
n.1: Delays should be a last resort.
n.2: Transport is essential for a delivery campaign.
n.3: Budget increases must be justified.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager needs a structured document that sets out the types and quantities of people, equipment and materials required across the project's activities. Which document typically details the types and quantities of resources required for project activities?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A resource breakdown structure (RBS) lists all resources needed for the project.

n.1: The risk register records risks, not resources.
n.2: Marketing strategy is not a project resource tool.
n.3: The issue log records project issues.
n.4: Communication plans do not list resource requirements.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A software development project needs access to a secure testing environment. What should be checked before scheduling the test phase?
o: The format of the weekly highlight report to the project board
The availability of the testing environment and required personnel
The number of change requests raised during the build phase
The power/interest grid for stakeholders in the wider test community
The supplier's reimbursement method for the testing licences
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Before scheduling testing, the project manager must confirm that the secure test environment and the people needed to run the tests are available when planned, since both are constrained resources.

n.0: The format of the highlight report concerns communication, not the scheduling of the test phase.
n.2: The number of change requests is a scope control measure and does not show whether testing can go ahead.
n.3: The power/interest grid informs stakeholder engagement, not whether the environment and testers are free.
n.4: How the licences are paid for is a commercial matter, not a check on availability.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When staffing a project with several distinct work packages, the project manager assesses both how many people and which specific competencies will be needed. Why is it important to determine both the number and the skills of people needed for a project?
o: To reduce the amount of documentation the team produces
To ensure all required tasks are completed to the right standard
To ensure every team member carries an identical workload
To allow the project deadline to be brought forward
To keep the overall staffing cost as low as possible
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Right skills and headcount ensure activities are completed properly and on time.

n.0: Team motivation should be supported, not minimised.
n.2: Communication is always essential.
n.3: Efficient resource planning should support timely delivery.
n.4: Cost control is important, but not the primary reason.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is assessing which factors could affect whether key resources will be available when the schedule requires them. Which of the following would NOT be considered when assessing the availability of resources?
o: A team member’s annual leave during the project
The hourly charge-out rate of each resource
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Availability is about whether a resource can be used when needed. A charge-out rate affects cost and the budget, not whether the resource is available.

n.0: Where materials are held affects whether they can be on site when needed.
n.1: Maintenance takes equipment out of service.
n.2: Commitments to other projects limit availability.
n.3: Annual leave reduces availability.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A refurbishment project depends on a small number of qualified electricians who are in high demand across other jobs. When building the schedule for the electrical work, what should the project manager consider?
o: The format of the monthly progress report to the client
Electrician availability and timing of electrical tasks
The reimbursement method in the main contract
The benefits profile for the refurbished building
The number of change requests already logged
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: With scarce, in-demand electricians, the schedule must be built around when they are available, with the electrical tasks sequenced and timed to match, or the work will be delayed.

n.0: The report format is a communication decision and does not affect electrician scheduling.
n.2: The reimbursement method decides how the contractor is paid, not when the electricians are available.
n.3: The benefits profile describes expected benefits, not the timing of electrical work.
n.4: The number of change requests reflects scope pressure, not the availability of qualified electricians.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager on a construction project is working out what resources will be needed and when they must arrive on site. Which of these is a typical step when determining the resources for a construction project?
o: Identify tasks, estimate quantities, and check supplier lead times
Set the management reserve for unidentified risks
Prepare the stakeholder communication schedule for site neighbours
Agree the acceptance criteria for the finished build with the client
Calculate the earned value of the work completed so far
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource requirements are built from the activities: identify the tasks, estimate the quantities needed, then check availability and supplier lead times so resources arrive on time.

n.1: Management reserve is a budget matter held by the sponsor, not a resource planning step.
n.2: Communication scheduling is stakeholder management.
n.3: Acceptance criteria are part of quality planning, not determining resources.
n.4: Earned value measures performance during delivery; it does not determine resource needs.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project needs specialist analytics work that the organisation's own staff are not trained for and cannot cover within the timeframe. Why might a project require external resources rather than just using internal staff?
o: To access specialist skills or additional capacity not available in-house
To remove the need to manage any project risks
To transfer full accountability for delivery onto the supplier
To guarantee the work will always cost less overall
To avoid having to plan the project schedule internally
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: External resources are often needed when internal staff lack the required skills or availability.

n.1: Risks can never be fully eliminated.
n.2: The aim is efficiency, not unnecessary complexity.
n.3: Good resource planning supports scheduling, not ignores it.
n.4: Quality should always be maintained or improved.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project team must use a shared meeting space that is often booked for other purposes. What’s the best approach to ensuring this resource is available when needed?
o: Replace all project meetings with email updates instead
Reduce the number of project meetings held each week
Book the meeting space well in advance and confirm reservations
Reserve the space exclusively for senior management use
Hold meetings only when the space is unexpectedly free
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Advance booking and confirmation is the best way to secure a shared resource.

n.0: Not all issues can be resolved via email.
n.1: Meeting frequency should meet project needs.
n.3: Resource allocation should be based on project need, not status.
n.4: Meetings may be necessary for project progress.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is drawing up the list of resources that will be required to deliver the project's activities. Which of the following is NOT a resource that may be required for project delivery?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The critical path is a feature of the schedule (the longest sequence of dependent activities), not a resource that delivery consumes or uses.

n.1: Software is a re-usable resource.
n.2: Money is a replenishable (consumable) resource.
n.3: Hired equipment is a re-usable resource.
n.4: Materials are consumable resources.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A facilities upgrade must be carried out overnight to avoid disrupting daytime operations, so some tasks are scheduled during night shifts. What is an important consideration for the project manager when planning these activities?
o: Apply the daytime productivity rates unchanged to every night task
Rely on the operations team to supervise the night-time work
Plan to cover any gaps with unplanned overtime as they arise
Check if those resources (people, equipment) can be accessed at night
Schedule the night tasks first and confirm the resources at a later date
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Night work can only go ahead if the people, equipment, site access and support it needs are actually available at night, so this must be confirmed before those activities are scheduled.

n.0: Productivity at night is often lower, so daytime rates may understate durations; this is an estimating error.
n.1: Operations staff have their own duties; supervision of project work must be planned, not assumed.
n.2: Relying on unplanned overtime is a sign of poor planning and risks fatigue and cost overruns.
n.4: Scheduling before confirming resources risks a plan that cannot be delivered; availability must come first.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager wants a graphical view showing how demand for particular resources rises and falls across the project timeline. Which tool can help visualise when specific resources will be needed during a project?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A resource histogram graphically shows resource requirements over time.

n.1: Risk logs track risks, not resources.
n.2: Lessons learned are collected at project end.
n.3: PBS details deliverables, not resource needs by time.
n.4: The PID describes the project but doesn’t visualise resource needs.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project’s timeline is tight and relies on a key supplier’s materials. What should the project manager confirm before starting work?
o: The supplier can deliver materials when needed
The supplier’s preferred payment terms and invoicing dates
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: With a tight timeline that depends on the supplier, the critical check is that materials will be available when the schedule needs them (lead times and capacity).

n.0: An annual report shows financial standing but not delivery timing.
n.1: The tender score was used at selection; it does not confirm delivery.
n.3: Warranty applies after delivery and does not protect the timeline.
n.4: Payment terms are a commercial matter, not whether materials will arrive on time.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is preparing the organisational breakdown structure (OBS) for a new IT system implementation. Why is the OBS important before creating a RACI matrix?
o: It provides the overall strategy for mitigating the project risks
It sets the sequence and dates of project activities
It finalises the list of materials the project needs
It identifies all roles and reporting lines needed for assigning responsibilities
It establishes the total budget for the whole project
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The OBS defines project roles, which is the foundation for building a responsibility matrix like RACI.

n.0: Risk mitigation is handled through other processes.
n.1: The schedule is not defined by the OBS.
n.2: Materials are detailed in other documents.
n.4: Budgeting is managed separately from OBS.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager introduces a matrix to make clear who does the work, who is answerable for it, who gives input and who is kept informed for each activity. What is the primary function of a responsibility assignment matrix (RACI)?
o: To summarise and then prioritise all of the main project risks
To record all of the financial transactions made during the project
To list out every single activity contained in the project schedule
To describe the detailed technical requirements of each project deliverable
To clarify who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for project tasks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A RACI matrix clarifies roles and responsibilities for each task or deliverable.

n.0: Risks are managed elsewhere.
n.1: Financial records are kept separately from the RACI.
n.2: The schedule may reference the RACI, but is a different document.
n.3: Technical requirements are detailed in specifications, not the RACI.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Before assigning roles across a RACI matrix, a project manager first maps out the project's teams and reporting lines. When developing a RACI matrix, why is it important to have an accurate organisational breakdown structure?
o: It takes the place of formal stakeholder analysis work
It guarantees the project will be delivered on time
It ensures all necessary roles are identified for assignment of responsibilities
It sets the format used for the communication plan
It removes the need for any project risk management
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: An accurate OBS is essential to ensure all roles are covered and responsibilities can be allocated effectively.

n.0: Stakeholder analysis remains a separate activity.
n.1: Finishing on time depends on many factors beyond the OBS and RACI.
n.3: The OBS does not dictate communication formats.
n.4: Risk management is still required.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A construction project is delivered by separate design, build and test teams, and the project manager needs to allocate responsibilities clearly across them. How can the organisational breakdown structure help with responsibility allocation?
o: It maps teams and individuals, providing clarity for the RACI matrix
It determines the construction materials that the project will require
It documents the local building codes that will apply here
It calculates the overtime payments that are owed to staff
It sets the calendar dates for each of the project milestones
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The OBS shows who is in each team, making it possible to assign RACI roles clearly.

n.1: Materials are managed elsewhere.
n.2: Regulations are a compliance issue, not for the OBS.
n.3: OBS does not deal with payroll.
n.4: Milestone dates come from the project plan, not the OBS.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is explaining to the team the advantages that a RACI matrix brings to how the project is run. Which of the following is NOT a typical benefit of using a RACI matrix in project management?
o: It guarantees all project risks are removed
It highlights gaps or overlaps in responsibility
It helps avoid confusion over roles
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A RACI does not remove risks but clarifies responsibilities.

n.0: RACI supports communication about who does what.
n.2: Accountability is made clear by the RACI.
n.3: Gaps and overlaps are easier to spot with a RACI.
n.4: Avoiding role confusion is a key RACI benefit.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project’s OBS is incomplete and missing key roles. What is a potential risk if the RACI is created from this incomplete structure?
o: The risk register will be unnecessary
There will be no need for quality assurance
All team members will have too many tasks
The project will always finish ahead of schedule
Important responsibilities may not be assigned
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: If key roles are missing, important tasks may be unassigned or overlooked in the RACI.

n.0: Risk management is always required.
n.1: Quality must always be checked regardless of structure.
n.2: Under-assignment is just as likely as over-assignment.
n.3: Schedules are not directly controlled by the RACI.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is filling in a RACI matrix for a series of engineering tasks and wants to make sure each of the four role letters is applied correctly against every activity. In the RACI matrix, what does the 'C' stand for?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: 'C' in RACI stands for Consulted, indicating those who provide input before a decision or action.

n.0: Calculated is not a RACI role.
n.1: Completed refers to tasks, not RACI roles.
n.2: Certified is unrelated to responsibility assignment.
n.3: Controlled is not part of RACI.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In a product launch project, the marketing manager is marked as 'A' for a task in the RACI. What does this mean?
o: They must perform the task directly
They are only consulted if issues arise
They only provide information, not decisions
The marketing manager is Accountable for the task’s completion
They have no involvement with the task
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: 'A' means Accountable, the person who must answer for task completion, not always the doer.

n.0: Responsibility is 'R'; accountability is about oversight.
n.1: Consulted are included, but accountability is a separate role.
n.2: Consulted ('C') provide input, not just information.
n.4: No involvement would mean no entry in the matrix.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager wants both a clear picture of the team structure and a precise breakdown of who is responsible for each activity. Why might a project manager use both an organisational breakdown structure and a RACI matrix?
o: To show how project costs map onto each work package
To ensure roles are defined and responsibilities are clearly allocated
To sequence activities and identify the critical path
To compare the demand for each resource with its availability over time
To record the products the project will deliver
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The OBS shows who is in the project organisation; combined with the WBS it produces a RACI matrix that allocates responsibility for each work package, with one person accountable.

n.0: Mapping costs to work packages is the cost breakdown structure.
n.2: Sequencing and the critical path come from network analysis.
n.3: Demand against availability is shown on a resource histogram.
n.4: Products are recorded in the product breakdown structure.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager takes the organisational breakdown structure and maps its teams and individuals against the project's activities. What is a direct output of linking the organisational breakdown structure (OBS) to project activities?
o: A revised layout plan for the office
A maintenance schedule for the project equipment
A detailed financial forecast for the project
A prioritised chart of the project risks
A clear responsibility assignment matrix (such as RACI)
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The OBS feeds directly into responsibility matrices by showing who can be assigned to what.

n.0: Office layout is unrelated to project responsibilities.
n.1: Maintenance schedules are resource management tools.
n.2: Financial forecasts are created elsewhere.
n.3: Risk charts are based on risk analysis, not OBS.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: While reviewing a project's RACI matrix, the project manager notices that one important task has no Accountable person assigned to it. What problem could this create?
o: Stakeholders will stop receiving any updates on the project progress
Lack of clear ownership may result in the task being overlooked
The overall project cost will rise without any warning
The project will be completed ahead of its schedule
Every team member will refuse to attempt the task
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Without an accountable person, no one is ultimately responsible for ensuring completion.

n.0: Communication gaps are possible but the main issue is accountability.
n.2: Costs may rise due to inefficiency, but this is not automatic.
n.3: A missing accountable role usually delays tasks.
n.4: Team members may try to help, but lack clear direction.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In a scenario where multiple people are marked 'R' for a single task in the RACI, what risk can arise?
o: Automatic success across the whole project
Duplication of effort or confusion over responsibility
The complete elimination of all project risks
Clearer and stronger lines of individual accountability
A reduced need for team communication overall

n.2: Risks are always present.
n.3: Accountability may actually become less clear.
n.4: Communication needs may increase to resolve confusion.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is working through a RACI matrix and assigning one of the four role letters to each stakeholder against every activity. In a RACI matrix, what does the 'I' stand for?

n.3: Instructed is not used in RACI.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project team has produced an organisational breakdown structure showing who sits in which team, but has not yet developed a RACI matrix. What is a potential disadvantage of this?
o: The complete removal of every single project risk involved
The immediate failure of the entire project delivery effort
Lack of clarity on exactly who does what for each activity
The automatic approval of all of the project documents
No further requirement to carry out any stakeholder analysis

n.1: Lack of RACI does not guarantee failure, but increases confusion.

n.4: Stakeholder analysis is still needed.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why should the OBS be regularly updated throughout a project?
o: Because it finalises the total budget for the project
Because it locks the RACI matrix at project start
Because it removes every risk the project might face
Because it sets the quality standards for the deliverables
Because roles or team members can change, affecting RACI assignments
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Updates to the OBS ensure new roles or staff changes are reflected in responsibility assignment.

n.2: Risks must always be managed, not avoided through documentation.
n.3: Quality standards are managed separately.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager ensures that every entry in the RACI matrix maps back to the real teams and reporting lines set out in the organisational breakdown structure. Which is a direct benefit of aligning the RACI matrix with the organisational breakdown structure?
o: Allows a single person to fill every project role
Guarantees the project will finish under its budget
Removes the requirement to keep any project documentation
Ensures responsibility assignments match actual team roles and reporting lines
Removes the need for any regular progress reporting altogether
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Alignment with the OBS ensures the RACI reflects how the project team actually functions.

n.1: Cost depends on many factors.
n.2: Documentation remains important.
n.4: Progress reporting is always required.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: On a project that has been reorganised, the RACI matrix still reflects the old team layout and no longer matches how the project is actually staffed. What can happen as a result of this mismatch?
o: The immediate closure of the whole project
A reduced need for communication between members
Faster and easier decision making across the team
The automatic identification of every project risk
Confusion and missed responsibilities due to misaligned assignments

n.3: Risks must still be actively identified and managed.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is planning a project delivered through a sequence of distinct, non-overlapping phases and needs to decide how resources will be committed to the work. Which of the following best describes resource allocation in a linear (waterfall) life cycle?
o: Resources are assigned at random all throughout the whole project
Resource allocation is decided only once the whole project closes
Resources are allocated in advance to each phase, following a sequential plan
Resources can never be adjusted after they are first assigned
All resources are shared across every phase at the same time
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: In linear life cycles, resources are assigned to each sequential phase as per the plan.

n.0: Allocation is structured, not random.
n.1: Allocation must occur before closure to deliver the work.
n.3: Resource needs may be reviewed at stage gates.
n.4: Simultaneous resource sharing is more typical of iterative cycles.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project is being delivered through repeated cycles of building, reviewing and refining the product, and the project manager must decide how resources will be committed. In an iterative project life cycle, how are resources typically allocated?
o: Resources are only required for the final stage
Resources are allocated to support repeated cycles of development and review
Resources are only financial, not human or material
Resource allocation follows a strict, unchanging plan
All resources are assigned at the start and never reallocated
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Iterative cycles require flexible allocation to allow for frequent review and adjustment.

n.2: Human and material resources are also required.
n.3: Plans may change as iterations progress.
n.4: Iterative life cycles adapt allocation as the project evolves.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project uses a linear life cycle to build a bridge. What is a typical resource categorisation for this project?
o: Only financial resources considered right across the whole project
All resources assigned only during the initial design phase
Resources categorised only after the whole project has finished
Resources grouped by phase, such as design, build, and test teams
No resources needed at all for the build phase
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: In linear cycles, resources are assigned according to sequential project phases.

n.0: Many resource types are involved.
n.1: Each phase needs its own allocation.
n.2: Resource planning happens before execution.
n.4: The build phase is resource-intensive.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is comparing how resources are committed in a linear, sequential approach with how they are committed in an iterative, cyclical one. How does resource allocation differ between linear and iterative life cycles?
o: Iterative cycles require more flexible resource allocation as priorities may shift each iteration
Linear life cycles will rely only on financial resources all throughout
Linear cycles require resources to be allocated at random each phase
Both approaches will always follow exactly the same fixed resource plan
Iterative cycles never make any use of the available material resources
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Iterative cycles demand flexibility to adjust resources as work is reprioritised in each cycle.

n.2: Linear allocation is structured, not random.
n.3: Plans are tailored to the life cycle.
n.4: Material resources may be needed in all cycles.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager wants to organise the project's resources into standard groupings that apply regardless of the life cycle being used. What is a common method of categorising resources in any project life cycle?
o: Using the order in which suppliers are paid
By type: human, material, equipment, and financial
By colour coding the project schedule
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Standard categories are human, material, equipment, and financial.

n.0: Payment order is an administrative concern.
n.2: Alphabetical order is unrelated to resource management.
n.3: Sponsor preference is not a method of categorisation.
n.4: Colour coding is a scheduling, not a resourcing tool.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A software development project using an iterative approach needs test resources for every cycle. What does this illustrate about resource allocation?
o: Certain resources must be available repeatedly, not just once
Material resources are not used in software projects
Financial resources are always more important
Resource allocation is not required in iterative projects
Resources are only needed at the end
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Iterative cycles require certain resources to be scheduled for multiple rounds.

n.1: Material resources (like hardware) can be necessary.
n.2: Financial and non-financial resources may be equally critical.
n.3: Resource allocation is required in every life cycle.
n.4: Some resources are needed throughout, not just at the end.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project is being delivered through a strict sequence of phases, each of which must be completed before the next begins. What is a key consideration when allocating resources in this linear project life cycle?
o: Delaying every resource decision until the project reaches closure
Assigning resources to project phases based on purely random selection
Ignoring the specific skill requirements of each team member
Ensuring resources are available in each defined phase before moving on
Revising the plan after every phase without any justification
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Each phase must have resources in place before that phase can proceed in a linear model.

n.0: Delays in allocation can jeopardise delivery.
n.1: Allocation should be structured, not random.
n.2: Skills are essential for task completion.
n.4: Plans should only change when justified.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In an iterative cycle, a project manager adjusts resource allocation after each sprint review. What is the main benefit of this approach?
o: It removes the need to manage a project budget
It allows resources to be aligned with changing priorities and feedback
It avoids any need at all to involve project stakeholders
It fixes the team structure from start to finish
It ensures the project will never encounter any risk
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Iterative approaches benefit from flexible resource allocation in response to new information.

n.0: Budgeting is still necessary.
n.2: Stakeholder input is important in all cycles.
n.3: Teams may change between sprints or iterations.
n.4: Risks must always be managed, regardless of allocation.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: On a sequentially phased project, resources for a later phase have not been secured in time for when that phase is due to start. What is a typical risk of this poor resource allocation in a linear life cycle?
o: All of the project risks will be completely eliminated altogether
Additional project resources will simply be created by default here
The whole project will turn iterative instead of staying linear
Project phases may be delayed if resources are not available as scheduled
Stakeholder engagement will automatically rise right across the whole project
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: If resources are not available when needed, sequential phases will be delayed.

n.0: Poor allocation increases risks.
n.1: Resource creation requires planning and investment.
n.2: The life cycle model does not change automatically.
n.4: Engagement is a separate management area.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager expects priorities to shift often and people and equipment to be moved between tasks repeatedly as the work evolves. In which life cycle is it most common to reassign resources between tasks as priorities change frequently?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Frequent reassignment is a hallmark of iterative cycles, supporting adaptability.

n.0: Adaptation happens in all project stages if needed.
n.1: All phases may require resource reassignment in iterative cycles.
n.3: Linear cycles tend to keep allocations fixed per phase.
n.4: Resource allocation is not restricted to procurement or testing.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A construction project uses a linear life cycle. Which of the following resources is most likely categorised and allocated at the start of the build phase?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Tangible resources for the build phase are identified and allocated before work starts.

n.1: Support staff and testers are needed in later stages.
n.2: Testing comes after the build phase.
n.3: Marketing consultants are more relevant post-build.
n.4: Sponsors provide governance, not build resources.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project team delivers work through successive iterations, adjusting who works on what at the start of each cycle. Which statement best summarises resource allocation in an iterative project?
o: External supplier resources are excluded from every iteration's allocation
Resources are reassigned as work priorities and tasks evolve each cycle
Only the financial budget is treated as an allocatable project resource
Resources are categorised only once, during the initiation phase alone
Resources are committed in full at project start and never reassigned
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resources are regularly adjusted to suit current iteration needs.

n.0: Suppliers may be used in any project.
n.2: Human, material, and equipment resources also matter.
n.3: Categorisation is essential for both cycle types.
n.4: This is a feature of linear cycles.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What does resource categorisation help with in project management?
o: Avoiding the need for stakeholder input
Identifying what is needed and planning when each type is required
Eliminating all risks from the project
Ensuring the project always finishes early
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Categorisation aids in precise planning and avoids shortages or bottlenecks.

n.0: Resources are always finite.
n.1: Stakeholder input is important.
n.3: Risks are managed, not eliminated by categorisation.
n.4: Finishing early depends on many factors.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: An iterative project is running two development cycles that overlap in time, and each cycle draws on the same small pool of specialist testers and equipment during the same period. What is a potential resource allocation challenge in this situation?
o: All resources are automatically available when needed
Resources can only be allocated to one task per project
Competing demand for the same resources in different cycles
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Overlaps can cause conflicts when different cycles require the same people or equipment.

n.0: Regular review is needed in all cycles.
n.1: Availability must be managed, not assumed.
n.2: Sequential phases are a feature of linear, not iterative, cycles.
n.3: Resources may be multitasked in iterative projects.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager wants to group and commit all the resources needed for each phase up front, before any of the work in that phase starts. Which type of project life cycle is most likely to categorise resources for each distinct phase before work begins?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Linear cycles categorise and allocate resources in advance, phase by phase.

n.0: Iterative cycles assign resources for each iteration.
n.2: Hybrid approaches may use either method.
n.3: Risk-driven allocation is part of risk management, not a life cycle.
n.4: Procurement is a component, not a cycle type.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Between iterations on an agile-style project, the team pauses to reassess how people and equipment are deployed before starting the next cycle. What is a key benefit of these resource allocation reviews in iterative life cycles?
o: Guarantees the resource budget remains fixed across all iterations
Removes the need for any planning meetings between iterations
Confirms that upfront planning at project start is unnecessary
Ability to adapt resource allocation to changing project needs
Sets a final allocation that later reviews cannot alter
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Reviewing allocation lets the team respond to new priorities and information each cycle.

n.0: Budgets may change if priorities shift.
n.1: Meetings are still required for communication.
n.2: Initial planning is always necessary.
n.4: Risks must still be managed.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which statement best defines resource smoothing in project management?
o: Adjusting activities within their float so that resource usage does not exceed limits
Increasing the project scope to use more resources
Assigning resources without regard for availability
Reducing the quality of project deliverables
Delaying the project end date to match available resources
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing uses available float to even out resource demand without affecting project end dates.

n.1: Scope is not increased for smoothing.
n.2: Smoothing always considers resource constraints.
n.3: Quality should not be sacrificed for resource adjustments.
n.4: Delaying the end date is resource levelling, not smoothing.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What distinguishes resource levelling from resource smoothing?
o: Smoothing is only used in agile projects
Levelling always increases the project’s budget
Resource levelling may change the project’s end date; smoothing does not
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling can extend the schedule to resolve conflicts, while smoothing only uses available float.

n.0: Both techniques can be used in different methodologies.
n.1: Budget impacts depend on the project.
n.2: Neither technique removes all risks.
n.4: Smoothing considers constraints, levelling may require schedule changes.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager adjusts the timing of non-critical tasks to keep resource usage below a set threshold, without affecting the end date. What technique is being used?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing shifts activities within float to balance resources but keeps the project on schedule.

n.0: Scope creep refers to uncontrolled scope change.
n.1: Procurement is unrelated.
n.2: Levelling might impact the schedule.
n.4: Risk avoidance is a separate activity.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager finds that several team members are scheduled to work on multiple activities at the same time, exceeding their available capacity. The end date may be delayed to resolve resource conflicts
The critical path remains unchanged despite the resource conflicts
Activities are compressed so the project finishes earlier than planned

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling resolves resource clashes by allowing schedule adjustments, potentially causing delays.

n.2: Risks must always be managed.
n.3: Levelling can require more time, not less.
n.4: Costs may rise or fall depending on adjustments.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: During planning, a project manager reviews a resource histogram that shows uneven peaks and troughs in team utilisation, but the agreed delivery date cannot move. The manager decides to apply resource smoothing to the schedule. Which of the following best describes the main goal of this technique?

Keep resource usage within limits without extending the project’s critical path

n.2: Communication is always important.
n.3: Overtime should be avoided if possible.
n.4: Scope is not increased by smoothing.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling delays activities to ensure resources are available, even if the project runs longer.

n.1: Exploitation is about using opportunities, not rescheduling.
n.2: Fast tracking involves parallel activities, not delay.
n.3: Scope expansion is not relevant here.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of resource smoothing?

It keeps the critical path unchanged

It allows the project end date to change
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing does not allow the project end date to slip.

n.2: Staying within resource limits is the aim.
n.3: Smoothing is preferred with fixed deadlines.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project team is finalising its schedule and finds that resource demand repeatedly exceeds what is available. The sponsor has confirmed that the completion date is not fixed and can flex if needed. In this situation, why might the team choose resource levelling instead of smoothing?

When deadlines are flexible and avoiding resource overload is critical
When only the financial budget needs rebalancing across tasks
When resource availability constraints can be safely disregarded entirely
When accelerating delivery outweighs any resource overload concerns

n.3: Ignoring constraints risks failure.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A new project manager is learning about scheduling techniques and is comparing resource smoothing and resource levelling before applying one to a plan with over-committed staff. Setting aside their differences in how they treat the end date, what do both techniques have in common?
o: They both aim to resolve resource over-allocation
They ignore the project’s resource constraints
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Both techniques deal with matching resources to the needs of the schedule.

n.1: Stakeholder communication remains important.
n.2: Durations may stay the same or increase.
n.4: Constraints are considered in both.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A software development project has a fixed release date, and the network shows that some non-critical tasks have available float. The project manager applies resource smoothing to deal with periods where developers are over-allocated. Which result is expected from this approach?
o: Additional resources are hired to keep every task on time
Resource availability limits are raised so no tasks need shifting
The project end date slips later to resolve the conflicts
Non-critical tasks are shifted within their float to avoid resource overloads
Critical path tasks are delayed to relieve the resource overloads
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing keeps the project on time by using float on non-critical tasks.

n.1: Critical activities remain unchanged.
n.2: Budget may not change.
n.4: Delays are avoided in smoothing.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is deciding between resource smoothing and resource levelling for a plan where the demand on specialist staff is uncertain and the sponsor has agreed the completion date can move if necessary. Which scenario would require resource levelling instead of smoothing?
o: No resource conflicts exist anywhere across the project schedule
The critical path must stay unchanged throughout the delivery
The project end date is flexible and resource availability is unpredictable
Resource usage already remains comfortably within the agreed limits
All project deadlines are fixed and the end date is immovable
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling is used when deadlines can move to resolve resource shortages.

n.1: Critical path changes may occur with levelling.
n.3: If there are no conflicts, neither method is needed.
n.4: Smoothing is used for fixed deadlines.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How does resource smoothing impact the project’s critical path?
o: It does not alter the critical path or extend project duration
It increases the number of critical activities
It always shortens the critical path
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing adjusts non-critical tasks, leaving the critical path unchanged.

n.0: Delays are not introduced in smoothing.
n.2: The type of resources may not change.
n.3: Smoothing does not add new critical activities.
n.4: The critical path remains the same length.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is worried that the current plan will push several team members beyond their available hours, yet the contractual delivery date cannot be moved under any circumstances. Which technique is the most suitable for the project manager to apply in this situation?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing is appropriate when deadlines must be maintained, and resource usage needs to be controlled.

n.0: Risk transfer is about managing threats.
n.1: Random allocation is not a valid technique.
n.3: Quality should not be compromised.
n.4: Levelling may cause delays.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project is operating with very limited specialist resources and a tightly packed schedule that contains little float. The project manager intends to rely on resource smoothing alone to manage periods of over-allocation. What is a potential risk of taking only this approach on such a resource-constrained project?
o: The project budget can never be exceeded under smoothing
Every scheduling risk is eliminated once smoothing is applied
Resource limits may still be breached if float is insufficient
All resource conflicts are guaranteed to be fully resolved
The project will always finish ahead of its planned schedule
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: If there isn’t enough float, smoothing alone may not resolve overallocation.

n.1: Risks must always be managed.
n.3: Some conflicts may persist.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the primary purpose of resource levelling?
o: To keep all activities within their float
To adjust the timing of activities so resource limits are not exceeded, even if it extends the project
To shorten the project’s overall schedule

n.4: Budgets may or may not be affected.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: On a delivery schedule, an activity that lies on the critical path is finished ahead of its planned finish date, and no other constraints currently limit the work that follows. The project manager is assessing what this means for the timeline. What is the most likely impact?
o: Other dependent activities will be delayed as a result
Float will increase evenly across all of the remaining activities
The critical path through the network will be eliminated
The project will automatically finish ahead of its deadline

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A two-day delay occurs on an activity shown as critical. No resources were added, no activities were overlapped and the logic was not changed, yet the forecast completion date is unaffected. What is the most plausible explanation?

Critical activities always carry some float

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is examining a network diagram and needs to work out which activities lie on the critical path by applying the correct defining test. She wants to reason from the underlying rule rather than a general impression. Which situation most accurately indicates that an activity is on the critical path?

It is the first activity in the schedule
It has the longest duration in the project

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When monitoring progress, a project manager reviews only the activities on the critical path and pays no attention to those carrying small amounts of float. A colleague warns him that this narrow focus is hazardous. What risk does concentrating solely on the critical path create?

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is reviewing a schedule and wants to anticipate which type of change would shift the critical path and thereby alter the overall duration. She is weighing several possible adjustments to different activities. Which change is most likely to alter the critical path?

Increasing the duration of a critical activity
Reducing the duration of a non-critical activity with float

She needs to interpret correctly what this value is telling her about the project's position. What does negative float on this activity indicate?

The critical path has been shortened
The activity is delaying the project completion

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A sponsor has asked the project manager to bring the planned completion date forward and is pressing for the most effective scheduling response. The manager is deciding where to direct compression effort within the network. Which action would most effectively reduce the overall project duration?

Extending the durations of critical activities
Reducing the duration of critical activities
Shortening the duration of non-critical activities

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: An assessor asks a project manager to explain precisely what makes an activity 'critical' within a network diagram. The manager must set out its true defining attributes rather than a loose impression of importance. Which TWO characteristics define a critical activity?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical activities have zero float and directly influence completion.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager has been building a schedule while taking no account of the float on various activities as he plans and sequences the work. Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Midway through delivery, a project manager wants to anticipate which developments could cause the critical path to shift to a different sequence of activities. He is considering several things that might happen across the network. Which TWO scenarios could cause a change in the critical path?

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager is briefing an apprentice on how float behaves within a schedule. She wants the apprentice to retain only the statements that are accurate and to set aside the misconceptions. Which TWO statements about float are correct?

Float is fixed throughout the project
