Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A review of a project's plan finds that its milestones have been described vaguely, with no clear criteria for when each is reached. The sponsor asks what problems such loosely defined milestones are likely to cause. Which TWO risks arise from poorly defined milestones?
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Poor definition leads to unclear progress and ineffective decision-making.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A Cost Breakdown Structure (CBS) shows costs exceeding budget, but the Work Breakdown Structure appears accurate. What is the most likely issue?
o: The product breakdown structure was left partially incomplete
Key dependencies between activities are missing from the network
The stakeholders have not been properly engaged throughout
The project schedule contains errors in its activity durations
Costs are not properly aligned to work packages
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: CBS must align with WBS; misalignment leads to inaccurate cost tracking.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: During planning for a product launch, a project manager deliberately structures the Cost Breakdown Structure so that it mirrors the Work Breakdown Structure. What is the primary benefit of aligning the two structures in this way?
o: Faster execution of the project activities
Clear linkage between costs and deliverables
Reduced overall stakeholder involvement in reporting
Simplified management of the project risks
Improved accuracy of the project schedule
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Aligning CBS with WBS ensures costs are traceable to deliverables.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A sponsor asks a project manager to explain what the Cost Breakdown Structure is intended to achieve on a capital project. Which statement best describes the purpose of a Cost Breakdown Structure?
o: Organises project costs in alignment with work packages
Defines the deliverables the project must produce
Sequences project activities according to their dependencies
Records identified project risks and their responses
Assigns responsibilities for delivering each work package
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: CBS structures costs in relation to work packages for control.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: On an ongoing project, a project manager finds that expenditure is only being recorded and reported at a high, whole-project level rather than against individual work packages. What limitation does tracking costs at this level create?
o: Inability to establish the total project budget
Poor assurance over the quality of deliverables
Limited visibility of cost performance at work package level
Reduced traceability of scope to stakeholder requirements
Weaker control over the sequencing of activities
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: High-level tracking reduces visibility and control over specific work areas.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: Which outcome indicates poor alignment between CBS and WBS?
o: Costs are traceable to specific deliverables
Budget variances are difficult to explain
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Misalignment makes cost variances unclear and difficult to manage.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: Which TWO practices improve alignment between CBS and WBS?
o: Separating cost tracking from scope definition
Tracking costs at project level only
Mapping costs directly to work packages
Ensuring consistent structure between cost and work breakdowns
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Alignment requires direct mapping and consistent structure.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager has just approved the scope and is preparing to build a detailed, bottom-up budget for the work to be delivered. Before any cost figures can be assembled with confidence, what is the first essential step the project manager should take?
o: Assign tasks randomly to available staff
Identify and list all project tasks and required resources
Increase the project’s contingency fund without analysis
Book meeting rooms for the project team
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Identifying all tasks and resources is crucial to ensure all costs are captured in the budget.

n.0: Random task assignment is not best practice.
n.2: Contingency must be based on actual analysis.
n.3: Marketing slogans are unrelated to budgeting.
n.4: Meetings support planning but don’t drive budget creation.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager is assembling a detailed project budget and wants a recognised way to organise and group the various costs into categories so nothing is overlooked. Which tool is commonly used to structure and group costs when creating a project budget?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: A CBS organises costs by category, activity or resource, aiding clarity and control.

n.1: Stakeholder plans are for communication, not budgeting.
n.2: Procurement schedules support purchasing, not structuring costs.
n.3: Risk matrices are not budgeting tools.
n.4: Work package descriptions detail scope, not costs.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project team uses a cost breakdown structure (CBS) to prepare their budget. What is the key advantage of this approach?
o: It automatically shortens the overall project delivery schedule
It removes the need to identify any project risks at all
It guarantees the project will deliver a financial profit
It ensures all cost elements are identified and tracked systematically
It removes the need for any stakeholder input on costs
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: CBS makes sure all costs are captured and assigned, supporting complete budgeting.

n.0: The schedule is managed independently of budgeting.
n.1: Risks still require separate management.
n.2: Budgets do not guarantee profits.
n.4: Stakeholder involvement is still important.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager is drawing up the cost estimate for a new office fit-out and wants to make sure the budget captures every relevant category of spend. Which of the following is typically included when creating a project budget?
o: Planned value, earned value and actual cost
Labour, materials, equipment, and contingency allowances
Direct labour and materials only, with no contingency allowance
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: A project budget is built from cost estimates for labour, materials and equipment, plus contingency for identified risks.

n.0: PV, EV and AC are earned value measures used to monitor the budget, not budget categories.
n.1: Outputs, outcomes and benefits define scope and value, not budget categories.
n.3: Registers are control records, not elements of a budget.
n.4: Omitting contingency leaves no provision for risks, and equipment costs are missing.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager decides to use a cost breakdown structure to bring order to the many costs on a construction project. When applying this technique, how are the costs usually organised within it?
o: By grouping costs according to deliverables, activities, or resource types
By grouping costs according to which stakeholder requested them
By listing every cost alphabetically according to the supplier name
By assigning each cost to a work package at random
By ordering costs solely on how frequently they recur
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Grouping by deliverables, activities or resources helps ensure costs are not missed.

n.1: Requests do not define the structure; planning does.
n.2: Supplier name order is not practical for budgeting.
n.3: Random assignment leads to confusion and errors.
n.4: Frequency matters, but structure is more important.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager is setting up the CBS for a major IT upgrade. What information should be included in each CBS category?
o: Purchase order numbers and supplier contact details for each
Subjective opinions on whether each listed cost is justified
The names of external stakeholders linked to each cost
Estimated costs, responsible person, and timeline for each element
Colour codes and formatting preferences for each cost element
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Each CBS element should list its cost, who manages it, and the timing.

n.0: Birthdays are not relevant.
n.1: Objective data is required for budget control.
n.2: Stakeholder names belong in other plans.
n.4: Colour codes may help visually, but aren’t required.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project budget is developed using both a work breakdown structure (WBS) and a cost breakdown structure (CBS). How do these two tools work together?
o: The WBS captures direct costs while the CBS captures indirect
The WBS plays no part in developing the project budget
WBS defines the work; CBS assigns and tracks costs for each work package
The CBS entirely removes the need to build a WBS
The CBS is applied only to procurement-related project costs
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: WBS outlines all tasks; CBS organises the cost side for each element, supporting budget accuracy.

n.0: Both structures may include various cost types.
n.1: Budgeting is a key WBS use.
n.3: Both tools are needed for full budget planning.
n.4: CBS is for all project costs.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: Why is contingency typically included when creating a budget?
o: To fund a reward for the project sponsor
To provide extra funds for team lunches
To make the project appear more costly
To cover identified risks if they occur
To allow suppliers to be paid early
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Contingency is a reserve of time or money for identified (known) risks, controlled and drawn down through governance. Unknowns are covered by a management reserve, held by the sponsor or board.

n.0: Rewarding the sponsor is not a project cost or a risk reserve.
n.1: Team costs should be budgeted directly; contingency is for identified risks.
n.2: Contingency is a justified reserve for risk, not padding to inflate the budget.
n.4: Payment timing is a cash-flow matter, not what contingency is for.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A programme office is encouraging its project managers to adopt a cost breakdown structure when preparing budgets, and one manager asks what practical advantage this offers. Which of the following is a benefit of using a CBS in budget creation?
o: It increases accuracy and makes tracking actual costs easier
It removes every financial risk from the project entirely
It automatically speeds up the budget approval process
It replaces the need for all other budgeting tools
It can be applied only to construction sector projects
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: A CBS supports precise, trackable budgeting and cost control.

n.1: Risks still require other management.
n.2: Approvals may still take time.
n.3: CBS works alongside other tools.
n.4: CBS can be used for any project.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: While creating a budget, a project team identifies several cost categories that overlap between work packages. What should they do?
o: Clarify and separate costs in the CBS to avoid double-counting
Transfer all the overlapping costs into the contingency reserve
Reassign the overlapping costs to individual stakeholders instead
Merge the overlapping costs into one line for simplicity
Leave the overlap unresolved and proceed with the budgeting
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: CBS should be checked for clarity, with each cost assigned once to the appropriate work package.

n.1: Contingency is not for planned costs.
n.2: Stakeholders are not responsible for budget categories.
n.3: Combining costs risks confusion and inaccuracy.
n.4: Double-counting leads to budget errors.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager is classifying the costs in a project budget so they can be forecast accurately over the delivery period. The manager needs to identify a cost that stays the same regardless of how much activity takes place. Which of the following is an example of a fixed cost in a project budget?
o: Utility bills that vary each month
Monthly office rent for the project duration
Cost of materials ordered as needed
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Fixed costs remain constant regardless of project activity, like monthly rent.

n.0: Utility bills may fluctuate.
n.1: Commissions depend on performance.
n.2: Hourly wages are variable costs.
n.4: Materials vary with project needs.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project team is budgeting for software licences, which are paid once regardless of project output. What type of cost is this?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Licences paid once are fixed, not dependent on project activity volume.

n.0: Incremental is not the standard cost category here.
n.1: They may be direct, but the defining feature here is being fixed.
n.2: Variable costs change with activity.
n.3: Indirect costs are less easily attributed to a specific output.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: In a construction project, the cost of concrete used depends on how much is needed for each phase. What is this cost category?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Material costs that change with project activity are variable costs.

n.0: Sunk costs are already incurred.
n.1: Indirect costs are less directly linked to the activity.
n.3: Overhead refers to general business expenses.
n.4: Fixed costs do not vary with project output.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager is reviewing costs on a construction project and wants to identify spend that can be traced directly to the deliverable being produced. Which of the following is an example of a direct cost in project budgeting?
o: Electricity supplied to the company head office building
Wages of the site team working on the deliverable
Annual premiums for the company-wide insurance cover
Depreciation charged on the corporate vehicle fleet overall
Salaries of the central office administration support staff
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Direct costs are clearly linked to a project deliverable or activity.

n.0: HQ utilities are typically indirect.
n.2: Insurance is indirect.
n.3: Depreciation is a general business expense.
n.4: Admin is an indirect cost.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: When building a project budget, a project manager allocates a proportional share of the organisation's company-wide IT support function to the project, as it cannot be tied to any single activity. What type of cost is this best described as?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Indirect costs cannot be traced to a single activity, like shared IT support.

n.0: Indirect can be fixed or variable, but are defined by allocation method.
n.1: Marginal costs are for each additional unit produced.
n.3: Direct costs link clearly to the project’s output.
n.4: Variable is based on activity, not sharing.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager is categorising expenditure and wants to identify a cost that changes in proportion to the amount of work carried out during delivery. Which of the following is most likely to be considered a variable cost in the project?
o: Monthly insurance premiums paid at a set fixed rate
Annual office lease payments fixed by the contract
Printing costs that increase with the number of reports produced
One-off fees paid for the initial project planning
The fixed salary of the permanent project manager
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Variable costs change with the volume of activity, like printing.

n.0: Insurance is usually fixed over time.
n.1: Leases are typically fixed.
n.3: Planning fees are not volume dependent.
n.4: Permanent salaries are often fixed.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A finance manager reviewing a project budget asks the project manager to clearly separate direct costs from indirect costs before the budget is approved. Why is it important to distinguish between direct and indirect costs in project budgeting?
o: To remove the need to maintain a cost breakdown structure
To enable accurate assignment of costs to specific deliverables or activities
To make the project budget appear more detailed and complex
To reduce the amount of ongoing cost tracking required
To automatically inflate the project’s overall contingency allowance
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Accurate allocation supports project control and performance analysis.

n.0: CBS remains a key budgeting tool.
n.2: Complexity is not the goal.
n.3: Tracking is always needed.
n.4: Contingency should be evidence-based.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project engages several external consultants who are each paid an agreed hourly rate for the time they spend working specifically on project deliverables. When preparing the budget, how should the cost of these consultants be categorised?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Hourly consultants’ costs are variable and directly attributable to project activity.

n.0: They are not fixed as they vary with hours worked.
n.1: Overhead is a broad term and less precise here.
n.3: Consultant costs are not purely overhead.
n.4: They are direct, not indirect, as they link to deliverables.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager is separating costs that can be attributed to a specific deliverable from those that support the wider organisation. Which of the following costs is most likely to be classified as an indirect cost in the project budget?
o: Materials purchased for a specific deliverable
A share of company head office electricity bills
Hourly wages of an on-site technician
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Shared office expenses are typically indirect and allocated across projects.

n.0: Hire for project tasks is direct.
n.1: Materials for deliverables are direct.
n.2: Subcontractor payments are direct.
n.4: Wages directly linked to work are direct.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: The project’s total cost increases as more units are produced, but the cost per unit falls. What is this an example of?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Economies of scale mean that per-unit costs decrease as production volume increases.

n.0: Direct costs can behave differently.
n.2: Fixed costs remain unchanged.
n.3: Overhead is shared, but may not fall per unit.
n.4: Sunk costs have already been incurred.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: Which statement about fixed costs is TRUE?
o: They remain unchanged regardless of project activity level
They are only found in construction projects
They always increase as project activity increases
They are not included in budgets
They are the same as variable costs
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Fixed costs do not fluctuate with the level of project output.

n.1: Fixed costs exist in all types of projects.
n.2: Variable costs change with activity.
n.3: Fixed costs must be included.
n.4: They are different to variable costs.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: Why might indirect costs be allocated across multiple projects?
o: To inflate the project’s apparent cost
To ensure no project ever runs a deficit
Because they are always variable costs
To avoid using a cost breakdown structure
Because they cannot be traced to a single project or deliverable
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Indirect costs support multiple projects and need fair allocation.

n.0: The goal is accuracy, not inflation.
n.1: Deficits depend on performance, not cost allocation.
n.2: Indirect costs can be fixed or variable.
n.3: A CBS helps manage costs.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project sponsor asks the project manager to explain how direct and indirect costs differ, so the board understands how the budget has been structured. What is the main difference between direct and indirect costs?
o: Direct costs are simply another name for overhead costs
Indirect costs are never included within any project budget
Direct costs are always variable while indirect costs are fixed
Indirect costs relate solely to project travel expenses
Direct costs can be specifically identified with a project activity, indirect costs cannot
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Direct costs relate clearly to one project activity; indirect costs are shared.

n.0: Overhead is an example of indirect cost.
n.1: Indirect costs must be budgeted.
n.2: Direct can be fixed or variable.
n.3: Travel can be direct or indirect.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager reviewing the latest cost report notices that the project's variable costs have risen sharply this period, while fixed costs are unchanged. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this increase in variable costs?
o: Increase in the quantity of work or deliverables produced
An overestimate of the project’s contingency reserve
A reduction in the number of assigned project staff
A delay in reaching the project’s closure phase
A sudden rise in the fixed monthly office rent
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Variable costs rise when project output increases.

n.1: Contingency overestimation does not increase real costs.
n.2: Staff reduction may lower costs, not increase them.
n.3: Delays may affect costs but not variable cost drivers.
n.4: Rent is a fixed cost.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager is explaining to a new team member how general business expenses such as rent and utilities are treated in the project accounts, as these support all work rather than any one task. Which is the best description of overhead costs in a project?
o: Costs incurred solely during the project’s closure phase
Contingency allowances set aside for identified project risks
Direct costs specifically assigned to each project deliverable
Costs that vary directly with the volume of output
General business expenses not linked to a single project activity
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Overheads are indirect costs, e.g., rent, utilities, that support all activities.

n.0: Overheads are ongoing.
n.1: Contingency is for unknowns, not overheads.
n.2: Direct costs are easily linked to activities.
n.3: Fixed costs do not change with output.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project budget must include both direct and indirect costs. Which of these is a common mistake when including indirect costs?
o: Recording subcontractor labour as a direct project cost
Allocating a fair share of overheads to every active project
Failing to allocate a share of company-wide overheads to the project
Reviewing the indirect cost apportionment at each budget review
Assigning purchased materials directly to the relevant work package
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Indirect costs such as overheads must be fairly allocated to every project.

n.0: Materials are typically direct.
n.1: Subcontractor costs are direct.
n.3: Project duration affects cost, but is not an indirect cost itself.
n.4: Fixed costs must be included.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: To recover a slipping deadline, a project manager authorises the delivery team to work additional hours over the coming weeks. When the next cost report is produced, which cost type would this decision most likely cause to increase?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Overtime is a variable cost, rising with additional work hours.

n.0: Fixed costs remain constant.
n.1: Overtime is typically a direct, variable cost.
n.2: Incremental cost is the cost of producing one extra unit, which may apply here but is not the main classification.
n.3: Sunk costs have already been paid.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project sponsor questions why the project manager records both the unchanging monthly costs and the costs that rise and fall with activity levels throughout the project. Why is it necessary to track both fixed and variable costs in a project?
o: To avoid the project being subject to financial audits
To control total spending and understand cost drivers throughout the project
To remove the need for any further budget reviews
To ensure that only direct project costs are ever tracked
To justify lowering the project’s agreed quality requirements
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Tracking both helps control spending and supports informed decision making.

n.0: Audits are always possible.
n.2: Budget reviews are essential for control.
n.3: All cost types must be tracked.
n.4: Quality should always be maintained.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager is reviewing a list of costs and needs to identify the one item that would normally be treated as an indirect or overhead cost rather than being charged directly to the deliverables. Which of the following is NOT typically considered a direct project cost?
o: Consultant fees for specific project tasks
Wages for labour hired to build a product
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: General management salaries are indirect or overhead costs.

n.0: Equipment hire is direct if used only on this project.
n.1: Consultants assigned to specific tasks are direct.
n.2: Project-specific labour is direct.
n.4: Raw materials are direct costs.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager prepares a budget that captures labour, materials and equipment but overlooks the share of shared organisational overheads that the project should carry. If the budget omits these indirect costs, what is a likely consequence?
o: The total cost will be underestimated, risking budget overruns
The project’s contingency will always be sufficient
The project will finish under budget
No impact, as indirect costs are always covered elsewhere
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Missing indirect costs means the budget is incomplete and overruns are more likely.

n.1: Contingency is for uncertainty, not omissions.
n.2: Direct and indirect costs are separate.
n.3: Finishing under budget is unlikely if costs are missed.
n.4: Indirect costs must be covered in each project.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager notices the actual cost is significantly higher than the earned value. What does this indicate about project performance?
o: The actual cost is lower than planned
The project is ahead of schedule
The budget has not been set
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: If actual cost exceeds earned value, it means the project has spent more than the value of work performed—it's over budget.

n.0: The actual cost is higher, not lower, than planned.
n.1: Ahead of schedule relates to schedule performance, not cost.
n.2: Scope change can affect costs, but this scenario specifically highlights over-budget status.
n.4: Budgets are already set in earned value analysis.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: Midway through delivery, a project manager needs a technique that compares actual progress and spend against the plan and also supports forecasting how the project is likely to finish. Which cost control technique is used to compare actual project performance against planned performance and forecast future trends?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Earned value analysis allows comparison of actual vs. planned performance and enables forecasting.

n.0: WBS is a planning tool, not a cost control technique.
n.1: Resource levelling manages resources, not budgets.
n.2: Monte Carlo simulation analyses risk, not direct cost control.
n.4: Risk assessment deals with uncertainties, not cost performance.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: At a monthly review, a project manager reports that the project's cost performance index (CPI) has been calculated as 0.8. What does this value suggest about the project's financial position?
o: The cost baseline was not set
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: A CPI less than 1 means costs are higher than earned value, indicating the project is over budget.

n.0: CPI above 1 would indicate under budget.
n.1: Cost baseline is a separate project management element.
n.2: A CPI of 1 would indicate on budget.
n.4: Budget approval is not related to CPI.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: In a review meeting, your sponsor asks for a forecast of the project’s final cost. Which metric would you use?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Estimate at completion (EAC) forecasts the total expected project cost at completion.

n.0: Stakeholder register is unrelated to budget forecasting.
n.2: Risk exposure is not a financial forecast.
n.3: Schedule variance measures time performance, not cost.
n.4: Planned value shows scheduled work, not final cost.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: During a progress review, a project manager calculates that the schedule performance index (SPI) for the current reporting period is less than 1. What does this indicate about the project?
o: The project is ahead of schedule
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: An SPI below 1 means less work has been completed than planned at this point—behind schedule.

n.0: SPI above 1 would indicate ahead of schedule.
n.1: SPI is about schedule, not cost.
n.2: Underspend relates to cost, not schedule.
n.3: Scope clarity is not measured by SPI.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: At the end of a reporting period, a project has recorded an earned value of £100,000 for the work completed, while the actual cost incurred to date is £120,000. Based on these figures, what is the cost variance for the project?

n.0: A positive £20,000 would indicate EV is greater than AC.
n.1: Zero means no variance, which is not the case here.
n.3: £120,000 is the actual cost, not the variance.
n.4: £100,000 is the earned value, not the variance.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager reviewing the latest figures notes that the actual costs recorded to date are lower than the planned value for the same point in the schedule. On the basis of this comparison alone, the project is considered to be:
o: Under budget, as less has been spent than planned
Over budget, as spending is lagging the plan
Ahead of schedule, as costs are below plan
Behind schedule, as spending is below plan
Not determinable without knowing earned value
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Cost performance compares earned value with actual cost (CV = EV - AC), and schedule performance compares EV with PV. AC against PV alone mixes the two: spending may be low simply because less work has been done, so neither cost nor schedule status can be concluded.

n.0: Low spend may just reflect less work done; without EV you cannot tell whether that work cost more or less than budgeted.
n.1: Spending less than planned does not show overspending; EV is needed.
n.2: Schedule status needs EV compared with PV, not AC.
n.3: Low spend hints at slow progress but does not prove it; schedule variance is EV - PV.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: After a risk event materialises and pushes up costs, the client asks the project manager for an updated view of the likely final project cost. Which action should the project manager take in response?
o: Ignore the change until project closure
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: After a risk event, the estimate at completion should be updated to reflect the revised forecast.

n.0: Ignoring the change leads to inaccurate forecasts.
n.1: Scope changes require formal approval.
n.2: Removing contingency reduces risk coverage, not forecast accuracy.
n.4: Continuing with the old forecast ignores the updated situation.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: At a review meeting, a project manager confirms that the project's earned value for the period is exactly equal to its planned value. What does this equality mean about the project's progress?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Earned value equals planned value means actual work completed matches the plan.

n.0: Cost overrun relates to AC vs. EV.
n.2: Slippage would mean EV < PV.
n.3: Quality issues are not assessed here.
n.4: This says nothing about budget, only schedule.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: After a scope reduction, the sponsor wants the project budget re-estimated by costing each remaining work package in the updated WBS and adding the results together. Which estimating technique is this?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: Costing each work package from the WBS and adding them up is bottom-up (analytical) estimating, the most accurate method once the scope is well defined.

n.1: The Delphi technique builds consensus among anonymous experts over several rounds; it does not cost the WBS line by line.
n.2: Analogous estimating bases the figure on a similar past project, not on costing each work package.
n.3: Parametric estimating multiplies a unit rate from historical data by a quantity rather than summing work packages.
n.4: Critical path analysis finds the longest path through the schedule; it is not a cost estimating technique.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project manager preparing a status report calculates the cost variance for the current period as £5,000, a positive figure. What does this positive cost variance indicate about the project?
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: A positive cost variance means the project has spent less than the value of work performed—under budget.

n.0: Scope change is not directly shown by cost variance.
n.1: Pending change requests don't affect cost variance until approved.
n.2: Cost variance relates to budget, not schedule.
n.3: Over budget would result in a negative cost variance.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: Following several change requests, a project manager recalculates the estimate at completion (EAC) and finds it is now higher than the original budget at completion (BAC). What does this comparison suggest about the project?
o: The project is ahead of schedule
Forecasted costs exceed the original budget
Less work is required than planned
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: EAC higher than BAC means the project is now expected to cost more than originally budgeted.

n.0: Schedule is not indicated by EAC vs BAC.
n.2: Quality criteria are unrelated to these budget terms.
n.3: EAC > BAC means overspend, not underspend.
n.4: Scope or work content is not shown by these metrics.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: The monthly report shows an earned value (EV) of £60,000, an actual cost (AC) of £65,000, and a planned value (PV) of £70,000. Which statement is correct?
o: The project is ahead of schedule and under budget
The project is behind schedule but under budget
The project is behind schedule and over budget
The project is on schedule and on budget
The project is over budget but ahead of schedule
Budgeting & Cost Control.w: EV < PV = behind schedule; EV < AC = over budget.

n.0: Both schedule and cost performance are worse than planned.
n.1: Under budget would require EV > AC.
n.3: The project is behind schedule but not under budget.
n.4: EV < PV, so not ahead of schedule.

Budgeting & Cost Control.q: A project sponsor is being briefed on the various ways earned value management can support a project during delivery. From the following list, which is NOT a valid use of earned value management (EVM)?

n.3: Planning is always required.
n.4: Feedback is still valuable.

Quality.q: A project manager reviews quality control data gathered over several reporting periods and notices certain defects appearing again and again. How can trend analysis in quality control help the project team?
o: By allowing agreed requirements to be quietly revised downward
By confirming that no further project changes will be required
By highlighting recurring issues so corrective action can be taken
By replacing the need for ongoing quality measurement activity
By lowering the priority the team gives to customer feedback
Quality.w: Trend analysis enables teams to spot and address patterns before they escalate.

n.0: Requirements should not be ignored.
n.1: Changes may still be needed.
n.3: Measurement is still required.
n.4: Feedback should always be considered.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team identifies a potential supplier delay but takes no further action. At which stage of the risk process has the team stopped?
Risk & Issue Management.w: The team has identified the risk but has not progressed to analysis or response.

n.1: Closure occurs after resolution.
n.2: Monitoring follows response planning.
n.3: No response has been defined.
n.4: No analysis has been carried out.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk has been identified and assessed as high probability but low impact. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Convert the risk into an issue
Define and implement an appropriate response strategy
Risk & Issue Management.w: All assessed risks require an appropriate response proportional to their impact and likelihood.

n.0: Assessment does not justify closure.
n.1: A risk is not yet an issue.
n.2: Ignoring risks increases exposure.
n.3: Escalation may not be necessary.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager realises that multiple risks have been identified but not analysed. What is the primary consequence of this gap?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Without analysis, risks cannot be prioritised or managed effectively.

n.1: Documentation is not the core concern.
n.2: Flexibility is not improved.
n.3: Engagement is secondary.
n.4: Communication is not the main issue.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk response has been implemented, but nobody is tracking whether it is working or whether the risk is changing. Which stage of the risk process is being neglected?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Monitoring runs throughout the project: it tracks risks, their triggers and the effectiveness of the responses put in place.

n.0: The risk has already been identified.
n.1: Closure happens once a risk has passed or occurred, not while it is still live.
n.3: The risk has already been analysed.
n.4: A response has already been chosen and implemented.

Risk & Issue Management.q: At a review meeting, a project team agrees a response to a newly identified risk and immediately marks that risk as closed in the register. The project manager challenges this decision. Why is closing the risk at this point problematic?
o: The response has not been implemented or validated
The project timeline has not been updated
The stakeholders have not been informed
The risk owner has not been assigned
The risk has not been analysed properly
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks should only be closed once they are no longer relevant or have been fully resolved.

n.1: Timeline updates are secondary.
n.2: Communication is not the main issue.
n.3: Ownership is separate.
n.4: Analysis may already have occurred.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is running a risk identification workshop for a new project and wants the team to generate a meaningful and relevant set of risks. Which scenario best demonstrates effective risk identification?
o: Concentrating only on the highest-impact risks currently known
Allocating risk owners informally without documenting the risks
Identifying risks based on previous project experience and current context
Excluding low-probability risks to keep the register manageable
Recording every conceivable risk without filtering or prioritisation
Risk & Issue Management.w: Effective identification considers both historical data and project-specific factors.

n.0: All risks should be considered initially.
n.1: Documentation is essential.
n.3: Low-probability risks may still matter.
n.4: Unfiltered lists reduce clarity.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During risk assessment, a genuine threat to a key milestone is recorded but wrongly judged to be low impact, so it receives little attention. If this assessment error goes unnoticed, what is the most likely outcome?
o: The risk may be under-prioritised and inadequately managed
The project will avoid all consequences
The risk will convert into an issue immediately
The risk will be closed early
Risk & Issue Management.w: Incorrect analysis leads to poor prioritisation and ineffective response.

n.1: Consequences are likely.
n.2: Escalation is not automatic.
n.3: Conversion depends on occurrence.
n.4: Closure is not guaranteed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team has identified and analysed a significant risk to delivery and now needs to decide how it will be handled, for example by avoiding, reducing or transferring it. Which stage of the risk management process determines the appropriate response strategy?
Risk & Issue Management.w: The response stage decides and plans how each risk will be handled (for a threat: avoid, reduce, transfer or accept) and assigns an owner to carry it out.

n.0: Identification finds and records risks; it does not decide how to handle them.
n.1: Closure removes risks that have passed or occurred and captures lessons.
n.2: Analysis assesses probability and impact to prioritise risks; it informs, but does not choose, the response.
n.3: Monitoring tracks risks and how well responses are working.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk that once threatened a project's schedule has been mitigated successfully and no longer poses any credible threat to the objectives. As the project manager updates the risk register, what is the correct next step for this risk?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks should be formally closed when no longer relevant.

n.0: Formal closure is required.
n.1: Escalation is not needed.
n.3: Transfer is not applicable.
n.4: Reanalysis is unnecessary.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which TWO activities are part of risk analysis?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Analysis evaluates likelihood and impact.

n.0: Ownership is separate.
n.1: Lessons learned occur post-project.
n.2: Closure is later.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which TWO outcomes result from effective risk monitoring?
o: Early identification of changes in risk status
Risk & Issue Management.w: Monitoring ensures risks are controlled and responses remain valid.

n.2: Planning is still required.
n.3: Success is not guaranteed.
n.4: Risks cannot be eliminated.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A supplier failure has already delayed a key deliverable, and the delay is forecast to breach the schedule tolerance delegated to the project manager. How should this situation be classified and managed?
o: As an issue, logged and escalated to the sponsor
As a risk, to be analysed and given a response
As a dependency, to be monitored on the schedule
As an assumption, to be validated with the supplier
As a constraint, to be recorded in the plan
Risk & Issue Management.w: The problem has happened and is forecast to breach delegated tolerance, so it is an issue: the project manager logs and assesses it and escalates it to the sponsor to agree a resolution. A problem that stays within tolerance would be handled by the project manager day to day.

n.1: A risk is an uncertain future event; this delay has already happened.
n.2: The supplier link may be a dependency, but the delay itself is a realised problem beyond tolerance.
n.3: Assumptions are things taken as true for planning; this is a realised failure.
n.4: Constraints are known limits set at the outset, not problems that arise during delivery.

Risk & Issue Management.q: An issue is raised in the log during delivery, but competing priorities mean no owner is assigned and no action is taken for several weeks. As the project manager reviews the log, what is the most likely consequence of this inaction?
o: The issue will reduce stakeholder expectations
The issue will automatically convert into a risk
The issue will resolve itself without intervention
The issue may escalate and increase impact on the project
The issue will be closed during reporting cycles
Risk & Issue Management.w: Delays in addressing issues typically increase their severity and impact.

n.0: Expectations may worsen.
n.1: Issues do not convert into risks.
n.2: Issues rarely resolve without action.
n.4: Closure requires resolution.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Midway through delivery, a team member reports a technical failure that is already affecting a key deliverable. What should the project manager do first?
o: Leave it until the next reporting cycle is due
Escalate it to the sponsor before any assessment is made
Assess its impact against the delegated tolerances
Log it and wait for the next scheduled review
Re-record the problem as a risk in the register
Risk & Issue Management.w: The project manager first logs the problem and assesses its impact. If it can be resolved within delegated tolerances it is managed day to day; if it breaches, or is about to breach, tolerance it is an issue and is escalated to the sponsor.

n.0: Leaving a live failure unassessed risks a larger breach later.
n.1: Whether to escalate depends on tolerances, which is only known after assessing the impact.
n.3: Waiting lets the impact grow; the problem needs assessing now.
n.4: It has already happened, so it is not an uncertain risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is dealing with an issue whose resolution would require decisions and funding that sit well beyond their delegated authority. Recognising this limit, what is the most appropriate next step?
o: Escalate the issue to the appropriate governance level
Delay action until more information is available
Assign it to another team member
Convert it into a risk for future tracking
Risk & Issue Management.w: Escalation ensures issues beyond authority are addressed at the correct level.

n.1: Delaying worsens impact.
n.2: Closure requires resolution.
n.3: Authority is still required.
n.4: Issues are not future risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager maintaining an issue log must decide which entries to raise to a higher level and which to resolve within the team. When making these judgements, which factor most strongly determines whether an issue should be escalated?
o: The project's documentation and audit standards
The overall size of the team
Risk & Issue Management.w: Escalation is based on impact and whether it exceeds authority.

n.0: Reporting cycles are secondary.
n.1: Documentation does not drive escalation.
n.2: Stakeholder count is not decisive.
n.4: Team size is irrelevant.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager chooses to delay addressing a known issue to avoid stakeholder concern. What is the most likely outcome?
o: Faster resolution once more information becomes available
Improved team performance through fewer delivery interruptions
A temporary reduction in overall project risk exposure
Improved stakeholder confidence through reduced early disruption
Increased impact and reduced control over the issue
Risk & Issue Management.w: Delaying action increases the likelihood and severity of negative outcomes.

n.0: Resolution is delayed.
n.1: Performance may decline.
n.2: Risk increases.
n.3: Trust may decrease.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A problem has occurred on a project and is forecast to breach the cost tolerance delegated to the project manager. Which action best demonstrates effective issue management?
o: Waiting to see whether the problem resolves itself
Closing it in the log before it has been resolved
Log and assess it, then escalate it to the sponsor
Escalating every day-to-day problem to the sponsor
Ignoring it because the overspend looks fairly small
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue is a problem that has occurred and is breaching, or about to breach, delegated tolerances. The project manager logs it, assesses its impact and escalates it to the sponsor to agree a resolution. Anticipating problems before they happen is risk management, not issue management.

n.0: Delay lets the impact grow and leaves the sponsor unaware of a tolerance breach.
n.1: Issues are tracked to closure once the agreed resolution has been carried out.
n.3: Problems within tolerance are handled day to day by the project manager; only those beyond tolerance are escalated.
n.4: A forecast breach of tolerance is outside the project manager's authority to absorb.

Risk & Issue Management.q: While reviewing the issue log for a long-running project, a project manager notices several very similar issues have been raised and resolved individually over recent weeks. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this pattern?
o: The recurring issues are routine and can be ignored
Each issue should simply be closed as quickly as possible
The issues are coincidental and should be handled individually
There may be an underlying root cause not being addressed
The project is performing efficiently despite the recurrences
Risk & Issue Management.w: Recurring issues indicate systemic problems requiring root cause analysis.

n.0: Ignoring worsens the problem.
n.1: Closure without resolution is ineffective.
n.2: Patterns suggest linkage.
n.4: Performance is likely poor.

Risk & Issue Management.q: When should an issue be formally closed?
o: When the issue is fully resolved and no longer impacts the project
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure requires resolution and no remaining impact.

n.0: Escalation is not closure.
n.2: Communication alone is insufficient.
n.3: Too early.
n.4: Planning is not resolution.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which TWO actions are part of effective issue handling?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Effective handling requires assessment and action.

n.1: Ignoring risks escalation.
n.2: Delay increases impact.
n.3: Closure requires resolution.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which TWO conditions justify issue escalation?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Escalation is needed when impact is high or authority exceeded.

n.0: Documentation is not the trigger.
n.2: Resolved issues are closed.
n.3: Minor issues do not require escalation.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project identifies that adopting a new automation tool could reduce delivery time but may introduce integration risks. How should this be classified?
o: Both a threat and an opportunity
A fixed constraint on the project
An opportunity for project objectives only
A threat to project objectives only
Neither a risk nor an issue
Risk & Issue Management.w: Some risks have both positive and negative potential outcomes depending on how they are managed.

n.1: It is not a fixed limitation.
n.2: There is also potential downside.
n.3: There is also potential benefit.
n.4: It is clearly a risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is coaching a new team member on risk terminology and explains that risk covers more than just possible problems. To clarify the concept, which statement best distinguishes a threat from an opportunity in risk management?
o: A threat arises earlier in delivery than an opportunity
A threat creates uncertainty, whereas an opportunity removes it
A threat is internal, whereas an opportunity is external
A threat always carries greater impact than an opportunity
A threat negatively impacts objectives, whereas an opportunity positively impacts them
Risk & Issue Management.w: Threats have negative effects, while opportunities have positive effects on objectives.

n.0: Timing does not define type.
n.1: Both introduce uncertainty.
n.2: Both can be internal or external.
n.3: Impact varies.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During risk identification, a project manager concentrates only on things that could go wrong and pays no attention to uncertain events that could benefit the project. What is the most likely consequence of overlooking opportunities in this way?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Ignoring opportunities means potential gains are not realised.

n.0: Opportunities are not risks.
n.1: Documentation is unrelated.
n.2: Confidence may decrease.
n.4: Delivery is not improved.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which situation is most clearly an opportunity risk?
o: A supplier may fail to deliver on time
A team member might leave unexpectedly
A new technology could accelerate project delivery if successfully implemented
Risk & Issue Management.w: Opportunities represent positive potential outcomes.

n.0: This is a threat.
n.1: This is a threat.
n.2: This is a threat.
n.3: This is a constraint/threat.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project sponsor questions why the risk register includes potential upside events as well as threats to the project. The project manager explains the rationale. Why is it important to treat opportunities as part of the risk process?
o: To simplify the project's risk documentation requirements
To reduce the stakeholder involvement required in delivery
To eliminate every threat to the project entirely
To add extra detail and complexity to risk planning
To ensure both positive and negative uncertainties are managed
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk management includes both threats and opportunities.

n.0: Documentation is not the focus.
n.1: Stakeholders remain important.
n.2: Threats cannot be eliminated.
n.3: Complexity is not the goal.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team identifies a chance to adopt an innovative method that could deliver benefits, but decides not to pursue it because of the uncertainty involved. In choosing to forgo the opportunity, what is the key trade-off being made?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Choosing not to pursue an opportunity sacrifices potential benefits to reduce risk.

n.0: Not relevant.
n.1: Not applicable.
n.3: Not the main trade-off.
n.4: Irrelevant.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best represents a threat risk?
o: A new tool that increases efficiency
A chance to reduce project duration
A potential cost saving from supplier negotiation
A possible delay due to regulatory approval
Risk & Issue Management.w: Threats represent negative impacts such as delays.

n.0: This is an opportunity.
n.1: This is an opportunity.
n.2: This is an opportunity.
n.3: This is an opportunity.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project identifies a risk that could either increase costs or reduce them depending on supplier performance. How should this risk be treated?
o: As both a threat and an opportunity
As a fixed constraint on the budget
As an opportunity for the budget only
As a threat to the budget only
Risk & Issue Management.w: Some risks have dual outcomes depending on how they unfold.

n.0: It has not occurred.
n.2: This is not fixed.
n.3: There is also potential loss.
n.4: There is also potential benefit.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager structures the risk analysis so that the team examines only the negative uncertainties facing the project. Considering how this narrows the process, what is the main risk of focusing only on threats during risk analysis?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Ignoring opportunities limits potential value creation.

n.0: Irrelevant.
n.2: Not the main risk.
n.3: Performance may suffer.
n.4: Not the core issue.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which approach best reflects balanced risk management?
o: Managing both threats and opportunities systematically
Risk & Issue Management.w: Balanced management considers both positive and negative uncertainties.

n.1: All risks should be assessed.
n.2: Incomplete approach.
n.3: Incomplete approach.
n.4: Closure requires resolution.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which TWO characteristics define opportunity risks?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Opportunities are uncertain events with positive impacts.

n.0: Risks are uncertain.
n.2: Risks are not certain.
n.4: This describes threats.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which TWO characteristics define threat risks?
o: Potential to cause delays or cost increases
Risk & Issue Management.w: Threats negatively impact project objectives.

n.1: Opportunity.
n.3: Opportunity.
n.4: Not applicable.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project risk has been assigned to a senior engineer who is responsible for monitoring its overall status but not implementing specific actions. What role is the engineer fulfilling?
Risk & Issue Management.w: The risk owner is accountable for the overall management and monitoring of the risk.

n.0: Action owners implement responses, not oversee the risk.
n.1: Functional managers are not necessarily risk owners.
n.2: Sponsor has governance responsibility.
n.3: Issue manager deals with realised problems.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk response has been agreed that requires a specific mitigation plan to be put into effect. As roles are allocated, the project manager needs to be clear who will actually carry out the mitigation activities. Who is most responsible for carrying out this action?
Risk & Issue Management.w: The risk action owner is responsible for executing the agreed response actions.

n.0: Risk owner oversees but does not necessarily execute.
n.1: The PM coordinates but does not always execute.
n.3: Stakeholders are not directly responsible.
n.4: Board provides governance.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team assigns the same person as both risk owner and action owner for all risks. What is the main concern with this approach?
o: It guarantees faster resolution of every identified risk
It oversimplifies risk reporting to the point of uselessness
It removes the need for any ongoing monitoring
It may reduce accountability clarity and effectiveness of control
It substantially increases the documentation effort per risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: Separating roles improves clarity, oversight, and effectiveness.

n.0: No guarantee of speed.
n.1: Oversimplification can be risky.
n.2: Monitoring is still required.
n.4: Documentation is not the main issue.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the primary responsibility of a risk owner?
o: Ensuring the risk is monitored and managed appropriately
Risk & Issue Management.w: The risk owner is accountable for overall management and control of the risk.

n.1: Implementation is for action owners.
n.2: Closure requires validation.
n.3: Not all risks require escalation.
n.4: Budgeting is unrelated.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is explaining the different responsibilities within the risk process to the team, using practical examples. Which situation best illustrates the role of a risk action owner?
o: Implementing a mitigation plan for a specific risk
Reporting overall project progress to stakeholders
Approving governance decisions across the whole project
Monitoring the overall risk status over time
Documenting and maintaining the full risk register
Risk & Issue Management.w: Action owners are responsible for executing specific response actions.

n.1: Reporting is not specific to action owners.
n.2: Governance is not their role.
n.3: Monitoring is the risk owner’s responsibility.
n.4: Documentation is broader.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk owner accepts responsibility for several risks but never nominates anyone to carry out the agreed response activities. As delivery continues, what is the most likely outcome of this omission?
o: Increased stakeholder confidence in risk handling
Improved accountability across the whole risk process
Faster resolution of the identified risks
A reduced need for ongoing risk monitoring
Lack of clear responsibility for implementing responses
Risk & Issue Management.w: Without action owners, responses may not be executed effectively.

n.0: Confidence may drop.
n.1: Accountability decreases.
n.2: Resolution may be delayed.
n.3: Monitoring is still required.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is deciding who to appoint as the owner of a significant risk that will need active management throughout delivery. When making this appointment, which factor most strongly determines who should be assigned as a risk owner?
o: Level of authority and ability to manage the risk
The current availability and workload of the individual
The stated preference of key project stakeholders
The project's documentation and record-keeping standards
The seniority of the individual within the organisation
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk owners need authority and capability to manage risks effectively.

n.1: Availability is not sufficient.
n.2: Preference is not objective.
n.3: Documentation is irrelevant.
n.4: Seniority alone is insufficient.

Risk & Issue Management.q: When setting up the risk management approach, a project manager separates the person accountable for overseeing each risk from those tasked with carrying out specific responses. Why is it important to distinguish between the risk owner and the risk action owner?
o: To increase the volume of risk reporting required
To simplify project communication by removing roles
To reduce the overall cost of the project
To remove the need for ongoing risk monitoring
To ensure clear accountability for both oversight and execution
Risk & Issue Management.w: Clear distinction ensures effective management and execution.

n.0: Reporting is secondary.
n.1: Communication still requires structure.
n.2: Cost is not the main reason.
n.3: Monitoring remains essential.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk action owner reports that all the mitigation activities assigned to them for a particular risk have now been completed. Following good risk management practice, what should happen next?
o: The risk owner should review and confirm whether the risk can be closed
The risk should be closed immediately with no further review needed
The risk should be reassigned directly to a different action owner
The risk should be escalated straight to the project sponsor for action
The completed outcome should be recorded but otherwise left unactioned
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure requires confirmation that the risk is no longer relevant.

n.1: Closure requires validation.
n.2: Reassignment is unnecessary.
n.3: Escalation may not be needed.
n.4: Outcome must be reviewed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which TWO responsibilities belong to a risk owner?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk owners oversee management and ensure responses are appropriate.

n.0: Closure requires validation.
n.2: All risks should be considered.
n.3: Execution is for action owners.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which TWO responsibilities belong to a risk action owner?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Action owners execute and report on risk responses.

n.0: Assignment is not their role.
n.1: Budget approval is governance.
n.4: Closure requires oversight.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project sponsor questions why the project manager is investing effort in identifying and managing uncertainty on a new product launch. What is a primary benefit of effective risk management in projects?
o: It reduces the need for stakeholder engagement
It increases the likelihood of project success
It shortens the project duration automatically
It guarantees zero issues will occur
Risk & Issue Management.w: Effective risk management makes project success more likely by anticipating and managing uncertainties.

n.0: Stakeholder engagement is always important, regardless of risk management.
n.1: Risks can be reduced or managed, not eliminated entirely.
n.3: Risk management does not directly shorten duration.
n.4: Issues may still arise, even with good risk management.

Risk & Issue Management.q: When building the budget for a project with significant uncertainty, the project manager deliberately sets aside a sum of money to be drawn on only if identified risks actually occur. What is this budget called?
Risk & Issue Management.w: A contingency fund is used to cover unexpected risks that arise during a project.

n.0: Quality reserves are related to quality assurance, not risk.
n.1: Stakeholder funds are not standard in risk management.
n.2: Profit margin is not a risk management tool.
n.4: Stage gates control progress, not contingency.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager wants a single controlled document in which to capture all identified threats and opportunities for a project, together with the planned responses to each. Which document records this?
Risk & Issue Management.w: The risk register captures details of all project risks and their management responses.

n.0: The issue log records active issues, not risks.
n.1: Change control forms track changes, not risks.
n.2: The business case justifies the project, not risks.
n.3: The project brief outlines the project, not risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During start up of a project exposed to volatile external conditions, the project manager develops plans for how the team will act if certain identified risks occur. What is the main purpose of contingency planning in projects?
o: To build additional profit margin into the project budget
To limit the need for stakeholder risk communication
To serve as a substitute for detailed project planning
To ensure the project can respond effectively to unforeseen events
To remove every identified threat before the project begins
Risk & Issue Management.w: Contingency planning prepares the team for unexpected events, improving resilience.

n.0: Contingency is for control, not for increasing costs.
n.1: Stakeholder communication is always needed.
n.2: Project planning and contingency planning work together.
n.4: Elimination of all risk is impossible.

Risk & Issue Management.q: The risk register for an outdoor construction project identifies a potential schedule delay caused by adverse weather during a critical phase. Which action by the project manager best demonstrates good risk management?
o: Adding extra team members without adjusting the schedule
Developing a plan to accelerate work if bad weather occurs
Cancelling progress reviews to protect the contingency time
Removing the weather risk from the project register entirely
Waiting to react only once the weather actually deteriorates
Risk & Issue Management.w: Planning in advance what to do if the risk occurs (a fallback or contingency plan) is good risk management.

n.0: Adding people without a plan increases cost without managing the risk.
n.2: Reviews are needed to monitor risks; cancelling them weakens control.
n.3: The risk still exists and must stay on the register until it passes.
n.4: Waiting until the risk happens is unplanned and reactive.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is deciding whether problems that have already occurred should be captured in a different log from potential future threats. Which of the following is a benefit of recording issues separately from risks?
o: It removes the need for issue management
It hides problems from the team
It allows more effective tracking and resolution
It makes the risk register redundant
Risk & Issue Management.w: Separating issues from risks ensures appropriate attention and tailored actions.

n.0: Issue management is still required.
n.1: Transparency is improved by clear records.
n.3: The risk register remains an essential tool.
n.4: Good documentation supports clarity, not bureaucracy.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A newly appointed project manager is being coached on how project management distinguishes between the terms 'risk' and 'issue' when managing uncertainty. What is the difference between a risk and an issue?
o: Risks affect only cost, whereas issues affect only the schedule
The two terms describe exactly the same thing in practice
An issue is a future opportunity; a risk is an active problem
Issues are future threats; risks are current problems being managed
A risk is a potential event; an issue has already occurred
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks are potential events, while issues are current problems that must be managed.

n.0: Risks can be schedule or quality related as well.
n.1: There is a clear distinction between risks and issues.
n.2: Opportunities are a type of risk, not issue.
n.3: Issues are current, risks are potential.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A threat previously recorded in the risk register has now actually happened and is affecting the project. As project manager following good practice, what is your next step?
o: Release the contingency budget back to the wider organisation
Expand the project scope to offset the resulting impact
Move the item from the risk register to the issue log
Treat the event as resolved and take no further action
Delete every planned risk response from the project plan
Risk & Issue Management.w: Once a risk occurs, it is tracked and managed as an issue going forward.

n.0: Contingency may still be needed to resolve the issue.
n.1: Scope changes are not standard for issue management.
n.3: Issues require management, not ignorance.
n.4: Risk responses may still be needed for other risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A sponsor asks a project manager to justify the time spent preparing responses for events that may never happen on a project operating in an uncertain environment. What is the main benefit of contingency planning in risk management?
o: It allows rapid response to unexpected events
It removes the need for insurance
It ensures no issues ever arise
Risk & Issue Management.w: Contingency planning enables the project to adapt quickly when risks occur.

n.1: Insurance may still be required in some cases.
n.2: Issues can arise even with planning.
n.3: Uncertainty is always present in projects.
n.4: Budgets should remain realistic.

Risk & Issue Management.q: The project manager identifies a major risk with a high impact. What should be included in the risk response plan?
o: Assigning the risk to the project team without a plan
A specific contingency action or reserve
Ignoring the risk until it happens
Risk & Issue Management.w: High-impact risks need defined responses, such as contingency actions or reserves.

n.0: Reducing documentation can undermine risk management.
n.1: Closure is only for extreme circumstances.
n.2: Ownership alone is not enough without a plan.
n.4: Risks must be managed proactively.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A group of stakeholders is nervous about the level of uncertainty surrounding a complex project. How does effective risk management benefit stakeholder confidence?
o: It removes the need for communication
It shortens the approval process automatically
It demonstrates proactive control over uncertainty

Risk & Issue Management.q: Whether a project is delivered through a linear or an iterative life cycle, its manager applies structured risk and issue management throughout. Regardless of the life cycle chosen, what is the ultimate goal of these risk and issue management processes?
o: To satisfy audit requirements without affecting the eventual project outcome
To support successful project delivery by controlling uncertainty and resolving problems
To generate a comprehensive risk record for the organisation's insurers
To transfer accountability for outcomes from the manager to the sponsor
To remove all uncertainty so that no risks can ever materialise
Risk & Issue Management.w: Managing risks and issues increases the chance of delivering projects on time, on budget, and to scope.

n.0: Good management supports timely completion.
n.2: Project managers are still essential.
n.3: Documentation supports control, not bureaucracy.
n.4: Stakeholder engagement remains important.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During response planning, a project manager decides to change the project plan so that a particular threat can no longer arise at all. Which risk response strategy is being used to completely remove the threat from the project in this way?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Avoiding a risk removes the threat by changing plans or processes.

n.0: Enhancing relates to opportunities, not threats.
n.2: Rejecting is not a formal risk response.
n.3: Sharing is for opportunities, not threats.
n.4: Accepting means tolerating the risk, not removing it.

Risk & Issue Management.q: To protect the project against the possibility of expensive equipment being stolen from site, a project team takes out an insurance policy that would cover the financial loss. Which risk response does purchasing this insurance represent?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Transferring a risk means shifting its impact to a third party, such as an insurer.

n.0: Enhancing is for increasing opportunities, not threats.
n.1: Exploiting is for opportunities, not threats.
n.2: Acceptance means no proactive action is taken.
n.3: Reduction means lessening probability or impact, not shifting risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What does it mean to 'accept' a risk?
o: To assign the risk to another party
To change the plan so the threat is completely eliminated
To exploit the risk for benefit
To enhance the probability of occurrence
To acknowledge and tolerate it without proactive action
Risk & Issue Management.w: Accepting a threat means consciously tolerating it and monitoring it, with no proactive action (often with a fallback plan if it occurs).

n.0: Passing it to another party is transfer.
n.1: Removing the risk entirely is avoidance.
n.2: Exploit is an opportunity response.
n.3: Enhance is an opportunity response.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager increases testing and reviews to lower the chance of a software defect. What is this approach called?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Reduction means taking action to decrease the probability or impact of a risk.

n.0: Reject is not a formal risk response.
n.1: Sharing is not relevant to threats.
n.2: Acceptance involves no action.
n.4: Transfer would shift risk to another party.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager identifies a positive risk that could bring significant benefit to the project and wants to take deliberate action to make certain that it actually happens. Which response is best suited to an opportunity the manager wants to ensure is realised?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Exploiting means ensuring an opportunity occurs and maximising the benefit.

n.1: Transfer is used for threats.
n.2: Reduce is a threat response.
n.3: Avoid is used for threats.
n.4: Reject is not a standard response.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team joins forces with another organisation to deliver an innovation that neither party could have achieved on its own, allocating the opportunity to the partner best placed to realise it. Which risk response does this arrangement represent?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Sharing means allocating opportunity to a partner best able to realise it.

n.0: Acceptance means no active attempt to realise the opportunity.
n.1: Avoid is for threats, not opportunities.
n.2: Reject is not a formal positive risk response.
n.4: Reduction is for threats.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is a proactive risk response?
o: Waiting until the risk has materialised
Taking action before the risk occurs to prevent or reduce its impact
Documenting the risk without further action
Risk & Issue Management.w: Proactive responses are preventative, aiming to avoid or reduce risks before they happen.

n.0: Ignoring risks is poor management.
n.1: Reactive responses happen after the risk materialises.
n.3: Delays can worsen the outcome.
n.4: Documentation alone does not manage risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is a reactive risk response?
o: Taking action in advance of the risk
Transferring risk before the project starts
Enhancing opportunities in the planning stage
Responding after the risk event has occurred
Risk & Issue Management.w: Reactive responses are taken once a risk has materialised.

n.0: Avoidance is proactive.
n.1: Proactive responses are taken before the event.
n.2: Transfer can be proactive or reactive depending on timing.
n.3: Enhancement is a proactive response for opportunities.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager decides not to pursue a new opportunity as it doesn't align with the project objectives. What response is this?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Rejecting is a valid response for opportunities that do not add value or fit the strategy.

n.1: Enhancing increases probability or impact.
n.2: Acceptance means tolerating without action.
n.3: Exploiting seeks to maximise the benefit.
n.4: Sharing means collaborating to realise an opportunity.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During response planning, a project manager looks for ways to make a favourable event both more likely to occur and more beneficial if it does. Which response strategy is concerned with increasing the likelihood or impact of a positive risk in this way?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Enhancement aims to make opportunities more likely or impactful.

n.0: Reject is not a formal response to enhance opportunities.
n.1: Transfer is about passing risk to another party.
n.3: Avoid is for threats.
n.4: Reduction is for negative risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager negotiates a contract clause under which a specialist supplier accepts responsibility for a specific technical risk and its consequences. What is this risk response called?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Transferring risk assigns responsibility for the impact to another party.

n.1: Sharing is mainly for opportunities.
n.2: Reduction means lowering probability/impact, not assigning responsibility.
n.3: Enhance is used for opportunities.
n.4: Avoidance is about removing the risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team knows a risk is unlikely but chooses to do nothing until it happens. What response is this?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Acceptance is choosing to tolerate a risk, taking no action until it materialises.

n.0: Share is for opportunities.
n.1: Transfer moves risk to another party.
n.2: Avoidance seeks to remove the risk proactively.
n.4: Exploit is for opportunities.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is selecting an appropriate response for a threat identified in the risk register. Considering the standard responses available for threats, which of the following is NOT one of them?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Exploit is a response for positive risks (opportunities), not threats.

n.1: Acceptance is for threats as well as opportunities.
n.2: Reduction manages threats.
n.3: Avoid is a threat response.
n.4: Transfer is for threats.

Risk & Issue Management.q: To manage the risk that newly installed equipment might fail, a project manager purchases a warranty under which the manufacturer would bear the cost of any failure. Which risk response does taking out this warranty represent?
Risk & Issue Management.w: A warranty shifts some or all risk of equipment failure to another party.

n.0: Acceptance is passive, not proactive.
n.2: Avoidance eliminates the risk entirely.
n.3: Enhance is for opportunities, not threats.
n.4: Reduction lowers risk probability/impact, not responsibility.

Risk & Issue Management.q: The team decides to add resources to increase the chance of delivering an early benefit. What risk response is this?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Enhance means taking action to make an opportunity more likely or impactful.

n.0: Transfer is for negative risks.
n.1: Exploit ensures the opportunity will definitely occur.
n.2: Avoid is for negative risks.
n.4: Acceptance involves no proactive steps.

Risk & Issue Management.q: To keep a software development project away from a period when key staff would be unavailable, the project manager reschedules the build so it no longer overlaps with the peak holiday season. Which risk response does this rescheduling represent?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Avoiding a risk removes it from the project by changing the schedule or plan.

n.0: Exploiting is for opportunities.
n.1: Acceptance means tolerating the risk.
n.2: Reduction lessens the probability or impact, but doesn't remove the risk.
n.4: Sharing is for opportunities.

Risk & Issue Management.q: An opportunity to gain extra funding arises, and the project manager forms a partnership to secure it. Which response is this?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Sharing is about collaborating so both parties benefit from the opportunity.

n.1: Acceptance means no action is taken.
n.2: Avoidance is for threats.
n.3: Reduction is for threats.
n.4: Rejection is not pursuing the opportunity.

Risk & Issue Management.q: The project sponsor chooses not to act on a minor risk due to its low impact. What risk response is this?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Acceptance is appropriate when the risk is low and the cost to act outweighs the benefit.

n.0: Avoidance removes the risk.
n.2: Enhance is for positive risks (opportunities).
n.3: Reject is for opportunities not pursued.
n.4: Transfer is for shifting risk to another party.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the main purpose of transferring a risk?
o: To increase the chance of an opportunity
To change plans so the threat can no longer affect the project at all
To record the risk and take no further action
To lower the probability of the threat occurring
To pass its impact to a third party, such as an insurer or supplier
Risk & Issue Management.w: Transfer passes the financial impact (and sometimes management) of a threat to a third party such as an insurer or supplier, though the risk itself may remain.

n.0: Increasing an opportunity's chance is enhance.
n.1: Changing plans to eliminate the threat is avoidance.
n.2: Recording it and taking no action is acceptance.
n.3: Lowering probability is reduction.
