Increase directive oversight to reduce dependency on individual judgement
Adopt a delegating approach, focusing on outcomes rather than task-level control
Leadership.w: High competence and commitment justify a delegating style focused on outcomes rather than control.

n.0: Minimal communication risks misalignment despite strong performance.
n.1: Over-governance slows decision-making without clear benefit.
n.2: Excessive supervision can reduce motivation and autonomy in a capable team.
n.3: Increased control is unnecessary and counterproductive at high maturity.

Leadership.q: A project team demonstrates strong technical ability but resists taking accountability for decisions. Work is completed, but ownership is unclear. Which leadership style adjustment is MOST appropriate?
o: Increase task direction to ensure all decisions are made by the project manager
Escalate accountability issues to governance without team intervention
Delegate all decision-making authority immediately to force accountability
Use a supporting style to build confidence and encourage shared ownership
Reduce involvement to allow accountability to emerge naturally
Leadership.w: Supporting style helps build confidence and ownership when competence exists but willingness is limited.

n.0: Taking over decisions reduces opportunities for ownership development.
n.1: Escalation avoids addressing the behavioural issue within the team.
n.2: Immediate delegation without support risks reinforcing avoidance behaviour.
n.4: Passive leadership does not actively develop accountability.

Leadership.q: A team member who was previously reliable begins underperforming after being assigned unfamiliar tasks. Which leadership response BEST reflects situational leadership?
o: Escalate the performance issue to senior management immediately
Shift to a more directive and coaching approach to support capability development
Remove the individual from the task to maintain overall team performance
Maintain the same level of delegation to reinforce expectations of independence
Ignore the issue to avoid damaging morale
Leadership.w: Reduced competence in a new context requires more guidance and coaching to rebuild performance.

n.0: Immediate escalation bypasses appropriate leadership intervention.
n.2: Removing the individual prevents learning and development.
n.3: Maintaining delegation ignores the change in capability requirements.
n.4: Ignoring the issue risks further decline in performance.

Leadership.q: A project manager notices that different team members respond inconsistently to the same leadership approach. What is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
o: Inconsistency indicates poor team discipline rather than leadership issues
Variation in response suggests the team lacks technical competence
The team should align to the leader’s preferred style rather than the reverse
A single leadership style should be applied consistently to ensure fairness
Leadership style should be adapted to individual needs and levels of development
Leadership.w: Situational leadership requires adapting style to individual capability and motivation rather than applying a uniform approach.

n.0: The issue relates to leadership adaptation, not necessarily discipline.
n.1: Response variation is not solely linked to technical competence.
n.2: Effective leadership aligns to team needs, not personal preference.
n.3: Consistency in style does not address differing development levels.

Leadership.q: A project manager leads an experienced software team that consistently delivers high-quality work, yet members have grown resistant because they feel every task is being checked and controlled. Given the team's capability, which leadership change is MOST appropriate?
o: Escalate resistance as a behavioural issue requiring intervention
Continue close supervision to maintain control over outputs
Increase reporting requirements to improve visibility
Reassign tasks to reduce dependency on the team
Reduce task-level control and focus on outcome-based leadership
Leadership.w: High capability requires less control; reducing micromanagement restores autonomy and motivation.

n.0: Escalation avoids adapting leadership style.
n.1: Maintaining control reinforces the cause of resistance.
n.2: Increased reporting adds control rather than addressing autonomy.
n.3: Reassignment does not address underlying leadership mismatch.

Leadership.q: A project manager oversees a newly assembled team that is enthusiastic and eager to contribute, but whose members produce work of uneven quality and still lack full competence in some tasks. Which leadership approach BEST reflects effective adaptation to this situation?
o: Applying strict control to eliminate performance variation
Delegating fully to leverage motivation and encourage independence
Reducing interaction to avoid interfering with motivation
Coaching through guidance while encouraging involvement in decisions
Escalating performance issues without direct intervention
Leadership.w: Coaching balances guidance with engagement when motivation is high but capability is uneven.

n.0: Strict control may reduce motivation despite capability gaps.
n.1: Delegation assumes consistent competence which is not present.
n.2: Reduced interaction fails to support capability development.
n.4: Escalation does not replace leadership responsibility.

Leadership.q: A project manager applying a situational leadership approach is deciding how much direction and support to offer different members of the delivery team, whose experience and attitudes vary. Which TWO factors MOST directly influence the appropriate leadership style?
o: Team member motivation and willingness to perform
Team member competence in relation to the task
Project budget constraints and cost pressures
Leadership.w: Situational leadership is primarily based on competence and commitment (motivation) of team members.

n.1: Reporting expectations influence communication, not leadership style selection.
n.3: Budget pressures affect decisions but not directly leadership style choice.
n.4: Governance context may influence constraints but is not the primary driver.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to develop the capability of team members while still guiding delivery, and chooses to adopt a coaching leadership style during the project. Which TWO leadership behaviours are MOST aligned with that style?
o: Escalating performance issues without direct team engagement
Maintaining strict control over task execution and decision-making
Providing clear direction while encouraging team input on decisions
Supporting problem-solving while developing individual capability
Allowing full autonomy with minimal oversight or guidance
Leadership.w: Coaching combines direction with support, helping develop competence while involving the team.

n.0: Escalation avoids leadership engagement.
n.1: Strict control aligns with directive style.
n.4: Full autonomy reflects delegation, not coaching.

Leadership.q: A project manager has taken on a newly formed team whose members are unfamiliar with the work and unclear about task priorities. Considering when firmer guidance is warranted, which TWO scenarios MOST justify a shift towards a more directive leadership style?
o: A high-performing team consistently delivers without supervision
A team lacks experience and shows confusion over task priorities
A mature team demonstrates strong ownership and accountability
A new team is unfamiliar with processes and requires structured guidance
An experienced team requests greater autonomy over decisions
Leadership.w: Low competence and uncertainty require directive leadership to provide clarity and structure.

n.0: High-performing teams do not require increased direction.
n.2: Mature teams benefit from delegation rather than direction.
n.4: Requests for autonomy suggest readiness for less directive styles.

Leadership.q: A project manager applies the same leadership style to every team regardless of their experience or maturity. Reflecting on the consequences of not adapting the approach, which TWO risks are MOST associated with this failure?
o: Increased autonomy leading to faster decision-making in all cases
Improved clarity in task allocation across all team levels
Decreased performance due to insufficient guidance for inexperienced members
Enhanced trust between leader and team regardless of context
Reduced engagement due to over-control of capable team members
Leadership.w: Misalignment leads to disengagement in capable teams and confusion in inexperienced teams.

n.0: Autonomy is not always beneficial if capability is low.
n.1: Clarity is not guaranteed when leadership style is misaligned.
n.3: Trust is often reduced when leadership is inappropriate.

Leadership.q: A project team has recently formed and members are unclear about roles, hesitant to contribute, and rely heavily on the project manager for direction. Which stage of team development is MOST evident?
o: Norming, where shared understanding and cohesion are already established
Adjourning, where focus shifts to closure and disbanding activities
Storming, where conflict dominates and individuals challenge authority openly
Performing, where the team operates autonomously with minimal oversight
Forming, where individuals seek clarity and depend on leadership for structure
Leadership.w: Forming is characterised by uncertainty, dependency on the leader, and lack of clarity about roles and expectations.

n.0: Norming reflects established cohesion, which is not yet present.
n.1: Adjourning relates to project closure, not early-stage team behaviour.
n.2: Storming involves visible conflict and challenges, not initial uncertainty and reliance.
n.3: Performing requires maturity and autonomy not evident here.

Leadership.q: A project team begins to openly challenge decisions, question authority, and experience interpersonal conflict as individuals assert their viewpoints. What is the MOST appropriate interpretation?
o: The team is regressing due to ineffective leadership and requires restructuring
The team is adjourning and disengaging from project objectives
The team has reached performing and is optimising its decision-making approach
The team is norming, as members establish stable working relationships
The team is in storming, where conflict is a natural part of development
Leadership.w: Storming involves conflict and challenges as individuals assert themselves and roles are negotiated.

n.0: Conflict does not necessarily indicate regression; it is a natural stage.
n.1: Adjourning is related to project closure, not active conflict.
n.2: Performing reflects stability and effectiveness, not conflict.
n.3: Norming involves reduced conflict and increased cohesion.

Leadership.q: A team has resolved earlier conflicts and now collaborates effectively, with clear roles and shared understanding of objectives. Which stage BEST describes this behaviour?
o: Forming, where roles and expectations are still unclear
Norming, where cohesion and mutual understanding develop
Adjourning, where focus is on project completion and disengagement
Performing, where the team is fully autonomous and optimised
Leadership.w: Norming is characterised by collaboration, clarity, and reduced conflict following the storming phase.

n.0: Forming lacks the clarity and cohesion described.
n.2: Storming would involve ongoing conflict, not resolution.
n.3: Adjourning relates to closure, not team cohesion.
n.4: Performing reflects higher autonomy and productivity beyond norming.

Leadership.q: A high-performing team consistently delivers outputs, adapts to challenges without escalation, and requires minimal direction from the project manager. Which stage is MOST applicable?
o: Storming, where team members challenge each other frequently
Performing, where the team operates efficiently and independently
Norming, where collaboration exists but autonomy is limited
Forming, where leadership direction is critical to progress
Adjourning, where focus shifts away from delivery activities
Leadership.w: Performing reflects high autonomy, efficiency, and adaptability with minimal supervision.

n.0: Storming is characterised by conflict, not efficiency.
n.2: Norming involves collaboration but not full autonomy.
n.3: Forming requires strong leadership and lacks autonomy.
n.4: Adjourning occurs at the end of the project lifecycle.

Leadership.q: A project team that was previously cohesive begins to experience renewed conflict after a significant change in scope and the introduction of new members. What is the MOST appropriate interpretation?
o: The team is progressing towards performing as project complexity gradually increases
The team is norming as it adapts to the new challenges
The team is adjourning due to reduced focus on delivery
The team has returned to storming due to changes in structure and context
The team has failed to maintain performance and should be replaced
Leadership.w: Teams can revert to earlier stages such as storming when changes disrupt established dynamics.

n.0: Performing would not involve renewed conflict.
n.1: Norming reflects stability, not renewed disruption.
n.2: Adjourning is unrelated to mid-project changes.
n.4: Regression does not imply failure requiring replacement.

Leadership.q: During the early stages of a project, the team avoids conflict and appears polite but lacks honest discussion about issues. Which stage is MOST likely?
o: Adjourning, where engagement is reduced as the project ends
Performing, where problems are addressed proactively
Storming, where conflict is openly expressed and challenged
Forming, where individuals avoid conflict and seek acceptance
Norming, where trust allows open discussion of issues
Leadership.w: Forming is characterised by politeness and avoidance of conflict as individuals seek acceptance.

n.0: Adjourning is unrelated to early-stage behaviour.
n.1: Performing teams address issues directly and effectively.
n.2: Storming involves open conflict, not avoidance.
n.4: Norming allows for more honest communication.

Leadership.q: A project manager notices that despite high technical capability, the team struggles to agree on approaches and decisions, leading to delays. Which stage BEST explains this behaviour?
o: Norming, where consensus is easily reached and roles are clear
Performing, where decisions are made efficiently without conflict
Forming, where capability is still developing and roles are unclear
Storming, where disagreements and competing views affect progress
Adjourning, where focus is on closing activities rather than decisions
Leadership.w: Storming is characterised by conflict and difficulty in decision-making despite capability.

n.0: Norming implies smoother decision-making and alignment.
n.1: Performing teams resolve decisions efficiently.
n.2: Forming would involve uncertainty rather than strong disagreement.
n.4: Adjourning is not relevant to decision-making challenges.

Leadership.q: Partway through the project, a newly formed team has begun openly disagreeing over roles and priorities, with tension rising between individuals as they compete for influence. At this stage of team development, which leadership response is MOST appropriate?
o: Apply strict control to suppress disagreement and enforce compliance
Provide facilitation to manage conflict and clarify roles and expectations
Delegate all decisions to the team to encourage independence
Escalate interpersonal issues immediately to senior stakeholders
Avoid intervening to allow conflicts to resolve without influence
Leadership.w: During storming, leaders should facilitate resolution of conflict and provide clarity to guide the team forward.

n.0: Suppressing disagreement can damage trust and cohesion.
n.2: Full delegation may worsen unresolved conflict.
n.3: Escalation avoids addressing team dynamics directly.
n.4: Non-intervention can allow conflict to escalate.

Leadership.q: After an earlier period of conflict, a project team has settled down, with members now cooperating well and working towards agreed goals. Which TWO characteristics are MOST associated with this stage of team development?
o: Frequent conflict and challenges to authority
Strong collaboration and mutual support among team members
Clear roles and shared understanding of objectives
High dependency on the project manager for direction
Avoidance of interaction to minimise disagreement
Leadership.w: Norming involves clarity, collaboration, and mutual support following resolution of earlier conflicts.

n.0: Frequent conflict is typical of the storming stage.
n.3: High dependency is more typical of forming.
n.4: Avoidance of interaction reflects forming behaviour.

Leadership.q: A project manager steps back from a team that is going through a period of disagreement over roles and authority, leaving the tensions unaddressed. If the storming stage is not managed effectively, which TWO outcomes are MOST likely to result?
o: Immediate transition to high performance without intervention
Improved cohesion due to unresolved disagreements
Prolonged conflict leading to reduced team performance
Breakdown in trust and communication within the team
Faster progression to adjourning due to conflict resolution
Leadership.w: Poorly managed storming leads to sustained conflict and reduced trust, impacting performance.

n.0: High performance does not emerge without resolving conflict.
n.1: Unresolved disagreements damage cohesion rather than improve it.
n.4: Adjourning is unrelated to conflict progression.

Leadership.q: A project sponsor asks the project manager whether a delivery team has fully matured, having observed how it now operates day to day. Which TWO scenarios would indicate that the team has reached the performing stage of development?
o: The team relies on structured guidance for all decisions
The team avoids taking ownership of decisions
The team consistently delivers outputs with minimal supervision
The team experiences frequent unresolved conflict
The team adapts to changes without requiring direction from the project manager
Leadership.w: Performing teams demonstrate autonomy, adaptability, and consistent delivery.

n.0: Reliance on guidance reflects earlier stages.
n.1: Avoiding ownership indicates lack of maturity.
n.3: Frequent conflict suggests storming.

Leadership.q: A project manager is meeting a newly assembled team for the first time, where members are uncertain about their responsibilities and how the project will operate. At this forming stage, which TWO leadership actions are MOST appropriate?
o: Providing clear direction and defining roles and expectations
Allowing the team to resolve uncertainties without intervention
Establishing structure and outlining processes for the team
Encouraging full autonomy and minimal oversight
Leadership.w: Forming requires structure, clarity, and direction to guide the team.

n.1: Non-intervention leaves uncertainty unresolved.
n.2: Delegation assumes readiness that is not present.
n.4: Autonomy is inappropriate when the team lacks clarity.

Leadership.q: A technically strong project team is generating many ideas but repeatedly fails to convert them into practical actions. Which Belbin team role would MOST directly address this gap?
o: Resource Investigator, by identifying external contacts and opportunities
Implementer, by turning concepts into structured and workable plans
Plant, by introducing more original ideas and alternative solutions
Monitor Evaluator, by assessing ideas for logic and strategic fit
Specialist, by providing deeper knowledge in a narrow technical area
Leadership.w: An Implementer is useful where ideas need to be converted into practical plans and organised action.

n.0: A Resource Investigator looks outward for opportunities and contacts, not implementation discipline.
n.2: A Plant would add more ideas, but the team already has enough ideas and lacks practical conversion.
n.3: A Monitor Evaluator assesses options but does not primarily turn ideas into action.
n.4: A Specialist provides expertise, but the issue is execution rather than technical depth.

Leadership.q: A project team has several capable specialists but meetings drift, decisions are delayed, and people leave unclear about ownership. Which Belbin role is MOST needed?
o: Teamworker, because the team needs someone to maintain harmony and avoid friction
Plant, because the team needs more creative challenge and unconventional thinking
Co-ordinator, because the team needs someone to clarify objectives and delegate effectively
Completer Finisher, because the team needs someone focused mainly on checking the final detail
Specialist, because the team needs additional expert knowledge to improve decisions
Leadership.w: A Co-ordinator helps clarify goals, draw out contributions, and allocate responsibilities, which directly addresses unclear ownership.

n.0: A Teamworker supports cohesion, but this scenario requires role clarity and delegation.
n.1: A Plant may increase ideas, but the problem is lack of coordination and ownership.
n.3: A Completer Finisher helps with accuracy and final checks, not meeting direction.
n.4: More expertise does not solve unclear ownership or weak meeting control.

Leadership.q: A project manager notices that one team member regularly identifies risks in proposed options, challenges weak assumptions, and avoids being swayed by enthusiasm. Which Belbin role does this BEST indicate?
o: Implementer, because they convert decisions into organised practical work
Monitor Evaluator, because they judge options objectively and test reasoning
Resource Investigator, because they explore external opportunities and stakeholder links
Teamworker, because they reduce tension and maintain cooperation
Shaper, because they push the team to overcome obstacles and maintain momentum
Leadership.w: A Monitor Evaluator provides objective judgement, evaluates options, and challenges weak reasoning.

n.0: An Implementer focuses on practical delivery, not critical assessment of options.
n.2: A Resource Investigator is outward-looking rather than focused on internal evaluation.
n.3: A Teamworker supports relationships, not analytical challenge.
n.4: A Shaper drives progress and challenge, but the emphasis here is objective evaluation.

Leadership.q: A project is approaching a key handover. Most deliverables are complete, but there are recurring minor defects in documentation and test evidence. Which Belbin role would add MOST value?
o: Co-ordinator, by redistributing responsibilities across the wider project team
Resource Investigator, by finding external lessons learned from similar projects
Completer Finisher, by checking detail and driving work through to closure
Shaper, by increasing pace and challenging the team to work harder
Plant, by proposing alternative ways to redesign the solution before handover
Leadership.w: A Completer Finisher is valuable near closure because they focus on accuracy, detail, and final completion.

n.0: A Co-ordinator may help allocation, but the dominant issue is detail and completion.
n.1: External lessons may help, but they do not directly resolve immediate defects.
n.3: A Shaper may increase urgency but could worsen defects if detail is not controlled.
n.4: A Plant may create unnecessary redesign when the main issue is final quality control.

Leadership.q: A team is technically competent but conflict is increasing because strong personalities dominate discussions. Which Belbin role would BEST help stabilise collaboration?
o: Plant, by adding creative disruption to challenge current thinking
Monitor Evaluator, by ranking all proposals against objective criteria
Teamworker, by improving cooperation and reducing interpersonal friction
Specialist, by increasing the depth of subject matter expertise available
Shaper, by pushing harder for progress despite interpersonal resistance
Leadership.w: A Teamworker helps maintain relationships, reduce friction, and support collaboration when interpersonal tension is affecting the team.

n.0: A Plant may create further challenge, which may not stabilise conflict.
n.1: Objective evaluation may support decisions but does not primarily manage relationships.
n.3: Additional expertise does not directly address interpersonal tension.
n.4: A Shaper can be useful for momentum but may intensify conflict.

Leadership.q: A project is losing momentum because the team discusses issues extensively but avoids difficult decisions. Which Belbin role is MOST likely missing?
o: Shaper, because the team needs challenge, drive, and pressure to act
Completer Finisher, because the team needs final checking of completed outputs
Plant, because the team needs more ideas before deciding on direction
Specialist, because the team lacks detailed knowledge of technical constraints
Teamworker, because the team needs more emphasis on harmony and inclusion
Leadership.w: A Shaper challenges inertia, drives progress, and pushes the team through obstacles and indecision.

n.1: A Completer Finisher is more relevant when outputs need final accuracy checks.
n.2: More ideas may increase discussion rather than action.
n.3: The issue is not lack of knowledge but reluctance to make decisions.
n.4: More harmony may worsen avoidance if the issue is lack of challenge.

Leadership.q: A team member has strong external networks, brings back information about supplier capability, and identifies opportunities the project team had not considered. Which Belbin role is MOST evident?
o: Resource Investigator, because they explore external ideas, contacts, and opportunities
Monitor Evaluator, because they critically assess all the options before decisions are made
Implementer, because they organise practical work from agreed decisions
Completer Finisher, because they ensure the final output is accurate and complete
Co-ordinator, because they allocate work and clarify team responsibilities
Leadership.w: A Resource Investigator is outward-facing and brings in contacts, opportunities, and external information.

n.1: A Monitor Evaluator assesses ideas but is not defined by external networking.
n.2: An Implementer converts plans into action rather than sourcing external opportunities.
n.3: A Completer Finisher focuses on detail and completion, not external exploration.
n.4: A Co-ordinator focuses on team objectives and delegation, not external networking.

Leadership.q: A project manager uses Belbin analysis and discovers several Plants but no Monitor Evaluator. What is the MOST likely risk?
o: The team may avoid conflict so strongly that poor behaviour goes unchallenged
The team may generate creative options without sufficient objective assessment
The team may complete work carefully but resist all new ideas
The team may lack specialist knowledge needed for technical decisions
The team may over-rely on external contacts and neglect internal delivery
Leadership.w: Multiple Plants may produce ideas, but without a Monitor Evaluator those ideas may not be tested objectively before action.

n.0: This relates more to an overemphasis on harmony, not absence of evaluation.
n.2: This describes overemphasis on completion or caution, not excess creative idea generation.
n.3: The absence of a Monitor Evaluator does not automatically mean lack of specialist knowledge.
n.4: This would suggest too much Resource Investigator behaviour.

Leadership.q: When selecting people for a new project team, a project manager plans to use Belbin team roles to inform how the team is built and managed. Regarding the appropriate use of this model, which statement is MOST appropriate?
o: Belbin roles are mainly used to rank team members by leadership potential
Belbin roles determine formal authority within the project organisation structure
Belbin roles should be used to permanently label individuals and restrict their tasks
Belbin roles replace the need for defined project roles and responsibilities
Belbin roles help identify behavioural contributions and possible team balance gaps
Leadership.w: Belbin roles describe behavioural contributions and can help a project manager understand team balance and gaps.

n.0: Belbin is not a ranking system for leadership potential.
n.1: Belbin roles are behavioural, not formal authority positions.
n.2: Belbin should not be used to rigidly label or limit individuals.
n.3: Belbin does not replace formal project roles and responsibilities.

Leadership.q: A project team has generated plenty of creative ideas but is struggling to turn them into completed, dependable outputs. Using Belbin team roles, which TWO roles are MOST likely to help the team move from idea generation to reliable delivery?
o: Implementer, by organising ideas into practical work
Completer Finisher, by checking accuracy and driving closure
Plant, by adding more creative and unconventional possibilities
Teamworker, by reducing tension and supporting cooperation
Resource Investigator, by bringing in external opportunities
Leadership.w: Implementers convert ideas into practical plans, while Completer Finishers help ensure outputs are completed accurately.

n.2: A Plant helps generate ideas, but the issue is moving beyond ideas.
n.3: A Teamworker helps cooperation but is not the main delivery conversion role.
n.4: A Resource Investigator brings external input but does not primarily ensure delivery.

Leadership.q: A project manager reviewing the Belbin profile of a team wants to identify who is most likely to question assumptions and drive decisions rather than smooth relationships or carry out the work. Which TWO Belbin roles are MOST associated with challenge and evaluation rather than harmony or delivery execution?
o: Shaper, by pushing the team through obstacles and complacency
Monitor Evaluator, by judging options objectively and logically
Teamworker, by maintaining relationships and reducing conflict
Completer Finisher, by checking for omissions and errors near completion
Implementer, by creating workable plans from agreed ideas
Leadership.w: Shapers challenge and drive action, while Monitor Evaluators challenge the quality of reasoning and decisions.

n.2: Teamworkers focus on cohesion and relationships rather than challenge.
n.3: Completer Finishers focus on final detail, not broad evaluation or challenge.
n.4: Implementers focus on practical execution, not challenge or evaluation.

Leadership.q: A project manager reviews the Belbin profiles of a delivery team and finds that most members share very similar role preferences, giving the team little variety in how it works. Which TWO risks can arise from this lack of balance?
o: The team will be unable to agree any stakeholder requirements
The project manager loses all formal authority over allocating tasks
Team members will be unable to carry out their functional job roles
Important behaviours may be missing from the team’s working approach
The team may overuse one style of contribution and create blind spots
Leadership.w: A team with similar behavioural preferences may lack important contributions and develop blind spots.

n.0: Requirements definition may be affected indirectly, but it is not impossible because of role imbalance.
n.1: Belbin roles do not remove formal authority from the project manager.
n.2: Belbin imbalance does not invalidate governance arrangements.

Leadership.q: A project manager is considering how best to apply Belbin team roles when forming and running the project team. Which TWO statements show an appropriate use of Belbin roles by the project manager?
o: Replacing stakeholder analysis with team role assessment
Selecting only one preferred role for each person and ignoring context
Treating role labels as fixed job titles for the rest of the project
Identifying missing behavioural contributions before they affect performance
Using role preferences to improve team balance and task allocation
Leadership.w: Belbin is useful for understanding behavioural contribution, team balance, and potential gaps.

n.0: Belbin supports team understanding but does not replace stakeholder analysis.
n.1: People may contribute differently depending on context and team need.
n.2: Belbin roles should not become fixed job titles.

Leadership.q: A project team is meeting deadlines but quality is declining because members are rushing work to avoid criticism from a demanding sponsor. Which leadership action would MOST improve sustainable performance?
o: Ask the sponsor to communicate directly with team members to increase urgency
Increase pressure on the team to maintain delivery pace and avoid stakeholder concern
Move quality checks to the end of each stage so progress is not disrupted
Rebalance expectations by reinforcing quality standards and creating space for honest escalation
Reward individuals who deliver fastest to reinforce the required pace
Leadership.w: Leadership influences performance by shaping conditions for motivation, quality and honest communication. The project manager should reduce fear-driven behaviour while maintaining standards.

n.0: Direct sponsor pressure may increase anxiety and reduce team ownership.
n.1: More pressure may protect pace briefly but is likely to worsen quality and motivation.
n.2: Delaying quality checks does not address the motivational problem causing poor work.
n.4: Rewarding speed can reinforce the behaviour that is damaging quality.

Leadership.q: A capable project team has become passive because the project manager makes all meaningful decisions. What is the MOST likely leadership impact on performance?
o: The team may lose ownership and reduce discretionary effort
The team may become more efficient because decision-making is centralised
The team may require fewer communications because accountability is removed
The team will usually become more innovative due to clearer control
The team will avoid conflict and therefore perform more consistently
Leadership.w: Excessive control can reduce ownership, motivation and initiative, especially where the team is capable of contributing to decisions.

n.1: Centralised decisions can sometimes be faster but often reduce engagement and initiative.
n.2: Removing accountability is more likely to weaken performance than improve communication.
n.3: Innovation usually falls when team members are denied meaningful influence.
n.4: Avoiding conflict does not necessarily improve performance or commitment.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to improve motivation after several team members say their work feels disconnected from the overall project purpose. Which response is MOST appropriate?
o: Reduce stakeholder contact so the team can focus on assigned tasks
Explain how their deliverables contribute to outcomes and stakeholder value
Increase reporting frequency so team members remain visibly accountable
Offer informal praise without changing how work is framed
Reallocate work randomly to create variety and reduce boredom
Leadership.w: Connecting work to purpose and outcomes can improve intrinsic motivation by helping team members understand the value of their contribution.

n.0: Reducing stakeholder contact may further weaken understanding of project value.
n.2: More reporting may increase control but does not address lack of purpose.
n.3: Praise alone may help morale briefly but does not connect work to meaning.
n.4: Random reallocation may create disruption and does not address purpose.

Leadership.q: A project manager publicly blames individuals for defects during team meetings. Defects are then hidden until late in delivery. What is the BEST explanation of the performance issue?
o: The quality process is too detailed and should be simplified immediately
The team is likely in a performing stage and needs less intervention
The project manager should increase individual performance tracking
The team lacks technical competence and needs additional formal training
The leadership climate is discouraging openness and weakening problem reporting
Leadership.w: Blame-based leadership damages psychological safety, causing people to hide issues rather than raise them early.

n.0: Simplifying the process does not address the leadership behaviour causing hiding.
n.1: A performing team would normally surface and resolve issues proactively.
n.2: More tracking may increase fear and further reduce openness.
n.3: The issue described is concealment caused by fear, not necessarily lack of competence.

Leadership.q: A team member has strong capability but is demotivated because their contribution is rarely recognised and they have little influence over how work is done. Which leadership response is MOST likely to improve performance?
o: Escalate the issue as poor attitude before changing leadership approach
Increase involvement, recognise contribution, and give appropriate autonomy
Move the individual to lower-risk tasks until motivation improves
Focus only on contractual obligations and expected outputs
Set more detailed task instructions to remove uncertainty
Leadership.w: Recognition, involvement and autonomy can increase motivation where capability is already strong but commitment is falling.

n.0: Escalating attitude without addressing leadership factors misses the cause.
n.2: Lower-risk tasks may further reduce motivation and perceived value.
n.3: A narrow focus on obligation is unlikely to create discretionary effort.
n.4: More instruction may worsen frustration if the person already has capability.

Leadership.q: A project manager introduces a small amount of constructive challenge, clearer goals and regular feedback. Team performance improves without additional resources. What does this MOST clearly demonstrate?
o: Leadership behaviour can influence performance conditions
Motivation is mainly controlled by financial incentives
Resource availability is usually irrelevant to project results
Performance issues are normally solved by tighter governance
Team development models replace the need for planning
Leadership.w: Leadership affects performance by influencing clarity, challenge, feedback, confidence and motivation, even without changing resources.

n.1: The scenario shows non-financial leadership factors improving motivation.
n.2: Resources still matter, but they are not the only performance driver.
n.3: Governance alone does not explain improved motivation and performance.
n.4: Leadership and team development support planning; they do not replace it.

Leadership.q: A project manager notices that team members only do the minimum required and rarely suggest improvements. Which leadership issue is MOST likely present?
o: The project schedule is probably too detailed for the team to interpret
The team may lack motivation because leadership has not encouraged ownership
The team is overperforming and should be given fewer opportunities to contribute
The communication plan is unnecessary because team members understand their tasks
The project sponsor has delegated too much authority to the project manager
Leadership.w: Minimum-effort behaviour often indicates limited ownership, weak motivation or lack of empowerment, all of which leadership can influence.

n.0: The scenario is about effort and initiative, not schedule interpretation.
n.2: The behaviour indicates underuse of capability, not overperformance.
n.3: Understanding tasks does not mean motivation and ownership are sufficient.
n.4: Delegated authority to the project manager does not directly explain low initiative.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to use recognition and reward to lift the performance of the delivery team over the course of the project. Which approach is MOST likely to be effective?
o: Use recognition mainly to compensate for unclear objectives
Recognise only senior team members because their work has greater project impact
Recognise visible effort only at the end of the project to avoid distraction
Link recognition to specific behaviours and outcomes that support project objectives
Give identical praise to all team members regardless of contribution
Leadership.w: Recognition is most useful when it is specific, timely and connected to behaviours that improve project performance.

n.0: Recognition cannot compensate for lack of clear objectives.
n.1: Recognition should reflect contribution, not seniority alone.
n.2: Delayed recognition loses impact and may not reinforce desired behaviours.
n.4: Generic praise can feel meaningless and may not influence performance.

Leadership.q: A team is under pressure and morale is falling. The project manager responds by clarifying priorities, removing blockers and protecting the team from unnecessary disruption. Which impact is MOST likely?
o: The project constraints will disappear because team morale has improved
The team may sustain performance because leadership has reduced avoidable friction
The team will need no further monitoring because motivation has been restored
The sponsor will no longer require progress information from the project manager
The team will automatically move to performing without further leadership effort
Leadership.w: Removing barriers and clarifying priorities can protect motivation and enable sustained performance under pressure.

n.0: Leadership can influence performance but cannot remove project constraints.
n.2: Improved motivation does not remove the need for monitoring.
n.3: Sponsor reporting remains necessary regardless of morale.
n.4: Team development still requires ongoing leadership and context awareness.

Leadership.q: A project manager is looking for ways to keep the delivery team motivated and performing well throughout a demanding project. Which TWO leadership behaviours are MOST likely to improve motivation and project team performance?
o: Providing clear objectives and explaining the purpose behind the work
Avoiding difficult conversations to maintain short-term harmony
Using pressure as the main method of sustaining delivery pace
Increasing control over every task regardless of team competence
Giving timely feedback that helps individuals improve
Leadership.w: Clear purpose and useful feedback help team members understand expectations, improve capability and sustain motivation.

n.1: Avoiding difficult conversations can allow performance issues to continue.
n.2: Pressure alone may produce short-term effort but often damages sustainable performance.
n.3: Excessive control can reduce autonomy and motivation.

Leadership.q: Under a project manager who has grown increasingly controlling, the team's behaviour has shifted over recent weeks. Reflecting on how people now respond to the leadership style, which TWO signs suggest leadership is negatively affecting team performance?
o: Capable individuals stop offering suggestions or challenge
Team members hide problems until formal reviews
The team uses lessons learned to improve its approach
Team members understand priorities and escalate early risks
The team asks for clarification when requirements are ambiguous
Leadership.w: Concealing issues and withholding contribution indicate a leadership climate that may be reducing trust, motivation and ownership.

n.2: Using lessons learned shows positive improvement behaviour.
n.3: Early escalation and clear priorities indicate healthy performance behaviours.
n.4: Seeking clarification is usually constructive rather than negative.

Leadership.q: A project manager leads a technically strong team whose members have become passive and reluctant to take initiative on their work. To rebuild commitment, which TWO actions would BEST help the project manager increase ownership in this capable but disengaged team?
o: Focus solely on individual underperformance rather than team conditions
Increase approval layers so decisions feel controlled
Delegate appropriate authority while keeping outcomes clear
Remove all accountability until morale has improved
Involve the team in decisions that affect how work is delivered
Leadership.w: Involvement and appropriate delegation increase ownership while still maintaining clarity over outcomes.

n.0: Focusing only on individuals may ignore leadership and team environment causes.
n.1: More approval layers usually reduce autonomy and engagement.
n.3: Removing accountability weakens ownership rather than building it.

Leadership.q: A project manager under schedule pressure begins driving the team mainly through deadlines, criticism and fear of consequences. Considering the effect of this style, which TWO risks are MOST associated with relying mainly on pressure and fear to drive project performance?
o: Quality normally improves because people feel safer challenging issues
Short-term compliance may replace genuine commitment
Learning and improvement may reduce because people avoid exposing problems
Trust is likely to increase because expectations are strict
Team members may become more willing to report mistakes early
Leadership.w: Fear-based leadership can produce compliance but reduces openness, learning, commitment and long-term performance.

n.0: People are less likely to challenge quality issues when they fear blame.
n.3: Strictness without safety often reduces trust.
n.4: Fear usually reduces early reporting of mistakes.

Leadership.q: A project manager reviewing how to keep the team engaged draws on Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory to distinguish elements that merely prevent dissatisfaction from those that genuinely motivate. According to that theory, which of the following is considered a hygiene factor?
Leadership.w: In Herzberg’s model, hygiene factors (e.g., salary, company policy) prevent dissatisfaction but don’t drive satisfaction.

n.1: Recognition is a motivator that increases satisfaction.
n.2: Achievement is a motivator, not a hygiene factor.
n.3: Opportunities for growth are motivators.
n.4: Responsibility falls under motivators in Herzberg’s theory.

Leadership.q: A project manager is using Maslow's hierarchy of needs to understand what drives team members at different points on a project. According to Maslow, ______ needs must be fulfilled before safety needs become a priority.
Leadership.w: Physiological needs (food, water, shelter) are the most basic and must be met first in Maslow’s pyramid.

n.0: Cognitive needs are not one of Maslow’s original five levels.
n.2: Self-actualisation is the highest level.
n.3: Esteem is higher up the hierarchy than safety.
n.4: Love/belonging comes after safety needs.

Leadership.q: A newly appointed team leader is studying McGregor's Theory X to understand the assumptions it makes about how workers behave and how they should be managed. Which of these is NOT a principle of Theory X?
Leadership.w: Theory X assumes people dislike work and need direction; the idea that employees are self-motivated contradicts Theory X.

n.0: Close supervision is characteristic of Theory X managers.
n.1: Under Theory X, people are seen as preferring direction over autonomy.
n.3: Theory X holds that workers avoid responsibility.
n.4: Theory X views work as undesirable and employees as reluctant.

Leadership.q: A project manager is applying Maslow's hierarchy of needs to the workplace and wants to illustrate each level with a fitting example. Which of the following pairings correctly matches a Maslow need with an example?
Leadership.w: Love/belonging needs include social connections and supportive relationships within the team.

n.0: Salary is tied to physiological or safety needs, not self-actualisation.
n.1: A comfortable workspace relates to safety, not esteem.
n.2: Team events are social (belonging), not safety needs.
n.3: Mentorship addresses esteem or self-actualisation, not basic physiological needs.

Leadership.q: A project manager introduces performance bonuses hoping to lift a demotivated team, yet after several weeks morale and engagement remain stubbornly low. Which motivational theory best explains why the financial incentive failed to improve satisfaction?
Leadership.w: Herzberg’s model suggests that while bonuses (a hygiene factor) prevent dissatisfaction, they don’t create true motivation or job satisfaction.

n.0: Theory Y assumes employees are self-motivated, not about hygiene factors.
n.1: Motivation factors (e.g., recognition) do drive satisfaction, but bonuses are hygiene factors.
n.2: Maslow’s model doesn’t distinguish hygiene versus motivators.
n.4: Self-actualisation is the highest need, unrelated to simple bonuses.

Leadership.q: In Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory, “recognition” falls under which category?
Leadership.w: Recognition is considered a motivator in Herzberg’s theory, driving job satisfaction.

n.0: Safety needs are part of Maslow’s model, not Herzberg’s.
n.1: Hygiene factors include salary and work conditions, not recognition.
n.2: Recognition is exclusively a motivator.
n.3: Recognition clearly affects satisfaction, so it cannot be neither.

Leadership.q: A project manager reflecting on what ultimately drives high-performing individuals turns to the top of Maslow's hierarchy of needs. Which of the following statements best describes Maslow's concept of self-actualisation?
Leadership.w: Self-actualisation is the highest level in Maslow’s hierarchy, where one realises full personal potential.

n.0: Physiological needs are the most basic level.
n.1: Job security relates to safety needs.
n.2: Safety needs concern personal security and health.
n.3: Social bonds are love/belonging needs.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to adopt a leadership style built on the assumption that team members are naturally ambitious, enjoy their work, and willingly take on responsibility. Which motivational approach rests on that assumption?
Leadership.w: Theory Y posits that employees are self-motivated, enjoy work, and seek responsibility.

n.0: Physiological needs are Maslow’s most basic level.
n.1: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction but don’t motivate.
n.2: Safety needs are a basic level in Maslow’s model.
n.3: Theory X assumes employees dislike work.

Leadership.q: A leader redesigns roles to give team members clear goals and growth paths. What impact is this most likely to have?
Leadership.w: Clarified goals and development opportunities satisfy motivators like achievement and growth, boosting motivation.

n.0: It doesn’t negatively affect social needs.
n.1: It’s unrelated to basic physiological needs.
n.2: Conflict may reduce but not necessarily be eliminated.
n.3: Role clarity addresses motivators, not hygiene dissatisfaction.

Leadership.q: A project manager is checking their understanding of Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, which separates the factors that prevent dissatisfaction from those that actively create satisfaction. Which of the following dual-fact statements about Herzberg's theory is correct?
o: Safety needs are motivators AND they include company policy
Self-actualisation is a hygiene factor AND includes salary
Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction AND they create high motivation
Physiological needs motivate performance AND include teamwork
Motivators drive satisfaction AND include factors like recognition
Leadership.w: Herzberg’s motivators (e.g., recognition) truly drive job satisfaction and motivation.

n.0: Safety needs are Maslow’s, not Herzberg’s motivators.
n.1: Self-actualisation is Maslow’s top level, not a hygiene factor, and salary is hygiene.
n.2: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction but don’t create motivation.
n.3: Physiological needs and teamwork belong to different models.

Leadership.q: A project manager is tracing the order of the five levels in Maslow's hierarchy of needs to understand how team members' priorities progress. In Maslow's model, which need directly follows love and belonging?
Leadership.w: Esteem needs come after social (love/belonging) in Maslow’s hierarchy.

n.0: Cognitive is not one of Maslow’s original five levels.
n.1: Self-actualisation is the final level.
n.2: Physiological needs are the first level.
n.3: Safety is the second level, before social.

Leadership.q: A project manager is comparing McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y to decide how much direction and oversight a particular team requires. Which of the following statements contrasting Theory X and Theory Y is FALSE?
o: Theory Y sees work as a natural activity
Theory X views employees as lazy
Theory Y trusts employees to self-direct
Theory X assumes workers seek responsibility
Leadership.w: Theory X assumes employees avoid responsibility, not that they seek it.

n.0: Theory Y regards work as inherently satisfying.
n.1: Theory X indeed views people as lazy.
n.2: Theory X managers use close control and supervision.
n.3: Theory Y trusts self-direction and autonomy.

Leadership.q: A team's morale steadily declines because leadership concentrates solely on enforcing process compliance and never acknowledges good work or achievement. Which motivational model best explains this dip in morale?
Leadership.w: Ignoring recognition (a motivator) while focusing on hygiene factors leads to dissatisfaction per Herzberg.

n.0: McClelland’s model is a different needs theory.
n.1: Theory Z relates to Japanese management styles.
n.2: Maslow doesn’t separate hygiene vs. motivators.
n.4: Theory Y is about self-motivation, not hygiene neglect.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to introduce something that will genuinely raise team members' job satisfaction rather than merely stop them becoming dissatisfied. Within Herzberg's theory, which of the following is a motivator that directly enhances job satisfaction?
Leadership.w: Recognition is a motivator that fosters satisfaction; the others are hygiene factors.

n.1: Salary is a hygiene factor.
n.2: Supervision quality is treated as hygiene in Herzberg’s model.
n.3: Working conditions are hygiene factors.
n.4: Policy is a hygiene factor.

Leadership.q: A project manager is reviewing the five levels that Maslow originally set out in his hierarchy of needs. Which of the following is NOT one of Maslow's original five levels of need?
Leadership.w: Cognitive needs (knowledge, understanding) were later additions; not part of the original five.

n.1: Physiological is level 1.
n.2: Safety is level 2.
n.3: Belonging (love) is level 3.
n.4: Esteem is level 4.

Leadership.q: According to McGregor, which assumption underlies Theory Y?
o: Work is a source of satisfaction
Leadership.w: Theory Y holds that work can be as natural and satisfying as play when conditions are right.

n.1: Theory Y recognises non-monetary motivators like achievement.
n.2: Theory X managers favour close supervision.
n.3: That’s a Theory X assumption.
n.4: Theory X assumes avoidance of responsibility.

Leadership.q: Which pairing is correct in Herzberg’s model?
Leadership.w: Company policy is a hygiene factor; recognition is a motivator, salary is hygiene, etc.

n.0: Salary is hygiene, not a motivator.
n.2: Supervision quality is hygiene in Herzberg’s theory.
n.3: Recognition is a motivator, not hygiene.
n.4: Working conditions are hygiene factors.

Leadership.q: A project leader deliberately gives team members greater autonomy and encourages their personal growth and development in their roles. In Maslow's hierarchy, which need level is this leader primarily addressing?
Leadership.w: Autonomy and growth support self-actualisation, Maslow’s highest need level.

n.0: Basic survival needs are not about autonomy.
n.1: Safety is about security and stability.
n.2: Belonging is about social connections.
n.3: Esteem covers respect and recognition, not autonomy.

Leadership.q: A project manager is testing their grasp of Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory by pairing one factor that merely prevents dissatisfaction with one that actively drives satisfaction. Which combination correctly describes a hygiene factor and a motivator?
Leadership.w: Salary is a hygiene factor; recognition is a motivator in Herzberg’s framework.

n.0: Recognition is motivator but company policy is hygiene.
n.1: Both are hygiene factors.
n.2: Achievement is a motivator but working conditions are hygiene.
n.3: Supervision is hygiene; growth is a motivator.

Leadership.q: Which of these statements about Maslow’s hierarchy is FALSE?
o: People pursue higher needs once lower are met
Esteem needs involve recognition and respect
Leadership.w: Physiological needs (food, water, shelter) are essential, not optional.

n.0: True: belonging is about social bonds.
n.1: True: higher needs emerge after lower ones are satisfied.
n.2: True: esteem relates to respect and recognition.
n.4: True: safety needs cover security aspects.

Leadership.q: A manager who subscribes to McGregor's Theory X believes staff will not perform unless closely directed and monitored. According to Theory X, management must apply ______ to get results from employees.
Leadership.w: Theory X assumes employees must be controlled or coerced to achieve objectives.

n.0: Theory X distrusts employees, preferring control.
n.1: Self-direction contradicts the Theory X view.
n.2: Autonomy is a Theory Y principle.
n.3: Empowerment aligns with Theory Y, not X.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants team members to feel a genuine sense of personal achievement in their day-to-day work. Applying Herzberg's two-factor theory, which of the following is a motivator most likely to create that feeling?
Leadership.w: Achievement is explicitly identified as a motivator in Herzberg’s model.

n.1: Salary is hygiene, not a motivator.
n.2: Policy is a hygiene factor.
n.3: Supervision quality is treated as hygiene.
n.4: Working conditions are hygiene factors.

Leadership.q: A project manager is reviewing Herzberg's two-factor theory. Which of the following is NOT one of the factors named in the theory?
Leadership.w: Physiological needs are the base level of Maslow's hierarchy; Herzberg's theory names hygiene factors and motivators instead.

n.0: Job security is a hygiene factor that prevents dissatisfaction.
n.1: Achievement is a core motivator.
n.2: Supervision is a hygiene factor that prevents dissatisfaction.
n.3: Recognition is explicitly a motivator.

Leadership.q: A team leader deliberately rotates responsibilities so that each member is regularly stretched, challenged and kept engaged by varied, meaningful work. Which underlying assumption about people at work does this leadership behaviour best illustrate?
Leadership.w: Task variety and challenge align with Theory Y’s assumption that work can be intrinsically motivating.

n.0: Herzberg’s motivators include recognition and achievement, but task rotation is Theory Y style.
n.2: Theory X is about control, not intrinsic motivation.
n.3: Safety needs are about stability, not variety.
n.4: Hygiene factors don’t drive engagement.

Leadership.q: While reviewing Herzberg's two-factor theory ahead of an engagement survey, a project manager wants to distinguish the hygiene factors that prevent dissatisfaction from the motivators that drive satisfaction. Which of the following is NOT a hygiene factor?
Leadership.w: Recognition is a motivator; the others are hygiene factors that prevent dissatisfaction.

n.0: Working conditions are hygiene factors.
n.2: Salary is a hygiene factor.
n.3: Company policy is a hygiene factor.
n.4: Job security is treated as a hygiene factor.

Leadership.q: A project manager is deciding how much autonomy to give a capable team. Drawing on McGregor's work, which statement best describes the Theory Y set of assumptions the manager would hold about their employees?
o: They dislike work and must be coerced
They seek responsibility and are self-motivated
Leadership.w: Theory Y posits that employees are inherently motivated and seek responsibility when given the chance.

n.0: That describes Theory X.
n.2: Theory Y assumes less need for close supervision.
n.3: Theory Y associates employees with adaptability.
n.4: Theory Y acknowledges non-monetary motivators like achievement.

Leadership.q: A project manager reflects on Maslow's hierarchy of needs to understand what drives a valued team member who seeks respect, recognition and standing within the group. Which level of the hierarchy do these needs correspond to?
Leadership.w: Esteem needs involve feelings of accomplishment, respect by others, and confidence.

n.0: Safety is about security and stability.
n.1: Belonging covers social connections.
n.2: Self-actualisation is achieving one’s full potential.
n.4: Physiological needs are basic survival needs.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants a single set of actions that will both reduce dissatisfaction and actively motivate the team, addressing hygiene factors and motivators together as Herzberg describes. Which of the following approaches would most likely satisfy both needs simultaneously?
o: Raising salaries WITHOUT enriching the job content
Improving workplace facilities AND offering credit for high performance
Improving job security AND increasing supervision levels
Delegating more responsibility AND creating clearer routes to advancement
Enforcing stricter policies AND closely monitoring attendance
Leadership.w: Working conditions are a Herzberg hygiene factor (reduces dissatisfaction) and recognition for achievement is a motivator (creates satisfaction), so this pair addresses both.

n.0: Pay is a hygiene factor; without enriching the work there is no motivator.
n.2: Job security and supervision are both hygiene factors; neither actively motivates.
n.3: Responsibility and advancement are both motivators; no hygiene factor is addressed, so dissatisfaction may remain.
n.4: Policies and supervision are hygiene factors, and tightening them is more likely to increase dissatisfaction.

Leadership.q: A newly appointed manager tends to supervise closely and control the team tightly, believing this reflects human nature at work. Which of the following is a core assumption of McGregor's Theory X that would underpin this behaviour?
Leadership.w: Theory X assumes that people inherently avoid work and need external control to perform.

n.0: Intrinsic motivation is a Theory Y concept.
n.1: Theory X assumes the opposite.
n.2: That aligns with Theory Y.
n.4: Self-direction is a Theory Y belief.

Leadership.q: A project manager notices that one item from Herzberg's list of motivators also corresponds to the higher levels of Maslow's hierarchy of needs. Which of the following motivators does Herzberg include that Maslow places near the top of his hierarchy?
Leadership.w: Recognition (a motivator) aligns with Maslow’s self-esteem or self-actualisation levels.

n.0: Working conditions are hygiene.
n.1: Salary is a hygiene factor.
n.2: Company policy is hygiene.
n.3: Supervision is treated as hygiene.

Leadership.q: After a project manager began publicly praising individuals for their specific contributions during team meetings, overall productivity noticeably improved. Which motivational theory does this outcome best illustrate?
Leadership.w: Public praise is a motivator (recognition) in Herzberg’s framework, boosting satisfaction and performance.

n.0: McClelland’s model is different, focusing on acquired needs.
n.2: Safety needs are unrelated to recognition.
n.3: Hygiene factors don’t motivate performance.
n.4: Theory X would not emphasize praise.

Leadership.q: A project manager is drawing out the practical leadership lessons of Maslow's hierarchy of needs when managing a diverse team. Which of the following is NOT a sound implication of the model for how a leader should act?
Leadership.w: Not every employee aspires immediately to self-actualisation; leaders must meet lower-order needs first.

n.0: True: belonging is key.
n.1: True: basic needs form the foundation.
n.2: True: esteem needs involve recognition.
n.3: True: security is a safety need.

Leadership.q: Over the course of a project a manager finds themselves shifting between a supportive, encouraging manner and a more directive, hands-on one with different team members. According to situational leadership thinking, why would a leader need to vary their style in this way?
o: To follow the organisation's standard leadership policy
To reduce the need for delegation
To maintain a consistent management approach
To avoid making decisions under uncertainty
To match the team's competence and commitment levels
Leadership.w: Situational leadership holds that there is no single best style: the leader adapts to each person's competence and commitment, directing those new to a task and moving to supporting or delegating as capability and confidence grow.

n.0: Situational leadership responds to followers' needs, not to a fixed organisational policy on style.
n.1: Varying style usually increases delegation as competence grows; reducing delegation is not the aim.
n.2: A consistent approach for everyone is the opposite of situational leadership, which varies style by person and task.
n.3: The model is about matching style to followers, not avoiding decisions under uncertainty.

Leadership.q: A project manager notices that her new team members lack experience with the software development process. She shifts from a delegating style to a directing style. What was her primary reason for changing style?
o: She aimed to increase team autonomy
She wanted to reduce her own workload
Team members required more guidance due to low competence
The project deadline was not mentioned as influencing her decision
Leadership.w: She provided more direction because inexperienced team members needed clear guidance to perform tasks.

n.0: Her aim was to provide guidance, not to increase autonomy.
n.1: Reducing her own workload is not a factor in style adaptation.
n.2: Corporate policy did not mandate the change in the scenario.
n.4: Deadlines were not cited; the change was driven by team competence.

Leadership.q: A project manager is choosing the most appropriate leadership style for a piece of work being handed to a particular group. Which pair of situational factors is most important to weigh up when making that choice?
Leadership.w: Situational leadership matches style to the followers' readiness (competence and commitment) for the particular task, so how able and willing the group is, and how complex the work is, drive the choice.

n.0: Budget and contract type affect commercial arrangements, not the leadership style a group needs.
n.2: Training schedules and reporting lines are organisational arrangements, not measures of readiness.
n.3: Hierarchy and job titles show formal position, not whether people are able and willing to do this task.
n.4: Team size and duration may affect logistics, but the model focuses on readiness for the task.

Leadership.q: After taking over a cross-functional team with tight deadlines and varying skill levels, a new manager must decide how much direction and support to provide. Which of the following pairs of factors should he assess before choosing his leadership approach?
Leadership.w: Situational leadership adapts the amount of direction and support to the followers' competence (and commitment) and to the situation, such as urgency or crisis.

n.1: The sponsor's seniority and reporting format do not reflect the team's readiness.
n.2: Budget and contract type affect commercial management, not how much direction and support the team needs.
n.3: Market conditions may affect the business case but do not tell the manager how much to direct or support the team.
n.4: Meeting frequency and templates are administrative choices, not leadership style factors.

Leadership.q: Leaders adapt their style based on the ______ of their followers, such as their ability and willingness to perform tasks.
Leadership.w: In situational leadership, style is matched to follower readiness: their ability (competence) and willingness (commitment) to perform the specific task.

n.0: Team roles, as in Belbin, describe behavioural strengths within a team, not readiness for a task.
n.1: Working location may affect how a leader communicates, but the theory adapts style to readiness.
n.3: Personality type, as in Myers-Briggs, describes preferences, not ability and willingness for a task.
n.4: Seniority is formal position; a senior person can still be new to a task and need direction.

Leadership.q: A leader working with a remote team notices morale is low due to isolation. To improve motivation, she adopts a more ______ style, offering support and encouragement through regular check-ins.
Leadership.w: A supportive style addresses team morale by offering encouragement and assistance.

n.0: Delegating involves less leader involvement, unsuitable for low morale.
n.1: Directive style focuses on instructions, not morale support.
n.3: Autocratic emphasizes control, not supportive engagement.
n.4: Hands-off is similar to delegating and does not provide needed support.

Leadership.q: A project manager reviews the circumstances that would justify adapting their leadership style during delivery. Which of the following is NOT a factor that would typically prompt such a change of style?
Leadership.w: Physical office layout does not influence the need to adapt leadership style.

n.0: Task complexity is a key driver in adapting style.
n.1: Time constraints can prompt a more directive approach.
n.2: Crisis severity often necessitates a style change.
n.3: Follower readiness directly influences style choice.

Leadership.q: During an urgent crisis, a leader shifts to an autocratic style to make rapid decisions. Which of the following was NOT a reason for this change?
o: To accelerate decision-making under time pressure
Because the situation had high stakes
Leadership.w: Gathering broad input is not consistent with an autocratic approach in a crisis.

n.1: Critical need for quick action justifies autocratic control.
n.2: Time pressure in a crisis justifies faster decision-making.
n.3: High stakes support an autocratic approach when speed is vital.
n.4: Uncertainty often leads leaders to take a more directive stance.

Leadership.q: A project manager applying situational leadership theory recognises that the appropriate style is not fixed but should shift according to particular characteristics. According to the theory, a leader should adapt their style based on the characteristics of the _____.
Leadership.w: Situational leadership matches the style to follower characteristics such as ability and willingness.

n.0: Market trends affect business planning, not direct style adaptation.
n.2: Physical environment is not a core situational leadership factor.
n.3: Corporate strategy guides goals, not follower-focused style changes.
n.4: Industry context influences business strategy but not immediate style choice.

Leadership.q: A seasoned sales team has high expertise and confidence. The leader delegates tasks and decision-making to them. Why did the leader adopt a delegating style?
o: The team demonstrated high competence and commitment
The leader lacked time to support
Leadership.w: Delegating is appropriate when team members are both capable and motivated to work independently.

n.1: The scenario described high morale, not low morale.
n.2: Increased oversight would require a directive style, not delegation.
n.3: Delegation was based on team capability, not the leader’s time constraints.
n.4: The schedule was not mentioned as influencing his decision.

Leadership.q: A project manager oversees an experienced, capable and motivated sub-team who need very little direction to deliver. Under the situational leadership model, which pair of conditions indicates that a delegating style is appropriate here?
o: High follower competence and low commitment
Low follower competence and high commitment
High follower competence and high commitment
Low follower competence and low commitment
Leadership.w: Delegating is suited to followers who are both skilled (competent) and motivated (committed).

n.0: High competence with low commitment may need a supportive style.
n.1: Low competence with high commitment requires coaching.
n.2: Moderate levels typically call for a facilitating style, not full delegation.
n.4: Low competence and commitment require a directive approach.

Leadership.q: After onboarding a skilled development team, a manager observes they are both capable and highly motivated. Which of the following pairs of factors did the manager assess when selecting his leadership style?
Leadership.w: He evaluated team competence and motivation to choose the appropriate style.

n.0: Reporting and policies are not core situational leadership factors.
n.1: Task complexity and culture were not mentioned as decision drivers.
n.3: Risk and stakeholder count do not directly determine style in this model.
n.4: Budget and team size did not inform his leadership choice here.

Leadership.q: A project manager is briefing colleagues on why the same leadership approach cannot simply be reapplied to every project and team. Contingency theory asserts that there is no ______ leadership style that suits every situation.
Leadership.w: Contingency theory rejects the idea of a universal (‘one-size-fits-all’) leadership style.

n.0: Hands-off is a style, not the theory’s concept.
n.1: Autocratic is a style, not what the theory rejects universally.
n.3: Participative is a style, not the theory’s rejected concept.
n.4: Transformational is a leadership style, not the concept described.

Leadership.q: During a company merger, a leader seeks input from both legacy teams to foster collaboration. He uses a ______ approach to involve employees in decisions.
Leadership.w: A participative approach invites team members to share ideas and influence decisions.

n.1: Directive focuses on giving instructions, not collaboration.
n.2: Delegating grants autonomy but does not actively involve employees in decision-making.
n.3: Autocratic excludes employee input.
n.4: Transactional centres on exchanges, not joint decision-making.

Leadership.q: A manufacturing manager finds routines well established and the team highly skilled and committed, so he delegates almost all decisions. Which of the following factors was NOT relevant in prompting this change?
Leadership.w: Market volatility was not a factor in deciding to delegate to a skilled, committed team working on routine tasks; situational leadership favours delegating when competence and commitment are high.

n.0: High competence justified the decision to delegate.
n.1: An experienced team needs little direction, which supports delegating.
n.2: High commitment allowed the manager to trust the team.
n.3: Clear procedures supported a delegating style.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to help capable team members grow and take ownership rather than simply telling them what to do. Why is adopting a coaching style particularly valuable for the development of the team?
o: It encourages individuals to develop their own solutions
It removes the need for team meetings
It ensures tasks are always completed faster
It is required by law in all organisations
It focuses solely on task allocation
Leadership.w: Coaching helps team members grow by guiding them to find their own answers and build confidence.

n.1: Team meetings remain valuable in any style.
n.2: Speed is not the main reason for using a coaching style.
n.3: Coaching is not a legal requirement.
n.4: Task allocation is directive, not coaching.

Leadership.q: An experienced leader agrees to act as a mentor to a newly appointed project manager over the coming months. What is the main benefit of taking this mentoring approach for the new manager?
o: It reduces the mentoring leader's own workload
It guarantees the project will be successful
It helps the new manager gain skills and confidence
It speeds up the completion of all tasks
It removes all conflict from within the team
Leadership.w: Mentoring provides guidance, support and builds confidence in less experienced colleagues.

n.0: Responsibility for leadership remains with the leader.
n.1: Project success can't be guaranteed by mentoring alone.
n.3: Mentoring focuses on development, not task speed.
n.4: Conflicts can still arise even with mentoring.

Leadership.q: Emotional intelligence enables leaders to:
o: Recognise and manage their own emotions and those of others
Leadership.w: Leaders with emotional intelligence are better at understanding and managing both their emotions and the team's.

n.0: Disagreements can still occur; EI helps manage them.
n.1: Deadlines are important, but not the only concern.
n.2: Technical skills alone are insufficient for effective leadership.
n.4: Team morale should not be ignored.

Leadership.q: A project sponsor asks a senior colleague to mentor a promising team member. Which of the following is a key feature that distinguishes a mentoring leadership style from other approaches?
o: Offering long-term guidance based on experience
Leadership.w: Mentors support others with advice and guidance based on their experience, usually over a longer period.

n.1: Daily task assignment is a directive style, not mentoring.
n.2: Personal growth is key to mentoring.
n.3: Mentoring often involves giving feedback.
n.4: Mentoring supports development, not just deadlines.

Leadership.q: A team member is capable but is struggling with self-confidence and doubts their ability to take on new work. If the project manager adopts a coaching approach, how can it best help this individual?
o: By focusing only on technical training
By encouraging self-reflection and setting personal goals
By assigning more complex work immediately
Leadership.w: Coaching supports confidence through guided reflection and achievable goals.

n.0: Technical training is helpful, but coaching is more holistic.
n.2: Ignoring the issue won't support the team member's growth.
n.3: Increasing complexity too soon may undermine confidence further.
n.4: Delegating all responsibilities may overwhelm the team member.

Leadership.q: A project manager regularly asks the team questions to help them discover solutions rather than providing answers. What leadership style is being demonstrated?
Leadership.w: Coaching involves guiding team members to find their own answers, building independence.

n.0: Laissez-faire involves minimal leader involvement.
n.1: Transactional is based on reward/punishment, not guidance.
n.3: Autocratic style gives instructions, not questions.
n.4: Micromanaging involves excessive control, not coaching.

Leadership.q: Two team members are in open disagreement and tensions are rising within the project team. Why is emotional intelligence so important for a project manager who wants to resolve this conflict effectively?
o: It removes the need for feedback
It ensures the leader always gets their way
It helps leaders understand different perspectives and manage reactions
It enables leaders to ignore problems until they disappear
Leadership.w: Leaders with emotional intelligence can empathise and manage team tensions effectively.

n.0: Feedback is still needed, even with EI.
n.1: Effective conflict management is not about 'winning'.
n.3: Formal processes may still be needed.
n.4: Ignoring issues leads to unresolved conflict.

Leadership.q: A project manager is setting realistic expectations for a mentoring arrangement they are establishing with a junior colleague. Which of the following is NOT a benefit that mentoring typically delivers in a project environment?
o: Ongoing professional development of the mentee
Leadership.w: Mentoring focuses on development, not instant task completion.

n.0: Mentoring transfers experience and insights.
n.2: Mentoring develops professionals.
n.3: Mentoring supports career goals.
n.4: Mentoring builds confidence.

Leadership.q: A mentor notices their mentee is visibly upset after receiving some critical feedback on their work. How does the mentor's emotional intelligence support them in handling this situation?
o: By immediately ending the mentoring relationship
By enabling empathy and constructive support
By focusing only on task deadlines
