Leadership.w: EI allows mentors to respond constructively and supportively to emotional reactions.

n.0: Ending the relationship does not solve issues.
n.1: Only positive feedback is not realistic or helpful.
n.3: Deadlines alone do not address emotional needs.
n.4: Ignoring feelings harms trust.

Leadership.q: Which action best demonstrates a leader using emotional intelligence?
o: Recognising a team member's frustration and discussing it privately
Delegating all work to the most senior team member
Leadership.w: Emotionally intelligent leaders acknowledge and address team emotions.

n.1: Dismissing concerns is not emotionally intelligent.
n.2: Limited communication can miss emotional cues.
n.3: Ignoring morale is a leadership weakness.
n.4: Delegation should be balanced and fair.

Leadership.q: A coaching style of leadership is most effective when:
o: There is no need for development
Team members need support to develop new skills
Leadership.w: Coaching is best used when growth and skill development are needed.

n.0: Schedule alone doesn't determine leadership style.
n.1: Experts may benefit more from autonomy than coaching.
n.2: Coaching is about development.
n.3: Routine tasks require less coaching.

Leadership.q: A project manager who consistently demonstrates strong emotional intelligence has led several teams over recent years. What is a common outcome typically seen among the teams that such a leader manages?
o: A focus only on individual achievement
Leadership.w: EI builds trust and improves team cooperation.

n.0: Staff turnover can still occur.
n.1: Some conflict is inevitable; EI helps manage it.
n.3: Feedback is important in any leadership style.
n.4: EI promotes collaboration over competition.

Leadership.q: A project sponsor encourages an experienced project manager to spend time mentoring several junior members of staff over the coming year. From the organisation's perspective, what is the primary intended benefit of establishing this mentoring arrangement?
Leadership.w: Mentoring builds skills and confidence in junior staff.

n.0: Documentation is still needed.
n.1: The purpose is development, not reducing workload.
n.2: Mentoring isn't focused on task speed.
n.3: The goal is growth, not sponsor visibility.

Leadership.q: An organisation is introducing a significant change and staff are anxious about what it means for them. Why might a project manager with high emotional intelligence be better placed to support such a change initiative?
o: They avoid all discussions about change
They focus only on the technical details
They can recognise and address emotional responses to change
They use a single leadership style for every situation
Leadership.w: EI helps leaders support people through the uncertainty and stress of change.

n.0: Avoiding discussion increases resistance to change.
n.1: Change success depends on emotional and technical aspects.
n.3: Flexibility is vital in leadership.
n.4: Ignoring feedback harms change adoption.

Leadership.q: A mentor helps a team member learn how to manage stress at work. This approach is most closely linked to which leadership element?
Leadership.w: Helping others manage stress is a sign of emotional intelligence.

n.0: Policies don't directly address emotions.
n.1: Budgeting is unrelated to stress management.
n.2: Technical skills alone don't address stress.
n.4: Task allocation is not focused on personal support.

Leadership.q: A project manager is regarded by colleagues as having strong emotional intelligence. Which of the following behaviours would be least likely to be shown by such a leader when working with their team?
o: Adapting communication style to the audience
Leadership.w: Leaders with EI pay attention to emotions and do not ignore them.

n.1: Adapting communication is part of EI.
n.2: EI leaders recognise achievements.
n.3: Active listening is a key EI trait.
n.4: Regular feedback is common for EI leaders.

Leadership.q: A coaching leadership style is likely to result in:
o: All decisions being made by the leader
Leadership.w: Coaching empowers team members to solve problems and grow independently.

n.0: Motivation usually increases with coaching.
n.1: Coaching encourages shared decision-making.
n.2: Coaching reduces misunderstandings.
n.4: Development is a key aim of coaching.

Leadership.q: A project manager is preparing to give a team member some difficult performance feedback. What role does emotional intelligence play in how the manager handles this feedback conversation?
o: It replaces the need for regular communication
It helps leaders deliver feedback constructively and sensitively
It allows leaders to ignore team responses
It removes the need to provide feedback
It guarantees that all feedback is positive
Leadership.w: EI helps leaders consider emotions when delivering and responding to feedback.

n.0: EI enhances, not replaces, communication.
n.2: Ignoring responses is not a feature of EI.
n.3: Feedback remains important.
n.4: Not all feedback will be positive, but EI helps manage this.

Leadership.q: A leader encourages a team member to reflect on their performance and set new goals. This is an example of:
Leadership.w: Coaching focuses on personal reflection and growth.

n.0: Autocratic leadership does not encourage team input.
n.1: Directive style gives instructions, not promotes reflection.
n.3: Micromanagement does not promote reflection.
n.4: Laissez-faire is hands-off and does not foster goal setting.

Leadership.q: A project manager is using Tuckman's model to explain to a sponsor how a newly assembled team will develop over time before it becomes fully effective. What is the correct order of the stages in Tuckman's model of team development?
Leadership.w: Tuckman's model describes team development as Forming, Storming, Norming, then Performing.

n.1: This mixes up the stages and their correct order.
n.2: This sequence does not follow the model's stages.
n.3: Storming is not the initial stage in Tuckman's model.
n.4: This order is incorrect according to Tuckman's model.

Leadership.q: A project team faces conflicts as members adjust to roles and responsibilities. Which stage of team development does this best describe?
Leadership.w: Storming is the stage where conflicts and disagreements are most common.

n.1: Adjourning is when the team disbands.
n.2: Forming is when the team comes together.
n.3: Performing is characterised by effective, harmonious work.
n.4: Norming follows storming and is about resolving conflict.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to ensure the team includes someone who can generate original ideas and imaginative solutions to difficult problems. In Belbin's model of team roles, which role is characterised by this creative, idea-generating contribution?
Leadership.w: The Plant is the creative innovator in Belbin’s team roles.

n.1: Implementers focus on turning ideas into action.
n.2: Co-ordinators focus on clarifying goals.
n.3: Shapers challenge the team to improve.
n.4: Completer Finishers focus on accuracy and detail.

Leadership.q: A project manager is observing a team as it settles down after early friction, with members increasingly cooperating and beginning to trust one another. During which stage of team development are relationships and trust most likely to be built?
Leadership.w: Norming is when team members resolve differences and build stronger relationships.

n.0: Adjourning is when the team is finishing up and separating.
n.1: Storming is conflict-prone, not relationship-building.
n.2: Performing is when teams work efficiently, having built trust earlier.
n.3: Forming is when members are just getting to know each other.

Leadership.q: A project manager is reflecting on what sets a genuinely high-performing team apart from an ordinary working group. According to Katzenbach and Smith, high-performing teams are distinguished by which of the following?
o: A focus on individual goals rather than shared ones
Minimal communication between the individual team members
Mutual accountability and a strong commitment to a common purpose
Rigidly fixed role definitions for every member
A large team size and a strict reporting hierarchy
Leadership.w: Katzenbach and Smith highlight mutual accountability and commitment as critical to team performance.

n.0: Common purpose, not just individual goals, drives performance.
n.1: Effective teams communicate frequently.
n.3: Roles may be flexible in high-performing teams.
n.4: High-performing teams may be small and flexible.

Leadership.q: A project manager observes that one team member is especially good at clarifying the team's objectives and delegating work appropriately to the right people. According to Belbin, which team role does this member most likely fulfil?
Leadership.w: The Co-ordinator clarifies goals and delegates tasks within Belbin's model.

n.1: Monitor Evaluators provide critical analysis.
n.2: Resource Investigators explore opportunities.
n.3: Teamworkers help with cohesion.
n.4: Specialists offer in-depth expertise.

Leadership.q: A project team has been working together productively for some time, and the project manager wants to keep it effective through the maintenance stage of its life. Which factor is most important for sustaining ongoing team effectiveness at this stage?
o: Repeatedly assigning members the same tasks
Speed of the initial team formation
A focus only on short-term goals
Leadership.w: Ongoing communication and feedback sustain team effectiveness.

n.0: Ignoring conflict can harm team functioning.
n.2: Task variety can help maintain motivation.
n.3: Formation is only the first step.
n.4: Both short- and long-term goals matter.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to select a team model that assigns people to roles according to their individual behavioural strengths and weaknesses. Which of the following models focuses on team roles in this way?
Leadership.w: Belbin’s model defines nine team roles based on behavioural strengths.

n.0: Katzenbach and Smith focus on performance.
n.1: Hackman focuses on conditions for team effectiveness.
n.2: Tuckman describes stages, not roles.
n.3: Margerison McCann focuses on work preferences.

Leadership.q: A team is working together smoothly, solving problems with little oversight and achieving goals. What team stage does this describe?
Leadership.w: The performing stage is when a team works independently and effectively.

n.0: Forming is about coming together, not peak performance.
n.1: Adjourning is the disbandment stage.
n.2: Norming focuses on resolving differences.
n.3: Storming is marked by conflict.

Leadership.q: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) is used to:
o: Assign financial roles within a team
Identify personality preferences and support team diversity
Leadership.w: MBTI is used to understand personality differences, aiding in building diverse teams.

n.0: MBTI does not assign financial roles.
n.2: It does not set deadlines.
n.3: Attendance is not measured by MBTI.
n.4: Resource allocation is not the focus of MBTI.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants a newly formed team to progress quickly from the forming stage to the norming stage so that it settles down and begins working well together. Which factor is most likely to influence how quickly this transition happens?
o: The size of the physical workspace
The choice of project management software
The level of trust built among team members
Leadership.w: Trust helps team members resolve conflicts and progress more quickly through the stages.

n.0: Workspace size is less important than team cohesion.
n.1: Software helps with tools, not relationships.
n.2: Funding impacts resources, not team dynamics.
n.3: Meeting frequency alone does not drive development.

Leadership.q: A project manager observes that a team is beset by ongoing disagreements, with members openly challenging one another and roles that remain unclear. Which stage of team development are they most likely experiencing?
Leadership.w: The storming stage is marked by conflict and the clarification of roles.

n.0: Adjourning occurs at project close.
n.1: Forming is when the team is just coming together.
n.2: Norming comes after storming, with increased harmony.
n.4: Performing is characterised by high effectiveness, not conflict.

Leadership.q: A project manager is assigning roles and wants someone who will scrutinise the work closely for errors and make sure deliverables are completed to a high standard. Which of the following best describes the 'Completer Finisher' role in Belbin's team model?
o: Drives the team forward and challenges any inertia
Clarifies the team's objectives and delegates the work
Pays attention to detail and ensures work is finished accurately
Brings new contacts and fresh ideas into the team
Provides scarce specialist knowledge and key technical skills to the team
Leadership.w: Completer Finishers are detail-oriented and ensure tasks are finished thoroughly.

n.0: Shapers drive teams forward.
n.1: Co-ordinators clarify objectives.
n.3: Resource Investigators bring in ideas and contacts.
n.4: Specialists provide deep expertise.

Leadership.q: A project has been delivered and the team is about to disband and move on to other assignments, reaching the adjourning stage of its development. During this stage, what should the project manager's main focus be?
o: Resolving the last of the conflicts
Leadership.w: Adjourning is about closure and acknowledging team accomplishments as the group disbands.

n.0: Objectives are set at the beginning, not at adjourning.
n.1: Trust building is a focus of the early stages.
n.2: Conflicts are typically resolved earlier.
n.3: Roles are usually winding down, not being assigned.

Leadership.q: According to Hackman, one condition for effective teams is:
o: A clear, engaging direction or purpose
No overlap in team member skills
Leadership.w: Hackman states that a compelling direction is essential for team effectiveness.

n.0: Remote working is not a requirement.
n.1: Optimal team size varies; 20 is often too large.
n.3: Some overlap can help with flexibility.
n.4: Deadlines are important for team output.

Leadership.q: A project manager is briefing a dispersed team at the start of a new phase, where members will collaborate mainly through online tools rather than face to face. A mentor advises being especially deliberate about setting out what is required. Why should leaders of virtual teams be proactive about clarifying expectations?
o: Expectations matter far less in remote settings
Remote work makes it easier for misunderstandings to occur
Online teams can safely rely on assumptions
Virtual teams have no real need for defined roles
Clear expectations tend to reduce team accountability
Leadership.w: Explicit expectations help prevent confusion and increase accountability in virtual settings.

n.0: Clear expectations are always important.
n.2: Assumptions lead to problems.
n.3: Clear roles are crucial virtually.
n.4: Clarity increases, not reduces, accountability.

Leadership.q: A project manager uses a mix of instant messaging, video calls, and shared documents for their hybrid team. This is an example of:
o: Adapting leadership style to meet diverse communication needs
Depending on formal email as the sole channel
Prioritising in-person meetings over all technology
Restricting team input to reduce distractions
Delegating every decision to the wider team
Leadership.w: Hybrid teams benefit when leaders use multiple channels to reach everyone effectively.

n.1: Email alone can be limiting.
n.2: Hybrid teams rely on technology.
n.3: Input should be encouraged.
n.4: Leaders should stay involved.

Leadership.q: A programme relies on a virtual team drawn from offices in Europe, Asia and North America, with members from a range of cultural backgrounds. The team leader wants to get the best from everyone across these differences. Which leadership approach is most effective for managing global virtual teams?
Leadership.w: Time zones and cultural differences require flexible, sensitive leadership for global teams.

n.0: Fixed times can exclude some members.
n.1: Written memos are often insufficient.
n.2: Feedback remains vital.
n.4: In-person meetings are impractical for global teams.

Leadership.q: A project manager who has always led co-located teams is asked to run an entirely remote team for the first time. Reflecting on what will matter most in this new setting, the manager considers which qualities to strengthen. In virtual teams, what leadership trait becomes even more critical?
Leadership.w: Clear, regular communication is vital for remote team cohesion and effectiveness.

n.0: Interaction should be maintained.
n.1: Office hours are often flexible.
n.3: Physical presence is less relevant virtually.
n.4: Feedback should be increased, not reduced.

Leadership.q: A member of a virtual project team has delivered strong results but confides that their achievements go unnoticed because they are rarely seen at the office. The team leader wants to keep this person motivated and engaged. How should leadership respond?
o: Regularly acknowledge and celebrate remote contributions
Leadership.w: Recognition is crucial for remote staff to feel valued and engaged.

n.0: Remote members must not be overlooked.
n.1: Recognition supports morale.
n.3: Meetings help build team identity.
n.4: All achievements should be acknowledged.

Leadership.q: An experienced manager used to leading from the office is frustrated that the informal, face-to-face style that worked well before is falling flat with a newly remote team. A colleague explains why the old approach struggles online. Why might traditional face-to-face leadership styles not work for virtual teams?
o: Virtual teams have no need for leadership
Remote teams lack in-person cues and spontaneous interaction
Feedback is unnecessary in remote settings
All virtual teams operate the same way
Digital tools replace all management needs
Leadership.w: Virtual teams require new methods due to lack of informal, face-to-face communication.

n.0: Leadership remains essential.
n.2: Feedback is still critical.
n.3: Each virtual team is unique.
n.4: Tools help but don’t replace leadership.

Leadership.q: After deliberately adapting the way they lead a mix of office-based and home-working staff, a project manager reviews the outcomes at the end of a phase. The changes have had a clear positive effect on the team. What is a common benefit of adapting leadership styles for virtual and hybrid teams?
o: Increased engagement and inclusion for all members
Ignoring time zones and individual needs
Leadership.w: Adapted leadership ensures everyone is included and feels part of the team.

n.1: Misunderstandings should be reduced, not increased.
n.2: Time zones and needs must be considered.
n.3: Office politics is less relevant to virtual/hybrid teams.
n.4: A variety of communication tools should be used.

Leadership.q: A project manager is leading a hybrid team where some members attend the office daily while others work remotely full time. Anticipating problems, the manager lists the difficulties that hybrid leadership must actively manage. Which of the following is a challenge that hybrid team leaders must address?
o: Restricting development opportunities for remote staff
Discouraging the use of digital communication tools
Arranging every team meeting as in-person only
Cutting back the team's use of collaborative software
Ensuring equal access to information for all team members
Leadership.w: Hybrid leaders must prevent information silos and ensure everyone has access.

n.0: Opportunities must be equal.
n.1: Digital communication is essential.
n.2: Meetings should be accessible to all.
n.3: Collaboration tools are necessary.

Leadership.q: Early in a remote project, the team leader recognises that members who cannot see each other day to day need a firm foundation of confidence in their leader and one another. The leader focuses on the behaviour most likely to build this. What leadership skill is especially important for building trust in virtual teams?
Leadership.w: Trust is built when leaders are transparent and communicate regularly.

n.1: Feedback should be regular and ongoing.
n.2: Virtual relationships also matter.
n.3: Transparency requires openness.
n.4: Check-ins are important for remote teams.

Leadership.q: A hybrid project team is struggling, with home-based members reporting feelings of isolation while office staff carry on largely unaffected. The project manager is asked to intervene before morale drops further. What leadership response is best?
o: Increase written reporting so remote work is more visible
Give remote staff more autonomy and fewer check-ins
Foster team building and frequent, inclusive communication
Move all updates to email so people can read them later
Require all collaborative work to take place in the office
Leadership.w: Isolation in hybrid teams is tackled by deliberately building relationships and trust and by regular, inclusive communication, so remote members are involved as fully as office staff and proximity bias is avoided.

n.0: More reporting increases monitoring rather than connection, and can signal distrust to remote staff.
n.1: Autonomy has value, but fewer check-ins would increase the isolation remote members already feel.
n.3: Moving everything to email reduces real-time contact and is likely to deepen isolation.
n.4: Requiring office-based collaboration excludes home-based members and ignores the hybrid arrangement.

Leadership.q: A project manager is establishing ways of working for a virtual team that will rely on email, chat and video across different working hours. A stakeholder asks why the manager is spending time defining how and when people should communicate. Why should virtual team leaders set clear communication protocols?
o: To limit the amount of feedback the team gives
To leave team members uncertain about their roles
To reduce day-to-day interaction between members
To avoid misunderstandings and ensure information is shared consistently
To keep project updates accessible only to leaders
Leadership.w: Protocols help teams know how, when, and where to communicate.

n.0: Feedback is important for remote teams.
n.1: Clear protocols reduce, not increase, confusion.
n.2: Interaction should be encouraged.
n.4: Updates should be accessible to all.

Leadership.q: To keep a hybrid team connected, a leader introduces regular virtual check-ins and moves the team onto shared collaborative platforms for its day-to-day work. Reviewing the impact after several weeks, the leader assesses the effect on the team. What is the likely result?
Leadership.w: Regular check-ins and shared tools keep all team members connected and engaged.

n.0: Role clarity improves with communication.
n.1: Engagement typically rises with inclusion.
n.2: Hybrid leadership should include all staff.
n.4: Sharing of ideas should increase.

Leadership.q: A project sponsor asks a manager to reflect on the pitfalls of leading dispersed teams, having seen previous virtual projects suffer from poor coordination. The manager considers the errors most often made by remote-team leaders. What is a common leadership mistake when managing virtual teams?
o: Scheduling regular virtual check-ins with the team
Using several communication channels to reach everyone
Recognising the achievements of remote staff members
Assuming all members receive information equally without confirmation
Encouraging open feedback from all team members
Leadership.w: Leaders must check that all team members are informed and included.

n.0: Check-ins are good practice.
n.1: Multiple channels help reach everyone.
n.2: Recognition is positive.
n.4: Feedback is important in virtual teams.

Leadership.q: An organisation is deciding whether to invest in developing leaders who can adapt their style for hybrid and virtual working. The sponsor asks the project manager to set out the business case for doing so. Which is an advantage of adapting leadership for hybrid and virtual teams?
Leadership.w: Adapted leadership attracts and retains diverse talent and enables flexible work.

n.1: Technology use should increase.
n.2: Accountability should remain strong.
n.3: Innovation usually increases with good leadership.
n.4: Politics can be reduced with transparency.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is reviewing recruitment processes to ensure no candidates are treated less favourably due to a protected characteristic. Which of the following is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Sexual orientation is one of the nine protected characteristics in the Equality Act 2010, so treating a candidate less favourably because of it is unlawful discrimination.

n.0: Educational background is not one of the nine protected characteristics; relevant qualifications may be required where the role genuinely needs them.
n.2: Socio-economic background is not a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010, even though it is an important diversity factor.
n.3: Length of employment is not a protected characteristic, although it can affect some employment rights.
n.4: Working-hour preferences are not a protected characteristic, although flexible working requests have their own rules.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project team member explains that their religious practices require time for observance that clashes with certain scheduled activities, and they feel excluded as a result. The project manager wants to respond appropriately. Which action best supports diversity and inclusion?
o: Adjusting team activities to accommodate religious observances
Discouraging any mention of personal beliefs
Requiring all team members to work the same schedule
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Accommodating religious practices supports inclusion and respects diversity.

n.0: Limiting discussions can create an unwelcoming environment.
n.1: Ignoring requests undermines inclusion.
n.3: Discouraging mention of beliefs can reduce openness.
n.4: Uniform schedules may disadvantage those with religious commitments.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: During an equality and diversity briefing, a project manager reviews a list of attributes to identify those that UK equality law specifically protects from discrimination. Which of the following is NOT considered a protected characteristic under UK equality law?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Job title is not a protected characteristic; the others are protected by law.

n.1: Race is a protected characteristic.
n.2: Sex is a protected characteristic.
n.3: Religion or belief is protected.
n.4: Disability is protected.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is reviewing how the team supports members through significant life circumstances, mindful of the duties set out in equality legislation. Complete the statement. In a diverse project team, respecting colleagues' needs related to _____ helps prevent discrimination based on protected characteristics.
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Pregnancy and maternity are protected characteristics requiring careful consideration.

n.0: Software preferences do not relate to diversity law.
n.2: Deadlines relate to project delivery, not diversity.
n.3: Annual leave is a standard benefit, not a protected characteristic.
n.4: Performance reviews are unrelated to protected characteristics.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: When assigning roles on a new project, a project manager must ensure that no team member is treated unfairly because of an attribute protected under equality law. Considering the options below, a project manager must avoid discrimination based on which of the following characteristics?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Age is one of the nine protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010, so roles must not be assigned less favourably because of it.

n.0: A home postcode is not a protected characteristic, though relying on it could indirectly disadvantage some groups.
n.1: Socio-economic status is not one of the nine protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010.
n.3: Body weight is not a protected characteristic in itself, unless it relates to a disability.
n.4: Length of service is not a protected characteristic, although it can relate to other employment rights.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: While drafting an inclusion policy, a project manager needs to identify attributes that UK equality legislation explicitly safeguards from discrimination. Looking at the pairs below, which pair of characteristics are both protected under the Equality Act 2010?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Race and religion or belief are both among the nine protected characteristics in the Equality Act 2010.

n.0: Disability is protected, but educational background is not.
n.1: Age is protected, but caring responsibilities are not one of the nine protected characteristics.
n.3: Sex is protected, but socio-economic background is not a protected characteristic.
n.4: Sexual orientation is protected, but appearance is not one of the nine characteristics.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A team member returning from maternity leave requests flexible working hours. As a manager, how should you respond to support diversity and inclusion?
o: Suggest she takes unpaid leave instead
Consider her request and explore reasonable adjustments
Insist all staff have identical hours
Deny the request as it disrupts the team routine
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Reasonable adjustments for maternity are part of inclusive management.

n.0: Suggesting unpaid leave ignores her legal rights.
n.2: Rigid policies may not accommodate protected needs.
n.3: Refusing requests outright may constitute discrimination.
n.4: Ignoring requests can create a non-inclusive environment.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is checking that team members are not disadvantaged because of their personal relationship status, in line with equality legislation. Which of the following characteristics is protected to prevent discrimination in marriage and civil partnership?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Marriage and civil partnership are protected characteristics under equality law.

n.0: Job roles are not protected characteristics.
n.1: Project management is a job function, not a protected characteristic.
n.2: Driving licences are unrelated to equality law.
n.3: Home ownership is not relevant to diversity protections.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project team consists of members of different ages, religions, and sexual orientations. What is the most important principle for the project manager to follow?
o: Restrict conversation strictly to work topics
Overlook diversity issues to avoid difficulty
Treat all team members equally and with respect
Allocate tasks based on members' ages
Group team members according to their background
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Equal treatment is the foundation of diversity and inclusion.

n.0: Diversity is about the whole person, not just work tasks.
n.1: Ignoring issues does not create an inclusive culture.
n.3: Assigning tasks by age is discriminatory.
n.4: Grouping by background can be discriminatory.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: During an audit of the team's inclusion practices, a project manager reviews a list of attributes and must identify which one falls outside the scope of equality legislation. Which is NOT a characteristic protected by diversity and inclusion legislation?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Management style is not protected by equality law.

n.0: Religion or belief is protected by law.
n.1: Sexual orientation is protected.
n.3: Pregnancy and maternity are protected.
n.4: Disability is a protected characteristic.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A colleague requests time off for a religious holiday. How should a manager respond to align with diversity and inclusion principles?
o: Discuss options to accommodate the request
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Discussing options promotes inclusion and respects protected characteristics.

n.0: Refusing without discussion is not inclusive.
n.1: Requiring proof is unnecessary and may be discriminatory.
n.2: Discouraging requests undermines inclusion.
n.3: Only allowing annual leave may not respect religious needs.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is ensuring the team's policies protect colleagues who are expecting a baby or have recently given birth, in line with equality law. Which characteristic is specifically protected to ensure fairness for those who are expecting or have recently had a child?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Pregnancy and maternity is the protected characteristic that specifically covers people who are pregnant or have recently given birth.

n.1: Parental leave is a statutory employment right, not a protected characteristic.
n.2: Marriage and civil partnership is protected, but it concerns marital status, not pregnancy or a new baby.
n.3: Family status is not a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010.
n.4: Caring responsibilities are not one of the nine protected characteristics.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: During a recruitment interview for a project role, a hiring manager asks a candidate about their plans to start a family. A colleague later raises concerns about the question. Which principle is being breached?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Questions about family plans can breach diversity and inclusion policies.

n.0: Project scheduling is not related.
n.1: Resource levelling concerns resources, not diversity.
n.3: Team size is unrelated to equality legislation.
n.4: Budget is not relevant here.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is compiling training material and needs to give the team a set of attributes that are all safeguarded by UK equality legislation. Reviewing the groupings below, which set includes only protected characteristics under UK equality law?
o: Race, age, sexual orientation, length of service
Sex, disability, gender reassignment, educational background
Disability, sex, religion or belief, carer status
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Age, sex, race and disability are all among the nine protected characteristics.

n.1: Length of service is not a protected characteristic.
n.2: Social class is not a protected characteristic.
n.3: Educational background is not a protected characteristic.
n.4: Carer status is not a protected characteristic.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: An employee who recently disclosed their sexual orientation to their manager is then passed over for a promotion they were expected to receive. The employee raises a grievance. Which type of discrimination might this represent?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Direct discrimination is treating someone less favourably due to a protected characteristic.

n.0: Annual leave is not related.
n.1: Probation is not relevant.
n.3: Feedback is unrelated here.
n.4: Objective assessments should be free of bias.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager wants to embed inclusive behaviours in the way the team works day to day, so that everyone contributes regardless of their background. Reviewing the options below, which of these is an example of inclusion in a project environment?
o: Encouraging participation from team members of all backgrounds
Making assumptions about team members’ abilities
Assigning tasks only to those with similar beliefs
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Inclusion involves valuing all team members equally.

n.0: Ignoring adjustments reduces inclusion.
n.2: Discouraging discussion undermines inclusion.
n.3: Assumptions can perpetuate bias.
n.4: This excludes those with different beliefs.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager introduces a policy supporting flexible working for parents and carers. Which protected characteristics is this likely to support?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Caring responsibilities still fall disproportionately on women, so flexible working supports fairness on grounds of sex, and it directly supports people who are pregnant or on maternity leave.

n.0: Working pattern and length of service are not protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010.
n.1: Socio-economic background is not protected, and the policy is not aimed at age.
n.3: Neither carer status nor family status is a protected characteristic.
n.4: Both are protected, but a policy for parents and carers has no particular link to race or gender reassignment.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A member of the project team discloses a disability and requests certain changes to help them carry out their work effectively. The project manager considers the right course of action. What should a project manager do?
o: Discuss and agree reasonable adjustments to support their participation
Decline the request without offering any explanation
Recommend the employee moves to another team
Demand medical proof before considering any change
Disregard the request and continue as normal
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Discussing and providing reasonable adjustments is essential for inclusion.

n.1: Denial without explanation is not inclusive.
n.2: Changing teams is not a solution.
n.3: Proof is not always necessary for reasonable adjustment.
n.4: Ignoring requests is discriminatory.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is reviewing the attributes that equality legislation protects so that no team member is treated unfairly because of their faith or convictions. Which characteristic is protected to help prevent discrimination due to personal beliefs?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Religion or belief protects people's religious and philosophical beliefs (including lack of belief), so it prevents discrimination because of faith or convictions.

n.0: Sexual orientation is protected but is not about faith or convictions.
n.1: Lifestyle choice is not a protected characteristic.
n.3: Race is protected, but it covers colour, nationality and ethnic or national origins, not beliefs.
n.4: Marriage and civil partnership is protected but concerns marital status, not beliefs.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project team includes members from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences. What is a key benefit of this diversity?
o: It guarantees all team members will agree
It increases the potential for innovative solutions
It reduces the need for project management
It ensures every decision is made quickly
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: A diverse team brings varied perspectives, leading to greater innovation.

n.0: Conflict can still occur, even in diverse teams.
n.1: Agreement is not guaranteed by diversity.
n.3: Project management remains essential regardless of diversity.
n.4: Diversity may require more time for decision-making.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager reviewing a newly assembled team observes that its members share very similar backgrounds and outlooks, offering few differing viewpoints. Considering the impact on delivery, the manager weighs the possible downsides. What could be a consequence of this?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: A lack of diversity can limit creative and innovative solutions.

n.0: Speed is not always related to team diversity.
n.1: Technical ability depends on skills, not diversity alone.
n.2: Customer feedback may become less varied and less useful.
n.4: Budget is determined by project needs, not diversity.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project sponsor is keen to build a team from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences, and asks the project manager what benefit this is most likely to bring. Incorporating diversity into a project team is most likely to improve which aspect?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Diversity fosters a positive working environment.

n.0: Regulations are external to team composition.
n.2: Equipment quality is not affected by team diversity.
n.3: Project phases are set by methodology, not diversity.
n.4: Project location is not influenced by diversity.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is encouraging the team to welcome a variety of viewpoints and approaches when tackling challenges. Reflecting on what this culture tends to produce, complete the statement. A team that embraces diverse thinking is more likely to:
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Diverse thinking leads to new ideas and innovation.

n.0: Diverse teams may need to work on communication.
n.1: Leadership is still needed to harness diversity.
n.2: Engagement with stakeholders should remain high.
n.4: Disagreement can still occur and be healthy.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is explaining to a sceptical colleague why diversity should be built into every stage of a project. The colleague lists several supposed justifications, one of which does not belong. Which of the following is NOT a reason to incorporate diversity throughout a project?
o: To create a positive work environment
To limit perspectives and simplify tasks
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Limiting perspectives goes against the benefits of diversity.

n.0: Diversity encourages creative solutions.
n.1: A positive environment is a benefit of diversity.
n.2: Diversity enhances problem-solving.
n.4: Diversity helps meet varied customer needs.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Wanting to draw on a wider range of viewpoints during a planning workshop, a project manager considers how best to encourage diverse thinking within the team. Which action is most likely to help?
o: Limiting discussions to a small group
Assigning all tasks to one person
Inviting input from all team members
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Encouraging input from everyone fosters diverse thinking.

n.0: Limiting discussion reduces diversity of thought.
n.1: One person may not represent diverse views.
n.3: Discouraging ideas stifles innovation.
n.4: Customer feedback can offer valuable perspectives.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project sponsor deliberately forms a team of people with varied backgrounds, skills and perspectives for an upcoming initiative. Considering the likely effect of this mix, complete the statement. A diverse project team is likely to:
o: Work without any need for communication
Generate a broader range of ideas
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Diversity brings more ideas and viewpoints.

n.0: No project is risk-free.
n.1: Communication is always needed.
n.2: Meetings may be more important to share views.
n.3: Immediate consensus is unlikely.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: An organisation is building a culture in which differences among colleagues are actively respected and welcomed on its projects. Considering how this shapes the team, complete the statement. A project team that values diversity is most likely to:
o: Allocate project roles through purely random selection
Limit the team's engagement with external customers
Concentrate only on members' technical skills
Create an environment where all team members feel valued
Base every decision solely on members' seniority
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Valuing diversity helps all team members feel respected and included.

n.0: Random role assignment may not make best use of skills.
n.1: Customer engagement is still important.
n.2: Diversity includes more than just technical skills.
n.4: Seniority-based decisions can overlook valuable perspectives.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project sponsor has set an objective of improving the working environment so that every member of the team feels respected and able to contribute. The project manager considers how to deliver this. Which approach supports this goal?
o: Selecting team members from only one department
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Inclusive practices support a positive environment.

n.0: Open discussion should be encouraged.
n.2: A single department limits diversity.
n.3: Feedback from all groups should be valued.
n.4: Cost reduction should not come at the expense of diversity.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project team is finding it difficult to crack a complex problem raised by an important customer, having exhausted its usual approaches. The project manager reflects on how a diverse team could break the deadlock. How can diversity help?
o: By providing a range of perspectives and ideas
By reducing the number of options considered
By ensuring only senior managers contribute
By focusing on previous solutions only
By eliminating the need for collaboration
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: A range of ideas from diverse members increases the chance of finding innovative solutions.

n.1: More options should be considered, not fewer.
n.2: Limiting input reduces diversity of thought.
n.3: Focusing only on the past may miss new ideas.
n.4: Collaboration remains important.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager actively encourages team members to bring differing viewpoints and approaches to how work is done. Considering the immediate effect of this on a project, what is a direct result of encouraging diverse thinking?
o: A focus only on existing processes
A greater potential for innovative outcomes
A guarantee of no project delays
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Diverse thinking directly supports innovation in project outcomes.

n.0: Multiple viewpoints are encouraged, not just one.
n.1: Diverse teams look for new solutions, not just existing ones.
n.3: Innovation does not guarantee no delays.
n.4: Documentation requirements are not related to team diversity.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: An organisation's customer base is expanding across different countries and cultures, and the project manager is considering how the delivery team should be composed in response. Why should a project team reflect this diversity?
o: To focus only on technical delivery
To better understand and meet customer needs
To limit the skills within the team
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: A diverse team can better relate to and serve a diverse customer base.

n.0: Good communication is always required.
n.1: Customer needs go beyond technical delivery.
n.2: Tradition may not meet diverse needs.
n.4: Limiting skills is not beneficial.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is explaining to newer team members the value of welcoming a wide range of perspectives when working through project challenges. Which explanation captures one of the main reasons for embracing diverse thinking within a project team?
o: It leads to more creative problem-solving
It removes the need for a project manager
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Diverse thinking brings creativity and innovation to projects.

n.1: Success is never guaranteed.
n.2: Stakeholder input should be encouraged.
n.3: Timelines may not be affected by diversity alone.
n.4: Project managers are still needed.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager encourages all team members to share their unique perspectives when developing new products. What is the likely result?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Encouraging unique perspectives boosts innovation and problem-solving.

n.0: Encouragement should increase ideas, not reduce them.
n.1: Speed is not guaranteed by diverse input.
n.2: Customer satisfaction is likely to increase, not be limited.
n.3: Budget is not necessarily affected.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is reflecting on how the mix of backgrounds and disciplines within the team adds value across the life cycle. Considering where varied perspectives make the greatest difference to outcomes, in which situation is the benefit of team diversity most clearly visible?
o: When the team faces complex challenges
When the project is fully automated
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Diversity helps most when dealing with complex, multi-faceted challenges.

n.0: Communication is always valuable.
n.1: Identical skills reduce diversity benefits.
n.2: Repetitive tasks show less benefit from diversity.
n.4: Automation does not remove the value of diverse thinking.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: During the concept phase, a project manager deliberately assembles a team drawn from different disciplines, backgrounds and experiences to explore how the requirements might be delivered. Compared with a very similar group, a team with such diverse perspectives is most likely to do what?
o: Develop a wider range of solutions to project issues
Struggle to adapt when circumstances change
Generate fewer discussions and shared ideas
Converge quickly on a single way of thinking
Depend entirely on their previous experience
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Diversity brings a broader set of ideas and potential solutions.

n.1: Adaptability increases, not decreases, with diverse teams.
n.2: Discussion and ideas should increase with diversity.
n.3: One way of thinking is a result of a lack of diversity.
n.4: Diversity encourages new approaches, not just old ones.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: While observing several planning meetings, a project manager notices that team members consistently pay more attention to the views of certain colleagues, even when others raise equally valid points. Which of the following is most likely to be influencing this behaviour within the team?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Consistently giving more weight to certain people's views, even when others are equally valid, is typical of unconscious bias (for example affinity bias or the halo effect).

n.0: Storming involves open disagreement and challenge, not a consistent pattern of favouring particular people.
n.2: Theory X is a manager's assumption that people need control; it does not explain the team favouring certain colleagues.
n.3: Information overload reduces attention to everything, not selectively to certain colleagues.
n.4: Role ambiguity causes confusion over responsibilities, not selective attention to certain people's views.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Which of the following best describes unconscious bias?
o: A deliberate decision to exclude someone
A preference or prejudice that operates without conscious awareness
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Unconscious bias is an unintentional, automatic tendency to favour or exclude.

n.0: Deliberate exclusion is conscious, not unconscious.
n.1: Project objectives do not relate to bias.
n.3: Stakeholder analysis is a project management tool.
n.4: Policies are formal documents, not biases.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is helping to recruit new members for a delivery team and wants to make sure candidates are assessed fairly and consistently. To minimise the impact of unconscious bias throughout the selection process, which approach would be most effective?
o: Hiring those most similar to existing staff
Using structured interviews with objective criteria
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Structured, objective interviews reduce the influence of unconscious bias.

n.0: Personal recommendations can reinforce bias.
n.1: Skipping interviews removes objective assessment.
n.2: Similarity bias excludes diversity.
n.4: Informal chats are more prone to bias.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is reviewing the ways in which they adapt their own behaviours so that every team member is treated fairly and can participate fully. Reviewing the following actions, which one is NOT an example of adapting behaviour to treat people fairly?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Ignoring flexibility requests is unfair and does not support inclusion.

n.1: Accessible materials are a fair adaptation.
n.2: Listening to feedback is inclusive.
n.3: Training helps fair treatment.
n.4: Adapting communication is inclusive.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: During delivery, a valued team member privately explains that they have a disability and asks for additional support to carry out their role effectively. As their project manager, what is the best way to respond to this request?
o: Refuse and say all employees are treated identically
Discuss reasonable adjustments and provide support
Remove the team member from the project
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Supporting reasonable adjustments is essential for fairness and inclusion.

n.0: Ignoring needs fails to support fair treatment.
n.1: Treating everyone identically may not address individual needs.
n.2: This is discriminatory and unfair.
n.4: Removing someone for requesting support is not inclusive.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is considering how unconscious bias can shape the way decisions are reached in regular team meetings. Thinking about the consequences of such bias on group discussion, which of the following is a direct effect of unconscious bias in team meetings?
o: All decisions are made by consensus
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Unconscious bias can cause some contributions to be undervalued.

n.0: Consensus does not always occur, especially if bias exists.
n.2: Team budget is not affected by bias directly.
n.3: Bias is unrelated to documentation needs.
n.4: Bias can increase risk, not decrease it.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project team includes individuals with a range of working styles, needs and communication preferences. The project manager wants to make sure each person is able to participate on an equal footing. Which of the following is a fair way to support an individual's contribution in a team?
o: Only recognising contributions from senior staff
Adapting communication methods to meet their needs
Expecting everyone to conform to a single style
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Adapting to individual needs facilitates fair participation.

n.0: Recognition should be inclusive of all.
n.2: A single style may exclude some team members.
n.3: Different preferences should be respected.
n.4: Feedback opportunities should be open to everyone.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A manager believes only certain backgrounds are suited to leadership roles, without realising this belief. This is an example of:
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: The manager holds a belief that shapes judgements about people without being aware of it, which is the definition of unconscious (implicit) bias.

n.0: Groupthink is a group's pressure towards consensus that suppresses challenge, not one person's hidden belief.
n.1: Indirect discrimination arises from a policy or practice applied to everyone that disadvantages a group, not from an individual's hidden belief.
n.2: Conscious bias is held knowingly; this manager does not realise they hold the belief.
n.4: Positive action is lawful steps to help under-represented groups, the opposite of the belief described.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: An organisation has recognised that unconscious bias may be affecting how work is allocated and how contributions are valued across its project teams. As part of its response, which method would help reduce the impact of unconscious bias in project teams?
o: Only assigning tasks to close friends
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Awareness and training can help identify and reduce unconscious bias.

n.0: Discouraging new ideas reduces diversity.
n.1: Feedback should be valued.
n.2: Avoidance perpetuates bias.
n.3: Nepotism is a form of bias.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager notices that one particular team member has their contributions frequently interrupted or dismissed during meetings, despite offering sound ideas. Looking for an explanation for this pattern of behaviour, which of the following could be a cause?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Unconscious bias can lead to some voices being undervalued.

n.1: Progress reporting is unrelated.
n.2: Job title is often a reflection, not a cause, of bias.
n.3: Risk management should not affect fairness in discussion.
n.4: Project goals do not cause this behaviour.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager is drawing up practical guidance for team leaders on treating people fairly and inclusively during delivery. To promote fair treatment within project teams, which pair of actions both help treat people fairly?
o: Listening actively and providing individual support
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Listening and supporting individuals are key to fair treatment.

n.0: All ideas should be valued.
n.1: Standardising may not meet individual needs.
n.3: Stereotyping is unfair.
n.4: Ignoring requests is not inclusive.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager adjusts the timing of team meetings so that members with caring responsibilities and differing working patterns can all attend and contribute. Which underlying principle does this decision most clearly support?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Adapting to individual needs is central to inclusion.

n.0: Cost is not the main principle here.
n.2: Risk avoidance is not directly related.
n.3: Hierarchy may reduce inclusion.
n.4: Inflexibility may exclude some team members.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A capable team member with strong relevant skills is repeatedly passed over when the project manager allocates the more challenging and high-profile tasks. Considering possible reasons for this recurring pattern, this may be due to what?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Bias, whether conscious or not, can affect fair allocation of tasks.

n.0: Scheduling is unrelated to task allocation fairness.
n.1: Budget approval does not affect allocation in this way.
n.2: Equipment issues are not a reason for overlooking contributions.
n.4: Regulations are not likely to be the cause here.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Which of the following statements about bias is correct?
o: Bias cannot be changed with training
Bias only occurs when someone is aware of their prejudice
Unconscious bias can affect decisions without the decision-maker realising
Bias always results in fair outcomes
Bias is unrelated to team performance
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Unconscious bias operates without awareness and can influence decisions.

n.0: Training can help reduce bias.
n.1: Bias can also be unconscious.
n.3: Bias typically undermines fairness.
n.4: Bias can harm team performance.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A team member is going through difficult personal circumstances, and the project manager agrees to give them extra time to complete their assigned tasks while the situation continues. This decision is best described as an example of what?
o: Acting in clear breach of company policy
Adapting behaviours to support individual needs
Showing favouritism unrelated to genuine need
Making an uncontrolled change to project scope
Mismanaging the allocation of team resources
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Supporting individuals’ needs enables fair contribution.

n.0: Adaptations should align with policy.
n.2: Support is based on individual need, not favouritism.
n.3: Scope changes are unrelated.
n.4: Providing support is not mismanagement.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager leads a team whose members have differing needs, abilities and working preferences, and wants everyone to be able to participate on an equal basis. Which practice best helps ensure that all team members can contribute fully?
o: Providing appropriate support and reasonable adjustments
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Support and adjustments enable full participation.

n.0: Processes should be adaptable when needed.
n.2: Needs should be addressed to ensure fairness.
n.3: Collaboration is important for inclusion.
n.4: Task assignment should reflect skills and needs.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: An experienced project professional is reviewing how they keep their capabilities aligned with a changing profession and evolving delivery methods. In this context, why is continuing professional development (CPD) important for project professionals?
o: It replaces the need for qualifications
It is only necessary for new employees
It helps maintain up-to-date knowledge and skills
It removes the need for team collaboration
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: CPD ensures knowledge, skills, and behaviours remain current and relevant.

n.0: Qualifications and CPD both have important roles.
n.1: CPD is important for all, not just new employees.
n.2: CPD supports growth but does not guarantee promotion.
n.4: Collaboration is still necessary regardless of CPD.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager routinely attends training events and actively seeks feedback on their performance from colleagues and stakeholders. Reflecting on why they take this approach, what is its main benefit to them as a professional?
o: Identifying and addressing personal competence gaps
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Regular training and feedback help address areas for improvement.

n.0: Behaviour and knowledge are as important as technical skills.
n.2: Feedback from all stakeholders is valuable.
n.3: Delegation is a management tool, not a development strategy.
n.4: CPD goes beyond formal education.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project professional is planning their continuing professional development for the year ahead and listing the activities it should involve. Of the following, which one is NOT typically included in genuine professional development?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Professional development requires engagement with new trends, not ignoring them.

n.0: Enhancing knowledge is central to CPD.
n.2: Developing skills is a core goal.
n.3: Identifying gaps is crucial for improvement.
n.4: Behaviours are as important as knowledge.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: An individual’s responsibility in professional development includes:
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Individuals should take an active role in recognising their learning needs.

n.0: Learning should be ongoing, not just mandatory.
n.1: Employer training should be supplemented by self-development.
n.2: Opportunities for learning should be embraced.
n.3: Feedback from peers supports growth.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: At the start of each year, a project professional sets specific goals for improving their skills and behaviours, then reviews their progress against those goals at regular intervals. This ongoing cycle is best described as an example of what?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Goal setting and review are key elements of CPD.

n.0: Budgeting is a project control process, not CPD.
n.1: Appraisals may support CPD but are not the same thing.
n.3: Negotiation is a skill, not a CPD process.
n.4: Risk management is separate from professional development.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Which aspect should continuing professional development address?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: All three areas—knowledge, skills, and behaviours—are vital for CPD.

n.0: Profits are not a CPD focus.
n.1: Deadlines are important, but not part of CPD content.
n.2: Office location is not relevant to CPD.
n.4: Meetings may support CPD but are not the focus.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project professional attends a hands-on workshop to learn how to use a new piece of project management software that their organisation is introducing. In terms of continuing professional development, what type of CPD does this represent?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Learning new software enhances skills.

n.1: Risk avoidance is unrelated.
n.2: Finance is not the focus here.
n.3: Learning is the opposite of ignoring gaps.
n.4: CPD is not just about compliance.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Within a project team, individuals are expected to keep their own capabilities current as the profession evolves. Thinking about who owns this responsibility, who is primarily responsible for identifying competence gaps in their own professional practice?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Individuals are responsible for recognising their own development needs.

n.0: Government does not monitor individual gaps.
n.2: Regulators set standards but do not identify individual needs.
n.3: Clients may give feedback, but are not responsible.
n.4: Competitors are not involved in CPD.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Which activity supports the identification of professional development needs?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Feedback helps reveal areas for growth and learning.

n.1: Reviews are useful for identifying gaps.
n.2: Sticking to old practices limits growth.
n.3: Responsibility helps develop new skills.
n.4: Training is essential for development.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project team member reflects on their recent performance and recognises a need for improvement in stakeholder communication. What is their next step?
o: Wait for the next annual appraisal
Ignore the issue and focus on other tasks
Create a plan to develop relevant communication skills
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Proactive planning for skill improvement is essential for CPD.

n.0: All aspects of performance matter.
n.1: Waiting delays improvement.
n.2: Relying on others does not develop your own skills.
n.3: Issues should be addressed directly.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager maintains a personal development plan (PDP) to guide their growth as a professional over the coming year. Considering how such a plan is intended to be used, what is the main purpose of a PDP?
o: To assign development tasks to other members of the project team
To log mandatory training that the organisation legally requires staff to hold
To set goals and track progress in knowledge, skills, and behaviours
To record the results of the annual team appraisal cycle
To capture project lessons learned for reuse on future work
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: A PDP helps structure and measure professional growth.

n.0: Attendance monitoring is not the PDP's main aim.
n.1: Budgets are not covered by a PDP.
n.3: Delegation is unrelated to development plans.
n.4: Risk management is separate.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager identifies that both they and their team have several competence gaps early in the delivery phase and decides to act on them straight away. What is a benefit of addressing competence gaps as soon as they are identified?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Prompt action improves outcomes for individuals and projects.

n.1: Costs can be controlled with good skills.
n.2: Addressing gaps can actually save time.
n.3: Collaboration remains important.
n.4: Motivation usually increases with growth.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Continuing professional development (CPD) should be:
o: Completed only at the start of a career
An ongoing process throughout a career
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: CPD is a lifelong, self-managed responsibility.

n.0: Individuals must play an active role.
n.1: CPD is necessary even for the fully qualified.
n.2: Skills, behaviours, and knowledge are all important.
n.3: CPD is not just for beginners.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: During a review, a project professional receives constructive criticism about the way they have been engaging stakeholders on their current project. Acting professionally, what should they do in response to this feedback?
o: Reflect and seek training to improve
Defend their current approach without review
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Responding to feedback with action leads to professional growth.

n.0: Responsibility for development is individual.
n.2: Ignoring feedback limits growth.
n.3: Development is always ongoing.
n.4: Openness to change is a strength.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Which action demonstrates an individual’s commitment to professional development?
o: Regularly reviewing their competence against industry standards
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Self-assessment ensures skills remain up to date and relevant.

n.0: Flexibility is important for growth.
n.2: Client feedback is valuable.
n.3: Learning new skills is essential.
n.4: Extra training shows commitment.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: While planning an upcoming phase, a project professional realises they lack knowledge in an area that will soon be important to their work. Taking a professional and proactive approach, what is their most appropriate action?
o: Seek learning opportunities to address the gap
Ask a colleague to do the work instead
Ignore the gap if it does not impact current tasks
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Actively seeking learning closes gaps and supports professional growth.

n.1: Delegation does not develop personal skills.
n.2: Management may not be aware of every gap.
n.3: Gaps can affect future work.
n.4: Proactive action is more effective.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project professional is discussing with their line manager how continuing professional development should work in practice and where responsibility for it sits. Which of the following best describes the individual's own role in continuing professional development?
o: Waiting for the line manager to schedule all development activity
Taking responsibility for identifying and addressing their own competence gaps
Recording development hours purely to satisfy professional membership audits
Completing only the formal training courses arranged by their employer
Focusing development effort only on their existing areas of strength
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Each professional is responsible for their ongoing growth.

n.0: Self-development is an individual’s responsibility.
n.2: Weaknesses must be addressed as well as strengths.
n.3: Development should be continuous, not just annual.
n.4: Development is a professional duty, not just a legal requirement.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager encourages their team to identify their own skills gaps and actively supports them in finding learning opportunities to close those gaps. Over time, what is the likely benefit of taking this approach?
o: Reduced need for future project governance reviews
Increased team capability and project success
Elimination of all skills gaps within the organisation
Automatic reduction in the overall project budget
Guaranteed retention of every trained team member
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Supporting development boosts team skills and project outcomes.

n.0: Capability and development reduce risk.
n.2: Motivation is likely to rise with support.
n.3: Staff are more likely to stay.
n.4: Knowledge transfer increases with learning.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Continuing professional development is most effective when:
o: It is completed once per career
It is planned, proactive, and ongoing
It is handled entirely by the employer
It focuses only on urgent issues
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Effective CPD requires planning and a proactive approach.

n.0: CPD is lifelong, not one-time.
n.1: Regularity and planning are key.
n.3: Individuals must play an active role.
n.4: All issues, not just urgent ones, should be addressed.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager needs authoritative, accountable guidance on good practice for managing their project and wants to draw on a credible source. Which of the following is a common source of specialist advice for a project manager?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Professional bodies, such as APM, publish good practice guidance, standards and codes of conduct and are accountable for their quality, which makes them a credible source of specialist advice.

n.0: Supplier sales staff have a commercial interest, so their advice is not independent.
n.2: General news sites report events; they do not provide authoritative professional guidance.
n.3: Peers' anecdotes can be useful but are unverified individual experience, not an accountable source.
n.4: Opinion columns reflect individual views and are not authoritative or accountable guidance.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Partway through delivery, a project encounters a complex legal issue that falls well outside the team's own knowledge and could have significant consequences if handled incorrectly. Where should the team seek advice on this matter?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Legal professionals are trained to give reliable advice on legal issues.

n.0: Friends and family are unlikely to have relevant expertise.
n.2: Intuition is not sufficient for legal matters.
n.3: Unmoderated chat rooms are not reliable.
n.4: Social events are not appropriate for legal advice.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager wants to align their working practices with recognised standards for the profession and is considering which body typically defines them. Which organisation typically sets the standards that should be followed in professional project management practice?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: APM and similar bodies set industry standards for project management.

n.0: Restaurants are unrelated to standards.
n.1: Sports teams do not issue professional standards.
n.3: Personal contacts do not set standards.
n.4: Social clubs are not relevant.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A team is unsure how to apply a particular health and safety standard. Where should they look for reliable guidance?
o: The Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD)
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: HSE provides authoritative guidance on health and safety standards.

n.0: Random searches are unreliable.
n.1: Personal blogs may lack accuracy and authority.
n.3: Marketing does not provide standards advice.
n.4: Unverified videos are not a professional source.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project professional is deciding where to turn for specialist advice on a difficult technical matter and wants to avoid sources that lack credibility or accountability. Of the following, which is NOT a reliable source of specialist advice?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Unofficial groups lack credibility and accountability.

n.0: Consultants can provide expert advice.
n.2: Regulators offer authoritative guidance.
n.3: Legal counsel offers reliable advice.
n.4: Standards bodies are trusted sources.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project manager wants to make sure the methods they are using reflect the latest recognised industry best practice before committing to an approach for the next phase. Where should they look to find this information?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Standards publications are up-to-date and credible.

n.0: Family opinions are not industry standards.
n.1: Search engines may yield unverified content.
n.2: Travel blogs are unrelated.
n.4: WhatsApp chats are not an official source.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project involves activities that must meet current regulatory requirements, and the project manager needs to be confident the compliance information they rely on is accurate and up to date. Which source is best for up-to-date information on regulatory compliance?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Official government sources publish current legislation and regulatory guidance and are updated when the rules change, so they are the most reliable source of up-to-date compliance information.

n.1: Textbooks are useful background but can be out of date once regulations change.
n.2: Supplier brochures promote products and may present regulations selectively.
n.3: A previous project's checklist may be out of date and may not match this project's activities.
n.4: Trade press summaries can lag behind changes and simplify the detail.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A project team will be handling significant amounts of personal data and needs authoritative guidance on the data protection standards they must meet. In the UK, where should they seek advice on this?
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: ICO is the official source for data protection standards.

n.0: Message boards are not authoritative.
n.2: Unrelated magazines lack relevance.
n.3: Online polls are not a professional source.
n.4: Anecdotes are not reliable guidance.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Midway through delivery, a new standard governing sustainability in projects is published and applies to work of the kind the team is undertaking. Acting professionally, what is the project manager's responsibility in this situation?
o: Apply the standard only to future projects, not current ones
Wait for the standard to become legally mandatory first
Ensure the project complies with the new standard
Adopt the standard only if it reduces project costs
Delegate compliance for the standard entirely to the sustainability team
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Managers must keep up to date and comply with new standards.

n.0: Previous standards may be out of date.
n.1: Ignoring guidance is non-compliant.
n.3: Informal contacts are not sufficient.
n.4: Proactive compliance prevents problems.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: During delivery, a project manager is faced with a technical question that lies clearly outside their own area of expertise but could affect a key decision. What is the best course of action for them to take?
o: Seek specialist advice from a qualified expert
Wait for the problem to resolve itself
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Seeking expert advice ensures correct handling of technical matters.

n.0: Lone attempts may lead to mistakes.
n.1: Delegation without guidance can be unsafe.
n.3: Problems rarely resolve themselves.
n.4: Ignoring technical issues is risky.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: A client asks for assurance that a project meets the latest industry standards. Where should the team find these standards?
o: General web searches and popular industry blogs
Competitors' published marketing brochures and case studies
Previous project documentation held in the archive
Relevant professional bodies and regulatory authorities
The project team's own accumulated delivery experience
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Professional and regulatory sources are authoritative for standards.

n.0: Personal storage may not have current documents.
n.1: Friends may lack specialist knowledge.
n.2: Old documents may not reflect current standards.
n.4: Entertainment sites do not host standards.

Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.q: Which pair both provide specialist advice to project professionals?
o: Trade press opinion pieces and personal acquaintances
Legal advisers and social media discussion groups
Professional bodies and unmoderated online forums
Diversity, Ethics & Professionalism.w: Industry consultants and regulatory agencies are both recognised specialist sources of advice and standards.

n.0: Neither opinion pieces nor acquaintances are authoritative specialist advice.
n.1: Standards bodies are specialist, but anecdotes are not a reliable source.
n.2: Legal advisers are specialist, but social media groups are not authoritative.
n.4: Professional bodies are specialist, but unmoderated forums are unverified.
